topic: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) Botanical Identification and Growth Habit
season: Warm season (plant outdoors in spring after all danger of frost has passed)
sunlight_requirement: Full sun (minimum 6–8+ hours of direct sunlight daily)
normal_appearance: Warm-season tender annual in temperate gardens (herbaceous perennial in tropical native range). Ascending, erect or sprawling vining plant (determinate bush types 3–4 ft tall; indeterminate vining types 6–10 ft tall). Documented dimensions: Height: 1 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in.; Width: 1 ft. 0 in. - 4 ft. 0 in.. Growth form: Ascending, Erect, Multi-stemmed, Spreading (growth rate: Rapid). Healthy tomato plants have alternate, odd-pinnately compound green leaves (4–10 inches long with 5–9 ovate to lanceolate leaflets with serrated/lobed margins), glandular hairy pubescent green stems with a characteristic herbal aroma, and upright vigorous apical growth without curling, spots, or wilting.
recommended_observations: Verify species identity (Solanum lycopersicum, family Solanaceae), growth habit (Ascending, erect or sprawling vining plant (determinate bush types 3–4 ft tall; indeterminate vining types 6–10 ft tall)), and expected seasonal adaptation before garden layout planning.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Lifecycle: Warm-season tender annual in temperate gardens (herbaceous perennial in tropical native range). Optimal growth 70–85°F (21–29°C) day and 60–70°F (16–21°C) night; blossom drop occurs below 55°F or above 90°F.
knowledge_text: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is a vegetable in the Solanaceae family grown as a warm-season tender annual in temperate gardens (herbaceous perennial in tropical native range). Characteristic growth habit: Ascending, erect or sprawling vining plant (determinate bush types 3–4 ft tall; indeterminate vining types 6–10 ft tall). Documented dimensions: Height: 1 ft. 0 in. - 10 ft. 0 in.; Width: 1 ft. 0 in. - 4 ft. 0 in.. Growth form: Ascending, Erect, Multi-stemmed, Spreading (growth rate: Rapid). Healthy tomato plants have alternate, odd-pinnately compound green leaves (4–10 inches long with 5–9 ovate to lanceolate leaflets with serrated/lobed margins), glandular hairy pubescent green stems with a characteristic herbal aroma, and upright vigorous apical growth without curling, spots, or wilting. The fruits or berries of the tomato are edible. They may be eaten raw, cooked, dried, or processed. They are a rich source of Vitamin A, Vitamin C, folic acid, and antioxidants. Lycopene is an antioxidant that gives the tomato its rich red color. Many plants will drop fruit when ripe or the fruit will come off easily. Tomatoes will continue to ripen once picked. Store them at room temperature.

topic: Tomato Sunlight Exposure and Light Intensity Requirements
sunlight_requirement: Full sun (minimum 6–8+ hours of direct sunlight daily) (Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day))
management_actions: Site Tomato where it receives full sun (minimum 6–8+ hours of direct sunlight daily). Orient rows and taller companion or trellised crops so they do not cast excessive shade.
prevention_actions: Insufficient light causes etiolated (leggy) stems, weak photosynthetic capacity, poor flower/fruit set or root/bulb sizing, and prolonged morning dew retention.
recommended_observations: Observe daily direct sunlight hours across the bed and check for shading from buildings, fences, trees, or taller garden crops.
knowledge_text: Sunlight requirement for Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Full sun (minimum 6–8+ hours of direct sunlight daily). Adequate daily photosynthetic light exposure is critical for vigorous growth, carbohydrate synthesis, and optimal yield and flavor.

topic: Tomato Aphids Management
problem_name: Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids)
causal_agent: Myzus persicae (Green Peach Aphid), Aphis gossypii (Melon/Cotton Aphid), Macrosiphum euphorbiae (Potato Aphid), Acyrthosiphon pisum (Pea Aphid), Aphis fabae (Black Bean Aphid), and Brevicoryne brassicae (Cabbage Aphid)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and flowering
season: Spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer)
humidity_conditions: Moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants)
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew.
symptom_keywords: soft pear-shaped insects under leaves, curled puckered shoot tips, sticky shiny honeydew, black sooty mold, white cast skins, ants tending stems
symptom_progression: Winged females (alates) land on succulent new shoots and give live birth parthenogenetically to nymphs that mature in 7–10 days, building dense colonies and transmitting non-persistent plant viruses within seconds of probing.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present).
similar_conditions: Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves)
risk_factors: Over-fertilization with high soluble nitrogen (which creates lush amino-acid-rich sap that accelerates aphid reproduction), broad-spectrum pyrethroid/carbamate insecticide sprays that kill ladybugs and parasitic wasps, ant tending, and greenhouse/indoors transplant carryover.
favorable_conditions: Mild temperatures (65–80°F) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth.
transmission_or_spread: Winged alate aphids disperse on wind currents from overwintering weeds, woody hosts (Prunus, Euonymus), or neighboring crops; ants also move aphids between plants.
management_actions: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides.
prevention_actions: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems) twice weekly during spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer) (60–82°F (15–28°C)); inspect for soft pear-shaped insects under leaves to distinguish Aphids from Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (direct stunting plus primary vector of CMV, PVY, PRSV, ZYMV, WMV, and BCMV)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–82°F (15–28°C) and moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants).
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Tomato Armyworms Management
problem_name: Armyworms (Beet, Yellowstriped, Fall, and Southern Armyworms)
causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. Beet Armyworm is olive-green with a prominent black spot on the thorax above the second pair of true legs; Yellowstriped Armyworm is velvety gray-black with two bright yellow-orange dorsal stripes and black triangular markings; Fall Armyworm has a prominent white inverted 'Y' suture on its dark head capsule and four black dots arranged in a square on the 8th abdominal segment.
symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for fuzzy tan/white scale-covered egg masses and crush or clip them off before they hatch; spray Bacillus thuringiensis aizawai (Bt aizawai is substantially more effective against Spodoptera armyworms than Bt kurstaki!) or spinosad while caterpillars are small (<1/2 inch) and windowpaning.
prevention_actions: Keep beds free of pigweed (Amaranthus) and lambsquarters (preferred egg-laying hosts for Beet Armyworm); cover fall brassica and leafy green plantings with floating row covers.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (whorl leaves (sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves to distinguish Armyworms from Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms.
severity_or_impact: High in late summer and fall
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Sweet potato, Beet, Swiss chard).

topic: Tomato Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Tomato Colorado Potato Beetle Management
problem_name: Colorado Potato Beetle
causal_agent: Leptinotarsa decemlineata
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, tender stems, and terminal shoots
growth_stage: Plant emergence through tuber bulking and fruiting
season: Late spring through summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Complete defoliation of potato and eggplant foliage by both adults and larvae: adults are robust, dome-shaped, oval beetles (3/8 inch / 10 mm long) with bright yellowish-orange wing covers marked with TEN distinct jet-black lengthwise stripes and black spots on the orange thorax; females lay clusters of 20–40 bright yellow-to-orange football-shaped eggs standing on end on the undersides of leaves; larvae are unmistakable humpbacked, soft-bodied, brick-red to salmon-orange grubs with two rows of black spots along each side and a shiny black head, which feed in groups on terminal shoots and deposit dark blackish-brown excrement.
symptom_keywords: dome-shaped yellow-orange beetle with ten black stripes, humpbacked brick-red grub larvae with two rows of black side spots, clusters of bright orange upright eggs under leaves, stripped potato and eggplant stems
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter 4–10 inches deep in the soil of last year's potato/eggplant bed and walk/fly to emerging plants in spring; eggs hatch in 4–9 days, and 4 larval instars devour foliage for 2–3 weeks before burrowing into soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from the False Potato Beetle (Leptinotarsa juncta, a harmless relative on horse nettle) because the true Colorado Potato Beetle has 10 clean black stripes on pale yellow wings, whereas the False Potato Beetle has a wide reddish-brown stripe down the center of each wing cover where two black stripes fuse; distinguish Colorado Potato Beetle egg clusters from Ladybug egg clusters only by checking for adult beetles/larvae nearby (they look very similar, though CPB eggs are slightly larger).
similar_conditions: False Potato Beetle, Beneficial Lady Beetle Eggs (do not crush orange upright egg clusters on crops OTHER than potato/eggplant/tomato, as those are ladybug eggs!), Blister Beetles
risk_factors: Planting potatoes or eggplants in or right next to last year's potato/eggplant bed, volunteer potatoes emerging from unharvested tubers, and heavy reliance on synthetic insecticides (Colorado Potato Beetle has evolved resistance to >50 classes of chemical insecticides!).
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny weather (75–86°F optimal).
transmission_or_spread: Adults emerge from overwintering soil burrows and walk several hundred yards (or fly on warm days >70°F) to locate Solanaceae hosts.
management_actions: Handpick striped adults and red humpbacked larvae into soapy water and crush orange egg clusters on the undersides of potato/eggplant leaves twice weekly; apply spinosad, azadirachtin (neem), or Bacillus thuringiensis tenebrionis (Bt san diego—a special beetle-specific strain of Bt, NOT caterpillar Bt kurstaki!) targeting newly hatched small 1st- and 2nd-instar red larvae.
prevention_actions: MULCH POTATOES WITH THICK STRAW AT EMERGENCE: applying a 4–6 inch layer of clean wheat or oat straw mulch over potato rows as soon as shoots emerge creates a physical roadblock for walking overwintered adults and cools the soil, while providing habitat for predatory stink bugs (Perillus bioculatus), damsel bugs, and pink spotted lady beetles (Coleomegilla maculata, which eat CPB eggs!); rotate potatoes and eggplants as far as possible from last year's nightshade bed.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (leaves, tender stems, and terminal shoots) twice weekly during late spring through summer (65–90°F (18–32°C)); inspect for dome-shaped yellow-orange beetle with ten black stripes to distinguish Colorado Potato Beetle from False Potato Beetle, Beneficial Lady Beetle Eggs (do not crush orange upright egg clusters on crops OTHER than potato/eggplant/tomato, as those are ladybug eggs!), Blister Beetles.
severity_or_impact: Critical on potato and eggplant (defoliation during potato bloom reduces tuber yield by 50–80%)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–90°F (18–32°C) and warm, sunny spring and summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Tomato Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm Management
problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin.
symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.
distinguishing_features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters).
similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.
prevention_actions: Plant early-maturing sweet corn cultivars as early in spring as soil temperature allows to harvest before peak late-summer moth flights; select sweet corn hybrids with tight, long husk extensions beyond the ear tip; encourage Trichogramma egg-parasitoid wasps and Orius minute pirate bugs (which eat earworm eggs on silks).

severity_or_impact: High (the #1 insect pest of sweet corn and a destructive borer in tomatoes, peppers, beans, and okra)

topic: Tomato Cucumber Beetles Management
problem_name: Cucumber Beetles (Striped and Spotted Cucumber Beetles)
causal_agent: Acalymma vittatum (Striped Cucumber Beetle) and Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi (Spotted Cucumber Beetle / Southern Corn Rootworm)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence through flowering and fruiting
season: Spring transplant/emergence through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oblong bright-yellow-green beetles with either three jet-black longitudinal stripes down the wing covers (Striped Cucumber Beetle) or twelve black spots (Spotted Cucumber Beetle); overwintered adults swarm emerging cucurbit cotyledons and young transplants in spring, chewing ragged holes through leaves, girdling tender stems, congregating inside open yellow cucurbit blossoms (chewing anthers/pistils and reducing fruit set), scarring the underside and rind of melons/pumpkins, and transmitting the fatal bacterium Erwinia tracheiphila (Bacterial Wilt); white brown-headed larvae feed underground on cucurbit, corn, and bean roots.
symptom_keywords: yellow beetle with three black stripes, yellow-green beetle with twelve black spots, chewed cucurbit cotyledons and stems, beetles packed inside squash blossoms, scarred pumpkin rinds, sudden bacterial wilt
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge when spring temperatures exceed 55–65°F, attracted strongly by cucurbitacin bitter compounds in emerging cucurbit seedlings; females lay orange-yellow eggs in soil cracks at the stem base, producing root-feeding larvae and a mid-summer second adult generation.
distinguishing_features: Striped Cucumber Beetle has 3 sharp black stripes on a yellow back with a black head and black abdomen underside (unlike Western Corn Rootworm, which has blurred stripes and a yellow abdomen); Spotted Cucumber Beetle is yellow-green with 12 black spots (unlike beneficial Pink Spotted Lady Beetles, which are pink/reddish-orange with spots on the thorax too).
similar_conditions: Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles
risk_factors: Uncovered spring cucurbit seedlings, cultivars high in cucurbitacins, and bacterial wilt reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny spring days (>60°F) during seedling emergence and bloom.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded field borders and weedy garden debris, flying into cucurbit beds as soon as seedlings crack the soil.
management_actions: Keep cucurbit seedlings and transplants completely covered under floating row covers or insect netting sealed at the edges from the day of planting until female flowers open (then remove covers for bee pollination); hand-vacuum beetles out of open squash blossoms early in the morning; apply kaolin clay (Surround) particle film or botanical pyrethrin/spinosad/neem sprays in the evening when bees are not inside flowers (squash blossoms close by afternoon!).
prevention_actions: Transplant robust 3-to-4-week-old cucurbit starts rather than direct-seeding in high-pressure gardens; plant a perimeter trap crop of 'Blue Hubbard' squash (which has extreme cucurbitacin levels that lure 85–90% of cucumber beetles away from cucumbers and melons!); mulch with straw to encourage wolf spiders and ground beetles.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds) twice weekly during spring transplant/emergence through autumn (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for yellow beetle with three black stripes to distinguish Cucumber Beetles from Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles.
severity_or_impact: Critical on cucumbers, melons, and squash (both from direct seedling destruction and as the sole vector of Bacterial Wilt)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm spring and summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Bottle gourd, Bitter gourd).

topic: Tomato Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Tomato Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites Management
problem_name: Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites (Tomato Russet Mite, Broad Mite, and Cyclamen Mite)
causal_agent: Aculops lycopersici (Tomato Russet Mite), Polyphagotarsonemus latus (Broad Mite), and Phytonemus pallidus (Cyclamen Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.
symptom_keywords: greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem, upward-moving bronzed papery leaves without webbing, stunted brittle downward-cupped terminal pepper shoots, rosetted distorted strawberry crown leaves, corky russeted fruit
symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).
distinguishing_features: Tomato Russet Mite is distinguished from Spider Mites by the complete absence of silk webbing or individual stipple dots and the greasy bronze-tan sheen on the lower stem; Broad Mite injury on pepper/strawberry terminal shoots mimics viral mosaic or 2,4-D herbicide drift, except leaf veins do not show Parallel 'strapping' and a 20x lens reveals tiny football-shaped eggs studded with rows of white polka-dot tubercles!
similar_conditions: 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites)
risk_factors: Warm weather, infested greenhouse transplants or strawberry crowns, and broad-spectrum insecticide use.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.
transmission_or_spread: Crawl between touching plants, blow on wind, or hitchhike phoretically on the legs of whiteflies and aphids (Broad Mite!).
management_actions: Apply wettable/micronized sulfur (highly effective against Eriophyid russet and broad mites, provided air temperature is below 85–90°F to avoid sulfur burn) or abamectin/horticultural oil early; rogue severely rosetted plants; clean and sanitize tomato stakes and cages at season's end.
prevention_actions: Purchase certified mite-free strawberry crowns and vegetable transplants; control whiteflies (which carry broad mites on their legs); rotate nightshades and destroy all volunteer solanaceous weeds (black nightshade, jimsonweed).

severity_or_impact: High (often misdiagnosed as blight or virus until lower foliage is completely bronzed or terminal buds abort)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and high humidity inside dense crowns (broad/cyclamen mites) or warm dry summer weather (tomato russet mite).
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Strawberry, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon).

topic: Tomato Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).

severity_or_impact: High on seedlings and young eggplant, radish, bok choy, arugula, turnip, and mustard greens
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny, dry spring weather.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Eggplant, Potato, Tomato, Pepper, Radish, Turnip, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Tomato Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Tomato Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)
causal_agent: Liriomyza sativae (Vegetable Leafminer), Liriomyza trifolii (American Serpentine Leafminer), and Pegomya hyoscyami (Spinach / Beet Leafminer)
affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering
risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.
management_actions: On Spinach, Swiss Chard, and Beets: flip leaves twice weekly to rub off the neat rows of chalk-white eggs on the underside BEFORE they hatch, and pinch/clip off any mined blotch leaves immediately (note: contact sprays like soapcannot reach maggots hidden inside the leaf epidermis, though spinosad and azadirachtin/neem have translaminar activity that penetrates into mines!); on Tomatoes, Beans, and Cucurbits, simply avoid broad-spectrum sprays so native Diglyphus parasitic wasps naturally suppress serpentine mines.
prevention_actions: Cover spinach, Swiss chard, and beet beds with floating row covers or fine insect netting from seeding through harvest (in beds rotated away from last year's chenopods); eradicate lambsquarters (Chenopodium album) weeds around the garden.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis) twice weekly during spring through autumn (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves to distinguish Leafminers from Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering.
severity_or_impact: High on spinach, Swiss chard, and beet greens (blotch mines ruin edible leaves); Low to Moderate on fruiting crops unless natural enemies are killed
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and mild-to-warm weather.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Spinach, Swiss chard, Beet, Amaranth, Lettuce, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Tomato Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes) twice weekly during cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights (45–75°F (7–24°C)); inspect for ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries to distinguish Slugs and Garden Snails from Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime).
severity_or_impact: High in cool, wet climates and on seedlings, lettuce, brassicas, and strawberries
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–75°F (7–24°C) and high humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Lettuce, Spinach, Swiss chard, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy).

topic: Tomato Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Tomato Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
affected_plant_parts: Developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.
symptom_keywords: shield-shaped green or brown bug, white bands on antennae of brown stink bug, cloudy yellow-white spots on ripe tomato and pepper skin, white spongy corky tissue under fruit skin, catfaced dimpled peaches and apples, black-and-orange harlequin bug with striped barrel eggs on kale
symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.

similar_conditions: Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface)
risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, sunny summer weather.

topic: Tomato Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! topic: Tomato Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Tomato Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms Management
problem_name: Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms
causal_agent: Manduca quinquemaculata (Tomato Hornworm) and Manduca sexta (Tobacco Hornworm)
affected_plant_parts: Upper canopy leaves, tender stems, blossoms, and green fruits
growth_stage: Mid-season vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Mid-to-late summer
humidity_conditions: Warm summer nights favoring hawk/sphinx moth flight and egg laying
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Sudden, dramatic defoliation of upper stems where entire compound leaves—including midribs and petioles—are chewed away overnight leaving bare stripped stalks, plus large gouged cavities chewed into the sides of green tomatoes; large, dark greenish-black barrel-shaped pellets of droppings ('frass', resembling miniature hand grenades) litter the lower leaves and ground directly beneath the well-camouflaged, 3-to-4-inch-long bright-green caterpillar with white diagonal side stripes and a prominent rear dorsal horn.
symptom_keywords: stripped bare upper tomato stems, large 3-4 inch green caterpillar with rear horn, white V or slash stripes on sides, large dark barrel-shaped frass pellets on lower leaves, gouged green fruit
symptom_progression: Large gray hawk/sphinx moths ('hummingbird moths') hover at dusk to lay single round pearly-green eggs on leaf undersides; caterpillars feed for 3–4 weeks (consuming 90% of their total foliage intake during their final 5–7 days in the 5th instar!) before burrowing 4–6 inches into soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Tomato Hornworm has 8 white V-shaped chevrons pointing forward along each side and a black/dark-blue rear horn; Tobacco Hornworm has 7 white diagonal slash stripes edged in black and a curved bright-red rear horn. Look for dark barrel-shaped frass pellets on lower leaves to spot the camouflaged caterpillar directly above!
similar_conditions: Tomato Fruitworm / Corn Earworm (bores a deep hole at the stem end of fruit rather than stripping whole upper branches), Deer browsing (rips jagged stems without leaving insect frass pellets)
risk_factors: High nightshade density, no-till beds where overwintering brown 'jug-handled' pupae survive undisturbed in the soil, and absence of parasitic braconid wasps.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (70–85°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adult sphinx moths (Carolina sphinx and five-spotted hawkmoth) migrate and fly from dusk to dawn.
management_actions: Handpick caterpillars from plants (a UV blacklight flashlight at night makes hornworms glow bright neon green against dark purple tomato foliage for effortless spotting!); CRITICAL: if a hornworm has dozens of small white rice-grain-like cocoons sticking up on its back, DO NOT kill it—those are the pupae of the beneficial parasitic wasp Cotesia congregata, which will hatch to parasitize dozens more hornworms! For young small larvae, spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt) or spinosad.
prevention_actions: Till or hand-fork tomato/pepper beds in late autumn or early spring to expose and destroy the large (2-inch), mahogany-brown, 'pitcher-handled' overwintering pupae in the top 4–6 inches of soil; plant dill, fennel, and sweet alyssum to nourish parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (upper canopy leaves, tender stems, blossoms, and green fruits) twice weekly during mid-to-late summer (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for stripped bare upper tomato stems to distinguish Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms from Tomato Fruitworm / Corn Earworm (bores a deep hole at the stem end of fruit rather than stripping whole upper branches), Deer browsing (rips jagged stems without leaving insect frass pellets).
severity_or_impact: High (just 2 or 3 large 5th-instar hornworms can strip a mature tomato or pepper plant bare in days)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm summer nights favoring hawk/sphinx moth flight and egg laying.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato).

topic: Tomato Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments

symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.

host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Tomato Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.)
problem_name: Anthracnose
causal_agent: Colletotrichum spp. (C. coccodes on Solanaceae; C. orbiculare on Cucurbits; C. lindemuthianum on Beans; C. acutatum / C. gloeosporioides on Fruits)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening and immature fruits, pods, leaves, petioles, and stems/canes
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit/pod maturation and post-harvest ripening
season: Warm, wet, humid summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>90%) and frequent splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum): Circular, sunken, water-soaked saucer-like lesions (1/4 to 1/2 inch across) on ripening or green fruits and bean pods that darken to brown or black with concentric rings of tiny black acervuli fruiting bodies; under warm humid conditions, the sunken centers exude sticky, gelatinous salmon-pink to orange spore masses; on cucurbit and bean leaves, reddish-brown to black angular or vein-delimited necrotic spots and elongated sunken stem/petiole cankers.
symptom_keywords: sunken circular fruit spots, salmon-pink sticky spore masses, concentric dark rings in sunken crater, dark vein-blackening on bean pods, tear-stain fruit streaks
symptom_progression: Spores splash onto green fruit or leaves, often establishing quiescent (latent) infections in green fruit skin that awaken and expand into sunken salmon-spored craters as the fruit ripens and softens.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by well-defined circular sunken ('thumbprint') craters on fruit and pods that produce slimy salmon-pink to orange conidial masses in humid weather.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot, Alternaria Black Mold, Phytophthora Fruit Rot, Cercospora Leaf Spot, Gummy Stem Blight
risk_factors: Fruits touching bare wet soil, overhead irrigation, saving seed from infected bean/cucurbit pods, and warm rainy weather during harvest.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–86°F) with frequent rainstorms and prolonged wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as microsclerotia or mycelium in crop residue, soil, and infected bean/cucurbit seeds; conidia are sticky and spread primarily by splashing rain, irrigation water, insects, and wet harvesting.
management_actions: Harvest ripe fruit promptly (do not allow overripe tomatoes, peppers, or berries to hang or rot on the ground); stake or trellis plants and mulch soil heavily with straw to prevent soil-to-fruit splash; never work in bean or cucurbit patches when foliage is wet; prune out dead twigs in mango/avocado/citrus canopies.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed and anthracnose-resistant bean and cucurbit cultivars; practice a 3-year crop rotation; use drip irrigation.
recommended_observations: Scout Tomato (ripening and immature fruits, pods, leaves, petioles, and stems/canes) weekly during warm, wet, humid summer weather (75–86°F (24–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Anthracnose from Bacterial Spot, Alternaria Black Mold, Phytophthora Fruit Rot, Cercospora Leaf Spot, Gummy Stem Blight.
severity_or_impact: High (primary cause of ripe fruit rot in tomatoes, peppers, strawberries, mangoes, papayas, avocados, and pod spots in beans)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–86°F (24–30°C) and high humidity (>90%) and frequent splashing rain.
host_range: Documented on Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin, Squash).
