topic: Eggplant Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Eggplant Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)
causal_agent: Liriomyza sativae (Vegetable Leafminer), Liriomyza trifolii (American Serpentine Leafminer), and Pegomya hyoscyami (Spinach / Beet Leafminer)
affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering
risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.

topic: Eggplant Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.

severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)

topic: Eggplant Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
affected_plant_parts: Developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.
symptom_keywords: shield-shaped green or brown bug, white bands on antennae of brown stink bug, cloudy yellow-white spots on ripe tomato and pepper skin, white spongy corky tissue under fruit skin, catfaced dimpled peaches and apples, black-and-orange harlequin bug with striped barrel eggs on kale
symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.
distinguishing_features: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug is identified by alternating light-and-dark bands on its antennae and along the flared rear edge of its abdomen (distinguishing it from beneficial predatory Rough Stink Bugs and Spined Soldier Bugs, which have pointed shoulder spines or thick piercing beaks); Harlequin Bug is unmistakable with its glossy black-and-fiery-orange shield and two-row clusters of black-and-white striped barrel eggs. Note: cloudy white spongy spots under tomato/pepper skin are Stink Bug feeding, NOT a fungal disease!
similar_conditions: Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface)
risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.
management_actions: Handpick adults, nymphs, and barrel-shaped egg clusters in the cool early morning by knocking them into a bucket of soapy water; cover high-value tomato, pepper, bean, and brassica beds with fine insect netting; vacuum Harlequin bugs off kale/collards.
prevention_actions: Plant a perimeter trap crop of early-maturing cowpeas/soybeans, sweet corn, or sunflowers (for green/brown stink bugs) or 'Cleome' spider flower / mustard greens (for Harlequin Bug) to intercept immigrating adults before they reach main crops; mow weedy borders BEFORE weeds go to seed.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for harlequin bug on brassicas)) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (70–92°F (21–33°C)); inspect for shield-shaped green or brown bug to distinguish Stink Bugs from Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface).
severity_or_impact: High (causes widespread 'cloudy spot' on tomatoes/peppers, catfacing on peaches/apples, shriveled beans/pecans, and severe scorching of kale/collards)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, sunny summer weather.

topic: Eggplant Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, peaches, celery, beans, tomatoes, and pomegranates
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Peach, Plum, Apple, Pear, Beans).

topic: Eggplant Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Eggplant Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms Management
problem_name: Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms
causal_agent: Manduca quinquemaculata (Tomato Hornworm) and Manduca sexta (Tobacco Hornworm)
affected_plant_parts: Upper canopy leaves, tender stems, blossoms, and green fruits
growth_stage: Mid-season vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Mid-to-late summer
humidity_conditions: Warm summer nights favoring hawk/sphinx moth flight and egg laying
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Sudden, dramatic defoliation of upper stems where entire compound leaves—including midribs and petioles—are chewed away overnight leaving bare stripped stalks, plus large gouged cavities chewed into the sides of green tomatoes; large, dark greenish-black barrel-shaped pellets of droppings ('frass', resembling miniature hand grenades) litter the lower leaves and ground directly beneath the well-camouflaged, 3-to-4-inch-long bright-green caterpillar with white diagonal side stripes and a prominent rear dorsal horn.
symptom_keywords: stripped bare upper tomato stems, large 3-4 inch green caterpillar with rear horn, white V or slash stripes on sides, large dark barrel-shaped frass pellets on lower leaves, gouged green fruit
symptom_progression: Large gray hawk/sphinx moths ('hummingbird moths') hover at dusk to lay single round pearly-green eggs on leaf undersides; caterpillars feed for 3–4 weeks (consuming 90% of their total foliage intake during their final 5–7 days in the 5th instar!) before burrowing 4–6 inches into soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Tomato Hornworm has 8 white V-shaped chevrons pointing forward along each side and a black/dark-blue rear horn; Tobacco Hornworm has 7 white diagonal slash stripes edged in black and a curved bright-red rear horn. Look for dark barrel-shaped frass pellets on lower leaves to spot the camouflaged caterpillar directly above!
similar_conditions: Tomato Fruitworm / Corn Earworm (bores a deep hole at the stem end of fruit rather than stripping whole upper branches), Deer browsing (rips jagged stems without leaving insect frass pellets)
risk_factors: High nightshade density, no-till beds where overwintering brown 'jug-handled' pupae survive undisturbed in the soil, and absence of parasitic braconid wasps.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (70–85°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adult sphinx moths (Carolina sphinx and five-spotted hawkmoth) migrate and fly from dusk to dawn.
management_actions: Handpick caterpillars from plants (a UV blacklight flashlight at night makes hornworms glow bright neon green against dark purple tomato foliage for effortless spotting!); CRITICAL: if a hornworm has dozens of small white rice-grain-like cocoons sticking up on its back, DO NOT kill it—those are the pupae of the beneficial parasitic wasp Cotesia congregata, which will hatch to parasitize dozens more hornworms! For young small larvae, spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt) or spinosad.
prevention_actions: Till or hand-fork tomato/pepper beds in late autumn or early spring to expose and destroy the large (2-inch), mahogany-brown, 'pitcher-handled' overwintering pupae in the top 4–6 inches of soil; plant dill, fennel, and sweet alyssum to nourish parasitic wasps.

topic: Eggplant Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).
severity_or_impact: High (causes direct sap depletion, sooty mold, Squash Silverleaf, irregular tomato ripening, and transmits Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus and Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Eggplant Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.)
problem_name: Anthracnose
causal_agent: Colletotrichum spp. (C. coccodes on Solanaceae; C. orbiculare on Cucurbits; C. lindemuthianum on Beans; C. acutatum / C. gloeosporioides on Fruits)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening and immature fruits, pods, leaves, petioles, and stems/canes
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit/pod maturation and post-harvest ripening
season: Warm, wet, humid summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>90%) and frequent splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Circular, sunken, water-soaked saucer-like lesions (1/4 to 1/2 inch across) on ripening or green fruits and bean pods that darken to brown or black with concentric rings of tiny black acervuli fruiting bodies; under warm humid conditions, the sunken centers exude sticky, gelatinous salmon-pink to orange spore masses; on cucurbit and bean leaves, reddish-brown to black angular or vein-delimited necrotic spots and elongated sunken stem/petiole cankers.
symptom_keywords: sunken circular fruit spots, salmon-pink sticky spore masses, concentric dark rings in sunken crater, dark vein-blackening on bean pods, tear-stain fruit streaks
symptom_progression: Spores splash onto green fruit or leaves, often establishing quiescent (latent) infections in green fruit skin that awaken and expand into sunken salmon-spored craters as the fruit ripens and softens.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by well-defined circular sunken ('thumbprint') craters on fruit and pods that produce slimy salmon-pink to orange conidial masses in humid weather.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot, Alternaria Black Mold, Phytophthora Fruit Rot, Cercospora Leaf Spot, Gummy Stem Blight
risk_factors: Fruits touching bare wet soil, overhead irrigation, saving seed from infected bean/cucurbit pods, and warm rainy weather during harvest.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–86°F) with frequent rainstorms and prolonged wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as microsclerotia or mycelium in crop residue, soil, and infected bean/cucurbit seeds; conidia are sticky and spread primarily by splashing rain, irrigation water, insects, and wet harvesting.
management_actions: Harvest ripe fruit promptly (do not allow overripe tomatoes, peppers, or berries to hang or rot on the ground); stake or trellis plants and mulch soil heavily with straw to prevent soil-to-fruit splash; never work in bean or cucurbit patches when foliage is wet; prune out dead twigs in mango/avocado/citrus canopies.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed and anthracnose-resistant bean and cucurbit cultivars; practice a 3-year crop rotation; use drip irrigation.

severity_or_impact: High (primary cause of ripe fruit rot in tomatoes, peppers, strawberries, mangoes, papayas, avocados, and pod spots in beans)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–86°F (24–30°C) and high humidity (>90%) and frequent splashing rain.

topic: Eggplant Bacterial Wilt (Southern Bacterial Wilt) (Ralstonia solanacearum)
problem_name: Bacterial Wilt (Southern Bacterial Wilt)
causal_agent: Ralstonia solanacearum
affected_plant_parts: Roots, xylem vascular system, stems, and potato tubers
growth_stage: Flowering and rapid fruit/tuber development
season: Hot, wet summer weather
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and warm wet soils
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Sudden, rapid wilting of the youngest upper leaves during the heat of the day, followed within 2–4 days by complete, irreversible collapse and death of the entire plant WHILE LEAVES REMAIN GREEN (no prior yellowing or leaf spotting); cutting the lower stem crosswise reveals dark brown water-soaked vascular tissue and greyish-white slimy bacterial ooze that streams out in milky threads when a cut stem section is suspended in a clear glass of water; in potato tubers, brown vascular ring rot and bacterial slime oozing from tuber eyes.
symptom_keywords: green wilt, sudden plant collapse without yellowing, bacterial streaming in water glass, slimy vascular ooze, brown tuber ring
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter roots through cultivation wounds or nematode feeding sites, rapidly multiplying and clogging xylem vessels with extracellular polysaccharide slime (EPS) so the green canopy wilts and dies in days.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Fusarium and Verticillium wilts by the rapid collapse of the entire plant while foliage is still bright green (without unilateral yellowing) and the positive 'water-glass bacterial streaming test' (milky white strands streaming from a cut stem suspended in clear water within 3–5 minutes).
similar_conditions: Fusarium Wilt, Verticillium Wilt, Southern Blight (white mycelium + sclerotia on outside of collar), Squash Vine Borer
risk_factors: Warm, wet, poorly drained soils, root-knot nematode feeding wounds, cultivating too deeply near roots, and planting in infested coastal/southern soils.
favorable_conditions: High soil temperatures (85–95°F) combined with high soil moisture.
transmission_or_spread: Persists for many years in deep soil layers, weed hosts, and infected seed potato tubers; spreads via contaminated soil, irrigation runoff, and root-to-root contact.
management_actions: Perform the clear-glass water streaming test to confirm; immediately uproot and bag infected plants; do not irrigate healthy beds with runoff from infested areas; clean soil from tools and boots.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g., 'Neptune', 'BHN 602', 'Hawai'i 7996') or graft heirloom tomatoes onto bacterial-wilt-resistant rootstocks ('RST-04-106', 'Maxifort', ' Armada'); control root-knot nematodes; rotate with non-host grasses/corn for 4+ years.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (roots, xylem vascular system, stems, and potato tubers) weekly during hot, wet summer weather (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Wilt (Southern Bacterial Wilt) from Fusarium Wilt, Verticillium Wilt, Southern Blight (white mycelium + sclerotia on outside of collar), Squash Vine Borer.
severity_or_impact: Critical (100% lethal to infected plants; extremely persistent in warm soils)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and warm wet soils.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Potato, Eggplant, Pepper, Banana).

topic: Eggplant Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot

topic: Eggplant Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury
risk_factors: Abundant perennial weeds (pokeweed, milkweed, chickweed, white cockle, nightshade, bindweed) harboring CMV near the garden and migrating winged aphids.
favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored non-persistently (stylet-borne) by >80 species of aphids (especially Green peach aphid Myzus persicae and Melon aphid Aphis gossypii); aphids acquire and transmit the virus in just 10–60 seconds of test probing (so insecticides cannot kill aphids fast enough to prevent transmission!).
management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.

topic: Eggplant Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot (Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani)
problem_name: Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot
causal_agent: Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani
affected_plant_parts: Germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line
growth_stage: Seed germination and cotyledon-to-first-true-leaf seedling stage
season: Early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil
humidity_conditions: Overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Pre-emergence damping-off: seeds turn soft, mushy, and brown and fail to emerge, leaving patchy gaps in rows; Post-emergence damping-off: healthy-looking cotyledon seedlings suddenly develop a water-soaked, pinched, thread-like brown or black constriction at the stem base right at the soil line ('wirestem' in brassicas when caused by Rhizoctonia) and topple over flat onto the soil while leaves are still green.
symptom_keywords: seedlings falling over at soil line, pinched thread-like stem base, wirestem, patchy seed emergence, mushy rotted seeds, water-soaked hypocotyl
symptom_progression: Soil-borne oomycetes and fungi attack slow-germinating seeds and tender unlignified hypocotyl tissue in wet soil, rotting the stem cortex within 24–48 hours so seedlings collapse.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the pinched, water-soaked or wiry brown constriction strictly at the soil line on young seedlings (whereas Cutworms completely sever the stem cleanly and Heat/Sunburn bleaches the stem white).
similar_conditions: Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling
risk_factors: Reusing unsterilized garden soil or dirty flats for indoor seed starting, overwatering, sowing too deeply or densely, cold soil temperatures delaying emergence, and poor airflow.
favorable_conditions: Cold, wet, poorly aerated soil or potting media with high seedling density and stagnant air.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oospores and sclerotia native to garden soils, splashed or carried on dirty pots, tools, and untreated seed.
management_actions: Discard damped-off seedling cells/trays immediately; allow the surface of seed-starting media to dry slightly between bottom-waterings; provide a gentle oscillating fan and heat mat (70–75°F) for indoor seedlings.
prevention_actions: Always use sterile, soilless seed-starting mix in clean sanitized trays (washed in 10% bleach); do not sow outdoors until soil reaches the crop's minimum germination temperature; sow at proper depth and thin promptly.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line) weekly during early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil (50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot from Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling.
severity_or_impact: High at seedling stage (can wipe out 50–100% of a seed tray or direct-sown row)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia and overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Pumpkin, Squash, Zucchini, Watermelon).

topic: Eggplant Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
problem_name: Early Blight
causal_agent: Alternaria solani (and Alternaria tomatophila)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, stems (collar rot), petioles, and fruit/tubers at stem end
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting and tuber bulking
season: Warm, humid mid-to-late summer
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>90% RH), heavy morning dew, or alternating wet and dry periods
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Dark brown to black circular-to-angular necrotic lesions (1/4 to 1/2 inch) containing characteristic target-like concentric rings ('bull's-eye' pattern), surrounded by a diffuse yellow chlorotic halo on older lower leaves; sunken dark leathery stem lesions near soil line ('collar rot') and dark sunken concentric-ringed fruit lesions at the calyx stem attachment.
symptom_keywords: concentric rings, target spot, bull's-eye lesion, lower leaf yellowing, yellow halo, dark brown leaf spot, collar rot, sunken stem-end fruit rot
symptom_progression: Begins on oldest lower leaves nearest the soil; lesions enlarge and coalesce causing entire lower leaves to turn yellow, brown, and defoliate progressively upward up the canopy, exposing fruit to sunscald.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by conspicuous concentric rings ('target-board' appearance) inside dark brown lesions 1/4–1/2 inch wide, whereas Septoria leaf spot produces much smaller (1/16–1/8 inch) numerous spots with pale gray centers and tiny black pycnidia specks without target rings.
similar_conditions: Septoria Leaf Spot, Target Spot (Corynespora cassiicola), Bacterial Spot, Late Blight, Gray Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Overwintered solanaceous crop debris, crowded foliage, overhead irrigation, nitrogen or potassium deficiency weakening older leaves, and heavy fruit load.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–85°F) accompanied by rain, heavy dew, or overhead watering that keeps leaves wet for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Conidia spores survive in infected plant debris, soil, and volunteer solanaceous weeds, splashing onto lower leaves via rain or irrigation water and spreading upward by wind and wet handling.
management_actions: Prune and destroy infected lower leaves early; apply organic mulch (straw/shredded leaves) immediately after planting to block soil-splash of conidia; irrigate only at the soil line via drip; apply labeled protectant fungicides (copper, chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or Bacillus subtilis biofungicides) when weather favors infection.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3–4 year crop rotation away from all Solanaceae (tomato, potato, eggplant, pepper); stake or cage plants and space adequately for rapid canopy drying; use certified disease-free seed/transplants and tolerant cultivars (e.g., 'Mountain Magic', 'Defiant', 'Iron Lady'); remove all crop debris at season end.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (older lower leaves, stems (collar rot), petioles, and fruit/tubers at stem end) weekly during warm, humid mid-to-late summer (75–85°F (24–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Early Blight from Septoria Leaf Spot, Target Spot (Corynespora cassiicola), Bacterial Spot, Late Blight, Gray Leaf Spot.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe premature defoliation, 30–50% yield loss, and secondary fruit sunscald)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–85°F (24–29°C) and high humidity (>90% rh), heavy morning dew, or alternating wet and dry periods.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Potato, Eggplant, Pepper).

topic: Eggplant Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
problem_name: Fusarium Wilt
causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum (host-specific formae speciales: f. sp. lycopersici, melongenae, tuberosi, niveum, melonis, cucumerinum, conglutinans, cepae, pisi, phaseoli, spinaciae, basilici, cubense)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Bright yellowing (chlorosis) and drooping of older lower leaves—classically starting on ONLY ONE SIDE of a leaf, one branch, or one side of the plant ('one-sided flagging')—which wilts during warm afternoons and eventually fails to recover at night; slicing the lower main stem or petiole lengthwise reveals a diagnostic reddish-brown to dark-brown discoloration of the water-conducting vascular ring while the central pith remains healthy.
symptom_keywords: one-sided yellowing, unilateral wilting, vascular browning, reddish-brown xylem ring, lower leaf yellowing, daytime wilting, stunted growth
symptom_progression: Fungus enters root tips or nematode wounds and colonizes xylem vessels; lower leaves yellow and wilt unilaterally, progressing upward until entire shoots brown, collapse, and die without soft stem rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity
risk_factors: Acidic sandy soils (pH <6.0), root-knot nematode infestations creating root entry wounds, high ammonium-nitrogen fertilization, and replanting susceptible cultivars in infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (80–90°F) and moisture stress during fruiting.
transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.
management_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants including roots immediately; do not compost infected stems; solarize soil in hot sunny climates; maintain soil pH near 6.5–7.0 using agricultural lime and use nitrate-nitrogen rather than ammonium-nitrogen.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'F', 'FF', or 'FFF' for Races 1, 2, 3 in tomato; Fusarium-resistant watermelon, melon, cabbage 'Yellows Resistant', pea, basil, and banana cultivars); control root-knot nematodes; practice 4–6 year crop rotations.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)) weekly during warm summer growing season (80–90°F (27–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Fusarium Wilt from Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity.
severity_or_impact: High (lethal systemic vascular wilt; soil remains infested for many years)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–90°F (27–32°C) and warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil ph and root-knot nematode feeding.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Eggplant, Pepper, Potato, Watermelon, Melon, Cucumber, Pumpkin).

topic: Eggplant Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').
symptom_keywords: fuzzy brownish-gray mold, dusty spore masses, stem pruning wound canker, blossom blight, berry gray rot, ghost spot rings on tomato
symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits) weekly during cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) from Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight.
severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, brambles, grapes, and high-tunnel tomatoes (major pre- and post-harvest fruit loss)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh), fog, rain, and poor air circulation.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Grape, Blueberry).

topic: Eggplant Leaf Mold, Target Spot, and Buckeye Rot (Passalora fulva)
problem_name: Leaf Mold, Target Spot, and Buckeye Rot
causal_agent: Passalora fulva (Tomato Leaf Mold), Corynespora cassiicola (Target Spot), and Phytophthora nicotianae (Buckeye Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Lower-to-middle leaves, stems, and low-hanging green fruits
growth_stage: Canopy closure and fruit development
season: Warm, humid summer weather or high-tunnel/greenhouse cultivation
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>85% RH) or soil splash onto low fruit
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Leaf Mold: pale greenish-yellow diffuse spots on the UPPER leaf surface matched directly underneath on the LOWER surface by velvety olive-green to grayish-purple patches of conidia; Target Spot: small brown-black spots with pale tan centers and concentric rings on leaves and sunken brown pitted lesions on fruit; Buckeye Rot: smooth, brown-and-grayish-green zonate concentric rings ('buckeye' pattern) on green fruit touching or near wet soil, remaining firm with a smooth skin until secondary rot sets in.
symptom_keywords: pale yellow upper leaf spots, velvety olive-green lower leaf mold, zonate brown-green buckeye rings on low fruit, target-like foliar spots
symptom_progression: High humidity (>85% RH) inside dense canopies or high tunnels triggers Leaf Mold on older leaves; rain splash from wet soil infects low-hanging green tomatoes with Buckeye Rot.
distinguishing_features: Leaf Mold is distinguished by the pale yellow blotches on top paired with velvety olive-green-to-purple mold strictly on the underside of the leaf; Buckeye Rot has smooth brown concentric bands on green fruit near the soil (unlike Late Blight fruit rot, which is rough, greasy, and accompanied by severe foliar blight).
similar_conditions: Early Blight, Late Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, Powdery Mildew, Blossom-End Rot
risk_factors: High tunnels/greenhouses with poor ventilation (>85% RH), unstaked vines allowing fruit to touch bare soil, and dense unpruned foliage.
favorable_conditions: Relative humidity above 85% at 70–80°F (Leaf Mold/Target Spot); warm wet soil splashing low fruit (Buckeye Rot).
transmission_or_spread: Conidia spread by air currents, worker clothing, and tools (Leaf Mold/Target Spot); sporangia/zoospores splash from soil (Buckeye Rot).
management_actions: Stake, cage, or trellis plants and prune lower leaves up to 12 inches off the mulched ground; ventilate high tunnels/greenhouses to keep relative humidity below 85%.
prevention_actions: Plant tomato cultivars carrying Cf resistance genes for Leaf Mold; mulch soil heavily with straw and use drip irrigation.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High in humid regions and high tunnels
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and high relative humidity (>85% rh) or soil splash onto low fruit.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Eggplant Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus and Choanephora Wet Rot (Bhendi yellow vein mosaic begomovirus)
problem_name: Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus and Choanephora Wet Rot
causal_agent: Bhendi yellow vein mosaic begomovirus (OYVMV) and Choanephora cucurbitarum (Blossom Blight / Wet Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Leaf veins, blades, blossoms, and young developing pods/fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through daily flowering and pod/fruit set
season: Hot, humid summer and monsoon/late-summer seasons
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>85% RH), frequent summer rains, or surging silverleaf whitefly populations
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus (OYVMV): a striking, vivid network of bright canary-yellow veins and veinlets enclosing small islands of green tissue across the leaf blade (or turning entire upper leaves solid yellow-cream), accompanied by stunted plants and small, pale yellowish-green, hard, fibrous pods; Choanephora Wet Rot (on Okra pods, Squash/Zucchini blossoms-and-fruits, Cowpea pods, and Pepper shoots): fading spent flowers fail to drop off the tip of the young pod or squash and quickly erupt in a dense beard of metallic whisker-like fungal stalks topped with tiny shiny black pinheads ('pins stuck in a pincushion'), rotting the attached blossom end of the young okra pod or squash into a soft watery brown mush.
symptom_keywords: vivid canary-yellow vein network on okra leaf, pale yellow fibrous okra pods, whiskers with shiny black pinheads on blossom end of young squash or okra pod, soft wet blossom-end rot
symptom_progression: Whiteflies transmit OYVMV persistently into phloem veins; Choanephora invades senescing day-old flower petals stuck to the tip of young okra pods or summer squash during humid rainy weather and grows into the fruit tip.
distinguishing_features: OYVMV is unmistakable due to the brilliant yellow net-like clearing of every major and minor leaf vein; Choanephora Wet Rot is distinguished from physiological Blossom-End Rot by the fuzzy whisker-like stalks tipped with tiny black pinhead sporangia covering the decaying blossom end!
similar_conditions: Blossom-End Rot (dry sunken leathery black patch from calcium/water stress WITHOUT whiskers or black pinheads), Iron/Magnesium Deficiency (yellow BETWEEN veins while veins stay green—the exact opposite of Yellow Vein Mosaic!)
risk_factors: High populations of silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) for OYVMV; dense canopies, overhead watering, and high humidity keeping spent flower petals stuck to young fruit tips for Choanephora.
favorable_conditions: Hot, humid weather (80–95°F) with whiteflies (OYVMV) or summer rain showers (Choanephora).
transmission_or_spread: OYVMV is transmitted persistently by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci (not seed-borne); Choanephora spores are spread by wind, rain splash, and flower-visiting bees/beetles.
management_actions: Rogue OYVMV-infected okra plants early and manage whiteflies with insecticidal soap or yellow sticky traps; for Choanephora Wet Rot, gently pluck spent wilted flower corollas off the tips of young squash and okra pods during humid rainy spells and harvest pods every 1–2 days.
prevention_actions: Plant OYVMV-resistant okra hybrids; space okra and summer squash generously for rapid morning sun drying of blossoms.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (leaf veins, blades, blossoms, and young developing pods/fruits) weekly during hot, humid summer and monsoon/late-summer seasons (78–95°F (26–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus and Choanephora Wet Rot from Blossom-End Rot (dry sunken leathery black patch from calcium/water stress WITHOUT whiskers or black pinheads), Iron/Magnesium Deficiency (yellow BETWEEN veins while veins stay green—the exact opposite of Yellow Vein Mosaic!).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (OYVMV stunts pod yield by 50–80%; Choanephora rots young squash and okra pods in wet summers)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 78–95°F (26–35°C) and high humidity (>85% rh), frequent summer rains, or surging silverleaf whitefly populations.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Okra, Squash, Zucchini, Cowpea, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Eggplant Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot (Phytophthora capsici)
problem_name: Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot
causal_agent: Phytophthora capsici (on Solanaceae, Cucurbits, Legumes); Phytophthora cactorum / P. fragariae (on Strawberry/Apple); Phytophthora cinnamomi / P. nicotianae (on Avocado, Citrus, Papaya, Blueberry, Rosemary, Sage)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown/collar (foot rot/gummosis), stems, leaves, and fruit ('buckeye rot' on tomato; white yeast-like powder on squash/pepper/watermelon)
growth_stage: Any stage after soil saturation or heavy rainfall
season: Warm, rainy summer weather or poorly drained wet soils
humidity_conditions: Saturated, waterlogged, or flooded soil (>24 hours of standing water) and splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Dark brown-to-black water-soaked lesion girdling the stem base/crown right above the soil line ('black shank' in pepper/squash; 'red stele' reddish-pink central root core in strawberry; 'foot rot/gummosis' cracking bark and oozing gum at graft union in citrus; feeder root blackening and canopy dieback in avocado/blueberry/rosemary), causing rapid permanent wilting; on pepper, cucurbit, and eggplant fruits, dark water-soaked blotches rapidly covered in a diagnostic dusting of white, yeast-like or powdered-sugar-like sporangia (on green tomato fruit touching soil, smooth brown 'buckeye rot' target rings).
symptom_keywords: black stem base collar rot, powdered-sugar white sporangia on fruit, buckeye rot on tomato, red stele root core in strawberry, citrus foot rot gummosis, avocado feeder root rot, sudden wilt after rain
symptom_progression: Swimming zoospores released in saturated soil chemotactically swim to roots and crowns, rotting the root system and stem collar within days and splashing onto low-hanging fruits.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished in pepper and cucurbits by the dark black basal stem girdling ('black shank') and the tight, flat, powdered-sugar-like white coating of sporangia on rotting fruit (unlike fluffy tall cottony Pythium or white fan-like Southern Blight with mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight, Pythium Cottony Leak, Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Sclerotinia White Mold
risk_factors: Poorly drained clay soils, low spots where rainwater puddles, over-irrigation, planting crowns/graft unions too deeply, and short rotations between peppers, eggplants, tomatoes, and cucurbits.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) combined with heavy rainfall or waterlogged soil.
transmission_or_spread: Thick-walled oospores survive in soil for 5–10+ years; motile biflagellate zoospores swim through soil water films and spread in surface runoff and ponded irrigation water.

topic: Eggplant Root-Knot Nematode Disease (Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla)
problem_name: Root-Knot Nematode Disease
causal_agent: Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla
affected_plant_parts: Root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting and root harvest
season: Warm growing season
temperature_range: 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla
humidity_conditions: Moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Above ground: patchy stunting, pale green-to-yellow chlorotic foliage resembling chronic nitrogen/micronutrient deficiency, premature wilting during warm sunny afternoons even when soil is moist, and poor fruit/pod yield; Below ground (diagnostic): uprooting the plant reveals swollen, beaded, irregular tumor-like root galls ('knots', 1/8 to 1 inch thick) that are an integral part of the root tissue itself, deformed forked/pimpled carrots and potatoes, and cracked sweet potatoes with a 'bearded' mass of stunted feeder roots.
symptom_keywords: swollen root galls, beaded knotted roots, afternoon wilting in moist soil, patchy stunting, forked galling on carrots, pimpled potato tubers
symptom_progression: Microscopic second-stage juveniles (J2) penetrate root tips and inject esophageal secretions that induce giant feeder cells and root galls, disrupting water and nutrient uptake and predisposing roots to Fusarium and Bacterial wilts.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION on legumes (Beans, Peas, Chickpea, Lentil, Soybean, Fenugreek): Root-knot nematode galls are swelling OF the structural root tissue itself and CANNOT be rubbed off, whereas beneficial nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium nodules are round pink-centered attachments on the side of the root that detach easily! On Brassicas, Clubroot causes much larger spindle-like clubs without female nematode egg masses.
similar_conditions: Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency
risk_factors: Warm sandy soils, continuous monoculture of susceptible vegetables (especially okra, tomato, cucurbits, carrot, bean), and introducing infested transplants or soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (75–90°F) in sandy loam soils.
transmission_or_spread: Microscopic soil-borne roundworms spread via infested transplants, seed tubers/slips, soil clinging to tools/shoes, and surface water runoff.
management_actions: Do not replant susceptible crops in galled spots; incorporate abundant organic compost right into beds to stimulate predatory soil fungi and microbes; solarize moist soil under clear UV plastic for 6–8 weeks in peak summer heat.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'N' or 'VFN' carrying the Mi-1 gene in tomato, 'Nemaguard'/'Guardian' rootstock in peach, 'Covington'/'Evangeline' in sweet potato, 'Charleston Belle' in pepper); rotate with non-host sweet corn, cereal rye, or French marigolds (Tagetes patula 'Single Gold'/'Nema-gone') planted as a solid cover crop.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots) weekly during warm growing season (75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Root-Knot Nematode Disease from Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency.
severity_or_impact: High (causes 30–80% yield loss and breaks genetic resistance to Fusarium and Bacterial wilts)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla and moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils.

topic: Eggplant Septoria Leaf Spot (Septoria lycopersici)
problem_name: Septoria Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Septoria lycopersici
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, stems, and calyces (rarely affects fruit directly)
growth_stage: First fruit set through harvest
season: Warm, wet summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, frequent rainfall, and extended leaf wetness
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Numerous small (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm), circular water-soaked spots on older lower leaves that mature into spots with dark brown margins and tan-to-light-gray centers dotted with tiny black pimple-like fruiting bodies (pycnidia, visible with a 10x hand lens); heavily spotted leaves turn yellow, wither, and drop.
symptom_keywords: small circular spots, gray center dark brown border, tiny black specks pycnidia, lower leaf spotting, progressive defoliation
symptom_progression: Starts on lowest leaves right after first fruit set; dozens of tiny spots coalesce, causing bottom-to-top defoliation that starves developing fruit and exposes them to sunscald.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Early Blight by smaller lesion size (1/16–1/8 inch vs 1/4–1/2 inch), pale gray-tan centers lacking concentric bull's-eye rings, and the presence of tiny black dot-like pycnidia embedded in the gray center; distinguished from Bacterial Spot by the gray center with pycnidia and lack of raised scabby fruit spots.
similar_conditions: Early Blight (Alternaria solani), Bacterial Spot (Xanthomonas spp.), Bacterial Speck, Gray Leaf Spot (Stemphylium)
risk_factors: Infected tomato crop residue left in soil, horse-nettle/nightshade weeds, staked equipment carrying spores, and overhead watering.
favorable_conditions: Extended periods of warm (68–77°F), rainy, or humid weather with splashing water.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters on infected tomato debris and solanaceous weeds (especially horsenettle Solanum carolinense); conidia ooze from pycnidia when wet and splash onto lower foliage.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves promptly; mulch soil with straw or plastic to stop rain splash; water only at the base via drip irrigation; apply copper or labeled protectant fungicides if wet weather persists.
prevention_actions: Rotate out of Solanaceae for 3 years; eradicate horsenettle and nightshade weeds around the garden; sanitize stakes and cages with 10% bleach between seasons; space and prune plants for airflow.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high humidity, frequent rainfall, and extended leaf wetness.

topic: Eggplant Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).
