topic: Eggplant Tobacco Mosaic Virus / Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV / ToMV) (Tobamovirus tabaci / Tobamovirus tomatotessellati)
problem_name: Tobacco Mosaic Virus / Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV / ToMV)
causal_agent: Tobamovirus tabaci / Tobamovirus tomatotessellati
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Seedling through fruiting
season: All growing seasons (including indoor seed starting and greenhouses)
humidity_conditions: Independent of humidity (spreads mechanically without water or insect vectors)
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Light-green and dark-green mosaic mottling across leaflets accompanied by leaf wrinkling, blistering, downward curling, and 'fern-leaf' / 'shoestring' distortion where leaflet blades narrow into ribbon-like strips; stunted overall plant growth; internal brown wall browning ('bronzing') and uneven blotchy yellow-red ripening on fruits.
symptom_keywords: light and dark green mosaic mottling, fern-leaf distortion, shoestring leaflets, leaf blistering, blotchy fruit ripening, internal fruit browning
symptom_progression: Enters through microscopic broken leaf hairs (trichomes) when plants are touched; systemic mosaic mottling and fern-leaf narrowing appear on newly expanding upper leaves 10–14 days after contact.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by alternating light/dark green mosaic islands on leaves, fern-like narrowing of young leaflets, and extreme stability on dry surfaces/hands (unlike CMV, TMV/ToMV is NOT transmitted by aphids but spreads rapidly via human hands and pruning tools).
similar_conditions: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV), Herbicide Drift (2,4-D/dicamba), Powdery Mildew, Physiological Blotchy Ripening
risk_factors: Handling tobacco products before touching plants, unsterilized pruning tools, contaminated seed coats, and reusing unwashed seedling trays or stakes.
favorable_conditions: Frequent hands-on pruning, tying, transplanting, and grafting operations.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely stable virus transmitted mechanically on workers' hands, clothing, pruning shears, and externally on contaminated seed coats; survives for years in dried plant debris and tobacco products.
management_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; wash hands thoroughly with soap and water and dip pruning tools in a 20% nonfat dry milk solution or 10% household bleach between plants; never smoke or handle tobacco near solanaceous plants.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (carrying Tm-2 or Tm-2^2 resistance genes in tomato and L genes in pepper); use certified virus-tested or trisodium-phosphate-treated seed; sanitize pots and stakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (leaves, stems, and fruits) weekly during all growing seasons (including indoor seed starting and greenhouses) (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tobacco Mosaic Virus / Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV / ToMV) from Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV), Herbicide Drift (2,4-D/dicamba), Powdery Mildew, Physiological Blotchy Ripening.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (reduces yield by 20–40% and causes blotchy unmarketable fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and independent of humidity (spreads mechanically without water or insect vectors).
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato).

topic: Eggplant Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) (Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae)
problem_name: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV)
causal_agent: Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae (Tomato spotted wilt virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Purpling, bronzing (metallic copper cast), and downward curling of young upper leaves accompanied by dark necrotic flecks or ringspots; dark brown necrotic streaks along petioles and terminal stems causing one-sided shoot tip dieback; on ripening tomato and pepper fruit, striking concentric yellow, orange, and green ringspots, marbled blotches, and raised bumps.
symptom_keywords: bronzing of upper leaves, concentric ringspots on fruit, necrotic stem streaks, terminal shoot dieback, stunted rosette, purple leaf veins
symptom_progression: Transmitted by adult thrips that acquired the virus as larvae; young terminal leaves bronze and develop necrotic specks, growth stunts severely, and fruits develop diagnostic target-like yellow/red ringspots.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by metallic bronzing and dark flecks on YOUNG upper leaves (unlike Early Blight on older lower leaves) and vivid yellow/orange concentric ringspots on ripening fruit.
similar_conditions: Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling
risk_factors: Abundant western flower thrips or tobacco thrips populations, nearby flowering weeds (chickweed, dandelion, spiny amaranth, buttercup) acting as virus reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather favoring thrips generation turnover and weed dry-down that drives thrips onto garden crops.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently and exclusively by thrips (especially Western flower thrips Frankliniella occidentalis and Tobacco thrips F. fusca); only larval thrips can acquire the virus by feeding on an infected plant, and emerging adults transmit it for life (not seed-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants so larval thrips cannot develop on them and spread virus to neighboring plants; use UV-reflective silver mulch to repel incoming adult thrips.
prevention_actions: Plant TSWV-resistant cultivars (carrying the Sw-5 gene in tomato, e.g., 'Amelia', 'Crista', 'Bella Rosa', 'Mountain Glory', or Tsw gene in pepper); eliminate winter/spring broadleaf weeds in a 30-ft perimeter around the garden BEFORE planting.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits) weekly during late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) from Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling.
severity_or_impact: High (severely stunts plants and renders ringed fruit unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Lettuce, Spinach, Celery, Beans).

topic: Eggplant Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) (Begomovirus coheni)
problem_name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
causal_agent: Begomovirus coheni (Tomato yellow leaf curl virus)
affected_plant_parts: New apical leaves, shoots, and flowers
growth_stage: Seedling transplant stage through flowering
season: Warm-to-hot summer and autumn seasons
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry conditions favoring silverleaf whitefly explosions
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): Severe stunting and upright, bushy 'bonsai-like' growth of shoot terminals; new upper leaflets are drastically reduced in size, thick and leathery, curled strongly UPWARD (cup-shaped) and inward, with bright yellow (chlorotic) leaf margins and interveinal areas (sometimes tinged purple on undersides); severe flower abscission results in almost no fruit set after infection.
symptom_keywords: upward leaf curling, yellow leaf margins, stunted bonsai-like shoot tips, small cupped leathery leaves, flower drop, whitefly vector
symptom_progression: Following feeding by viruliferous silverleaf whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), emerging apical leaves within 2–3 weeks stay tiny, cup upward with bright yellow borders, internodes shorten drastically, and blossoms drop.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Physiological Leaf Roll by affecting the NEW upper leaves with bright yellow margins, extreme leaflet size reduction, and severe stunting (whereas Physiological Leaf Roll curls older lower leaves upward while keeping them full-sized and green).
similar_conditions: Physiological Leaf Roll, Herbicide Drift (2,4-D), Broad/Russet Mite injury, Micronutrient (Zinc/Iron) Deficiency
risk_factors: High populations of silverleaf/sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), infected transplants, and overlapping warm-season solanaceous crops.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry weather (80–95°F) promoting rapid whitefly reproduction and migration.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci MEAM1/MED); not transmitted by seed or mechanical touch/pruning.
management_actions: Rogue and seal infected plants inside plastic bags immediately to prevent whiteflies from dispersing; manage whitefly nymphs and adults on undersides of leaves using insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or neem oil; install yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies.
prevention_actions: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato cultivars (carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, Ty-3 genes, e.g., 'Security 28', 'Tycoon', 'BHN 968') and lay UV-reflective silver plastic mulch at transplanting to repel whiteflies; inspect transplants carefully for whitefly nymphs before purchasing.
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (new apical leaves, shoots, and flowers) weekly during warm-to-hot summer and autumn seasons (77–95°F (25–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) from Physiological Leaf Roll, Herbicide Drift (2,4-D), Broad/Russet Mite injury, Micronutrient (Zinc/Iron) Deficiency.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (early infection causes up to 90–100% fruit loss due to blossom abortion)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–95°F (25–35°C) and warm, dry conditions favoring silverleaf whitefly explosions.
host_range: Documented on Eggplant (Solanum melongena, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Beans).

topic: Eggplant Verticillium Wilt (Verticillium dahliae)
problem_name: Verticillium Wilt
causal_agent: Verticillium dahliae (and Verticillium albo-atrum)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/tuber enlargement
season: Cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: Moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand
visible_symptoms: On Eggplant (Solanum melongena): V-shaped yellow chlorotic blotches developing at the margins and tips of older lower leaflets that soon turn brown and necrotic with a yellow halo; leaves wilt during the heat of the day (often affecting one side of a leaf or branch first); outer older leaves on strawberry crowns turn brown and collapse while inner leaves remain green initially; light tan-to-brown streaking is visible in the vascular tissue near the base of the stem.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesion on leaf margin, lower leaf wilting, light tan vascular streaking, outer crown collapse, stunting, midday flagging
symptom_progression: Microsclerotia germinate near root exudates, invade root cortex and xylem, and slowly plug water transport; plants become chronically stunted with progressive lower-leaf V-necrosis and reduced fruit size.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by characteristic V-shaped marginal yellow-and-brown fan lesions at leaflet tips, cooler temperature optimum (68–78°F vs 80–90°F for Fusarium wilt), and lighter tan vascular discoloration restricted closer to the lower stem.
similar_conditions: Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot
risk_factors: Planting susceptible crops (such as strawberry, raspberry, or eggplant) in soil where tomato, potato, pepper, or eggplant grew within the preceding 3–4 years; root-lesion nematode feeding.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild soil temperatures (68–78°F) in spring followed by warm summer transpiration stress.
transmission_or_spread: Survives in soil for 8–10+ years as microscopic dark resting bodies (microsclerotia) across a wide host range of >300 broadleaf crops and weeds (nightshades, lambsquarters, pigweed).
management_actions: Remove infected plants and roots; maintain even irrigation and balanced potassium nutrition to help moderately tolerant plants mature fruit; solarize infested garden beds under clear plastic for 6 weeks in midsummer.
prevention_actions: Plant Verticillium-resistant cultivars ('V' designation in tomatoes); NEVER plant strawberries, brambles, or eggplants where nightshade family crops grew in the past 4 years; rotate with non-host grasses, sweet corn, or brassicas (broccoli residue biofumigation reduces microsclerotia).
recommended_observations: Scout Eggplant (roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather (68–78°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Verticillium Wilt from Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes chronic stunting, defoliation, and plant death in highly susceptible hosts like eggplant, potato, and strawberry)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–78°F (20–25°C) and moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand.

topic: Potato Aphids Management
problem_name: Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids)

affected_plant_parts: Undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and flowering
season: Spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer)
humidity_conditions: Moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants)
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew.
symptom_keywords: soft pear-shaped insects under leaves, curled puckered shoot tips, sticky shiny honeydew, black sooty mold, white cast skins, ants tending stems
symptom_progression: Winged females (alates) land on succulent new shoots and give live birth parthenogenetically to nymphs that mature in 7–10 days, building dense colonies and transmitting non-persistent plant viruses within seconds of probing.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present).
similar_conditions: Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves)
risk_factors: Over-fertilization with high soluble nitrogen (which creates lush amino-acid-rich sap that accelerates aphid reproduction), broad-spectrum pyrethroid/carbamate insecticide sprays that kill ladybugs and parasitic wasps, ant tending, and greenhouse/indoors transplant carryover.
favorable_conditions: Mild temperatures (65–80°F) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth.
transmission_or_spread: Winged alate aphids disperse on wind currents from overwintering weeds, woody hosts (Prunus, Euonymus), or neighboring crops; ants also move aphids between plants.
management_actions: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides.
prevention_actions: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.

topic: Potato Colorado Potato Beetle Management
problem_name: Colorado Potato Beetle
causal_agent: Leptinotarsa decemlineata
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, tender stems, and terminal shoots
growth_stage: Plant emergence through tuber bulking and fruiting
season: Late spring through summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Complete defoliation of potato and eggplant foliage by both adults and larvae: adults are robust, dome-shaped, oval beetles (3/8 inch / 10 mm long) with bright yellowish-orange wing covers marked with TEN distinct jet-black lengthwise stripes and black spots on the orange thorax; females lay clusters of 20–40 bright yellow-to-orange football-shaped eggs standing on end on the undersides of leaves; larvae are unmistakable humpbacked, soft-bodied, brick-red to salmon-orange grubs with two rows of black spots along each side and a shiny black head, which feed in groups on terminal shoots and deposit dark blackish-brown excrement.
symptom_keywords: dome-shaped yellow-orange beetle with ten black stripes, humpbacked brick-red grub larvae with two rows of black side spots, clusters of bright orange upright eggs under leaves, stripped potato and eggplant stems
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter 4–10 inches deep in the soil of last year's potato/eggplant bed and walk/fly to emerging plants in spring; eggs hatch in 4–9 days, and 4 larval instars devour foliage for 2–3 weeks before burrowing into soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from the False Potato Beetle (Leptinotarsa juncta, a harmless relative on horse nettle) because the true Colorado Potato Beetle has 10 clean black stripes on pale yellow wings, whereas the False Potato Beetle has a wide reddish-brown stripe down the center of each wing cover where two black stripes fuse; distinguish Colorado Potato Beetle egg clusters from Ladybug egg clusters only by checking for adult beetles/larvae nearby (they look very similar, though CPB eggs are slightly larger).
similar_conditions: False Potato Beetle, Beneficial Lady Beetle Eggs (do not crush orange upright egg clusters on crops OTHER than potato/eggplant/tomato, as those are ladybug eggs!), Blister Beetles
risk_factors: Planting potatoes or eggplants in or right next to last year's potato/eggplant bed, volunteer potatoes emerging from unharvested tubers, and heavy reliance on synthetic insecticides (Colorado Potato Beetle has evolved resistance to >50 classes of chemical insecticides!).
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny weather (75–86°F optimal).
transmission_or_spread: Adults emerge from overwintering soil burrows and walk several hundred yards (or fly on warm days >70°F) to locate Solanaceae hosts.
management_actions: Handpick striped adults and red humpbacked larvae into soapy water and crush orange egg clusters on the undersides of potato/eggplant leaves twice weekly; apply spinosad, azadirachtin (neem), or Bacillus thuringiensis tenebrionis (Bt san diego—a special beetle-specific strain of Bt, NOT caterpillar Bt kurstaki!) targeting newly hatched small 1st- and 2nd-instar red larvae.

severity_or_impact: Critical on potato and eggplant (defoliation during potato bloom reduces tuber yield by 50–80%)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–90°F (18–32°C) and warm, sunny spring and summer weather.

topic: Potato Cucumber Beetles Management
problem_name: Cucumber Beetles (Striped and Spotted Cucumber Beetles)
causal_agent: Acalymma vittatum (Striped Cucumber Beetle) and Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi (Spotted Cucumber Beetle / Southern Corn Rootworm)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence through flowering and fruiting
season: Spring transplant/emergence through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oblong bright-yellow-green beetles with either three jet-black longitudinal stripes down the wing covers (Striped Cucumber Beetle) or twelve black spots (Spotted Cucumber Beetle); overwintered adults swarm emerging cucurbit cotyledons and young transplants in spring, chewing ragged holes through leaves, girdling tender stems, congregating inside open yellow cucurbit blossoms (chewing anthers/pistils and reducing fruit set), scarring the underside and rind of melons/pumpkins, and transmitting the fatal bacterium Erwinia tracheiphila (Bacterial Wilt); white brown-headed larvae feed underground on cucurbit, corn, and bean roots.
symptom_keywords: yellow beetle with three black stripes, yellow-green beetle with twelve black spots, chewed cucurbit cotyledons and stems, beetles packed inside squash blossoms, scarred pumpkin rinds, sudden bacterial wilt
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge when spring temperatures exceed 55–65°F, attracted strongly by cucurbitacin bitter compounds in emerging cucurbit seedlings; females lay orange-yellow eggs in soil cracks at the stem base, producing root-feeding larvae and a mid-summer second adult generation.
distinguishing_features: Striped Cucumber Beetle has 3 sharp black stripes on a yellow back with a black head and black abdomen underside (unlike Western Corn Rootworm, which has blurred stripes and a yellow abdomen); Spotted Cucumber Beetle is yellow-green with 12 black spots (unlike beneficial Pink Spotted Lady Beetles, which are pink/reddish-orange with spots on the thorax too).
similar_conditions: Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles
risk_factors: Uncovered spring cucurbit seedlings, cultivars high in cucurbitacins, and bacterial wilt reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny spring days (>60°F) during seedling emergence and bloom.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded field borders and weedy garden debris, flying into cucurbit beds as soon as seedlings crack the soil.
management_actions: Keep cucurbit seedlings and transplants completely covered under floating row covers or insect netting sealed at the edges from the day of planting until female flowers open (then remove covers for bee pollination); hand-vacuum beetles out of open squash blossoms early in the morning; apply kaolin clay (Surround) particle film or botanical pyrethrin/spinosad/neem sprays in the evening when bees are not inside flowers (squash blossoms close by afternoon!).
prevention_actions: Transplant robust 3-to-4-week-old cucurbit starts rather than direct-seeding in high-pressure gardens; plant a perimeter trap crop of 'Blue Hubbard' squash (which has extreme cucurbitacin levels that lure 85–90% of cucumber beetles away from cucumbers and melons!); mulch with straw to encourage wolf spiders and ground beetles.

topic: Potato Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.

topic: Potato Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites Management
problem_name: Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites (Tomato Russet Mite, Broad Mite, and Cyclamen Mite)
causal_agent: Aculops lycopersici (Tomato Russet Mite), Polyphagotarsonemus latus (Broad Mite), and Phytonemus pallidus (Cyclamen Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.
symptom_keywords: greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem, upward-moving bronzed papery leaves without webbing, stunted brittle downward-cupped terminal pepper shoots, rosetted distorted strawberry crown leaves, corky russeted fruit
symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).
distinguishing_features: Tomato Russet Mite is distinguished from Spider Mites by the complete absence of silk webbing or individual stipple dots and the greasy bronze-tan sheen on the lower stem; Broad Mite injury on pepper/strawberry terminal shoots mimics viral mosaic or 2,4-D herbicide drift, except leaf veins do not show Parallel 'strapping' and a 20x lens reveals tiny football-shaped eggs studded with rows of white polka-dot tubercles!
similar_conditions: 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites)
risk_factors: Warm weather, infested greenhouse transplants or strawberry crowns, and broad-spectrum insecticide use.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.
transmission_or_spread: Crawl between touching plants, blow on wind, or hitchhike phoretically on the legs of whiteflies and aphids (Broad Mite!).

topic: Potato Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).

topic: Potato Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Potato Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)
causal_agent: Liriomyza sativae (Vegetable Leafminer), Liriomyza trifolii (American Serpentine Leafminer), and Pegomya hyoscyami (Spinach / Beet Leafminer)
affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering
risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.
management_actions: On Spinach, Swiss Chard, and Beets: flip leaves twice weekly to rub off the neat rows of chalk-white eggs on the underside BEFORE they hatch, and pinch/clip off any mined blotch leaves immediately (note: contact sprays like soapcannot reach maggots hidden inside the leaf epidermis, though spinosad and azadirachtin/neem have translaminar activity that penetrates into mines!); on Tomatoes, Beans, and Cucurbits, simply avoid broad-spectrum sprays so native Diglyphus parasitic wasps naturally suppress serpentine mines.
prevention_actions: Cover spinach, Swiss chard, and beet beds with floating row covers or fine insect netting from seeding through harvest (in beds rotated away from last year's chenopods); eradicate lambsquarters (Chenopodium album) weeds around the garden.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis) twice weekly during spring through autumn (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves to distinguish Leafminers from Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering.
severity_or_impact: High on spinach, Swiss chard, and beet greens (blotch mines ruin edible leaves); Low to Moderate on fruiting crops unless natural enemies are killed
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and mild-to-warm weather.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Spinach, Swiss chard, Beet, Amaranth, Lettuce, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Potato Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Potato Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

topic: Potato Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms Management
problem_name: Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms
causal_agent: Manduca quinquemaculata (Tomato Hornworm) and Manduca sexta (Tobacco Hornworm)
affected_plant_parts: Upper canopy leaves, tender stems, blossoms, and green fruits
growth_stage: Mid-season vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Mid-to-late summer
humidity_conditions: Warm summer nights favoring hawk/sphinx moth flight and egg laying
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Sudden, dramatic defoliation of upper stems where entire compound leaves—including midribs and petioles—are chewed away overnight leaving bare stripped stalks, plus large gouged cavities chewed into the sides of green tomatoes; large, dark greenish-black barrel-shaped pellets of droppings ('frass', resembling miniature hand grenades) litter the lower leaves and ground directly beneath the well-camouflaged, 3-to-4-inch-long bright-green caterpillar with white diagonal side stripes and a prominent rear dorsal horn.
symptom_keywords: stripped bare upper tomato stems, large 3-4 inch green caterpillar with rear horn, white V or slash stripes on sides, large dark barrel-shaped frass pellets on lower leaves, gouged green fruit
symptom_progression: Large gray hawk/sphinx moths ('hummingbird moths') hover at dusk to lay single round pearly-green eggs on leaf undersides; caterpillars feed for 3–4 weeks (consuming 90% of their total foliage intake during their final 5–7 days in the 5th instar!) before burrowing 4–6 inches into soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Tomato Hornworm has 8 white V-shaped chevrons pointing forward along each side and a black/dark-blue rear horn; Tobacco Hornworm has 7 white diagonal slash stripes edged in black and a curved bright-red rear horn. Look for dark barrel-shaped frass pellets on lower leaves to spot the camouflaged caterpillar directly above!
similar_conditions: Tomato Fruitworm / Corn Earworm (bores a deep hole at the stem end of fruit rather than stripping whole upper branches), Deer browsing (rips jagged stems without leaving insect frass pellets)
risk_factors: High nightshade density, no-till beds where overwintering brown 'jug-handled' pupae survive undisturbed in the soil, and absence of parasitic braconid wasps.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (70–85°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adult sphinx moths (Carolina sphinx and five-spotted hawkmoth) migrate and fly from dusk to dawn.
management_actions: Handpick caterpillars from plants (a UV blacklight flashlight at night makes hornworms glow bright neon green against dark purple tomato foliage for effortless spotting!); CRITICAL: if a hornworm has dozens of small white rice-grain-like cocoons sticking up on its back, DO NOT kill it—those are the pupae of the beneficial parasitic wasp Cotesia congregata, which will hatch to parasitize dozens more hornworms! For young small larvae, spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt) or spinosad.
prevention_actions: Till or hand-fork tomato/pepper beds in late autumn or early spring to expose and destroy the large (2-inch), mahogany-brown, 'pitcher-handled' overwintering pupae in the top 4–6 inches of soil; plant dill, fennel, and sweet alyssum to nourish parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (upper canopy leaves, tender stems, blossoms, and green fruits) twice weekly during mid-to-late summer (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for stripped bare upper tomato stems to distinguish Tomato and Tobacco Hornworms from Tomato Fruitworm / Corn Earworm (bores a deep hole at the stem end of fruit rather than stripping whole upper branches), Deer browsing (rips jagged stems without leaving insect frass pellets).
severity_or_impact: High (just 2 or 3 large 5th-instar hornworms can strip a mature tomato or pepper plant bare in days)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm summer nights favoring hawk/sphinx moth flight and egg laying.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato).

topic: Potato Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures) weekly during mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Aster Yellows from Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High on carrots, lettuce, and celery (infected roots and heads are bitter and inedible)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement.

topic: Potato Bacterial Wilt (Southern Bacterial Wilt) (Ralstonia solanacearum)

causal_agent: Ralstonia solanacearum
affected_plant_parts: Roots, xylem vascular system, stems, and potato tubers
growth_stage: Flowering and rapid fruit/tuber development
season: Hot, wet summer weather
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and warm wet soils
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Sudden, rapid wilting of the youngest upper leaves during the heat of the day, followed within 2–4 days by complete, irreversible collapse and death of the entire plant WHILE LEAVES REMAIN GREEN (no prior yellowing or leaf spotting); cutting the lower stem crosswise reveals dark brown water-soaked vascular tissue and greyish-white slimy bacterial ooze that streams out in milky threads when a cut stem section is suspended in a clear glass of water; in potato tubers, brown vascular ring rot and bacterial slime oozing from tuber eyes.
symptom_keywords: green wilt, sudden plant collapse without yellowing, bacterial streaming in water glass, slimy vascular ooze, brown tuber ring
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter roots through cultivation wounds or nematode feeding sites, rapidly multiplying and clogging xylem vessels with extracellular polysaccharide slime (EPS) so the green canopy wilts and dies in days.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Fusarium and Verticillium wilts by the rapid collapse of the entire plant while foliage is still bright green (without unilateral yellowing) and the positive 'water-glass bacterial streaming test' (milky white strands streaming from a cut stem suspended in clear water within 3–5 minutes).

risk_factors: Warm, wet, poorly drained soils, root-knot nematode feeding wounds, cultivating too deeply near roots, and planting in infested coastal/southern soils.
favorable_conditions: High soil temperatures (85–95°F) combined with high soil moisture.
transmission_or_spread: Persists for many years in deep soil layers, weed hosts, and infected seed potato tubers; spreads via contaminated soil, irrigation runoff, and root-to-root contact.
management_actions: Perform the clear-glass water streaming test to confirm; immediately uproot and bag infected plants; do not irrigate healthy beds with runoff from infested areas; clean soil from tools and boots.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g., 'Neptune', 'BHN 602', 'Hawai'i 7996') or graft heirloom tomatoes onto bacterial-wilt-resistant rootstocks ('RST-04-106', 'Maxifort', ' Armada'); control root-knot nematodes; rotate with non-host grasses/corn for 4+ years.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (roots, xylem vascular system, stems, and potato tubers) weekly during hot, wet summer weather (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Wilt (Southern Bacterial Wilt) from Fusarium Wilt, Verticillium Wilt, Southern Blight (white mycelium + sclerotia on outside of collar), Squash Vine Borer.
severity_or_impact: Critical (100% lethal to infected plants; extremely persistent in warm soils)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and warm wet soils.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Potato, Eggplant, Pepper, Banana).

topic: Potato Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato (Streptomyces scabies)
problem_name: Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato
causal_agent: Streptomyces scabies (Common Scab - filamentous bacterium) and Rhizoctonia solani (Black Scurf)
affected_plant_parts: Underground tubers, stolons, stems, and swollen storage roots
growth_stage: Tuber initiation and early bulking (first 3–5 weeks after stolon tips swell)
season: Warm, dry soil conditions during early summer tuber set
humidity_conditions: Dry soil during the 4-week window of tuber initiation (for Common Scab); cool wet spring soil (for Black Scurf)
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Common Scab: circular-to-irregular, rough, raised corky brown wart-like crusts ('russet/superficial scab') or sunken crater-like corky pits ('pitted scab') up to 1/4 inch deep on the skin of potato tubers, beets, radishes, and turnips (with normal healthy above-ground foliage!); Black Scurf: hard, irregular, coal-black crusty specks on the potato tuber skin resembling dried bits of soil that will NOT wash off ('the dirt that won't wash off'), plus reddish-brown sunken cankers on underground sprouts in spring.
symptom_keywords: rough corky scabs on potato skin, sunken corky tuber pits, black scurf specks that won't wash off, reddish-brown underground stem cankers
symptom_progression: Streptomyces invades young tubers exclusively through immature unsuberized lenticels during the first 3–5 weeks of tuberization when soil is dry and pH is above 5.5; tubers remain completely edible once peeled.
distinguishing_features: Common Scab forms tan-brown corky raised or pitted skin lesions; Black Scurf forms jet-black superficial sclerotia crusts that look like tar or dried dirt stuck to the skin.
similar_conditions: Powdery Scab (Spongospora subterranea - forms small volcano-like pustules in cool wet soil), Colorado Potato Beetle/Wireworm holes, Physiological Enlarged Lenticels (white puffy dots in wet soil)
risk_factors: Soil pH above 5.5–6.0 (liming or applying wood ashes before potatoes/beets), applying fresh animal manure, dry soil during early tuber set, and planting scabby seed tubers.
favorable_conditions: Soil pH 5.8–7.8 combined with dry soil during the 4 weeks following stolon tip swelling.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne actinomycete/fungus and tuber-borne on infected seed potatoes.
management_actions: Keep soil consistently moist (near field capacity) during the critical 4–6 week window of tuber initiation (starting when stolon tips begin to swell, just before bloom)—moisture encourages beneficial antagonistic bacteria on lenticels that block Streptomyces!
prevention_actions: Maintain potato soil pH between 5.0 and 5.5 (never apply lime, wood ash, or fresh manure before planting potatoes); plant only certified scab-free seed tubers and scab-resistant cultivars (such as 'Superior', 'Norland', 'Chieftain', 'Russet Burbank', 'Goldrush').

severity_or_impact: Moderate (strictly cosmetic skin blemish on peeled tubers, though deep pits increase peeling waste and reduce storage life)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–80°F (20–27°C) and dry soil during the 4-week window of tuber initiation (for common scab); cool wet spring soil (for black scurf).
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Potato, Beet, Radish, Turnip, Carrot, Parsnip).

topic: Potato Early Blight (Alternaria solani)
problem_name: Early Blight
causal_agent: Alternaria solani (and Alternaria tomatophila)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, stems (collar rot), petioles, and fruit/tubers at stem end
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting and tuber bulking
season: Warm, humid mid-to-late summer
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>90% RH), heavy morning dew, or alternating wet and dry periods
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Dark brown to black circular-to-angular necrotic lesions (1/4 to 1/2 inch) containing characteristic target-like concentric rings ('bull's-eye' pattern), surrounded by a diffuse yellow chlorotic halo on older lower leaves; sunken dark leathery stem lesions near soil line ('collar rot') and dark sunken concentric-ringed fruit lesions at the calyx stem attachment.
symptom_keywords: concentric rings, target spot, bull's-eye lesion, lower leaf yellowing, yellow halo, dark brown leaf spot, collar rot, sunken stem-end fruit rot
symptom_progression: Begins on oldest lower leaves nearest the soil; lesions enlarge and coalesce causing entire lower leaves to turn yellow, brown, and defoliate progressively upward up the canopy, exposing fruit to sunscald.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by conspicuous concentric rings ('target-board' appearance) inside dark brown lesions 1/4–1/2 inch wide, whereas Septoria leaf spot produces much smaller (1/16–1/8 inch) numerous spots with pale gray centers and tiny black pycnidia specks without target rings.
similar_conditions: Septoria Leaf Spot, Target Spot (Corynespora cassiicola), Bacterial Spot, Late Blight, Gray Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Overwintered solanaceous crop debris, crowded foliage, overhead irrigation, nitrogen or potassium deficiency weakening older leaves, and heavy fruit load.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–85°F) accompanied by rain, heavy dew, or overhead watering that keeps leaves wet for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Conidia spores survive in infected plant debris, soil, and volunteer solanaceous weeds, splashing onto lower leaves via rain or irrigation water and spreading upward by wind and wet handling.
management_actions: Prune and destroy infected lower leaves early; apply organic mulch (straw/shredded leaves) immediately after planting to block soil-splash of conidia; irrigate only at the soil line via drip; apply labeled protectant fungicides (copper, chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or Bacillus subtilis biofungicides) when weather favors infection.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3–4 year crop rotation away from all Solanaceae (tomato, potato, eggplant, pepper); stake or cage plants and space adequately for rapid canopy drying; use certified disease-free seed/transplants and tolerant cultivars (e.g., 'Mountain Magic', 'Defiant', 'Iron Lady'); remove all crop debris at season end.

severity_or_impact: High (causes severe premature defoliation, 30–50% yield loss, and secondary fruit sunscald)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–85°F (24–29°C) and high humidity (>90% rh), heavy morning dew, or alternating wet and dry periods.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Potato, Eggplant, Pepper).

topic: Potato Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
problem_name: Fusarium Wilt
causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum (host-specific formae speciales: f. sp. lycopersici, melongenae, tuberosi, niveum, melonis, cucumerinum, conglutinans, cepae, pisi, phaseoli, spinaciae, basilici, cubense)

growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding

symptom_keywords: one-sided yellowing, unilateral wilting, vascular browning, reddish-brown xylem ring, lower leaf yellowing, daytime wilting, stunted growth

distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).

transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.

topic: Potato Root-Knot Nematode Disease (Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla)
problem_name: Root-Knot Nematode Disease
causal_agent: Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla
affected_plant_parts: Root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting and root harvest
season: Warm growing season
temperature_range: 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla
humidity_conditions: Moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Above ground: patchy stunting, pale green-to-yellow chlorotic foliage resembling chronic nitrogen/micronutrient deficiency, premature wilting during warm sunny afternoons even when soil is moist, and poor fruit/pod yield; Below ground (diagnostic): uprooting the plant reveals swollen, beaded, irregular tumor-like root galls ('knots', 1/8 to 1 inch thick) that are an integral part of the root tissue itself, deformed forked/pimpled carrots and potatoes, and cracked sweet potatoes with a 'bearded' mass of stunted feeder roots.
symptom_keywords: swollen root galls, beaded knotted roots, afternoon wilting in moist soil, patchy stunting, forked galling on carrots, pimpled potato tubers
symptom_progression: Microscopic second-stage juveniles (J2) penetrate root tips and inject esophageal secretions that induce giant feeder cells and root galls, disrupting water and nutrient uptake and predisposing roots to Fusarium and Bacterial wilts.

similar_conditions: Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency
risk_factors: Warm sandy soils, continuous monoculture of susceptible vegetables (especially okra, tomato, cucurbits, carrot, bean), and introducing infested transplants or soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (75–90°F) in sandy loam soils.
transmission_or_spread: Microscopic soil-borne roundworms spread via infested transplants, seed tubers/slips, soil clinging to tools/shoes, and surface water runoff.
management_actions: Do not replant susceptible crops in galled spots; incorporate abundant organic compost right into beds to stimulate predatory soil fungi and microbes; solarize moist soil under clear UV plastic for 6–8 weeks in peak summer heat.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'N' or 'VFN' carrying the Mi-1 gene in tomato, 'Nemaguard'/'Guardian' rootstock in peach, 'Covington'/'Evangeline' in sweet potato, 'Charleston Belle' in pepper); rotate with non-host sweet corn, cereal rye, or French marigolds (Tagetes patula 'Single Gold'/'Nema-gone') planted as a solid cover crop.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots) weekly during warm growing season (75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Root-Knot Nematode Disease from Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla and moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils.

topic: Potato Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).
