topic: Potato Tobacco Mosaic Virus / Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV / ToMV) (Tobamovirus tabaci / Tobamovirus tomatotessellati)
problem_name: Tobacco Mosaic Virus / Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV / ToMV)
causal_agent: Tobamovirus tabaci / Tobamovirus tomatotessellati
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Seedling through fruiting
season: All growing seasons (including indoor seed starting and greenhouses)
humidity_conditions: Independent of humidity (spreads mechanically without water or insect vectors)
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Light-green and dark-green mosaic mottling across leaflets accompanied by leaf wrinkling, blistering, downward curling, and 'fern-leaf' / 'shoestring' distortion where leaflet blades narrow into ribbon-like strips; stunted overall plant growth; internal brown wall browning ('bronzing') and uneven blotchy yellow-red ripening on fruits.
symptom_keywords: light and dark green mosaic mottling, fern-leaf distortion, shoestring leaflets, leaf blistering, blotchy fruit ripening, internal fruit browning
symptom_progression: Enters through microscopic broken leaf hairs (trichomes) when plants are touched; systemic mosaic mottling and fern-leaf narrowing appear on newly expanding upper leaves 10–14 days after contact.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by alternating light/dark green mosaic islands on leaves, fern-like narrowing of young leaflets, and extreme stability on dry surfaces/hands (unlike CMV, TMV/ToMV is NOT transmitted by aphids but spreads rapidly via human hands and pruning tools).
similar_conditions: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV), Herbicide Drift (2,4-D/dicamba), Powdery Mildew, Physiological Blotchy Ripening
risk_factors: Handling tobacco products before touching plants, unsterilized pruning tools, contaminated seed coats, and reusing unwashed seedling trays or stakes.
favorable_conditions: Frequent hands-on pruning, tying, transplanting, and grafting operations.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely stable virus transmitted mechanically on workers' hands, clothing, pruning shears, and externally on contaminated seed coats; survives for years in dried plant debris and tobacco products.
management_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; wash hands thoroughly with soap and water and dip pruning tools in a 20% nonfat dry milk solution or 10% household bleach between plants; never smoke or handle tobacco near solanaceous plants.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (carrying Tm-2 or Tm-2^2 resistance genes in tomato and L genes in pepper); use certified virus-tested or trisodium-phosphate-treated seed; sanitize pots and stakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (leaves, stems, and fruits) weekly during all growing seasons (including indoor seed starting and greenhouses) (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tobacco Mosaic Virus / Tomato Mosaic Virus (TMV / ToMV) from Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV), Herbicide Drift (2,4-D/dicamba), Powdery Mildew, Physiological Blotchy Ripening.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (reduces yield by 20–40% and causes blotchy unmarketable fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and independent of humidity (spreads mechanically without water or insect vectors).
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato).

topic: Potato Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) (Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae)
problem_name: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV)
causal_agent: Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae (Tomato spotted wilt virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): Purpling, bronzing (metallic copper cast), and downward curling of young upper leaves accompanied by dark necrotic flecks or ringspots; dark brown necrotic streaks along petioles and terminal stems causing one-sided shoot tip dieback; on ripening tomato and pepper fruit, striking concentric yellow, orange, and green ringspots, marbled blotches, and raised bumps.
symptom_keywords: bronzing of upper leaves, concentric ringspots on fruit, necrotic stem streaks, terminal shoot dieback, stunted rosette, purple leaf veins
symptom_progression: Transmitted by adult thrips that acquired the virus as larvae; young terminal leaves bronze and develop necrotic specks, growth stunts severely, and fruits develop diagnostic target-like yellow/red ringspots.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by metallic bronzing and dark flecks on YOUNG upper leaves (unlike Early Blight on older lower leaves) and vivid yellow/orange concentric ringspots on ripening fruit.
similar_conditions: Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling
risk_factors: Abundant western flower thrips or tobacco thrips populations, nearby flowering weeds (chickweed, dandelion, spiny amaranth, buttercup) acting as virus reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather favoring thrips generation turnover and weed dry-down that drives thrips onto garden crops.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently and exclusively by thrips (especially Western flower thrips Frankliniella occidentalis and Tobacco thrips F. fusca); only larval thrips can acquire the virus by feeding on an infected plant, and emerging adults transmit it for life (not seed-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants so larval thrips cannot develop on them and spread virus to neighboring plants; use UV-reflective silver mulch to repel incoming adult thrips.
prevention_actions: Plant TSWV-resistant cultivars (carrying the Sw-5 gene in tomato, e.g., 'Amelia', 'Crista', 'Bella Rosa', 'Mountain Glory', or Tsw gene in pepper); eliminate winter/spring broadleaf weeds in a 30-ft perimeter around the garden BEFORE planting.
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits) weekly during late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) from Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling.
severity_or_impact: High (severely stunts plants and renders ringed fruit unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Lettuce, Spinach, Celery, Beans).

topic: Potato Verticillium Wilt (Verticillium dahliae)
problem_name: Verticillium Wilt
causal_agent: Verticillium dahliae (and Verticillium albo-atrum)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/tuber enlargement
season: Cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: Moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand
visible_symptoms: On Potato (Solanum tuberosum): V-shaped yellow chlorotic blotches developing at the margins and tips of older lower leaflets that soon turn brown and necrotic with a yellow halo; leaves wilt during the heat of the day (often affecting one side of a leaf or branch first); outer older leaves on strawberry crowns turn brown and collapse while inner leaves remain green initially; light tan-to-brown streaking is visible in the vascular tissue near the base of the stem.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesion on leaf margin, lower leaf wilting, light tan vascular streaking, outer crown collapse, stunting, midday flagging
symptom_progression: Microsclerotia germinate near root exudates, invade root cortex and xylem, and slowly plug water transport; plants become chronically stunted with progressive lower-leaf V-necrosis and reduced fruit size.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by characteristic V-shaped marginal yellow-and-brown fan lesions at leaflet tips, cooler temperature optimum (68–78°F vs 80–90°F for Fusarium wilt), and lighter tan vascular discoloration restricted closer to the lower stem.
similar_conditions: Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot
risk_factors: Planting susceptible crops (such as strawberry, raspberry, or eggplant) in soil where tomato, potato, pepper, or eggplant grew within the preceding 3–4 years; root-lesion nematode feeding.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild soil temperatures (68–78°F) in spring followed by warm summer transpiration stress.
transmission_or_spread: Survives in soil for 8–10+ years as microscopic dark resting bodies (microsclerotia) across a wide host range of >300 broadleaf crops and weeds (nightshades, lambsquarters, pigweed).
management_actions: Remove infected plants and roots; maintain even irrigation and balanced potassium nutrition to help moderately tolerant plants mature fruit; solarize infested garden beds under clear plastic for 6 weeks in midsummer.
prevention_actions: Plant Verticillium-resistant cultivars ('V' designation in tomatoes); NEVER plant strawberries, brambles, or eggplants where nightshade family crops grew in the past 4 years; rotate with non-host grasses, sweet corn, or brassicas (broccoli residue biofumigation reduces microsclerotia).
recommended_observations: Scout Potato (roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather (68–78°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Verticillium Wilt from Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes chronic stunting, defoliation, and plant death in highly susceptible hosts like eggplant, potato, and strawberry)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–78°F (20–25°C) and moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand.
host_range: Documented on Potato (Solanum tuberosum, Solanaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Eggplant, Potato, Pepper, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Watermelon).

topic: Cucumber Aphids Management
problem_name: Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids)
causal_agent: Myzus persicae (Green Peach Aphid), Aphis gossypii (Melon/Cotton Aphid), Macrosiphum euphorbiae (Potato Aphid), Acyrthosiphon pisum (Pea Aphid), Aphis fabae (Black Bean Aphid), and Brevicoryne brassicae (Cabbage Aphid)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and flowering
season: Spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer)
humidity_conditions: Moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants)
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew.
symptom_keywords: soft pear-shaped insects under leaves, curled puckered shoot tips, sticky shiny honeydew, black sooty mold, white cast skins, ants tending stems
symptom_progression: Winged females (alates) land on succulent new shoots and give live birth parthenogenetically to nymphs that mature in 7–10 days, building dense colonies and transmitting non-persistent plant viruses within seconds of probing.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present).
similar_conditions: Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves)
risk_factors: Over-fertilization with high soluble nitrogen (which creates lush amino-acid-rich sap that accelerates aphid reproduction), broad-spectrum pyrethroid/carbamate insecticide sprays that kill ladybugs and parasitic wasps, ant tending, and greenhouse/indoors transplant carryover.
favorable_conditions: Mild temperatures (65–80°F) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth.
transmission_or_spread: Winged alate aphids disperse on wind currents from overwintering weeds, woody hosts (Prunus, Euonymus), or neighboring crops; ants also move aphids between plants.
management_actions: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides.
prevention_actions: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.

topic: Cucumber Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.

severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.

topic: Cucumber Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites Management
problem_name: Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites (Tomato Russet Mite, Broad Mite, and Cyclamen Mite)
causal_agent: Aculops lycopersici (Tomato Russet Mite), Polyphagotarsonemus latus (Broad Mite), and Phytonemus pallidus (Cyclamen Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.
symptom_keywords: greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem, upward-moving bronzed papery leaves without webbing, stunted brittle downward-cupped terminal pepper shoots, rosetted distorted strawberry crown leaves, corky russeted fruit
symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).
distinguishing_features: Tomato Russet Mite is distinguished from Spider Mites by the complete absence of silk webbing or individual stipple dots and the greasy bronze-tan sheen on the lower stem; Broad Mite injury on pepper/strawberry terminal shoots mimics viral mosaic or 2,4-D herbicide drift, except leaf veins do not show Parallel 'strapping' and a 20x lens reveals tiny football-shaped eggs studded with rows of white polka-dot tubercles!
similar_conditions: 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites)
risk_factors: Warm weather, infested greenhouse transplants or strawberry crowns, and broad-spectrum insecticide use.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.
transmission_or_spread: Crawl between touching plants, blow on wind, or hitchhike phoretically on the legs of whiteflies and aphids (Broad Mite!).
management_actions: Apply wettable/micronized sulfur (highly effective against Eriophyid russet and broad mites, provided air temperature is below 85–90°F to avoid sulfur burn) or abamectin/horticultural oil early; rogue severely rosetted plants; clean and sanitize tomato stakes and cages at season's end.
prevention_actions: Purchase certified mite-free strawberry crowns and vegetable transplants; control whiteflies (which carry broad mites on their legs); rotate nightshades and destroy all volunteer solanaceous weeds (black nightshade, jimsonweed).
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (tomato russet mite) or newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (broad and cyclamen mites)) twice weekly during warm-to-hot summer weather (russet/broad mite) or cool humid spring/fall (cyclamen mite) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem to distinguish Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites from 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites).
severity_or_impact: High (often misdiagnosed as blight or virus until lower foliage is completely bronzed or terminal buds abort)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and high humidity inside dense crowns (broad/cyclamen mites) or warm dry summer weather (tomato russet mite).
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Strawberry, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon).

topic: Cucumber Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)
causal_agent: Liriomyza sativae (Vegetable Leafminer), Liriomyza trifolii (American Serpentine Leafminer), and Pegomya hyoscyami (Spinach / Beet Leafminer)
affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering
risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.
management_actions: On Spinach, Swiss Chard, and Beets: flip leaves twice weekly to rub off the neat rows of chalk-white eggs on the underside BEFORE they hatch, and pinch/clip off any mined blotch leaves immediately (note: contact sprays like soapcannot reach maggots hidden inside the leaf epidermis, though spinosad and azadirachtin/neem have translaminar activity that penetrates into mines!); on Tomatoes, Beans, and Cucurbits, simply avoid broad-spectrum sprays so native Diglyphus parasitic wasps naturally suppress serpentine mines.
prevention_actions: Cover spinach, Swiss chard, and beet beds with floating row covers or fine insect netting from seeding through harvest (in beds rotated away from last year's chenopods); eradicate lambsquarters (Chenopodium album) weeds around the garden.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis) twice weekly during spring through autumn (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves to distinguish Leafminers from Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering.
severity_or_impact: High on spinach, Swiss chard, and beet greens (blotch mines ruin edible leaves); Low to Moderate on fruiting crops unless natural enemies are killed
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and mild-to-warm weather.
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Spinach, Swiss chard, Beet, Amaranth, Lettuce, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Cucumber Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).

topic: Cucumber Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.

topic: Cucumber Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Cucumber Squash Bug Management
problem_name: Squash Bug
causal_agent: Anasa tristis
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves, petioles, crown stems, and ripening winter squash/pumpkin rinds
growth_stage: Vine runner stage through late-summer fruit maturation
season: Late spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather and mulched/board-covered soil surfaces
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Large (5/8 inch / 16 mm), flat-backed, dark grayish-brown, shield-shaped adults (which emit a foul odor when crushed and scurry rapidly sideways under leaves or stems when approached) and teardrop-shaped spider-like nymphs with pale gray/green bodies and black legs; females lay diagnostic neat, geometric V-shaped clusters of 15–40 shiny, bronze-to-coppery-brown, football-shaped eggs glued tightly to the undersides of leaves in the V-angles between major veins; piercing-sucking feeding injects toxic saliva that causes yellow spots on leaves that turn dark brown and crisp, wilting whole runners ('Anasa wilt') and scarring winter squash and pumpkin rinds.
symptom_keywords: neat geometric clusters of shiny bronze-copper eggs in leaf vein angles, flat brownish-gray shield-shaped bug, gray teardrop nymphs with black legs, crisp brown scorched squash leaves, Anasa wilt of runners
symptom_progression: Unmated/mated adults overwinter under garden debris, boards, stones, and compost piles, flying to squash/pumpkin vines in late spring to lay bronze egg clusters; nymphs feed in dense aggregations for 4–6 weeks.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the neat clusters of 15–40 metallic bronze/copper-colored oval eggs arranged in V-angles between veins on the underside of squash and pumpkin leaves (unlike Ladybug eggs, which are bright yellow-orange spindles standing upright on end in tight clusters).
similar_conditions: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug (wider rounded shield shape, lays barrel-shaped white/green eggs), Beneficial Assassin Bugs (narrow head and curved beak), Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Winter squash and pumpkins (especially Hubbard, kabocha, acorn, and jack-o'-lantern pumpkins), overwintering vine debris, and thick dry mulch or wooden boards near beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in sheltered garden margins, woodpiles, and vine trash, flying into cucurbit beds in late spring.
management_actions: SCOUT AND CRUSH EGG CLUSTERS TWICE WEEKLY: flip squash/pumpkin leaves over and crush or scrape off the bronze egg clusters (or press a loop of duct tape onto the leaf underside to peel off the eggs without tearing the leaf!); lay a wooden board or shingle on the soil next to squash crowns at night—squash bugs congregate underneath by dawn, allowing you to flip the board each morning and crush them; spray insecticidal soap or neem oil ONLY against newly hatched young nymphs (hard-shelled adults are impervious to soaps!).
prevention_actions: Clean up and destroy all cucurbit vines and cull fruits immediately after autumn harvest; trellis vining squash and cucumbers off the ground; grow resistant cultivars ('Butternut', 'Royal Acorn', 'Sweet Cheese').
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (undersides of leaves, petioles, crown stems, and ripening winter squash/pumpkin rinds) twice weekly during late spring through autumn (70–92°F (21–33°C)); inspect for neat geometric clusters of shiny bronze-copper eggs in leaf vein angles to distinguish Squash Bug from Brown Marmorated Stink Bug (wider rounded shield shape, lays barrel-shaped white/green eggs), Beneficial Assassin Bugs (narrow head and curved beak), Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High on pumpkins, winter squash, and zucchini (can wilt and kill mature vines in mid-to-late summer)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, dry summer weather and mulched/board-covered soil surfaces.
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Bottle gourd).

topic: Cucumber Squash Vine Borer and Pickleworm Management
problem_name: Squash Vine Borer and Pickleworm
causal_agent: Melittia cucurbitae (Squash Vine Borer) and Diaphania nitidalis (Pickleworm)
affected_plant_parts: Hollow basal vine stems/crowns near the soil line (Squash Vine Borer) and blossoms/developing fruits (Pickleworm)
growth_stage: Runner elongation and early flowering through harvest
season: Mid-June through August (Squash Vine Borer); mid-to-late summer in warm regions (Pickleworm)
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer days
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Squash Vine Borer: a healthy, vigorous zucchini, summer squash, or pumpkin plant suddenly wilts catastrophically during midday heat and eventually collapses; close inspection of the basal 6–12 inches of the hollow stem near the soil line reveals longitudinal holes oozing wet, coarse, yellowish-green sawdust-like frass ('apple-sauce' mush), and slicing the stem lengthwise exposes 1 to 6 fat, wrinkled, creamy-white grub-like caterpillars (1 inch long) with brown heads hollowing out the vascular stem; Pickleworm: small greenish caterpillars (spotted when young, coppery-green when mature) bore clean circular entry holes into flower buds and developing cucumber, cantaloupe, and squash fruits, pushing wet frass out the hole and souring the fruit.
symptom_keywords: sudden wilting of whole zucchini or pumpkin vine, wet yellow-green sawdust frass oozing from base of stem, fat white caterpillar with brown head inside hollow vine, day-flying red-and-black wasp-mimic moth, circular bore holes in squash blossoms and fruit
symptom_progression: Day-flying clearwing moths (which look and buzz remarkably like red-and-black paper wasps with metallic-green forewings and hairy orange hind legs!) emerge from soil pupae in early summer and glue flat, oval, reddish-brown eggs singly near the base of squash stems; hatching larvae bore into the stem within hours.
distinguishing_features: Squash Vine Borer is distinguished from Bacterial Wilt and Fusarium Crown Rot by the piles of coarse, wet, yellow-green sawdust frass pushed out of holes near the base of the stem and the fat white brown-headed caterpillar inside.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Wilt (sticky white bacterial strands when stem is cut, spread by cucumber beetles, no sawdust frass), Squash Bug Wilting, Fusarium Crown Rot
risk_factors: Growing highly susceptible Cucurbita pepo (zucchini, yellow crookneck/straightneck, acorn squash, jack-o'-lantern pumpkin) and Cucurbita maxima (Hubbard, kabocha, giant pumpkin) without stem protection in regions east of the Rocky Mountains.
favorable_conditions: Warm early-to-mid summer days (starting around 900–1,000 growing degree days base 50°F, often when chicory blooms).
transmission_or_spread: Squash Vine Borer overwinters in the garden soil as a dark cocoon 1–2 inches deep; adult clearwing moths fly during the daytime in June/July.
management_actions: EMERGENCY VINE SURGERY: as soon as you see yellow sawdust frass at a stem hole, use a clean razor blade to slit the stem lengthwise (parallel to the vascular bundles, never across!) through the hole, puncture/remove the white borer larva, and immediately mound moist soil 3–4 inches deep over the slit stem and along runner nodes to stimulate auxiliary rooting; apply Bt kurstaki or spinosad to the lower stems weekly during June–July egg-laying (or inject liquid Bt directly into the hollow base of the stem with a syringe!).
prevention_actions: PLANT RESISTANT SPECIES: Cucurbita moschata ('Waltham Butternut' winter squash and 'Tromboncino' rampicante summer zucchini!) have solid, tough, thin stems that are naturally highly resistant to Squash Vine Borer! Wrap the bottom 6 inches of young bush zucchini stems with aluminum foil or nylon stocking barriers, or keep plants under row covers until female flowers open.

severity_or_impact: Critical on zucchini, summer squash, and pumpkins east of the Rockies (kills entire vines right as they begin fruiting)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, sunny summer days.

topic: Cucumber Stink Bugs Management

causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)

growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.

symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.

risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.
management_actions: Handpick adults, nymphs, and barrel-shaped egg clusters in the cool early morning by knocking them into a bucket of soapy water; cover high-value tomato, pepper, bean, and brassica beds with fine insect netting; vacuum Harlequin bugs off kale/collards.

topic: Cucumber Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Cucumber Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).
severity_or_impact: High (causes direct sap depletion, sooty mold, Squash Silverleaf, irregular tomato ripening, and transmits Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus and Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Cucumber Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Fertile, warm, well-drained sandy loam or loam amended with aged compost (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a fertile, warm, well-drained sandy loam or loam amended with aged compost adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Cucumber to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Prefers fertile, warm, well-drained sandy loam or loam amended with aged compost with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Cucumber Angular Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans)
problem_name: Angular Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans (Cucurbits) and Xanthomonas fragariae (Strawberry)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, petioles, stems, blossoms, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through fruiting
season: Cool-to-warm, rainy, windy spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, driving rain, overhead irrigation, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Small, water-soaked, translucent angular spots on leaves strictly bounded by fine leaf veins; under humid mornings, glistening milky-white droplets of bacterial exudate ooze from the lower surface of the lesions and dry into a thin, shiny, white crust or film; on cucurbits, tan necrotic spot centers soon dry out, tear, and fall away, leaving ragged angular 'shot-holes'; on cucumber/squash fruits, small circular water-soaked spots turn chalky white and crack, allowing soft-rot bacteria inside.
symptom_keywords: vein-bounded water-soaked angular spots, shiny white dried bacterial film on leaf underside, ragged angular shot-holes, chalky cracked fruit spots
symptom_progression: Seed- or debris-borne bacteria splash onto leaves; lesions expand up to vein boundaries, dry, and drop out as ragged holes while fruit lesions open pathways for belly/soft rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Cucurbit Downy Mildew by the shiny white dried bacterial crust on the underside of lesions (rather than purplish-gray fuzzy sporangia) and by the dry centers dropping out to leave ragged angular holes.
similar_conditions: Downy Mildew (yellow angular spots with purplish-gray fuzz underneath, no shot-holes or white crust), Anthracnose, Belly Rot
risk_factors: Contaminated seed, overhead sprinklers, working in cucumber or strawberry beds when foliage is wet, and short crop rotations.
favorable_conditions: Rainy weather at 68–80°F with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne (cucurbits) or crown-borne on nursery transplants (strawberry); spread rapidly down rows by splashing rain, sprinklers, hands, and harvest containers.
management_actions: Never cultivate, weed, or harvest cucumbers, squash, or strawberries when leaves are wet; switch to drip irrigation; apply fixed copper sprays early if bacterial spotting starts.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed and angular-leaf-spot-resistant cucumber hybrids; rotate cucurbits out of affected beds for 2–3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (leaves, petioles, stems, blossoms, and fruit surfaces) weekly during cool-to-warm, rainy, windy spring and early summer weather (65–82°F (18–28°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Angular Leaf Spot from Downy Mildew (yellow angular spots with purplish-gray fuzz underneath, no shot-holes or white crust), Anthracnose, Belly Rot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (defoliates vines and predisposes cucumber fruits to soft rot)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–82°F (18–28°C) and high humidity, driving rain, overhead irrigation, or heavy dew.
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cucumber, Zucchini, Squash, Pumpkin, Melon, Watermelon, Strawberry).

topic: Cucumber Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.)
problem_name: Anthracnose
causal_agent: Colletotrichum spp. (C. coccodes on Solanaceae; C. orbiculare on Cucurbits; C. lindemuthianum on Beans; C. acutatum / C. gloeosporioides on Fruits)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening and immature fruits, pods, leaves, petioles, and stems/canes
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit/pod maturation and post-harvest ripening
season: Warm, wet, humid summer weather

topic: Cucumber Bacterial Wilt of Cucurbits (Erwinia tracheiphila)
problem_name: Bacterial Wilt of Cucurbits
causal_agent: Erwinia tracheiphila
affected_plant_parts: Xylem vascular system, leaves, and individual vine runners
growth_stage: Cotyledon seedling stage through flowering and fruiting
season: Late spring and summer when cucumber beetles feed
humidity_conditions: Independent of rain (driven by cucumber beetle feeding activity)
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Dull-green limp wilting of single leaves with cucumber beetle feeding scars, rapidly followed by wilting of an entire individual vine runner while other runners appear temporarily healthy, and within 7–14 days complete collapse and death of the whole vine (note: Watermelon is genetically immune/resistant to Erwinia tracheiphila!); slicing a wilted stem near the crown, pressing the two cut ends together, and slowly pulling them apart sometimes draws fine, sticky, viscid white bacterial strands ('string test') or reveals creamy bacterial droplets on the cut xylem.

symptom_progression: Bacteria excreted in striped and spotted cucumber beetle frass enter open leaf/stem feeding or floral nectary wounds, multiply in xylem vessels, and plug water transport with bacterial gums until the vine wilts irreversibly.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by starting on individual leaves/runners with visible striped or spotted cucumber beetle chewing holes, the positive 'viscid string test' (or microscopic streaming in water), and the fact that watermelon is unaffected.
similar_conditions: Squash Vine Borer (shows sawdust-like yellow frass at base of squash/pumpkin stems), Fusarium Wilt (yellowing + brown vascular ring), Phytophthora Blight
risk_factors: Early-season feeding by striped (Acalymma vittatum) and spotted (Diabrotica undecimpunctata) cucumber beetles, especially between cotyledon emergence and flowering.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather (70–85°F) promoting heavy cucumber beetle emergence and feeding.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters inside the digestive tract of adult striped and spotted cucumber beetles and is transmitted exclusively via beetle feeding wounds and frass.
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy wilted vines so cucumber beetles cannot feed on them and spread bacteria to healthy plants; there is no cure once a plant is systemically infected.

topic: Cucumber Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot

affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.

topic: Cucumber Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury
risk_factors: Abundant perennial weeds (pokeweed, milkweed, chickweed, white cockle, nightshade, bindweed) harboring CMV near the garden and migrating winged aphids.
favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored non-persistently (stylet-borne) by >80 species of aphids (especially Green peach aphid Myzus persicae and Melon aphid Aphis gossypii); aphids acquire and transmit the virus in just 10–60 seconds of test probing (so insecticides cannot kill aphids fast enough to prevent transmission!).
management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits) weekly during late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) from Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stunting and deformed, warty, unmarketable fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal.
host_range: Documented on Cucumber (Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cucumber, Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Melon, Watermelon, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Cucumber Cucurbit Mosaic Viruses (ZYMV, WMV, SqMV) (Zucchini yellow mosaic virus)
problem_name: Cucurbit Mosaic Viruses (ZYMV, WMV, SqMV)
causal_agent: Zucchini yellow mosaic virus (ZYMV), Watermelon mosaic virus (WMV), and Squash mosaic virus (SqMV)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, vines, blossoms, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative runner growth through fruiting
season: Mid-to-late summer when winged aphids and cucumber beetles peak
humidity_conditions: Warm weather accelerating aphid flights and beetle feeding

symptom_keywords: warty bumpy mottled squash fruit, green-and-yellow color breaking on fruit, blistered mosaic vine leaves, shoestring fern-leaf distortion, stunted runners
symptom_progression: Winged aphids transmit ZYMV and WMV within 15–60 seconds of probing a leaf (while cucumber beetles transmit SqMV and SqMV can also be seed-borne); symptoms appear on all newly formed leaves and fruits within 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the dramatic green-and-yellow mosaic color-breaking and knobby wart-like bumps on developing squash, pumpkins, and cucumbers (note: silvery-white uniform leaf sheen alone without fruit bumps or mosaic distortion is either genetic variegation in zucchini or Squash Silverleaf from whiteflies, NOT a mosaic virus).
similar_conditions: Squash Silverleaf (uniform silver upper leaf surface from whiteflies), Genetic Silver Mottling along zucchini veins (normal trait), Herbicide Drift
risk_factors: Late-planted summer squash/pumpkins exposed to summer aphid flights, high cucumber beetle numbers, and weedy borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer weather with active transient winged aphids.
transmission_or_spread: ZYMV and WMV are transmitted non-persistently by >20 species of winged aphids; SqMV is seed-borne in melons/squash and transmitted by spotted and striped cucumber beetles.

topic: Cucumber Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot (Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani)
problem_name: Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot
causal_agent: Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani
affected_plant_parts: Germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line
growth_stage: Seed germination and cotyledon-to-first-true-leaf seedling stage
season: Early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil
humidity_conditions: Overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds
visible_symptoms: On Cucumber (Cucumis sativus): Pre-emergence damping-off: seeds turn soft, mushy, and brown and fail to emerge, leaving patchy gaps in rows; Post-emergence damping-off: healthy-looking cotyledon seedlings suddenly develop a water-soaked, pinched, thread-like brown or black constriction at the stem base right at the soil line ('wirestem' in brassicas when caused by Rhizoctonia) and topple over flat onto the soil while leaves are still green.
symptom_keywords: seedlings falling over at soil line, pinched thread-like stem base, wirestem, patchy seed emergence, mushy rotted seeds, water-soaked hypocotyl
symptom_progression: Soil-borne oomycetes and fungi attack slow-germinating seeds and tender unlignified hypocotyl tissue in wet soil, rotting the stem cortex within 24–48 hours so seedlings collapse.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the pinched, water-soaked or wiry brown constriction strictly at the soil line on young seedlings (whereas Cutworms completely sever the stem cleanly and Heat/Sunburn bleaches the stem white).
similar_conditions: Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling
risk_factors: Reusing unsterilized garden soil or dirty flats for indoor seed starting, overwatering, sowing too deeply or densely, cold soil temperatures delaying emergence, and poor airflow.
favorable_conditions: Cold, wet, poorly aerated soil or potting media with high seedling density and stagnant air.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oospores and sclerotia native to garden soils, splashed or carried on dirty pots, tools, and untreated seed.
management_actions: Discard damped-off seedling cells/trays immediately; allow the surface of seed-starting media to dry slightly between bottom-waterings; provide a gentle oscillating fan and heat mat (70–75°F) for indoor seedlings.
prevention_actions: Always use sterile, soilless seed-starting mix in clean sanitized trays (washed in 10% bleach); do not sow outdoors until soil reaches the crop's minimum germination temperature; sow at proper depth and thin promptly.
recommended_observations: Scout Cucumber (germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line) weekly during early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil (50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot from Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling.
severity_or_impact: High at seedling stage (can wipe out 50–100% of a seed tray or direct-sown row)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia and overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds.

topic: Cucumber Downy Mildew (Pseudoperonospora cubensis)
problem_name: Downy Mildew
causal_agent: Pseudoperonospora cubensis (Cucurbits); Peronospora destructor (Alliums); Peronospora farinosa f. sp. spinaciae (Spinach); Bremia lactucae (Lettuce); Hyaloperonospora brassicae (Brassicas); Peronospora belbahrii (Basil); Peronospora viciae (Peas); Plasmopara viticola (Grape)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves (upper chlorotic lesions and lower sporangiophore growth); shoots and young clusters in grape
growth_stage: Vegetative rosette/vine growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-warm, wet, humid, overcast weather with heavy morning dew
temperature_range: 58–75°F (14–24°C) (up to 82°F for cucurbit and basil downy mildew)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>85–95% RH) and minimum 4–6 hours of free leaf wetness from dew, fog, or rain
