topic: Beans Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm Management
problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin.
symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.
distinguishing_features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters).
similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.
prevention_actions: Plant early-maturing sweet corn cultivars as early in spring as soil temperature allows to harvest before peak late-summer moth flights; select sweet corn hybrids with tight, long husk extensions beyond the ear tip; encourage Trichogramma egg-parasitoid wasps and Orius minute pirate bugs (which eat earworm eggs on silks).
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear to distinguish Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm from European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm.
severity_or_impact: High (the #1 insect pest of sweet corn and a destructive borer in tomatoes, peppers, beans, and okra)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm weather and southerly summer wind currents.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea).

topic: Beans Cucumber Beetles Management
problem_name: Cucumber Beetles (Striped and Spotted Cucumber Beetles)
causal_agent: Acalymma vittatum (Striped Cucumber Beetle) and Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi (Spotted Cucumber Beetle / Southern Corn Rootworm)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence through flowering and fruiting
season: Spring transplant/emergence through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oblong bright-yellow-green beetles with either three jet-black longitudinal stripes down the wing covers (Striped Cucumber Beetle) or twelve black spots (Spotted Cucumber Beetle); overwintered adults swarm emerging cucurbit cotyledons and young transplants in spring, chewing ragged holes through leaves, girdling tender stems, congregating inside open yellow cucurbit blossoms (chewing anthers/pistils and reducing fruit set), scarring the underside and rind of melons/pumpkins, and transmitting the fatal bacterium Erwinia tracheiphila (Bacterial Wilt); white brown-headed larvae feed underground on cucurbit, corn, and bean roots.
symptom_keywords: yellow beetle with three black stripes, yellow-green beetle with twelve black spots, chewed cucurbit cotyledons and stems, beetles packed inside squash blossoms, scarred pumpkin rinds, sudden bacterial wilt
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge when spring temperatures exceed 55–65°F, attracted strongly by cucurbitacin bitter compounds in emerging cucurbit seedlings; females lay orange-yellow eggs in soil cracks at the stem base, producing root-feeding larvae and a mid-summer second adult generation.
distinguishing_features: Striped Cucumber Beetle has 3 sharp black stripes on a yellow back with a black head and black abdomen underside (unlike Western Corn Rootworm, which has blurred stripes and a yellow abdomen); Spotted Cucumber Beetle is yellow-green with 12 black spots (unlike beneficial Pink Spotted Lady Beetles, which are pink/reddish-orange with spots on the thorax too).
similar_conditions: Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles
risk_factors: Uncovered spring cucurbit seedlings, cultivars high in cucurbitacins, and bacterial wilt reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny spring days (>60°F) during seedling emergence and bloom.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded field borders and weedy garden debris, flying into cucurbit beds as soon as seedlings crack the soil.
management_actions: Keep cucurbit seedlings and transplants completely covered under floating row covers or insect netting sealed at the edges from the day of planting until female flowers open (then remove covers for bee pollination); hand-vacuum beetles out of open squash blossoms early in the morning; apply kaolin clay (Surround) particle film or botanical pyrethrin/spinosad/neem sprays in the evening when bees are not inside flowers (squash blossoms close by afternoon!).
prevention_actions: Transplant robust 3-to-4-week-old cucurbit starts rather than direct-seeding in high-pressure gardens; plant a perimeter trap crop of 'Blue Hubbard' squash (which has extreme cucurbitacin levels that lure 85–90% of cucumber beetles away from cucumbers and melons!); mulch with straw to encourage wolf spiders and ground beetles.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds) twice weekly during spring transplant/emergence through autumn (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for yellow beetle with three black stripes to distinguish Cucumber Beetles from Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles.

topic: Beans Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.

topic: Beans Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites Management
problem_name: Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites (Tomato Russet Mite, Broad Mite, and Cyclamen Mite)
causal_agent: Aculops lycopersici (Tomato Russet Mite), Polyphagotarsonemus latus (Broad Mite), and Phytonemus pallidus (Cyclamen Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.
symptom_keywords: greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem, upward-moving bronzed papery leaves without webbing, stunted brittle downward-cupped terminal pepper shoots, rosetted distorted strawberry crown leaves, corky russeted fruit
symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).
distinguishing_features: Tomato Russet Mite is distinguished from Spider Mites by the complete absence of silk webbing or individual stipple dots and the greasy bronze-tan sheen on the lower stem; Broad Mite injury on pepper/strawberry terminal shoots mimics viral mosaic or 2,4-D herbicide drift, except leaf veins do not show Parallel 'strapping' and a 20x lens reveals tiny football-shaped eggs studded with rows of white polka-dot tubercles!
similar_conditions: 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites)
risk_factors: Warm weather, infested greenhouse transplants or strawberry crowns, and broad-spectrum insecticide use.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.
transmission_or_spread: Crawl between touching plants, blow on wind, or hitchhike phoretically on the legs of whiteflies and aphids (Broad Mite!).
management_actions: Apply wettable/micronized sulfur (highly effective against Eriophyid russet and broad mites, provided air temperature is below 85–90°F to avoid sulfur burn) or abamectin/horticultural oil early; rogue severely rosetted plants; clean and sanitize tomato stakes and cages at season's end.
prevention_actions: Purchase certified mite-free strawberry crowns and vegetable transplants; control whiteflies (which carry broad mites on their legs); rotate nightshades and destroy all volunteer solanaceous weeds (black nightshade, jimsonweed).

severity_or_impact: High (often misdiagnosed as blight or virus until lower foliage is completely bronzed or terminal buds abort)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and high humidity inside dense crowns (broad/cyclamen mites) or warm dry summer weather (tomato russet mite).
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Strawberry, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon).

topic: Beans Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Beans Mexican Bean Beetle, Bean Leaf Beetle, Cowpea Curculio, and Pea Weevil Management
problem_name: Mexican Bean Beetle, Bean Leaf Beetle, Cowpea Curculio, and Pea Weevil
causal_agent: Epilachna varivestis (Mexican Bean Beetle), Cerotoma trifurcata (Bean Leaf Beetle), Chalcodermus aeneus (Cowpea Curculio), and Bruchus pisorum (Pea Weevil)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of trifoliate leaves, stems, flowers, green pods, and maturing seeds
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through pod fill and seed maturation
season: Late spring through summer
humidity_conditions: Moderate-to-high humidity (Mexican Bean Beetle thrives in humid mid-Atlantic/Appalachian/irrigated gardens; hot dry weather above 95°F kills its eggs and larvae)
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Mexican Bean Beetle (actually a plant-eating member of the Ladybird Beetle family!): coppery-brown to bronze dome-shaped adults (1/4 inch) with 16 small black spots arranged in 3 rows across the wing covers, and oval, bright canary-yellow larvae covered in 6 rows of long, branched, black-tipped spines ('fuzzy yellow hedgehogs') that feed on the undersides of bean leaves, scraping away lower tissue between veins to leave a delicate, lace-like skeletonized network ('windowpane lacework') that dries brown; Bean Leaf Beetle: small (1/5 inch) yellow, tan, or red beetles with a diagnostic black triangle right behind the thorax and 4 rectangular black spots that chew round holes in seedling leaves and scar pods; Cowpea Curculio & Pea Weevil: small (1/5 inch) black/brown snout weevils that puncture green pods to lay eggs inside swelling cowpeas or peas, leaving dark blister-like stings on the pod and a white C-shaped legless grub inside each seed.
symptom_keywords: lacy skeletonized bean leaves with intact vein network, fuzzy yellow spiny larvae under bean leaves, coppery-brown ladybug-like beetle with 16 black spots, beetle with black triangle behind neck chewing round holes in bean leaves, blister stings on cowpea pods with white grub inside seed
symptom_progression: Overwintered beetles colonize emerging bean/pea rows in spring; Mexican Bean Beetles lay clusters of 40–60 yellow upright eggs on leaf undersides, and spiny yellow larvae skeletonize foliage for 2–3 weeks before pupating into orange pupae glued by their tails to lower leaves.
distinguishing_features: Mexican Bean Beetle is easily distinguished from beneficial Lady Beetles because: (1) its thorax is plain bronze without white-and-black eye markings, (2) it has 16 small uniform black dots in 3 neat rows on a coppery shell, and (3) its larvae are bright yellow and covered in branched spines (whereas beneficial ladybug larvae are alligator-shaped black-and-orange predators!).
similar_conditions: Beneficial Lady Beetles (red/orange with white markings on black thorax and alligator-like black-and-orange larvae), Japanese Beetle (metallic green head with coppery wings feeding on upper leaf surface)
risk_factors: Successive plantings of bush, pole, and lima beans without break, dense humid foliage, and proximity to overwintering wooded leaf litter.
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid summer weather (70–85°F).
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in woody leaf litter and garden debris, flying to bean and pea rows in spring.
management_actions: Handpick coppery adults, spiny yellow larvae, and yellow egg clusters from the undersides of bean leaves; release the tiny parasitic wasp Pediobius foveolatus (which parasitizes Mexican Bean Beetle larvae, turning them into dark brown papery shells!); spray spinosad, neem oil, or pyrethrin on leaf undersides if skeletonization exceeds 20%; promptly pull and compost bush bean plants as soon as their main harvest finishes.
prevention_actions: Plant an early spring crop of bush snap beans (which often matures before Mexican Bean Beetle populations peak in mid-summer); rotate cowpeas and peas away from last year's legume beds and store dried peas/beans in sealed containers (freezing dried culinary seeds at 0°F for 4 days kills any internal bruchid seed weevils).
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (undersides of trifoliate leaves, stems, flowers, green pods, and maturing seeds) twice weekly during late spring through summer (68–88°F (20–31°C)); inspect for lacy skeletonized bean leaves with intact vein network to distinguish Mexican Bean Beetle, Bean Leaf Beetle, Cowpea Curculio, and Pea Weevil from Beneficial Lady Beetles (red/orange with white markings on black thorax and alligator-like black-and-orange larvae), Japanese Beetle (metallic green head with coppery wings feeding on upper leaf surface).
severity_or_impact: High on snap beans, lima beans, soybeans, cowpeas, and field/garden peas
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–88°F (20–31°C) and moderate-to-high humidity (mexican bean beetle thrives in humid mid-atlantic/appalachian/irrigated gardens; hot dry weather above 95°f kills its eggs and larvae).
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea, Lentil, Chickpea).
knowledge_text: Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) Mexican Bean Beetle, Bean Leaf Beetle, Cowpea Curculio, and Pea Weevil is a chewing beetle pest of legumes caused by Epilachna varivestis (Mexican Bean Beetle), Cerotoma trifurcata (Bean Leaf Beetle), Chalcodermus aeneus (Cowpea Curculio), and Bruchus pisorum (Pea Weevil). Plant an early spring crop of bush snap beans (which often matures before Mexican Bean Beetle populations peak in mid-summer); rotate cowpeas and peas away from last year's legume beds and store dried peas/beans in sealed containers (freezing dried culinary seeds at 0°F for 4 days kills any internal bruchid seed weevils).

topic: Beans Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Beans Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes) twice weekly during cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights (45–75°F (7–24°C)); inspect for ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries to distinguish Slugs and Garden Snails from Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime).
severity_or_impact: High in cool, wet climates and on seedlings, lettuce, brassicas, and strawberries
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–75°F (7–24°C) and high humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Lettuce, Spinach, Swiss chard, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy).

topic: Beans Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Beans Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Beans Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)

season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather

topic: Beans Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs Management
problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests
causal_agent: Cylas formicarius (Sweetpotato Weevil), Conoderus / Melanotus / Limonius spp. (Wireworms - Click Beetle larvae), and Phyllophaga / Popillia / Cyclocephala spp. (White Grubs - Scarab Beetle larvae)
affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod).
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet potato, Potato, Carrot, Beet, Radish, Turnip, Parsnip, Onion).

topic: Beans Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed.

topic: Beans Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Beans Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus (Potyvirus phaseovulgaris)
problem_name: Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus
causal_agent: Potyvirus phaseovulgaris (Bean common mosaic virus - BCMV) and Bean yellow mosaic virus (BYMV)

growth_stage: Seedling emergence through pod fill
season: Warm late spring and summer seasons

topic: Beans Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury

favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored non-persistently (stylet-borne) by >80 species of aphids (especially Green peach aphid Myzus persicae and Melon aphid Aphis gossypii); aphids acquire and transmit the virus in just 10–60 seconds of test probing (so insecticides cannot kill aphids fast enough to prevent transmission!).
management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.

host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cucumber, Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Melon, Watermelon, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Beans Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)

topic: Beans Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').

symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits) weekly during cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) from Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight.
severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, brambles, grapes, and high-tunnel tomatoes (major pre- and post-harvest fruit loss)

problem_name: Halo Blight and Common Bacterial Blight of Beans
causal_agent: Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. phaseolicola (Halo Blight) and Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. phaseoli (Common Bacterial Blight)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, stems, pods, and seeds
growth_stage: Seedling stage through pod fill
season: Cool-to-warm wet weather (60–73°F for Halo Blight; 80–90°F for Common Blight)
humidity_conditions: High humidity, driving rain, heavy morning dew, and overhead sprinklers
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Halo Blight: small angular water-soaked brown spots on leaflets surrounded by a wide, striking greenish-yellow (chlorotic) halo caused by phaseolotoxin; Common Bacterial Blight: larger irregular brown necrotic blotches on leaves with a narrow lemon-yellow border that coalesce and rag the leaf edges; on green pods, both cause circular water-soaked greasy spots that turn reddish-brown and sunken, sometimes oozing cream-or-yellow bacterial droplets.
symptom_keywords: wide yellow-green halo around small brown spot, greasy water-soaked spots on bean pods, reddish-brown sunken pod lesions, ragged brown leaf blotches
symptom_progression: Seed-borne bacteria infect cotyledons and splash onto trifoliate leaves; walking through or picking wet bean rows brushes bacteria along the entire row, causing widespread foliar scorching and spotted pods.
distinguishing_features: Halo Blight is distinguished by the broad pale-green/yellow toxin halo around a tiny angular brown pin-spot in cool weather (60–73°F), whereas Common Bacterial Blight has large brown dead blotches with a narrow bright yellow rim in hot weather (80–90°F).
similar_conditions: Bean Anthracnose (black sunken pod craters with salmon spores and blackened leaf veins), Bean Rust (cinnamon-brown powdery pustules), Sunscald
risk_factors: Saving home-grown bean seed from infected pods, cultivating or harvesting when leaves are wet with dew or rain, and overhead watering.
favorable_conditions: Splashing rain, windstorms, and wet foliage handling.

management_actions: STRICT RULE: never enter, weed, cultivate, or harvest bean patches when foliage is wet! Remove early symptomatic seedlings; use drip irrigation.
prevention_actions: Plant only certified western-grown (arid-region) pathogen-free bean seed and resistant cultivars; rotate out of all legumes for 2–3 years; never save seed from spotted pods.

topic: Beans Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot (Phytophthora capsici)
problem_name: Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot
causal_agent: Phytophthora capsici (on Solanaceae, Cucurbits, Legumes); Phytophthora cactorum / P. fragariae (on Strawberry/Apple); Phytophthora cinnamomi / P. nicotianae (on Avocado, Citrus, Papaya, Blueberry, Rosemary, Sage)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown/collar (foot rot/gummosis), stems, leaves, and fruit ('buckeye rot' on tomato; white yeast-like powder on squash/pepper/watermelon)
growth_stage: Any stage after soil saturation or heavy rainfall
season: Warm, rainy summer weather or poorly drained wet soils
humidity_conditions: Saturated, waterlogged, or flooded soil (>24 hours of standing water) and splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Dark brown-to-black water-soaked lesion girdling the stem base/crown right above the soil line ('black shank' in pepper/squash; 'red stele' reddish-pink central root core in strawberry; 'foot rot/gummosis' cracking bark and oozing gum at graft union in citrus; feeder root blackening and canopy dieback in avocado/blueberry/rosemary), causing rapid permanent wilting; on pepper, cucurbit, and eggplant fruits, dark water-soaked blotches rapidly covered in a diagnostic dusting of white, yeast-like or powdered-sugar-like sporangia (on green tomato fruit touching soil, smooth brown 'buckeye rot' target rings).
symptom_keywords: black stem base collar rot, powdered-sugar white sporangia on fruit, buckeye rot on tomato, red stele root core in strawberry, citrus foot rot gummosis, avocado feeder root rot, sudden wilt after rain
symptom_progression: Swimming zoospores released in saturated soil chemotactically swim to roots and crowns, rotting the root system and stem collar within days and splashing onto low-hanging fruits.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished in pepper and cucurbits by the dark black basal stem girdling ('black shank') and the tight, flat, powdered-sugar-like white coating of sporangia on rotting fruit (unlike fluffy tall cottony Pythium or white fan-like Southern Blight with mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight, Pythium Cottony Leak, Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Sclerotinia White Mold
risk_factors: Poorly drained clay soils, low spots where rainwater puddles, over-irrigation, planting crowns/graft unions too deeply, and short rotations between peppers, eggplants, tomatoes, and cucurbits.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) combined with heavy rainfall or waterlogged soil.
transmission_or_spread: Thick-walled oospores survive in soil for 5–10+ years; motile biflagellate zoospores swim through soil water films and spread in surface runoff and ponded irrigation water.
management_actions: Immediately remove infected plants and rotting fruits; improve surface drainage and never overwater; on citrus and fruit trees, keep mulch 6–12 inches away from the trunk and ensure the graft union is 4–6 inches above soil; on avocado, apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) and maintain a 6-inch coarse leaf/woodchip mulch mat.

severity_or_impact: Critical (causes rapid plant death after heavy rains and persistent soil infestation)

topic: Beans Powdery Mildew (Podosphaera xanthii & Erysiphe cichoracearum)
problem_name: Powdery Mildew
causal_agent: Podosphaera xanthii & Erysiphe cichoracearum (Cucurbits); Erysiphe polygoni (Legumes/Beets); Erysiphe cruciferarum (Brassicas); Erysiphe necator (Grape); Podosphaera aphanis (Strawberry); Podosphaera leucotricha (Apple); Leveillula taurica / Oidium neolycopersici (Solanaceae)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems, and occasionally flower buds/young fruit
growth_stage: Mid-season canopy closure through harvest
season: Mid-to-late summer and autumn (warm days and cool humid nights)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (50–90% RH) at night WITHOUT requiring free liquid water on leaves (liquid water actually inhibits spore germination!)
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Superficial white-to-light-gray talcum-powder-like patches of fungal mycelium and chains of conidia starting on shaded older leaves, petioles, and stems and expanding to cover both upper and lower leaf surfaces; affected leaves turn yellow, then brown and papery dry, and die prematurely, leaving fruits exposed to sunscald and low sugar (low Brix).
symptom_keywords: white powdery patches on leaves, talcum-powder coating, flour-like leaf dust, premature leaf yellowing and drying, upward leaf rolling in strawberry
symptom_progression: Airborne conidia land on dry leaves in humid air, sending haustoria into epidermal cells; white powdery colonies coalesce within 5–7 days, senescing the canopy from older shaded leaves outward.

topic: Beans Root-Knot Nematode Disease (Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla)
problem_name: Root-Knot Nematode Disease
causal_agent: Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla
affected_plant_parts: Root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting and root harvest
season: Warm growing season
temperature_range: 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla
humidity_conditions: Moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Above ground: patchy stunting, pale green-to-yellow chlorotic foliage resembling chronic nitrogen/micronutrient deficiency, premature wilting during warm sunny afternoons even when soil is moist, and poor fruit/pod yield; Below ground (diagnostic): uprooting the plant reveals swollen, beaded, irregular tumor-like root galls ('knots', 1/8 to 1 inch thick) that are an integral part of the root tissue itself, deformed forked/pimpled carrots and potatoes, and cracked sweet potatoes with a 'bearded' mass of stunted feeder roots.
symptom_keywords: swollen root galls, beaded knotted roots, afternoon wilting in moist soil, patchy stunting, forked galling on carrots, pimpled potato tubers
symptom_progression: Microscopic second-stage juveniles (J2) penetrate root tips and inject esophageal secretions that induce giant feeder cells and root galls, disrupting water and nutrient uptake and predisposing roots to Fusarium and Bacterial wilts.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION on legumes (Beans, Peas, Chickpea, Lentil, Soybean, Fenugreek): Root-knot nematode galls are swelling OF the structural root tissue itself and CANNOT be rubbed off, whereas beneficial nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium nodules are round pink-centered attachments on the side of the root that detach easily! On Brassicas, Clubroot causes much larger spindle-like clubs without female nematode egg masses.
similar_conditions: Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency
risk_factors: Warm sandy soils, continuous monoculture of susceptible vegetables (especially okra, tomato, cucurbits, carrot, bean), and introducing infested transplants or soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (75–90°F) in sandy loam soils.
transmission_or_spread: Microscopic soil-borne roundworms spread via infested transplants, seed tubers/slips, soil clinging to tools/shoes, and surface water runoff.
management_actions: Do not replant susceptible crops in galled spots; incorporate abundant organic compost right into beds to stimulate predatory soil fungi and microbes; solarize moist soil under clear UV plastic for 6–8 weeks in peak summer heat.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'N' or 'VFN' carrying the Mi-1 gene in tomato, 'Nemaguard'/'Guardian' rootstock in peach, 'Covington'/'Evangeline' in sweet potato, 'Charleston Belle' in pepper); rotate with non-host sweet corn, cereal rye, or French marigolds (Tagetes patula 'Single Gold'/'Nema-gone') planted as a solid cover crop.

topic: Beans Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods) weekly during moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity (65–80°F (18–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) from Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Asparagus, Sweet corn, Onion).
