topic: Beans Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).

topic: Beans Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) (Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae)
problem_name: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV)
causal_agent: Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae (Tomato spotted wilt virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Purpling, bronzing (metallic copper cast), and downward curling of young upper leaves accompanied by dark necrotic flecks or ringspots; dark brown necrotic streaks along petioles and terminal stems causing one-sided shoot tip dieback; on ripening tomato and pepper fruit, striking concentric yellow, orange, and green ringspots, marbled blotches, and raised bumps.
symptom_keywords: bronzing of upper leaves, concentric ringspots on fruit, necrotic stem streaks, terminal shoot dieback, stunted rosette, purple leaf veins
symptom_progression: Transmitted by adult thrips that acquired the virus as larvae; young terminal leaves bronze and develop necrotic specks, growth stunts severely, and fruits develop diagnostic target-like yellow/red ringspots.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by metallic bronzing and dark flecks on YOUNG upper leaves (unlike Early Blight on older lower leaves) and vivid yellow/orange concentric ringspots on ripening fruit.
similar_conditions: Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling
risk_factors: Abundant western flower thrips or tobacco thrips populations, nearby flowering weeds (chickweed, dandelion, spiny amaranth, buttercup) acting as virus reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather favoring thrips generation turnover and weed dry-down that drives thrips onto garden crops.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently and exclusively by thrips (especially Western flower thrips Frankliniella occidentalis and Tobacco thrips F. fusca); only larval thrips can acquire the virus by feeding on an infected plant, and emerging adults transmit it for life (not seed-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants so larval thrips cannot develop on them and spread virus to neighboring plants; use UV-reflective silver mulch to repel incoming adult thrips.
prevention_actions: Plant TSWV-resistant cultivars (carrying the Sw-5 gene in tomato, e.g., 'Amelia', 'Crista', 'Bella Rosa', 'Mountain Glory', or Tsw gene in pepper); eliminate winter/spring broadleaf weeds in a 30-ft perimeter around the garden BEFORE planting.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits) weekly during late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) from Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling.
severity_or_impact: High (severely stunts plants and renders ringed fruit unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction.
host_range: Documented on Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Lettuce, Spinach, Celery, Beans).

topic: Beans Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) (Begomovirus coheni)
problem_name: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
causal_agent: Begomovirus coheni (Tomato yellow leaf curl virus)
affected_plant_parts: New apical leaves, shoots, and flowers
growth_stage: Seedling transplant stage through flowering
season: Warm-to-hot summer and autumn seasons
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry conditions favoring silverleaf whitefly explosions
visible_symptoms: On Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris): Severe stunting and upright, bushy 'bonsai-like' growth of shoot terminals; new upper leaflets are drastically reduced in size, thick and leathery, curled strongly UPWARD (cup-shaped) and inward, with bright yellow (chlorotic) leaf margins and interveinal areas (sometimes tinged purple on undersides); severe flower abscission results in almost no fruit set after infection.
symptom_keywords: upward leaf curling, yellow leaf margins, stunted bonsai-like shoot tips, small cupped leathery leaves, flower drop, whitefly vector
symptom_progression: Following feeding by viruliferous silverleaf whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), emerging apical leaves within 2–3 weeks stay tiny, cup upward with bright yellow borders, internodes shorten drastically, and blossoms drop.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Physiological Leaf Roll by affecting the NEW upper leaves with bright yellow margins, extreme leaflet size reduction, and severe stunting (whereas Physiological Leaf Roll curls older lower leaves upward while keeping them full-sized and green).
similar_conditions: Physiological Leaf Roll, Herbicide Drift (2,4-D), Broad/Russet Mite injury, Micronutrient (Zinc/Iron) Deficiency
risk_factors: High populations of silverleaf/sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci), infected transplants, and overlapping warm-season solanaceous crops.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry weather (80–95°F) promoting rapid whitefly reproduction and migration.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci MEAM1/MED); not transmitted by seed or mechanical touch/pruning.
management_actions: Rogue and seal infected plants inside plastic bags immediately to prevent whiteflies from dispersing; manage whitefly nymphs and adults on undersides of leaves using insecticidal soap, horticultural oil, or neem oil; install yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies.
prevention_actions: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato cultivars (carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, Ty-3 genes, e.g., 'Security 28', 'Tycoon', 'BHN 968') and lay UV-reflective silver plastic mulch at transplanting to repel whiteflies; inspect transplants carefully for whitefly nymphs before purchasing.
recommended_observations: Scout Beans (new apical leaves, shoots, and flowers) weekly during warm-to-hot summer and autumn seasons (77–95°F (25–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) from Physiological Leaf Roll, Herbicide Drift (2,4-D), Broad/Russet Mite injury, Micronutrient (Zinc/Iron) Deficiency.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (early infection causes up to 90–100% fruit loss due to blossom abortion)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–95°F (25–35°C) and warm, dry conditions favoring silverleaf whitefly explosions.

topic: Peas Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Peas (Pisum sativum): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury
risk_factors: Abundant perennial weeds (pokeweed, milkweed, chickweed, white cockle, nightshade, bindweed) harboring CMV near the garden and migrating winged aphids.
favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored non-persistently (stylet-borne) by >80 species of aphids (especially Green peach aphid Myzus persicae and Melon aphid Aphis gossypii); aphids acquire and transmit the virus in just 10–60 seconds of test probing (so insecticides cannot kill aphids fast enough to prevent transmission!).
management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.
recommended_observations: Scout Peas (young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits) weekly during late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) from Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury.

topic: Peas Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot (Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani)

topic: Peas Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
problem_name: Fusarium Wilt
causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum (host-specific formae speciales: f. sp. lycopersici, melongenae, tuberosi, niveum, melonis, cucumerinum, conglutinans, cepae, pisi, phaseoli, spinaciae, basilici, cubense)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding

symptom_progression: Fungus enters root tips or nematode wounds and colonizes xylem vessels; lower leaves yellow and wilt unilaterally, progressing upward until entire shoots brown, collapse, and die without soft stem rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity

favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (80–90°F) and moisture stress during fruiting.
transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.

topic: Peas Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation

symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.

growth_stage: Seedling stage through pod fill
season: Cool-to-warm wet weather (60–73°F for Halo Blight; 80–90°F for Common Blight)

distinguishing_features: Halo Blight is distinguished by the broad pale-green/yellow toxin halo around a tiny angular brown pin-spot in cool weather (60–73°F), whereas Common Bacterial Blight has large brown dead blotches with a narrow bright yellow rim in hot weather (80–90°F).

topic: Peas Powdery Mildew (Podosphaera xanthii & Erysiphe cichoracearum)
problem_name: Powdery Mildew
causal_agent: Podosphaera xanthii & Erysiphe cichoracearum (Cucurbits); Erysiphe polygoni (Legumes/Beets); Erysiphe cruciferarum (Brassicas); Erysiphe necator (Grape); Podosphaera aphanis (Strawberry); Podosphaera leucotricha (Apple); Leveillula taurica / Oidium neolycopersici (Solanaceae)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems, and occasionally flower buds/young fruit
growth_stage: Mid-season canopy closure through harvest
season: Mid-to-late summer and autumn (warm days and cool humid nights)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (50–90% RH) at night WITHOUT requiring free liquid water on leaves (liquid water actually inhibits spore germination!)
visible_symptoms: On Peas (Pisum sativum): Superficial white-to-light-gray talcum-powder-like patches of fungal mycelium and chains of conidia starting on shaded older leaves, petioles, and stems and expanding to cover both upper and lower leaf surfaces; affected leaves turn yellow, then brown and papery dry, and die prematurely, leaving fruits exposed to sunscald and low sugar (low Brix).
symptom_keywords: white powdery patches on leaves, talcum-powder coating, flour-like leaf dust, premature leaf yellowing and drying, upward leaf rolling in strawberry
symptom_progression: Airborne conidia land on dry leaves in humid air, sending haustoria into epidermal cells; white powdery colonies coalesce within 5–7 days, senescing the canopy from older shaded leaves outward.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Downy Mildew because Powdery Mildew forms a bright white, flour-like powdery coating on BOTH upper and lower leaf surfaces that rubs off with a finger and thrives in dry warm weather without rain, whereas Downy Mildew forms yellow angular spots on top and purplish-gray fuzz strictly on the leaf underside in wet weather. On Zucchini/Pumpkin, distinguish from natural genetic silver-white vein mottling (which does not rub off and stays strictly along veins).
similar_conditions: Downy Mildew, Natural Silver Leaf Mottling (in zucchini/pumpkin), Spray Residue, Whitefly Waxy Secretions
risk_factors: Shaded areas, dense crowded foliage with poor airflow, late-season plantings, and excessive nitrogen fertilization.
favorable_conditions: Warm dry days (70–85°F) followed by cool humid nights that form high boundary-layer humidity without rain.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose wind-borne conidia blow in on air currents; some species overwinter as tiny black chasmothecia on bark, canes, or crop debris.
management_actions: Remove heavily mildewed oldest leaves; apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oil, neem oil, wettable sulfur (WARNING: never apply sulfur to melons/cucurbits above 85°F as it burns cucurbit foliage!), or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens biofungicides at first sign of white spots.
prevention_actions: Plant powdery-mildew-resistant (PMR) cultivars; site plants in full sun with wide spacing and trellis vines for maximum airflow; avoid excess nitrogen.

topic: Peas Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)

causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Peas (Pisum sativum): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.

topic: Peas White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Peas (Pisum sativum): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Peas (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) from Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stem girdling in beans/tomatoes, head drop in lettuce/cabbage, and storage rot in carrots)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours).
host_range: Documented on Peas (Pisum sativum, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Soybean, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Peas (Pisum sativum) Manganese (Mn) Deficiency ('Marsh Spot' of Pea Seeds & Young-Leaf Chlorosis): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Manganese (Mn) Deficiency ('Marsh Spot' of Pea Seeds & Young-Leaf Chlorosis)
affected_plant_parts: Young upper compound leaves and interior of maturing pea cotyledons
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through seed maturation in pods
season: Cool season (sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, 4–6 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall crop)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 55–70°F (13–21°C); tolerates light frost down to 28°F (though open flowers are damaged by hard frost); growth and flowering decline rapidly above 80–85°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Young upper leaflets develop diffuse pale yellow-green interveinal chlorosis while a relatively broad green halo remains around the veins; critically, during seed fill, a circular, sunken, dark-brown necrotic spot or hollow cavity forms on the flat inner surface of the pea cotyledons inside the pod ('marsh spot'), even when external pod appearance is normal.
symptom_keywords: peas, manganese (mn) deficiency, immobile in phloem (essential cofactor for photosystem ii water-splitting complex), young upper compound leaves and interior of maturing pea cotyledons, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Young to recently matured upper leaves and developing cotyledons of legume seeds. Foliar interveinal yellowing appears on upper leaves in alkaline or over-limed organic/sandy soils (pH > 6.8), followed by internal cotyledon necrosis during seed maturation.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Immobile in phloem (essential cofactor for Photosystem II water-splitting complex). Internal brown necrotic 'marsh spot' cavities in the center of mature pea cotyledons are uniquely diagnostic of Manganese deficiency in peas.
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Peas.
risk_factors: Over-limed or naturally alkaline soils (pH > 6.8–7.2), high-organic-matter muck or peaty soils at high pH where Mn2+ oxidizes to unavailable MnO2 complexes, or dry fluffy seedbeds.
favorable_conditions: Over-limed or naturally alkaline soils (pH > 6.8–7.2), high-organic-matter muck or peaty soils at high pH where Mn2+ oxidizes to unavailable MnO2 complexes, or dry fluffy seedbeds.

topic: Chickpea Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus (Potyvirus phaseovulgaris)
problem_name: Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus
causal_agent: Potyvirus phaseovulgaris (Bean common mosaic virus - BCMV) and Bean yellow mosaic virus (BYMV)
affected_plant_parts: Trifoliate leaves, stems, roots (in black root necrosis), and pods
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through pod fill
season: Warm late spring and summer seasons
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aphid migration
visible_symptoms: On Chickpea (Cicer arietinum): Distinct light-green, dark-green, and bright-yellow mosaic mottling on trifoliate leaves accompanied by dark-green vein banding, downward curling or 'cupping' of leaflet margins, puckered blisters along the midrib, and elongated narrow leaflets; plants infected early via seed are stunted with fewer, smaller, curved, greasy-looking pods; in bean cultivars carrying the dominant 'I' resistance gene exposed to necrotic BCMV/BCMNV strains at high temperatures, vascular 'black root' systemic necrosis streaks the stems brown-black and kills the plant.
symptom_keywords: puckered downward-cupped trifoliate leaves, dark-green vein banding, light-and-dark green bean leaf mosaic, stunted curved pods, systemic black root vascular necrosis
symptom_progression: Up to 30–50% of seeds harvested from an infected susceptible bean plant carry BCMV internally inside the embryo; emerging infected seedlings serve as focal points from which winged aphids spread the virus across the bean patch in seconds.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the downward-cupped, blistered trifoliate leaflets with dark-green puffy bubbles along the veins and mosaic light/dark green patterns.
similar_conditions: Potato Leafhopper 'Hopperburn' (triangular yellow V-shaped tip burn and curling without mosaic mottling), Bean Rust, Halo Blight
risk_factors: Saving and replanting home-saved bean or cowpea seed from virus-infected plants, planting susceptible heirloom cultivars, and nearby clover/gladiolus reservoirs (for BYMV).
favorable_conditions: Warm weather (75–85°F) with active winged aphids.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne at high rates (BCMV in common bean and cowpea mosaic viruses in cowpea) and transmitted non-persistently by transient winged aphids.
management_actions: Rogue and destroy mottled, downward-cupped bean seedlings as soon as they emerge so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; never save seed from mosaic-symptomatic bean or cowpea plants.
prevention_actions: Plant certified virus-free seed of BCMV-resistant bush and pole bean cultivars (carrying bc-1, bc-2, or bc-3 combined with the I gene); avoid planting beans adjacent to perennial white/red clover or gladiolus.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (reduces pod set by 30–70% when seed-borne)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–88°F (21–31°C) and warm weather favoring aphid migration.
host_range: Documented on Chickpea (Cicer arietinum, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea, Lentil, Chickpea).

topic: Chickpea Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot (Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani)
problem_name: Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot
causal_agent: Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani
affected_plant_parts: Germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line
growth_stage: Seed germination and cotyledon-to-first-true-leaf seedling stage
season: Early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil
humidity_conditions: Overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds
visible_symptoms: On Chickpea (Cicer arietinum): Pre-emergence damping-off: seeds turn soft, mushy, and brown and fail to emerge, leaving patchy gaps in rows; Post-emergence damping-off: healthy-looking cotyledon seedlings suddenly develop a water-soaked, pinched, thread-like brown or black constriction at the stem base right at the soil line ('wirestem' in brassicas when caused by Rhizoctonia) and topple over flat onto the soil while leaves are still green.
symptom_keywords: seedlings falling over at soil line, pinched thread-like stem base, wirestem, patchy seed emergence, mushy rotted seeds, water-soaked hypocotyl
symptom_progression: Soil-borne oomycetes and fungi attack slow-germinating seeds and tender unlignified hypocotyl tissue in wet soil, rotting the stem cortex within 24–48 hours so seedlings collapse.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the pinched, water-soaked or wiry brown constriction strictly at the soil line on young seedlings (whereas Cutworms completely sever the stem cleanly and Heat/Sunburn bleaches the stem white).
similar_conditions: Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling
risk_factors: Reusing unsterilized garden soil or dirty flats for indoor seed starting, overwatering, sowing too deeply or densely, cold soil temperatures delaying emergence, and poor airflow.
favorable_conditions: Cold, wet, poorly aerated soil or potting media with high seedling density and stagnant air.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oospores and sclerotia native to garden soils, splashed or carried on dirty pots, tools, and untreated seed.
management_actions: Discard damped-off seedling cells/trays immediately; allow the surface of seed-starting media to dry slightly between bottom-waterings; provide a gentle oscillating fan and heat mat (70–75°F) for indoor seedlings.
prevention_actions: Always use sterile, soilless seed-starting mix in clean sanitized trays (washed in 10% bleach); do not sow outdoors until soil reaches the crop's minimum germination temperature; sow at proper depth and thin promptly.
recommended_observations: Scout Chickpea (germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line) weekly during early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil (50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot from Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling.
severity_or_impact: High at seedling stage (can wipe out 50–100% of a seed tray or direct-sown row)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia and overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds.
host_range: Documented on Chickpea (Cicer arietinum, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Pumpkin, Squash, Zucchini, Watermelon).

Distinguishing features: Distinguished by the pinched, water-soaked or wiry brown constriction strictly at the soil line on young seedlings (whereas Cutworms completely sever the stem cleanly and Heat/Sunburn bleaches the stem white). topic: Chickpea Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
problem_name: Fusarium Wilt
causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum (host-specific formae speciales: f. sp. lycopersici, melongenae, tuberosi, niveum, melonis, cucumerinum, conglutinans, cepae, pisi, phaseoli, spinaciae, basilici, cubense)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding
visible_symptoms: On Chickpea (Cicer arietinum): Bright yellowing (chlorosis) and drooping of older lower leaves—classically starting on ONLY ONE SIDE of a leaf, one branch, or one side of the plant ('one-sided flagging')—which wilts during warm afternoons and eventually fails to recover at night; slicing the lower main stem or petiole lengthwise reveals a diagnostic reddish-brown to dark-brown discoloration of the water-conducting vascular ring while the central pith remains healthy.
symptom_keywords: one-sided yellowing, unilateral wilting, vascular browning, reddish-brown xylem ring, lower leaf yellowing, daytime wilting, stunted growth
symptom_progression: Fungus enters root tips or nematode wounds and colonizes xylem vessels; lower leaves yellow and wilt unilaterally, progressing upward until entire shoots brown, collapse, and die without soft stem rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity
risk_factors: Acidic sandy soils (pH <6.0), root-knot nematode infestations creating root entry wounds, high ammonium-nitrogen fertilization, and replanting susceptible cultivars in infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (80–90°F) and moisture stress during fruiting.
transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.
management_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants including roots immediately; do not compost infected stems; solarize soil in hot sunny climates; maintain soil pH near 6.5–7.0 using agricultural lime and use nitrate-nitrogen rather than ammonium-nitrogen.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'F', 'FF', or 'FFF' for Races 1, 2, 3 in tomato; Fusarium-resistant watermelon, melon, cabbage 'Yellows Resistant', pea, basil, and banana cultivars); control root-knot nematodes; practice 4–6 year crop rotations.

severity_or_impact: High (lethal systemic vascular wilt; soil remains infested for many years)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–90°F (27–32°C) and warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil ph and root-knot nematode feeding.
host_range: Documented on Chickpea (Cicer arietinum, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Eggplant, Pepper, Potato, Watermelon, Melon, Cucumber, Pumpkin).

topic: Chickpea White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Chickpea (Cicer arietinum): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.

distinguishing_features: Mexican Bean Beetle is easily distinguished from beneficial Lady Beetles because: (1) its thorax is plain bronze without white-and-black eye markings, (2) it has 16 small uniform black dots in 3 neat rows on a coppery shell, and (3) its larvae are bright yellow and covered in branched spines (whereas beneficial ladybug larvae are alligator-shaped black-and-orange predators!).

affected_plant_parts: Leaves, stems, tendrils, peduncles, pods, and seeds
growth_stage: Flowering through pod fill and maturity
season: Cool-to-moderate, rainy, humid spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: Frequent rain showers, heavy dew, and high canopy humidity (>85% RH)

similar_conditions: Bacterial Blight (translucent water-soaked angular lesions), Pea Powdery Mildew, Fusarium Root Rot
risk_factors: Planting infected seed, short rotations (<3 years between pea/lentil/chickpea crops), dense matted vine canopies, and rainy spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate temperatures (60–75°F) with frequent rain splash and wet foliage.

topic: Lentil Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus (Potyvirus phaseovulgaris)
problem_name: Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus
causal_agent: Potyvirus phaseovulgaris (Bean common mosaic virus - BCMV) and Bean yellow mosaic virus (BYMV)
affected_plant_parts: Trifoliate leaves, stems, roots (in black root necrosis), and pods
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through pod fill
season: Warm late spring and summer seasons
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aphid migration
visible_symptoms: On Lentil (Lens culinaris): Distinct light-green, dark-green, and bright-yellow mosaic mottling on trifoliate leaves accompanied by dark-green vein banding, downward curling or 'cupping' of leaflet margins, puckered blisters along the midrib, and elongated narrow leaflets; plants infected early via seed are stunted with fewer, smaller, curved, greasy-looking pods; in bean cultivars carrying the dominant 'I' resistance gene exposed to necrotic BCMV/BCMNV strains at high temperatures, vascular 'black root' systemic necrosis streaks the stems brown-black and kills the plant.
symptom_keywords: puckered downward-cupped trifoliate leaves, dark-green vein banding, light-and-dark green bean leaf mosaic, stunted curved pods, systemic black root vascular necrosis
symptom_progression: Up to 30–50% of seeds harvested from an infected susceptible bean plant carry BCMV internally inside the embryo; emerging infected seedlings serve as focal points from which winged aphids spread the virus across the bean patch in seconds.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the downward-cupped, blistered trifoliate leaflets with dark-green puffy bubbles along the veins and mosaic light/dark green patterns.
similar_conditions: Potato Leafhopper 'Hopperburn' (triangular yellow V-shaped tip burn and curling without mosaic mottling), Bean Rust, Halo Blight
risk_factors: Saving and replanting home-saved bean or cowpea seed from virus-infected plants, planting susceptible heirloom cultivars, and nearby clover/gladiolus reservoirs (for BYMV).
favorable_conditions: Warm weather (75–85°F) with active winged aphids.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne at high rates (BCMV in common bean and cowpea mosaic viruses in cowpea) and transmitted non-persistently by transient winged aphids.
management_actions: Rogue and destroy mottled, downward-cupped bean seedlings as soon as they emerge so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; never save seed from mosaic-symptomatic bean or cowpea plants.
prevention_actions: Plant certified virus-free seed of BCMV-resistant bush and pole bean cultivars (carrying bc-1, bc-2, or bc-3 combined with the I gene); avoid planting beans adjacent to perennial white/red clover or gladiolus.
recommended_observations: Scout Lentil (trifoliate leaves, stems, roots (in black root necrosis), and pods) weekly during warm late spring and summer seasons (70–88°F (21–31°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus from Potato Leafhopper 'Hopperburn' (triangular yellow V-shaped tip burn and curling without mosaic mottling), Bean Rust, Halo Blight.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (reduces pod set by 30–70% when seed-borne)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–88°F (21–31°C) and warm weather favoring aphid migration.
host_range: Documented on Lentil (Lens culinaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea, Lentil, Chickpea).

topic: Lentil Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot (Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani)
problem_name: Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot
causal_agent: Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani
affected_plant_parts: Germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line
growth_stage: Seed germination and cotyledon-to-first-true-leaf seedling stage
season: Early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil
humidity_conditions: Overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds
visible_symptoms: On Lentil (Lens culinaris): Pre-emergence damping-off: seeds turn soft, mushy, and brown and fail to emerge, leaving patchy gaps in rows; Post-emergence damping-off: healthy-looking cotyledon seedlings suddenly develop a water-soaked, pinched, thread-like brown or black constriction at the stem base right at the soil line ('wirestem' in brassicas when caused by Rhizoctonia) and topple over flat onto the soil while leaves are still green.
symptom_keywords: seedlings falling over at soil line, pinched thread-like stem base, wirestem, patchy seed emergence, mushy rotted seeds, water-soaked hypocotyl
symptom_progression: Soil-borne oomycetes and fungi attack slow-germinating seeds and tender unlignified hypocotyl tissue in wet soil, rotting the stem cortex within 24–48 hours so seedlings collapse.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the pinched, water-soaked or wiry brown constriction strictly at the soil line on young seedlings (whereas Cutworms completely sever the stem cleanly and Heat/Sunburn bleaches the stem white).
similar_conditions: Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling
risk_factors: Reusing unsterilized garden soil or dirty flats for indoor seed starting, overwatering, sowing too deeply or densely, cold soil temperatures delaying emergence, and poor airflow.
favorable_conditions: Cold, wet, poorly aerated soil or potting media with high seedling density and stagnant air.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oospores and sclerotia native to garden soils, splashed or carried on dirty pots, tools, and untreated seed.
management_actions: Discard damped-off seedling cells/trays immediately; allow the surface of seed-starting media to dry slightly between bottom-waterings; provide a gentle oscillating fan and heat mat (70–75°F) for indoor seedlings.
prevention_actions: Always use sterile, soilless seed-starting mix in clean sanitized trays (washed in 10% bleach); do not sow outdoors until soil reaches the crop's minimum germination temperature; sow at proper depth and thin promptly.
recommended_observations: Scout Lentil (germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line) weekly during early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil (50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot from Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling.
severity_or_impact: High at seedling stage (can wipe out 50–100% of a seed tray or direct-sown row)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia and overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds.
host_range: Documented on Lentil (Lens culinaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Pumpkin, Squash, Zucchini, Watermelon).

topic: Lentil Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Lentil (Lens culinaris): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.
host_range: Documented on Lentil (Lens culinaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Asparagus, Sweet corn, Onion).

topic: Lentil White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Lentil (Lens culinaris): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Lentil (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) from Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stem girdling in beans/tomatoes, head drop in lettuce/cabbage, and storage rot in carrots)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours).
host_range: Documented on Lentil (Lens culinaris, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Soybean, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Lentil Nutrient Requirements and Fertilization Schedule
growth_stage: Pre-plant bed preparation, active vegetative growth, and reproductive/storage organ development
management_actions: Inoculate with Rhizobium leguminosarum (pea/lentil group); require phosphorus and potassium with little to no added nitrogen
prevention_actions: Base fertilizer rates on a soil test and maintain soil pH at 6.0–7.5 to keep macronutrients and micronutrients bioavailable; avoid over-application of soluble nitrogen salts which can burn roots or skew vegetative-to-reproductive balance.
recommended_observations: Monitor shoot vigor, leaf color on both older lower leaves (mobile nutrients N, P, K, Mg) and new upper leaves (immobile nutrients Fe, Ca, B, Zn, Mn), and fruit/root set.
knowledge_text: Nutrition and fertilizer management for Lentil (Lens culinaris): Inoculate with Rhizobium leguminosarum (pea/lentil group); require phosphorus and potassium with little to no added nitrogen. Maintain soil pH within 6.0–7.5 to ensure optimal nutrient availability.

harvest_information: Pull or cut plants when the lowest pods turn tan-brown and seeds inside are hard (waiting until all top pods dry causes bottom pods to shatter); dry plants on a tarp and thresh out lens-shaped seeds
management_actions: Pull or cut plants when the lowest pods turn tan-brown and seeds inside are hard (waiting until all top pods dry causes bottom pods to shatter); dry plants on a tarp and thresh out lens-shaped seeds

topic: Soybean Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm Management
problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents

symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.

similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.

host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea).

topic: Soybean Cucumber Beetles Management
problem_name: Cucumber Beetles (Striped and Spotted Cucumber Beetles)
causal_agent: Acalymma vittatum (Striped Cucumber Beetle) and Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi (Spotted Cucumber Beetle / Southern Corn Rootworm)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence through flowering and fruiting
season: Spring transplant/emergence through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oblong bright-yellow-green beetles with either three jet-black longitudinal stripes down the wing covers (Striped Cucumber Beetle) or twelve black spots (Spotted Cucumber Beetle); overwintered adults swarm emerging cucurbit cotyledons and young transplants in spring, chewing ragged holes through leaves, girdling tender stems, congregating inside open yellow cucurbit blossoms (chewing anthers/pistils and reducing fruit set), scarring the underside and rind of melons/pumpkins, and transmitting the fatal bacterium Erwinia tracheiphila (Bacterial Wilt); white brown-headed larvae feed underground on cucurbit, corn, and bean roots.
symptom_keywords: yellow beetle with three black stripes, yellow-green beetle with twelve black spots, chewed cucurbit cotyledons and stems, beetles packed inside squash blossoms, scarred pumpkin rinds, sudden bacterial wilt
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge when spring temperatures exceed 55–65°F, attracted strongly by cucurbitacin bitter compounds in emerging cucurbit seedlings; females lay orange-yellow eggs in soil cracks at the stem base, producing root-feeding larvae and a mid-summer second adult generation.
distinguishing_features: Striped Cucumber Beetle has 3 sharp black stripes on a yellow back with a black head and black abdomen underside (unlike Western Corn Rootworm, which has blurred stripes and a yellow abdomen); Spotted Cucumber Beetle is yellow-green with 12 black spots (unlike beneficial Pink Spotted Lady Beetles, which are pink/reddish-orange with spots on the thorax too).
similar_conditions: Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles
risk_factors: Uncovered spring cucurbit seedlings, cultivars high in cucurbitacins, and bacterial wilt reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny spring days (>60°F) during seedling emergence and bloom.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded field borders and weedy garden debris, flying into cucurbit beds as soon as seedlings crack the soil.
management_actions: Keep cucurbit seedlings and transplants completely covered under floating row covers or insect netting sealed at the edges from the day of planting until female flowers open (then remove covers for bee pollination); hand-vacuum beetles out of open squash blossoms early in the morning; apply kaolin clay (Surround) particle film or botanical pyrethrin/spinosad/neem sprays in the evening when bees are not inside flowers (squash blossoms close by afternoon!).
prevention_actions: Transplant robust 3-to-4-week-old cucurbit starts rather than direct-seeding in high-pressure gardens; plant a perimeter trap crop of 'Blue Hubbard' squash (which has extreme cucurbitacin levels that lure 85–90% of cucumber beetles away from cucumbers and melons!); mulch with straw to encourage wolf spiders and ground beetles.

topic: Soybean Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Soybean Mexican Bean Beetle, Bean Leaf Beetle, Cowpea Curculio, and Pea Weevil Management
problem_name: Mexican Bean Beetle, Bean Leaf Beetle, Cowpea Curculio, and Pea Weevil
causal_agent: Epilachna varivestis (Mexican Bean Beetle), Cerotoma trifurcata (Bean Leaf Beetle), Chalcodermus aeneus (Cowpea Curculio), and Bruchus pisorum (Pea Weevil)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of trifoliate leaves, stems, flowers, green pods, and maturing seeds
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through pod fill and seed maturation
season: Late spring through summer
humidity_conditions: Moderate-to-high humidity (Mexican Bean Beetle thrives in humid mid-Atlantic/Appalachian/irrigated gardens; hot dry weather above 95°F kills its eggs and larvae)
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Mexican Bean Beetle (actually a plant-eating member of the Ladybird Beetle family!): coppery-brown to bronze dome-shaped adults (1/4 inch) with 16 small black spots arranged in 3 rows across the wing covers, and oval, bright canary-yellow larvae covered in 6 rows of long, branched, black-tipped spines ('fuzzy yellow hedgehogs') that feed on the undersides of bean leaves, scraping away lower tissue between veins to leave a delicate, lace-like skeletonized network ('windowpane lacework') that dries brown; Bean Leaf Beetle: small (1/5 inch) yellow, tan, or red beetles with a diagnostic black triangle right behind the thorax and 4 rectangular black spots that chew round holes in seedling leaves and scar pods; Cowpea Curculio & Pea Weevil: small (1/5 inch) black/brown snout weevils that puncture green pods to lay eggs inside swelling cowpeas or peas, leaving dark blister-like stings on the pod and a white C-shaped legless grub inside each seed.
symptom_keywords: lacy skeletonized bean leaves with intact vein network, fuzzy yellow spiny larvae under bean leaves, coppery-brown ladybug-like beetle with 16 black spots, beetle with black triangle behind neck chewing round holes in bean leaves, blister stings on cowpea pods with white grub inside seed
symptom_progression: Overwintered beetles colonize emerging bean/pea rows in spring; Mexican Bean Beetles lay clusters of 40–60 yellow upright eggs on leaf undersides, and spiny yellow larvae skeletonize foliage for 2–3 weeks before pupating into orange pupae glued by their tails to lower leaves.
distinguishing_features: Mexican Bean Beetle is easily distinguished from beneficial Lady Beetles because: (1) its thorax is plain bronze without white-and-black eye markings, (2) it has 16 small uniform black dots in 3 neat rows on a coppery shell, and (3) its larvae are bright yellow and covered in branched spines (whereas beneficial ladybug larvae are alligator-shaped black-and-orange predators!).
similar_conditions: Beneficial Lady Beetles (red/orange with white markings on black thorax and alligator-like black-and-orange larvae), Japanese Beetle (metallic green head with coppery wings feeding on upper leaf surface)
risk_factors: Successive plantings of bush, pole, and lima beans without break, dense humid foliage, and proximity to overwintering wooded leaf litter.
favorable_conditions: Warm, humid summer weather (70–85°F).
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in woody leaf litter and garden debris, flying to bean and pea rows in spring.
management_actions: Handpick coppery adults, spiny yellow larvae, and yellow egg clusters from the undersides of bean leaves; release the tiny parasitic wasp Pediobius foveolatus (which parasitizes Mexican Bean Beetle larvae, turning them into dark brown papery shells!); spray spinosad, neem oil, or pyrethrin on leaf undersides if skeletonization exceeds 20%; promptly pull and compost bush bean plants as soon as their main harvest finishes.
prevention_actions: Plant an early spring crop of bush snap beans (which often matures before Mexican Bean Beetle populations peak in mid-summer); rotate cowpeas and peas away from last year's legume beds and store dried peas/beans in sealed containers (freezing dried culinary seeds at 0°F for 4 days kills any internal bruchid seed weevils).

severity_or_impact: High on snap beans, lima beans, soybeans, cowpeas, and field/garden peas

topic: Soybean Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).
