topic: Soybean Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Soybean Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
affected_plant_parts: Developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.
symptom_keywords: shield-shaped green or brown bug, white bands on antennae of brown stink bug, cloudy yellow-white spots on ripe tomato and pepper skin, white spongy corky tissue under fruit skin, catfaced dimpled peaches and apples, black-and-orange harlequin bug with striped barrel eggs on kale
symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.
distinguishing_features: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug is identified by alternating light-and-dark bands on its antennae and along the flared rear edge of its abdomen (distinguishing it from beneficial predatory Rough Stink Bugs and Spined Soldier Bugs, which have pointed shoulder spines or thick piercing beaks); Harlequin Bug is unmistakable with its glossy black-and-fiery-orange shield and two-row clusters of black-and-white striped barrel eggs. Note: cloudy white spongy spots under tomato/pepper skin are Stink Bug feeding, NOT a fungal disease!
similar_conditions: Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface)
risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.
management_actions: Handpick adults, nymphs, and barrel-shaped egg clusters in the cool early morning by knocking them into a bucket of soapy water; cover high-value tomato, pepper, bean, and brassica beds with fine insect netting; vacuum Harlequin bugs off kale/collards.
prevention_actions: Plant a perimeter trap crop of early-maturing cowpeas/soybeans, sweet corn, or sunflowers (for green/brown stink bugs) or 'Cleome' spider flower / mustard greens (for Harlequin Bug) to intercept immigrating adults before they reach main crops; mow weedy borders BEFORE weeds go to seed.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for harlequin bug on brassicas)) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (70–92°F (21–33°C)); inspect for shield-shaped green or brown bug to distinguish Stink Bugs from Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface).
severity_or_impact: High (causes widespread 'cloudy spot' on tomatoes/peppers, catfacing on peaches/apples, shriveled beans/pecans, and severe scorching of kale/collards)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, sunny summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Okra, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea).

topic: Soybean Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.

similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Soybean Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.)

similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot, Alternaria Black Mold, Phytophthora Fruit Rot, Cercospora Leaf Spot, Gummy Stem Blight

topic: Soybean Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus (Potyvirus phaseovulgaris)
problem_name: Bean Common Mosaic Virus (BCMV) and Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus
causal_agent: Potyvirus phaseovulgaris (Bean common mosaic virus - BCMV) and Bean yellow mosaic virus (BYMV)
affected_plant_parts: Trifoliate leaves, stems, roots (in black root necrosis), and pods
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through pod fill
season: Warm late spring and summer seasons
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aphid migration
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Distinct light-green, dark-green, and bright-yellow mosaic mottling on trifoliate leaves accompanied by dark-green vein banding, downward curling or 'cupping' of leaflet margins, puckered blisters along the midrib, and elongated narrow leaflets; plants infected early via seed are stunted with fewer, smaller, curved, greasy-looking pods; in bean cultivars carrying the dominant 'I' resistance gene exposed to necrotic BCMV/BCMNV strains at high temperatures, vascular 'black root' systemic necrosis streaks the stems brown-black and kills the plant.
symptom_keywords: puckered downward-cupped trifoliate leaves, dark-green vein banding, light-and-dark green bean leaf mosaic, stunted curved pods, systemic black root vascular necrosis
symptom_progression: Up to 30–50% of seeds harvested from an infected susceptible bean plant carry BCMV internally inside the embryo; emerging infected seedlings serve as focal points from which winged aphids spread the virus across the bean patch in seconds.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the downward-cupped, blistered trifoliate leaflets with dark-green puffy bubbles along the veins and mosaic light/dark green patterns.
similar_conditions: Potato Leafhopper 'Hopperburn' (triangular yellow V-shaped tip burn and curling without mosaic mottling), Bean Rust, Halo Blight
risk_factors: Saving and replanting home-saved bean or cowpea seed from virus-infected plants, planting susceptible heirloom cultivars, and nearby clover/gladiolus reservoirs (for BYMV).
favorable_conditions: Warm weather (75–85°F) with active winged aphids.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne at high rates (BCMV in common bean and cowpea mosaic viruses in cowpea) and transmitted non-persistently by transient winged aphids.
management_actions: Rogue and destroy mottled, downward-cupped bean seedlings as soon as they emerge so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; never save seed from mosaic-symptomatic bean or cowpea plants.
prevention_actions: Plant certified virus-free seed of BCMV-resistant bush and pole bean cultivars (carrying bc-1, bc-2, or bc-3 combined with the I gene); avoid planting beans adjacent to perennial white/red clover or gladiolus.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (reduces pod set by 30–70% when seed-borne)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–88°F (21–31°C) and warm weather favoring aphid migration.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea, Lentil, Chickpea).

topic: Soybean Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cercospora Leaf Spot from Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (ruins marketable leaves on Swiss chard and spinach and weakens beet, carrot, and pepper plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh) and warm summer rains or overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beet, Swiss chard, Spinach, Amaranth, Carrot, Celery, Parsley, Pepper).

topic: Soybean Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot (Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani)
problem_name: Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot
causal_agent: Pythium spp., Phytophthora spp., and Rhizoctonia solani
affected_plant_parts: Germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line
growth_stage: Seed germination and cotyledon-to-first-true-leaf seedling stage
season: Early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil
humidity_conditions: Overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Pre-emergence damping-off: seeds turn soft, mushy, and brown and fail to emerge, leaving patchy gaps in rows; Post-emergence damping-off: healthy-looking cotyledon seedlings suddenly develop a water-soaked, pinched, thread-like brown or black constriction at the stem base right at the soil line ('wirestem' in brassicas when caused by Rhizoctonia) and topple over flat onto the soil while leaves are still green.
symptom_keywords: seedlings falling over at soil line, pinched thread-like stem base, wirestem, patchy seed emergence, mushy rotted seeds, water-soaked hypocotyl
symptom_progression: Soil-borne oomycetes and fungi attack slow-germinating seeds and tender unlignified hypocotyl tissue in wet soil, rotting the stem cortex within 24–48 hours so seedlings collapse.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the pinched, water-soaked or wiry brown constriction strictly at the soil line on young seedlings (whereas Cutworms completely sever the stem cleanly and Heat/Sunburn bleaches the stem white).
similar_conditions: Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling
risk_factors: Reusing unsterilized garden soil or dirty flats for indoor seed starting, overwatering, sowing too deeply or densely, cold soil temperatures delaying emergence, and poor airflow.
favorable_conditions: Cold, wet, poorly aerated soil or potting media with high seedling density and stagnant air.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oospores and sclerotia native to garden soils, splashed or carried on dirty pots, tools, and untreated seed.
management_actions: Discard damped-off seedling cells/trays immediately; allow the surface of seed-starting media to dry slightly between bottom-waterings; provide a gentle oscillating fan and heat mat (70–75°F) for indoor seedlings.
prevention_actions: Always use sterile, soilless seed-starting mix in clean sanitized trays (washed in 10% bleach); do not sow outdoors until soil reaches the crop's minimum germination temperature; sow at proper depth and thin promptly.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (germinating seeds, emerging hypocotyls, root tips, and seedling stems at the soil line) weekly during early spring or indoor seed starting in cool, wet soil (50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Damping-Off and Seedling Root Rot from Cutworm feeding (stems clipped cleanly), Fertilizer Salt Burn, Cold/Chilling Injury, Heat Stem Girdling.
severity_or_impact: High at seedling stage (can wipe out 50–100% of a seed tray or direct-sown row)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–68°F (10–20°C) for Pythium; 68–82°F for Rhizoctonia and overwatered, poorly drained, compacted, or high-humidity seedling trays and garden beds.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Pumpkin, Squash, Zucchini, Watermelon).

topic: Soybean Halo Blight and Common Bacterial Blight of Beans (Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. phaseolicola)
problem_name: Halo Blight and Common Bacterial Blight of Beans
causal_agent: Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. phaseolicola (Halo Blight) and Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. phaseoli (Common Bacterial Blight)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, stems, pods, and seeds

causal_agent: Podosphaera xanthii & Erysiphe cichoracearum (Cucurbits); Erysiphe polygoni (Legumes/Beets); Erysiphe cruciferarum (Brassicas); Erysiphe necator (Grape); Podosphaera aphanis (Strawberry); Podosphaera leucotricha (Apple); Leveillula taurica / Oidium neolycopersici (Solanaceae)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems, and occasionally flower buds/young fruit
growth_stage: Mid-season canopy closure through harvest
season: Mid-to-late summer and autumn (warm days and cool humid nights)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (50–90% RH) at night WITHOUT requiring free liquid water on leaves (liquid water actually inhibits spore germination!)
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Superficial white-to-light-gray talcum-powder-like patches of fungal mycelium and chains of conidia starting on shaded older leaves, petioles, and stems and expanding to cover both upper and lower leaf surfaces; affected leaves turn yellow, then brown and papery dry, and die prematurely, leaving fruits exposed to sunscald and low sugar (low Brix).
symptom_keywords: white powdery patches on leaves, talcum-powder coating, flour-like leaf dust, premature leaf yellowing and drying, upward leaf rolling in strawberry
symptom_progression: Airborne conidia land on dry leaves in humid air, sending haustoria into epidermal cells; white powdery colonies coalesce within 5–7 days, senescing the canopy from older shaded leaves outward.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Downy Mildew because Powdery Mildew forms a bright white, flour-like powdery coating on BOTH upper and lower leaf surfaces that rubs off with a finger and thrives in dry warm weather without rain, whereas Downy Mildew forms yellow angular spots on top and purplish-gray fuzz strictly on the leaf underside in wet weather. On Zucchini/Pumpkin, distinguish from natural genetic silver-white vein mottling (which does not rub off and stays strictly along veins).
similar_conditions: Downy Mildew, Natural Silver Leaf Mottling (in zucchini/pumpkin), Spray Residue, Whitefly Waxy Secretions
risk_factors: Shaded areas, dense crowded foliage with poor airflow, late-season plantings, and excessive nitrogen fertilization.
favorable_conditions: Warm dry days (70–85°F) followed by cool humid nights that form high boundary-layer humidity without rain.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose wind-borne conidia blow in on air currents; some species overwinter as tiny black chasmothecia on bark, canes, or crop debris.
management_actions: Remove heavily mildewed oldest leaves; apply potassium bicarbonate, horticultural oil, neem oil, wettable sulfur (WARNING: never apply sulfur to melons/cucurbits above 85°F as it burns cucurbit foliage!), or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens biofungicides at first sign of white spots.
prevention_actions: Plant powdery-mildew-resistant (PMR) cultivars; site plants in full sun with wide spacing and trellis vines for maximum airflow; avoid excess nitrogen.

topic: Soybean Root-Knot Nematode Disease (Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla)
problem_name: Root-Knot Nematode Disease
causal_agent: Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. arenaria, and M. hapla
affected_plant_parts: Root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting and root harvest
season: Warm growing season
temperature_range: 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla
humidity_conditions: Moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Above ground: patchy stunting, pale green-to-yellow chlorotic foliage resembling chronic nitrogen/micronutrient deficiency, premature wilting during warm sunny afternoons even when soil is moist, and poor fruit/pod yield; Below ground (diagnostic): uprooting the plant reveals swollen, beaded, irregular tumor-like root galls ('knots', 1/8 to 1 inch thick) that are an integral part of the root tissue itself, deformed forked/pimpled carrots and potatoes, and cracked sweet potatoes with a 'bearded' mass of stunted feeder roots.
symptom_keywords: swollen root galls, beaded knotted roots, afternoon wilting in moist soil, patchy stunting, forked galling on carrots, pimpled potato tubers
symptom_progression: Microscopic second-stage juveniles (J2) penetrate root tips and inject esophageal secretions that induce giant feeder cells and root galls, disrupting water and nutrient uptake and predisposing roots to Fusarium and Bacterial wilts.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION on legumes (Beans, Peas, Chickpea, Lentil, Soybean, Fenugreek): Root-knot nematode galls are swelling OF the structural root tissue itself and CANNOT be rubbed off, whereas beneficial nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium nodules are round pink-centered attachments on the side of the root that detach easily! On Brassicas, Clubroot causes much larger spindle-like clubs without female nematode egg masses.
similar_conditions: Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency
risk_factors: Warm sandy soils, continuous monoculture of susceptible vegetables (especially okra, tomato, cucurbits, carrot, bean), and introducing infested transplants or soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (75–90°F) in sandy loam soils.
transmission_or_spread: Microscopic soil-borne roundworms spread via infested transplants, seed tubers/slips, soil clinging to tools/shoes, and surface water runoff.
management_actions: Do not replant susceptible crops in galled spots; incorporate abundant organic compost right into beds to stimulate predatory soil fungi and microbes; solarize moist soil under clear UV plastic for 6–8 weeks in peak summer heat.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'N' or 'VFN' carrying the Mi-1 gene in tomato, 'Nemaguard'/'Guardian' rootstock in peach, 'Covington'/'Evangeline' in sweet potato, 'Charleston Belle' in pepper); rotate with non-host sweet corn, cereal rye, or French marigolds (Tagetes patula 'Single Gold'/'Nema-gone') planted as a solid cover crop.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (root tips, feeder roots, and underground tubers/taproots) weekly during warm growing season (75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Root-Knot Nematode Disease from Beneficial Rhizobium Nitrogen Nodules (on legumes), Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae on brassicas), Crown Gall (Agrobacterium), Drought/Nutrient Deficiency.
severity_or_impact: High (causes 30–80% yield loss and breaks genetic resistance to Fusarium and Bacterial wilts)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) for M. incognita; 65–77°F for northern M. hapla and moist, warm, light sandy or sandy-loam soils.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Soybean Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).

topic: Soybean Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) (Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae)
problem_name: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV)
causal_agent: Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae (Tomato spotted wilt virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Purpling, bronzing (metallic copper cast), and downward curling of young upper leaves accompanied by dark necrotic flecks or ringspots; dark brown necrotic streaks along petioles and terminal stems causing one-sided shoot tip dieback; on ripening tomato and pepper fruit, striking concentric yellow, orange, and green ringspots, marbled blotches, and raised bumps.
symptom_keywords: bronzing of upper leaves, concentric ringspots on fruit, necrotic stem streaks, terminal shoot dieback, stunted rosette, purple leaf veins
symptom_progression: Transmitted by adult thrips that acquired the virus as larvae; young terminal leaves bronze and develop necrotic specks, growth stunts severely, and fruits develop diagnostic target-like yellow/red ringspots.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by metallic bronzing and dark flecks on YOUNG upper leaves (unlike Early Blight on older lower leaves) and vivid yellow/orange concentric ringspots on ripening fruit.
similar_conditions: Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling
risk_factors: Abundant western flower thrips or tobacco thrips populations, nearby flowering weeds (chickweed, dandelion, spiny amaranth, buttercup) acting as virus reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather favoring thrips generation turnover and weed dry-down that drives thrips onto garden crops.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently and exclusively by thrips (especially Western flower thrips Frankliniella occidentalis and Tobacco thrips F. fusca); only larval thrips can acquire the virus by feeding on an infected plant, and emerging adults transmit it for life (not seed-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants so larval thrips cannot develop on them and spread virus to neighboring plants; use UV-reflective silver mulch to repel incoming adult thrips.
prevention_actions: Plant TSWV-resistant cultivars (carrying the Sw-5 gene in tomato, e.g., 'Amelia', 'Crista', 'Bella Rosa', 'Mountain Glory', or Tsw gene in pepper); eliminate winter/spring broadleaf weeds in a 30-ft perimeter around the garden BEFORE planting.
recommended_observations: Scout Soybean (young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits) weekly during late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) from Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling.
severity_or_impact: High (severely stunts plants and renders ringed fruit unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction.
host_range: Documented on Soybean (Glycine max, Fabaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Lettuce, Spinach, Celery, Beans).

topic: Soybean White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Soybean (Glycine max): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.

Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia). growth_stage: Bloom (R1–R2) through seed fill (R5) under heat or drought
season: Warm season (sow after last spring frost when soil temperature reaches 60–65°F)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 70–85°F (21–29°C); sensitive to frost; night temperatures play a key role in photoperiodic floral induction
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Developing pods abort and drop at the R3 stage, or full-sized green edamame pods remain completely flat ('pop-pods') or contain only 1 bean instead of 3 plump beans.
symptom_keywords: soybean, pod abortion & flat empty pods ('pop-pods') of soybean / edamame, poor pollination, misshapen fruit, bottlenecked fruit, nubbin berry, tip blanking, pod abortion, incomplete kernel fill
symptom_progression: High temperatures (>95°F) or water deficit during R3–R5 aborts fertilized embryos inside the pod.
distinguishing_features: Flat seedless pods with clean intact pod walls (unlike Stink bug feeding, which leaves dark internal puncture marks and deformed yeast-spotted seeds).
similar_conditions: Stink bug 'stay-green' syndrome and seed puncturing; Potassium deficiency.
risk_factors: Cold, rainy, or windy weather (<55°F) suppressing bee flight, extreme heat (>90–95°F) desiccating silks or killing pollen, planting sweet corn in single rows instead of blocks, or broad-spectrum insecticide use during bloom.
favorable_conditions: Cold, rainy, or windy weather (<55°F) suppressing bee flight, extreme heat (>90–95°F) desiccating silks or killing pollen, planting sweet corn in single rows instead of blocks, or broad-spectrum insecticide use during bloom.
management_actions: Hand-pollinate female cucurbit flowers in the morning using a soft brush or male flower, plant sweet corn in 4+ row blocks, and maintain soil moisture during silking and bloom.
prevention_actions: Conserve native bumblebees, squash bees, and honeybees by avoiding insecticide sprays on open blooms, provide wind-sheltered sunny beds, and ensure adequate boron and calcium nutrition.
recommended_observations: Examine the exact anatomical position of symptoms on Soybean (Developing R3–R5 pods at middle and upper nodes), review recent irrigation, temperature, pollination, and fertility logs, and confirm absence of fungal fruiting bodies or insect larvae.
severity_or_impact: Drastically reduces marketable 2- and 3-bean edamame pod grade.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Warm-season frost-sensitive annual legume (Glycine max: vegetable soybean / edamame and grain soybean). Optimal thermal regime: Optimal growth 70–85°F (21–29°C); sensitive to frost; night temperatures play a key role in photoperiodic floral induction.
host_range: Soybean (Glycine max, family Fabaceae) and physiologically similar legume crops.
knowledge_text: Pod Abortion & Flat Empty Pods ('Pop-Pods') of Soybean / Edamame in Soybean (Glycine max, family Fabaceae) is a non-infectious physiological disorder caused by insufficient bee/wind pollination or thermal pollen inactivation causing uneven seed-auxin gradients in developing fruit. Visual symptoms: Developing pods abort and drop at the R3 stage, or full-sized green edamame pods remain completely flat ('pop-pods') or contain only 1 bean instead of 3 plump beans. Progression: High temperatures (>95°F) or water deficit during R3–R5 aborts fertilized embryos inside the pod. Distinguishing features: Flat seedless pods with clean intact pod walls (unlike Stink bug feeding, which leaves dark internal puncture marks and deformed yeast-spotted seeds). Favorable conditions: Cold, rainy, or windy weather (<55°F) suppressing bee flight, extreme heat (>90–95°F) desiccating silks or killing pollen, planting sweet corn in single rows instead of blocks, or broad-spectrum insecticide use during bloom. Management and prevention: Hand-pollinate female cucurbit flowers in the morning using a soft brush or male flower, plant sweet corn in 4+ row blocks, and maintain soil moisture during silking and bloom. Conserve native bumblebees, squash bees, and honeybees by avoiding insecticide sprays on open blooms, provide wind-sheltered sunny beds, and ensure adequate boron and calcium nutrition.

topic: Soybean Watering, Irrigation Method, and Critical Moisture Stages
growth_stage: Seedling establishment, vegetative growth, flowering, and harvest-organ development
water_requirement: 1.0–1.5 inches per week; critical moisture stage is R3–R6 (pod development through full green seed fill)
management_actions: Supply 1.0–1.5 inches per week; critical moisture stage is R3–R6 (pod development through full green seed fill). Apply water directly to the root zone using drip irrigation or soaker hoses in the morning so any wet foliage dries rapidly.
prevention_actions: Avoid both acute drought stress (which stunts growth, drops blossoms, and impairs quality) and chronic overwatering/waterlogging (which suffocates feeder roots and promotes root/crown rots); avoid overhead watering late in the day.

knowledge_text: Water and irrigation requirements for Soybean (Glycine max): 1.0–1.5 inches per week; critical moisture stage is R3–R6 (pod development through full green seed fill). topic: Cabbage Aphids Management
problem_name: Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids)
causal_agent: Myzus persicae (Green Peach Aphid), Aphis gossypii (Melon/Cotton Aphid), Macrosiphum euphorbiae (Potato Aphid), Acyrthosiphon pisum (Pea Aphid), Aphis fabae (Black Bean Aphid), and Brevicoryne brassicae (Cabbage Aphid)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and flowering
season: Spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer)
humidity_conditions: Moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants)
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew.
symptom_keywords: soft pear-shaped insects under leaves, curled puckered shoot tips, sticky shiny honeydew, black sooty mold, white cast skins, ants tending stems
symptom_progression: Winged females (alates) land on succulent new shoots and give live birth parthenogenetically to nymphs that mature in 7–10 days, building dense colonies and transmitting non-persistent plant viruses within seconds of probing.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present).
similar_conditions: Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves)
risk_factors: Over-fertilization with high soluble nitrogen (which creates lush amino-acid-rich sap that accelerates aphid reproduction), broad-spectrum pyrethroid/carbamate insecticide sprays that kill ladybugs and parasitic wasps, ant tending, and greenhouse/indoors transplant carryover.
favorable_conditions: Mild temperatures (65–80°F) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth.
transmission_or_spread: Winged alate aphids disperse on wind currents from overwintering weeds, woody hosts (Prunus, Euonymus), or neighboring crops; ants also move aphids between plants.
management_actions: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides.
prevention_actions: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.
recommended_observations: Scout Cabbage (undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems) twice weekly during spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer) (60–82°F (15–28°C)); inspect for soft pear-shaped insects under leaves to distinguish Aphids from Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (direct stunting plus primary vector of CMV, PVY, PRSV, ZYMV, WMV, and BCMV)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–82°F (15–28°C) and moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants).
host_range: Documented on Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).
knowledge_text: Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata) Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids) is a sap-feeding insect pest caused by Myzus persicae (Green Peach Aphid), Aphis gossypii (Melon/Cotton Aphid), Macrosiphum euphorbiae (Potato Aphid), Acyrthosiphon pisum (Pea Aphid), Aphis fabae (Black Bean Aphid), and Brevicoryne brassicae (Cabbage Aphid). Visible signs and feeding damage on cabbage (undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew. Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present). Favored by mild temperatures (65–80°f) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth. (60–82°F (15–28°C)). Integrated pest management and prevention: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.

topic: Cabbage Armyworms Management
problem_name: Armyworms (Beet, Yellowstriped, Fall, and Southern Armyworms)
causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. Beet Armyworm is olive-green with a prominent black spot on the thorax above the second pair of true legs; Yellowstriped Armyworm is velvety gray-black with two bright yellow-orange dorsal stripes and black triangular markings; Fall Armyworm has a prominent white inverted 'Y' suture on its dark head capsule and four black dots arranged in a square on the 8th abdominal segment.
symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for fuzzy tan/white scale-covered egg masses and crush or clip them off before they hatch; spray Bacillus thuringiensis aizawai (Bt aizawai is substantially more effective against Spodoptera armyworms than Bt kurstaki!) or spinosad while caterpillars are small (<1/2 inch) and windowpaning.
prevention_actions: Keep beds free of pigweed (Amaranthus) and lambsquarters (preferred egg-laying hosts for Beet Armyworm); cover fall brassica and leafy green plantings with floating row covers.
recommended_observations: Scout Cabbage (whorl leaves (sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves to distinguish Armyworms from Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms.
severity_or_impact: High in late summer and fall
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather.
host_range: Documented on Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Sweet potato, Beet, Swiss chard).

topic: Cabbage Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime

similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.

severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.

topic: Cabbage Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Cabbage (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Cabbage Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).
recommended_observations: Scout Cabbage (cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of potato, sweetpotato, and striped flea beetles)) twice weekly during spring through mid-summer (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves to distinguish Flea Beetles from Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass).
severity_or_impact: High on seedlings and young eggplant, radish, bok choy, arugula, turnip, and mustard greens
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny, dry spring weather.
host_range: Documented on Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Eggplant, Potato, Tomato, Pepper, Radish, Turnip, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Cabbage Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Cabbage (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Cabbage Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Cabbage (seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes) twice weekly during cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights (45–75°F (7–24°C)); inspect for ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries to distinguish Slugs and Garden Snails from Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime).
severity_or_impact: High in cool, wet climates and on seedlings, lettuce, brassicas, and strawberries
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–75°F (7–24°C) and high humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds.
host_range: Documented on Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Lettuce, Spinach, Swiss chard, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy).
