topic: Cauliflower Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Cauliflower (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Cauliflower Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Deep, rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained loam with high organic matter (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
soil_ph: 6.5–7.0 (soil pH below 6.0 reduces molybdenum availability and induces 'whiptail' leaf deformity)
management_actions: Prepare a deep, rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained loam with high organic matter adjusted to pH 6.5–7.0 (soil pH below 6.0 reduces molybdenum availability and induces 'whiptail' leaf deformity) based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Cauliflower to verify soil pH (6.5–7.0 (soil pH below 6.0 reduces molybdenum availability and induces 'whiptail' leaf deformity)) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): Prefers deep, rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained loam with high organic matter with an optimal soil pH of 6.5–7.0 (soil pH below 6.0 reduces molybdenum availability and induces 'whiptail' leaf deformity). topic: Cauliflower Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Cauliflower (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) from Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.

topic: Cauliflower Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)
problem_name: Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg
causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits
growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions

symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak

favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.

topic: Cauliflower Black Rot of Crucifers (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris)
problem_name: Black Rot of Crucifers
causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
affected_plant_parts: Leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots
growth_stage: Seedling stage through heading and root maturity
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): Diagnostic V-shaped bright yellow (chlorotic) blotches initiating at the leaf margins (with the point of the 'V' directed inward toward the midrib) that turn tan-brown and papery dry; holding the V-shaped lesion up to the light reveals a network of jet-blackened veins inside the yellow/tan wedge; slicing the petiole or main stem crosswise shows a black-brown vascular ring; infected cabbage and cauliflower heads often develop secondary foul-smelling bacterial soft rot.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesions on leaf margin, blackened veins inside yellow wedge, black vascular ring in stem, marginal leaf blight
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter water pores (hydathodes) along the leaf edges inside morning guttation droplets, moving inward down the xylem veins to form V-shaped wedges and eventually invading the main stem vascular system.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Alternaria Leaf Spot and Downy Mildew by the classic V-shaped yellow marginal wedges with jet-black veins inside the lesion (Verticillium Wilt also causes V-shaped marginal yellowing, but lacks the crisp jet-black vein network inside the leaf blade and occurs in cooler weather).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins)
risk_factors: Saved or untreated brassica seed, infected transplants, cruciferous weeds, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and working in wet beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–86°F) with heavy morning dew/guttation and splashing rain.
transmission_or_spread: Primarily seed-borne (even 1 infected seed in 10,000 can cause an epidemic in transplant trays); survives up to 2 years in unrotted brassica stalks and spreads by splashing water and equipment.
management_actions: Remove infected plants early; never work in brassica beds when leaves are wet with morning dew or guttation droplets; use drip irrigation; copper sprays offer only limited suppression once established.
prevention_actions: Plant certified pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed (122°F/50°C for 25 minutes for cabbage/broccoli/brussels sprouts; 15 minutes for cauliflower/kale/turnip/bok choy) and black-rot-tolerant cultivars; rotate out of all Brassicaceae for 3 years; chop and bury brassica stalks immediately after harvest so they decompose.
recommended_observations: Scout Cauliflower (leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather (77–86°F (25–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Rot of Crucifers from Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins).
severity_or_impact: High (most destructive bacterial disease of brassicas worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–86°F (25–30°C) and high humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Cauliflower Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.
recommended_observations: Scout Cauliflower (taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)) weekly during warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils (68–77°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Clubroot from Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (persists in soil for up to 20 years and prevents marketable head or root formation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (ph <6.5).
host_range: Documented on Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Cauliflower Downy Mildew (Pseudoperonospora cubensis)
problem_name: Downy Mildew
causal_agent: Pseudoperonospora cubensis (Cucurbits); Peronospora destructor (Alliums); Peronospora farinosa f. sp. spinaciae (Spinach); Bremia lactucae (Lettuce); Hyaloperonospora brassicae (Brassicas); Peronospora belbahrii (Basil); Peronospora viciae (Peas); Plasmopara viticola (Grape)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves (upper chlorotic lesions and lower sporangiophore growth); shoots and young clusters in grape
growth_stage: Vegetative rosette/vine growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-warm, wet, humid, overcast weather with heavy morning dew
temperature_range: 58–75°F (14–24°C) (up to 82°F for cucurbit and basil downy mildew)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>85–95% RH) and minimum 4–6 hours of free leaf wetness from dew, fog, or rain
visible_symptoms: On Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): Upper leaf surface develops bright yellow (or pale greenish-yellow in watermelon/basil) angular blotches strictly bounded and squared-off by the leaf veins (giving a 'checkerboard' or 'stained-glass' appearance in cucumber, lettuce, spinach, and basil); on the corresponding UNDERSIDE of the leaf during humid mornings, a diagnostic velvety purplish-gray, violet-brown, or dark gray-black fuzzy down of sporangia develops; leaves rapidly turn necrotic brown, curl upward, and die ('wildfire' canopy collapse).
symptom_keywords: angular yellow leaf spots bounded by veins, purplish-gray fuzzy growth on leaf underside, checkerboard yellow blotches, upward curling brown dead leaves
symptom_progression: Wind-borne sporangia germinate in morning dew films; angular yellow blotches appear in 4–7 days and rapidly coalesce into necrotic brown sheets that crisp the mid-canopy leaves while leaving petioles standing upright.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Powdery Mildew by angular vein-delimited yellow spots on the upper leaf surface and dark purplish-gray/violet-black fuzzy sporulation restricted strictly to the LOWER leaf surface (in Basil Downy Mildew, dark gray-purple fuzz underneath yellow vein-bounded leaf zones is often mistaken for nitrogen deficiency!).
similar_conditions: Powdery Mildew, Angular Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans), Nitrogen/Magnesium Deficiency, Alternaria Leaf Blight
risk_factors: Late-summer plantings (when airborne cucurbit downy mildew sporangia arrive on storm fronts), overhead irrigation, night/evening watering, and dense shaded foliage.
favorable_conditions: Overcast, humid weather with night/morning temperatures of 58–75°F and heavy dew or fog.
transmission_or_spread: Airborne sporangia travel hundreds of miles on wind currents (cucurbit downy mildew moves northward annually from frost-free overwintering zones; basil downy mildew can also be seed-borne; spinach/brassica/grape/allium species overwinter as oospores in debris).
management_actions: Water strictly in the early morning via drip irrigation so leaves never stay wet overnight; remove infected leaves early; check regional forecasts (cdm.ipmpipe.org) and apply copper or targeted oomycete fungicides preventatively when risky weather occurs.
prevention_actions: Plant downy-mildew-resistant (DMR) cultivars (e.g., DMR cucumbers 'DMR 401'/'Bristol', resistant spinach races, 'Prospera'/'Rutgers Devotion' basil); trellis vines and space widely in full sun for rapid morning dew evaporation.
recommended_observations: Scout Cauliflower (leaves (upper chlorotic lesions and lower sporangiophore growth); shoots and young clusters in grape) weekly during cool-to-warm, wet, humid, overcast weather with heavy morning dew (58–75°F (14–24°C) (up to 82°F for cucurbit and basil downy mildew)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Downy Mildew from Powdery Mildew, Angular Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans), Nitrogen/Magnesium Deficiency, Alternaria Leaf Blight.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (can defoliate cucumber, melon, spinach, or basil plantings in 7–10 days)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 58–75°F (14–24°C) (up to 82°F for cucurbit and basil downy mildew) and high relative humidity (>85–95% rh) and minimum 4–6 hours of free leaf wetness from dew, fog, or rain.

topic: Cauliflower White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Cauliflower (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) from Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stem girdling in beans/tomatoes, head drop in lettuce/cabbage, and storage rot in carrots)

knowledge_text: Cauliflower (Brassica oleracea var. botrytis) White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) is a fungal disease caused by Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor). Symptoms on cauliflower (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith. Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia). topic: Broccoli Aphids Management
problem_name: Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids)
causal_agent: Myzus persicae (Green Peach Aphid), Aphis gossypii (Melon/Cotton Aphid), Macrosiphum euphorbiae (Potato Aphid), Acyrthosiphon pisum (Pea Aphid), Aphis fabae (Black Bean Aphid), and Brevicoryne brassicae (Cabbage Aphid)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and flowering
season: Spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer)
humidity_conditions: Moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants)
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew.
symptom_keywords: soft pear-shaped insects under leaves, curled puckered shoot tips, sticky shiny honeydew, black sooty mold, white cast skins, ants tending stems
symptom_progression: Winged females (alates) land on succulent new shoots and give live birth parthenogenetically to nymphs that mature in 7–10 days, building dense colonies and transmitting non-persistent plant viruses within seconds of probing.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present).
similar_conditions: Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves)
risk_factors: Over-fertilization with high soluble nitrogen (which creates lush amino-acid-rich sap that accelerates aphid reproduction), broad-spectrum pyrethroid/carbamate insecticide sprays that kill ladybugs and parasitic wasps, ant tending, and greenhouse/indoors transplant carryover.
favorable_conditions: Mild temperatures (65–80°F) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth.
transmission_or_spread: Winged alate aphids disperse on wind currents from overwintering weeds, woody hosts (Prunus, Euonymus), or neighboring crops; ants also move aphids between plants.
management_actions: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides.
prevention_actions: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (direct stunting plus primary vector of CMV, PVY, PRSV, ZYMV, WMV, and BCMV)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–82°F (15–28°C) and moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants).

topic: Broccoli Armyworms Management
problem_name: Armyworms (Beet, Yellowstriped, Fall, and Southern Armyworms)
causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for fuzzy tan/white scale-covered egg masses and crush or clip them off before they hatch; spray Bacillus thuringiensis aizawai (Bt aizawai is substantially more effective against Spodoptera armyworms than Bt kurstaki!) or spinosad while caterpillars are small (<1/2 inch) and windowpaning.
prevention_actions: Keep beds free of pigweed (Amaranthus) and lambsquarters (preferred egg-laying hosts for Beet Armyworm); cover fall brassica and leafy green plantings with floating row covers.

severity_or_impact: High in late summer and fall
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather.

topic: Broccoli Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Broccoli Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Broccoli Flea Beetles Management

growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather

similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)

topic: Broccoli Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Broccoli Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes) twice weekly during cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights (45–75°F (7–24°C)); inspect for ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries to distinguish Slugs and Garden Snails from Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime).
severity_or_impact: High in cool, wet climates and on seedlings, lettuce, brassicas, and strawberries
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–75°F (7–24°C) and high humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds.

topic: Broccoli Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
affected_plant_parts: Developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.
symptom_keywords: shield-shaped green or brown bug, white bands on antennae of brown stink bug, cloudy yellow-white spots on ripe tomato and pepper skin, white spongy corky tissue under fruit skin, catfaced dimpled peaches and apples, black-and-orange harlequin bug with striped barrel eggs on kale
symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.
distinguishing_features: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug is identified by alternating light-and-dark bands on its antennae and along the flared rear edge of its abdomen (distinguishing it from beneficial predatory Rough Stink Bugs and Spined Soldier Bugs, which have pointed shoulder spines or thick piercing beaks); Harlequin Bug is unmistakable with its glossy black-and-fiery-orange shield and two-row clusters of black-and-white striped barrel eggs. Note: cloudy white spongy spots under tomato/pepper skin are Stink Bug feeding, NOT a fungal disease!
similar_conditions: Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface)
risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.
management_actions: Handpick adults, nymphs, and barrel-shaped egg clusters in the cool early morning by knocking them into a bucket of soapy water; cover high-value tomato, pepper, bean, and brassica beds with fine insect netting; vacuum Harlequin bugs off kale/collards.
prevention_actions: Plant a perimeter trap crop of early-maturing cowpeas/soybeans, sweet corn, or sunflowers (for green/brown stink bugs) or 'Cleome' spider flower / mustard greens (for Harlequin Bug) to intercept immigrating adults before they reach main crops; mow weedy borders BEFORE weeds go to seed.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for harlequin bug on brassicas)) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (70–92°F (21–33°C)); inspect for shield-shaped green or brown bug to distinguish Stink Bugs from Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface).
severity_or_impact: High (causes widespread 'cloudy spot' on tomatoes/peppers, catfacing on peaches/apples, shriveled beans/pecans, and severe scorching of kale/collards)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, sunny summer weather.

problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)

topic: Broccoli Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Broccoli Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Fertile, well-drained loam or silt loam rich in organic matter (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
soil_ph: 6.0–7.0 (6.8–7.2 if clubroot is a risk)
management_actions: Prepare a fertile, well-drained loam or silt loam rich in organic matter adjusted to pH 6.0–7.0 (6.8–7.2 if clubroot is a risk) based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Broccoli to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0 (6.8–7.2 if clubroot is a risk)) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Broccoli Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Broccoli Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)
problem_name: Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg
causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits
growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Small water-soaked translucent spots around wounds, insect holes, sunscald patches, or hollow stems that rapidly expand within 24–72 hours into a wet, slimy, mushy, cream-to-tan liquified collapse of the fleshy parenchyma tissue (while the outer epidermis remains intact like a water-filled bag until broken), accompanied by an unmistakable, putrid, foul fishy/sulfurous stench (in brassicas, onions, and potatoes); in Potato Blackleg, an inky jet-black slimy decay rises from the decaying seed piece up the lower 4–8 inches of the green stem, yellowing and rolling upper leaves.
symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak
risk_factors: Insect feeding wounds (cabbageworms, onion/cabbage maggots, corn borers, slugs), harvesting bruising, washing vegetables in warm unchlorinated water, boron/calcium deficiency (hollow stem), and dome-less flat broccoli heads holding rainwater.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.
prevention_actions: Control insect pests (cabbageworms, root maggots, borers) that create entry wounds; select domed broccoli cultivars that shed rainwater; plant whole uncut certified seed potatoes or cure cut seed pieces at 55–60°F and 85% RH for 3–5 days before planting in warmed (>50°F) well-drained soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits) weekly during warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg from Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (destroys marketable cabbage/broccoli heads, peppers, and stored potatoes, carrots, and onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions.
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Potato, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy, Chinese cabbage, Lettuce).

topic: Broccoli Black Rot of Crucifers (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris)
problem_name: Black Rot of Crucifers
causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
affected_plant_parts: Leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots
growth_stage: Seedling stage through heading and root maturity
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Diagnostic V-shaped bright yellow (chlorotic) blotches initiating at the leaf margins (with the point of the 'V' directed inward toward the midrib) that turn tan-brown and papery dry; holding the V-shaped lesion up to the light reveals a network of jet-blackened veins inside the yellow/tan wedge; slicing the petiole or main stem crosswise shows a black-brown vascular ring; infected cabbage and cauliflower heads often develop secondary foul-smelling bacterial soft rot.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesions on leaf margin, blackened veins inside yellow wedge, black vascular ring in stem, marginal leaf blight
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter water pores (hydathodes) along the leaf edges inside morning guttation droplets, moving inward down the xylem veins to form V-shaped wedges and eventually invading the main stem vascular system.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Alternaria Leaf Spot and Downy Mildew by the classic V-shaped yellow marginal wedges with jet-black veins inside the lesion (Verticillium Wilt also causes V-shaped marginal yellowing, but lacks the crisp jet-black vein network inside the leaf blade and occurs in cooler weather).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins)
risk_factors: Saved or untreated brassica seed, infected transplants, cruciferous weeds, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and working in wet beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–86°F) with heavy morning dew/guttation and splashing rain.
transmission_or_spread: Primarily seed-borne (even 1 infected seed in 10,000 can cause an epidemic in transplant trays); survives up to 2 years in unrotted brassica stalks and spreads by splashing water and equipment.
management_actions: Remove infected plants early; never work in brassica beds when leaves are wet with morning dew or guttation droplets; use drip irrigation; copper sprays offer only limited suppression once established.
prevention_actions: Plant certified pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed (122°F/50°C for 25 minutes for cabbage/broccoli/brussels sprouts; 15 minutes for cauliflower/kale/turnip/bok choy) and black-rot-tolerant cultivars; rotate out of all Brassicaceae for 3 years; chop and bury brassica stalks immediately after harvest so they decompose.

topic: Broccoli Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.

topic: Broccoli Downy Mildew (Pseudoperonospora cubensis)
problem_name: Downy Mildew
causal_agent: Pseudoperonospora cubensis (Cucurbits); Peronospora destructor (Alliums); Peronospora farinosa f. sp. spinaciae (Spinach); Bremia lactucae (Lettuce); Hyaloperonospora brassicae (Brassicas); Peronospora belbahrii (Basil); Peronospora viciae (Peas); Plasmopara viticola (Grape)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves (upper chlorotic lesions and lower sporangiophore growth); shoots and young clusters in grape
growth_stage: Vegetative rosette/vine growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-warm, wet, humid, overcast weather with heavy morning dew
temperature_range: 58–75°F (14–24°C) (up to 82°F for cucurbit and basil downy mildew)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>85–95% RH) and minimum 4–6 hours of free leaf wetness from dew, fog, or rain
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Upper leaf surface develops bright yellow (or pale greenish-yellow in watermelon/basil) angular blotches strictly bounded and squared-off by the leaf veins (giving a 'checkerboard' or 'stained-glass' appearance in cucumber, lettuce, spinach, and basil); on the corresponding UNDERSIDE of the leaf during humid mornings, a diagnostic velvety purplish-gray, violet-brown, or dark gray-black fuzzy down of sporangia develops; leaves rapidly turn necrotic brown, curl upward, and die ('wildfire' canopy collapse).
symptom_keywords: angular yellow leaf spots bounded by veins, purplish-gray fuzzy growth on leaf underside, checkerboard yellow blotches, upward curling brown dead leaves
symptom_progression: Wind-borne sporangia germinate in morning dew films; angular yellow blotches appear in 4–7 days and rapidly coalesce into necrotic brown sheets that crisp the mid-canopy leaves while leaving petioles standing upright.

similar_conditions: Powdery Mildew, Angular Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans), Nitrogen/Magnesium Deficiency, Alternaria Leaf Blight
risk_factors: Late-summer plantings (when airborne cucurbit downy mildew sporangia arrive on storm fronts), overhead irrigation, night/evening watering, and dense shaded foliage.
favorable_conditions: Overcast, humid weather with night/morning temperatures of 58–75°F and heavy dew or fog.
transmission_or_spread: Airborne sporangia travel hundreds of miles on wind currents (cucurbit downy mildew moves northward annually from frost-free overwintering zones; basil downy mildew can also be seed-borne; spinach/brassica/grape/allium species overwinter as oospores in debris).
management_actions: Water strictly in the early morning via drip irrigation so leaves never stay wet overnight; remove infected leaves early; check regional forecasts (cdm.ipmpipe.org) and apply copper or targeted oomycete fungicides preventatively when risky weather occurs.
prevention_actions: Plant downy-mildew-resistant (DMR) cultivars (e.g., DMR cucumbers 'DMR 401'/'Bristol', resistant spinach races, 'Prospera'/'Rutgers Devotion' basil); trellis vines and space widely in full sun for rapid morning dew evaporation.
