topic: Broccoli White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Broccoli (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) from Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stem girdling in beans/tomatoes, head drop in lettuce/cabbage, and storage rot in carrots)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours).
host_range: Documented on Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Soybean, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Broccoli (Brassica oleracea var. italica) Heat Stress ('Bubble Head', Uneven Bead Size & Bracting) of Broccoli: Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management

growth_stage: Floral dome initiation and sizing when temperatures exceed 85–90°F
season: Cool season (transplant in early spring 2–4 weeks before last frost, or in midsummer for fall harvest)

topic: Kale Armyworms Management
problem_name: Armyworms (Beet, Yellowstriped, Fall, and Southern Armyworms)
causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather

symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for fuzzy tan/white scale-covered egg masses and crush or clip them off before they hatch; spray Bacillus thuringiensis aizawai (Bt aizawai is substantially more effective against Spodoptera armyworms than Bt kurstaki!) or spinosad while caterpillars are small (<1/2 inch) and windowpaning.

severity_or_impact: High in late summer and fall
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather.

topic: Kale Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Kale Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Kale Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).

topic: Kale Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.

severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Kale Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes) twice weekly during cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights (45–75°F (7–24°C)); inspect for ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries to distinguish Slugs and Garden Snails from Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime).
severity_or_impact: High in cool, wet climates and on seedlings, lettuce, brassicas, and strawberries
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–75°F (7–24°C) and high humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds.

topic: Kale Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
affected_plant_parts: Developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.
symptom_keywords: shield-shaped green or brown bug, white bands on antennae of brown stink bug, cloudy yellow-white spots on ripe tomato and pepper skin, white spongy corky tissue under fruit skin, catfaced dimpled peaches and apples, black-and-orange harlequin bug with striped barrel eggs on kale
symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.
distinguishing_features: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug is identified by alternating light-and-dark bands on its antennae and along the flared rear edge of its abdomen (distinguishing it from beneficial predatory Rough Stink Bugs and Spined Soldier Bugs, which have pointed shoulder spines or thick piercing beaks); Harlequin Bug is unmistakable with its glossy black-and-fiery-orange shield and two-row clusters of black-and-white striped barrel eggs. Note: cloudy white spongy spots under tomato/pepper skin are Stink Bug feeding, NOT a fungal disease!
similar_conditions: Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface)
risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.
management_actions: Handpick adults, nymphs, and barrel-shaped egg clusters in the cool early morning by knocking them into a bucket of soapy water; cover high-value tomato, pepper, bean, and brassica beds with fine insect netting; vacuum Harlequin bugs off kale/collards.
prevention_actions: Plant a perimeter trap crop of early-maturing cowpeas/soybeans, sweet corn, or sunflowers (for green/brown stink bugs) or 'Cleome' spider flower / mustard greens (for Harlequin Bug) to intercept immigrating adults before they reach main crops; mow weedy borders BEFORE weeds go to seed.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for harlequin bug on brassicas)) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (70–92°F (21–33°C)); inspect for shield-shaped green or brown bug to distinguish Stink Bugs from Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface).
severity_or_impact: High (causes widespread 'cloudy spot' on tomatoes/peppers, catfacing on peaches/apples, shriveled beans/pecans, and severe scorching of kale/collards)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, sunny summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Okra, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea).

topic: Kale Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

Visible signs and feeding damage on kale (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit. topic: Kale Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)
problem_name: Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg
causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits
growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Small water-soaked translucent spots around wounds, insect holes, sunscald patches, or hollow stems that rapidly expand within 24–72 hours into a wet, slimy, mushy, cream-to-tan liquified collapse of the fleshy parenchyma tissue (while the outer epidermis remains intact like a water-filled bag until broken), accompanied by an unmistakable, putrid, foul fishy/sulfurous stench (in brassicas, onions, and potatoes); in Potato Blackleg, an inky jet-black slimy decay rises from the decaying seed piece up the lower 4–8 inches of the green stem, yellowing and rolling upper leaves.
symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak
risk_factors: Insect feeding wounds (cabbageworms, onion/cabbage maggots, corn borers, slugs), harvesting bruising, washing vegetables in warm unchlorinated water, boron/calcium deficiency (hollow stem), and dome-less flat broccoli heads holding rainwater.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.
prevention_actions: Control insect pests (cabbageworms, root maggots, borers) that create entry wounds; select domed broccoli cultivars that shed rainwater; plant whole uncut certified seed potatoes or cure cut seed pieces at 55–60°F and 85% RH for 3–5 days before planting in warmed (>50°F) well-drained soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits) weekly during warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg from Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (destroys marketable cabbage/broccoli heads, peppers, and stored potatoes, carrots, and onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions.
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Potato, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy, Chinese cabbage, Lettuce).

topic: Kale Black Rot of Crucifers (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris)
problem_name: Black Rot of Crucifers
causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
affected_plant_parts: Leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots
growth_stage: Seedling stage through heading and root maturity
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Diagnostic V-shaped bright yellow (chlorotic) blotches initiating at the leaf margins (with the point of the 'V' directed inward toward the midrib) that turn tan-brown and papery dry; holding the V-shaped lesion up to the light reveals a network of jet-blackened veins inside the yellow/tan wedge; slicing the petiole or main stem crosswise shows a black-brown vascular ring; infected cabbage and cauliflower heads often develop secondary foul-smelling bacterial soft rot.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesions on leaf margin, blackened veins inside yellow wedge, black vascular ring in stem, marginal leaf blight
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter water pores (hydathodes) along the leaf edges inside morning guttation droplets, moving inward down the xylem veins to form V-shaped wedges and eventually invading the main stem vascular system.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Alternaria Leaf Spot and Downy Mildew by the classic V-shaped yellow marginal wedges with jet-black veins inside the lesion (Verticillium Wilt also causes V-shaped marginal yellowing, but lacks the crisp jet-black vein network inside the leaf blade and occurs in cooler weather).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins)
risk_factors: Saved or untreated brassica seed, infected transplants, cruciferous weeds, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and working in wet beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–86°F) with heavy morning dew/guttation and splashing rain.
transmission_or_spread: Primarily seed-borne (even 1 infected seed in 10,000 can cause an epidemic in transplant trays); survives up to 2 years in unrotted brassica stalks and spreads by splashing water and equipment.
management_actions: Remove infected plants early; never work in brassica beds when leaves are wet with morning dew or guttation droplets; use drip irrigation; copper sprays offer only limited suppression once established.
prevention_actions: Plant certified pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed (122°F/50°C for 25 minutes for cabbage/broccoli/brussels sprouts; 15 minutes for cauliflower/kale/turnip/bok choy) and black-rot-tolerant cultivars; rotate out of all Brassicaceae for 3 years; chop and bury brassica stalks immediately after harvest so they decompose.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather (77–86°F (25–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Rot of Crucifers from Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins).
severity_or_impact: High (most destructive bacterial disease of brassicas worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–86°F (25–30°C) and high humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Kale Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.
recommended_observations: Scout Kale (taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)) weekly during warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils (68–77°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Clubroot from Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (persists in soil for up to 20 years and prevents marketable head or root formation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (ph <6.5).
host_range: Documented on Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Kale Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
problem_name: Fusarium Wilt
causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum (host-specific formae speciales: f. sp. lycopersici, melongenae, tuberosi, niveum, melonis, cucumerinum, conglutinans, cepae, pisi, phaseoli, spinaciae, basilici, cubense)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding
visible_symptoms: On Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): Bright yellowing (chlorosis) and drooping of older lower leaves—classically starting on ONLY ONE SIDE of a leaf, one branch, or one side of the plant ('one-sided flagging')—which wilts during warm afternoons and eventually fails to recover at night; slicing the lower main stem or petiole lengthwise reveals a diagnostic reddish-brown to dark-brown discoloration of the water-conducting vascular ring while the central pith remains healthy.
symptom_keywords: one-sided yellowing, unilateral wilting, vascular browning, reddish-brown xylem ring, lower leaf yellowing, daytime wilting, stunted growth
symptom_progression: Fungus enters root tips or nematode wounds and colonizes xylem vessels; lower leaves yellow and wilt unilaterally, progressing upward until entire shoots brown, collapse, and die without soft stem rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity
risk_factors: Acidic sandy soils (pH <6.0), root-knot nematode infestations creating root entry wounds, high ammonium-nitrogen fertilization, and replanting susceptible cultivars in infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (80–90°F) and moisture stress during fruiting.
transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.

water_requirement: 1.0–1.5 inches per week; uniform soil moisture keeps leaves tender and succulent
management_actions: Supply 1.0–1.5 inches per week; uniform soil moisture keeps leaves tender and succulent. Apply water directly to the root zone using drip irrigation or soaker hoses in the morning so any wet foliage dries rapidly.
prevention_actions: Avoid both acute drought stress (which stunts growth, drops blossoms, and impairs quality) and chronic overwatering/waterlogging (which suffocates feeder roots and promotes root/crown rots); avoid overhead watering late in the day.
recommended_observations: Check soil moisture at a 2–4 inch depth before irrigating and monitor plants during peak transpiration and reproductive fill stages.
knowledge_text: Water and irrigation requirements for Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala): 1.0–1.5 inches per week; uniform soil moisture keeps leaves tender and succulent. Drip or soil-level irrigation combined with organic mulch conserves soil moisture and reduces foliar disease pressure.

topic: Radish Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Radish (Raphanus sativus): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Radish (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Radish (Raphanus sativus, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Radish Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Radish (Raphanus sativus): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).
recommended_observations: Scout Radish (cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of potato, sweetpotato, and striped flea beetles)) twice weekly during spring through mid-summer (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves to distinguish Flea Beetles from Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass).
severity_or_impact: High on seedlings and young eggplant, radish, bok choy, arugula, turnip, and mustard greens
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny, dry spring weather.
host_range: Documented on Radish (Raphanus sativus, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Eggplant, Potato, Tomato, Pepper, Radish, Turnip, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Radish Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Radish (Raphanus sativus): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Radish (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Radish (Raphanus sativus, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Radish Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs Management
problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests
causal_agent: Cylas formicarius (Sweetpotato Weevil), Conoderus / Melanotus / Limonius spp. (Wireworms - Click Beetle larvae), and Phyllophaga / Popillia / Cyclocephala spp. (White Grubs - Scarab Beetle larvae)
affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Radish (Raphanus sativus): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).
recommended_observations: Scout Radish (underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds) twice weekly during spring planting through autumn harvest (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil to distinguish Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs from Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod).
host_range: Documented on Radish (Raphanus sativus, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet potato, Potato, Carrot, Beet, Radish, Turnip, Parsnip, Onion).

knowledge_subtype: Pruning, Staking, Mulching, Thinning & Routine Care
topic: Radish Routine Garden Maintenance, Pruning, Support, and Weed Management
growth_stage: Established vegetative growth through harvest
management_actions: Thin crowded seedlings promptly as soon as cotyledons expand—crowded radishes fail to bulb and form only thin stringy roots
prevention_actions: Cultivate shallowly around plants to avoid severing surface feeder roots, keep mulch pulled slightly back from direct stem contact where crown rot is a risk, and sanitize pruning tools between plants.
recommended_observations: Check Radish weekly for structural support needs, weed competition, mulch depth, and pollinator activity.
knowledge_text: Routine maintenance and cultural care for Radish (Raphanus sativus): Thin crowded seedlings promptly as soon as cotyledons expand—crowded radishes fail to bulb and form only thin stringy roots.

knowledge_subtype: Soil Texture, pH, Drainage & Bed Preparation
topic: Radish Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Loose, friable, stone-free sandy loam or silt loam; heavy or crusted soil causes misshapen roots (Extension soil texture tags: Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage)
management_actions: Prepare a loose, friable, stone-free sandy loam or silt loam; heavy or crusted soil causes misshapen roots adjusted to pH 6.0–7.0 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Radish to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Radish (Raphanus sativus): Prefers loose, friable, stone-free sandy loam or silt loam; heavy or crusted soil causes misshapen roots with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–7.0. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.
secondary_source_name: Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden
evidence_notes: Soil texture, drainage, and pH requirements verified against University of Maryland Extension (HGIC) and Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden.

topic: Radish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Radish (Raphanus sativus): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Radish (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) from Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.
host_range: Documented on Radish (Raphanus sativus, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

Symptoms on radish (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks. Distinguishing features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
