topic: Carrot Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).

topic: Carrot Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.

topic: Carrot Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)
problem_name: Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg
causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits
growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): Small water-soaked translucent spots around wounds, insect holes, sunscald patches, or hollow stems that rapidly expand within 24–72 hours into a wet, slimy, mushy, cream-to-tan liquified collapse of the fleshy parenchyma tissue (while the outer epidermis remains intact like a water-filled bag until broken), accompanied by an unmistakable, putrid, foul fishy/sulfurous stench (in brassicas, onions, and potatoes); in Potato Blackleg, an inky jet-black slimy decay rises from the decaying seed piece up the lower 4–8 inches of the green stem, yellowing and rolling upper leaves.
symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak
risk_factors: Insect feeding wounds (cabbageworms, onion/cabbage maggots, corn borers, slugs), harvesting bruising, washing vegetables in warm unchlorinated water, boron/calcium deficiency (hollow stem), and dome-less flat broccoli heads holding rainwater.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.
prevention_actions: Control insect pests (cabbageworms, root maggots, borers) that create entry wounds; select domed broccoli cultivars that shed rainwater; plant whole uncut certified seed potatoes or cure cut seed pieces at 55–60°F and 85% RH for 3–5 days before planting in warmed (>50°F) well-drained soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Carrot (fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits) weekly during warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg from Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (destroys marketable cabbage/broccoli heads, peppers, and stored potatoes, carrots, and onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions.

topic: Carrot Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking) (Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum)
problem_name: Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking)
causal_agent: Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum
affected_plant_parts: Taproot tip (young seedlings) and mature taproot periderm/cortex
growth_stage: Seedling taproot elongation (Forking) and mid-to-late root sizing (Cavity Spot)
season: Cool, wet, poorly drained soil conditions
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture, compacted beds, or delayed harvest in wet autumn soils
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): Two distinct syndromes caused by the same soil-borne Pythium species: (1) Cavity Spot on mature carrots/parsnips: small, sunken, elliptical, horizontal (crosswise) greyish-brown to dark craters/cavities (1/8 to 1/2 inch wide) scattered along the side of an otherwise normal-sized taproot where the outer skin collapses over a shallow subsurface pocket; (2) Pythium Root Dieback: when Pythium kills the delicate apical meristem tip of a 1-to-3-week-old seedling taproot, the root loses apical dominance and splits into multiple 'forked', 'stubbed', or 'fanged' roots.
symptom_keywords: sunken horizontal elliptical pits on carrot root, crosswise root cavities, forked fanged taproots, stubbed stunted carrots, completely healthy green tops
symptom_progression: In spring, Pythium zoospores nip the young primary root tip causing forking; later in summer/autumn, infections along the secondary root emergence sites of the maturing taproot form sunken horizontal cavities under the periderm.
distinguishing_features: Cavity Spot is distinguished by horizontal (crosswise) elliptical sunken lesions with tattered skin margins and no insect tunnels inside (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots leave winding rust-colored tunnels filled with frass).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot tunnels, Root-Knot Nematode (round bead-like galls on lateral roots), Streptomyces Common Scab (raised corky warts in dry alkaline soil)
risk_factors: Poorly drained or compacted soils, over-irrigation, high soil nitrogen, growing carrots repeatedly in the same bed, and leaving mature carrots in wet soil too long in autumn.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate (59–68°F), wet soils.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oomycetes surviving as thick-walled oospores in soil and spreading via swimming zoospores in saturated soil pores.
management_actions: Harvest carrots and parsnips promptly once they reach marketable maturity rather than holding them in wet fall beds; avoid overwatering once roots size up.
prevention_actions: Grow carrots and parsnips on deep (10–12 inch) raised beds for rapid drainage; maintain soil pH around 6.5–6.8; plant Cavity-Spot-tolerant carrot hybrids (such as 'Bolero' or 'Napoli'); rotate out of umbellifers for 3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Carrot (taproot tip (young seedlings) and mature taproot periderm/cortex) weekly during cool, wet, poorly drained soil conditions (55–70°F (13–21°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking) from Carrot Rust Fly Maggot tunnels, Root-Knot Nematode (round bead-like galls on lateral roots), Streptomyces Common Scab (raised corky warts in dry alkaline soil).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (mars root appearance and causes severe taproot forking)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–70°F (13–21°C) and high soil moisture, compacted beds, or delayed harvest in wet autumn soils.
host_range: Documented on Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Parsnip, Beet, Radish, Turnip).

topic: Carrot Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.

symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (ruins marketable leaves on Swiss chard and spinach and weakens beet, carrot, and pepper plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh) and warm summer rains or overhead watering.

topic: Carrot Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato (Streptomyces scabies)
problem_name: Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato
causal_agent: Streptomyces scabies (Common Scab - filamentous bacterium) and Rhizoctonia solani (Black Scurf)
affected_plant_parts: Underground tubers, stolons, stems, and swollen storage roots
growth_stage: Tuber initiation and early bulking (first 3–5 weeks after stolon tips swell)
season: Warm, dry soil conditions during early summer tuber set
humidity_conditions: Dry soil during the 4-week window of tuber initiation (for Common Scab); cool wet spring soil (for Black Scurf)
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): Common Scab: circular-to-irregular, rough, raised corky brown wart-like crusts ('russet/superficial scab') or sunken crater-like corky pits ('pitted scab') up to 1/4 inch deep on the skin of potato tubers, beets, radishes, and turnips (with normal healthy above-ground foliage!); Black Scurf: hard, irregular, coal-black crusty specks on the potato tuber skin resembling dried bits of soil that will NOT wash off ('the dirt that won't wash off'), plus reddish-brown sunken cankers on underground sprouts in spring.
symptom_keywords: rough corky scabs on potato skin, sunken corky tuber pits, black scurf specks that won't wash off, reddish-brown underground stem cankers
symptom_progression: Streptomyces invades young tubers exclusively through immature unsuberized lenticels during the first 3–5 weeks of tuberization when soil is dry and pH is above 5.5; tubers remain completely edible once peeled.
distinguishing_features: Common Scab forms tan-brown corky raised or pitted skin lesions; Black Scurf forms jet-black superficial sclerotia crusts that look like tar or dried dirt stuck to the skin.
similar_conditions: Powdery Scab (Spongospora subterranea - forms small volcano-like pustules in cool wet soil), Colorado Potato Beetle/Wireworm holes, Physiological Enlarged Lenticels (white puffy dots in wet soil)
risk_factors: Soil pH above 5.5–6.0 (liming or applying wood ashes before potatoes/beets), applying fresh animal manure, dry soil during early tuber set, and planting scabby seed tubers.
favorable_conditions: Soil pH 5.8–7.8 combined with dry soil during the 4 weeks following stolon tip swelling.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne actinomycete/fungus and tuber-borne on infected seed potatoes.
management_actions: Keep soil consistently moist (near field capacity) during the critical 4–6 week window of tuber initiation (starting when stolon tips begin to swell, just before bloom)—moisture encourages beneficial antagonistic bacteria on lenticels that block Streptomyces!
prevention_actions: Maintain potato soil pH between 5.0 and 5.5 (never apply lime, wood ash, or fresh manure before planting potatoes); plant only certified scab-free seed tubers and scab-resistant cultivars (such as 'Superior', 'Norland', 'Chieftain', 'Russet Burbank', 'Goldrush').

topic: Carrot Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)

causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)

management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.

topic: Carrot Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Carrot (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).

topic: Carrot White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Carrot (Daucus carota subsp. sativus): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Carrot (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) from Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stem girdling in beans/tomatoes, head drop in lettuce/cabbage, and storage rot in carrots)

causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. Beet Armyworm is olive-green with a prominent black spot on the thorax above the second pair of true legs; Yellowstriped Armyworm is velvety gray-black with two bright yellow-orange dorsal stripes and black triangular markings; Fall Armyworm has a prominent white inverted 'Y' suture on its dark head capsule and four black dots arranged in a square on the 8th abdominal segment.
symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for fuzzy tan/white scale-covered egg masses and crush or clip them off before they hatch; spray Bacillus thuringiensis aizawai (Bt aizawai is substantially more effective against Spodoptera armyworms than Bt kurstaki!) or spinosad while caterpillars are small (<1/2 inch) and windowpaning.
prevention_actions: Keep beds free of pigweed (Amaranthus) and lambsquarters (preferred egg-laying hosts for Beet Armyworm); cover fall brassica and leafy green plantings with floating row covers.
recommended_observations: Scout Beet (whorl leaves (sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves to distinguish Armyworms from Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms.
severity_or_impact: High in late summer and fall
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather.

topic: Beet Cutworms Management

causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)

growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils

transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.

topic: Beet Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny, dry spring weather.

topic: Beet Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Beet (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Beet (Beta vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Beet Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)
causal_agent: Liriomyza sativae (Vegetable Leafminer), Liriomyza trifolii (American Serpentine Leafminer), and Pegomya hyoscyami (Spinach / Beet Leafminer)
affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering
risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.
management_actions: On Spinach, Swiss Chard, and Beets: flip leaves twice weekly to rub off the neat rows of chalk-white eggs on the underside BEFORE they hatch, and pinch/clip off any mined blotch leaves immediately (note: contact sprays like soapcannot reach maggots hidden inside the leaf epidermis, though spinosad and azadirachtin/neem have translaminar activity that penetrates into mines!); on Tomatoes, Beans, and Cucurbits, simply avoid broad-spectrum sprays so native Diglyphus parasitic wasps naturally suppress serpentine mines.
prevention_actions: Cover spinach, Swiss chard, and beet beds with floating row covers or fine insect netting from seeding through harvest (in beds rotated away from last year's chenopods); eradicate lambsquarters (Chenopodium album) weeds around the garden.

severity_or_impact: High on spinach, Swiss chard, and beet greens (blotch mines ruin edible leaves); Low to Moderate on fruiting crops unless natural enemies are killed
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and mild-to-warm weather.
host_range: Documented on Beet (Beta vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Spinach, Swiss chard, Beet, Amaranth, Lettuce, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests
causal_agent: Cylas formicarius (Sweetpotato Weevil), Conoderus / Melanotus / Limonius spp. (Wireworms - Click Beetle larvae), and Phyllophaga / Popillia / Cyclocephala spp. (White Grubs - Scarab Beetle larvae)
affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)

topic: Beet Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

knowledge_subtype: Soil Texture, pH, Drainage & Bed Preparation
topic: Beet Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Loose, friable, well-drained loam or sandy loam free of crusting (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
soil_ph: 6.2–7.0 (beets are highly sensitive to acidic soils below pH 6.0, where growth stunts severely)
management_actions: Prepare a loose, friable, well-drained loam or sandy loam free of crusting adjusted to pH 6.2–7.0 (beets are highly sensitive to acidic soils below pH 6.0, where growth stunts severely) based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Beet to verify soil pH (6.2–7.0 (beets are highly sensitive to acidic soils below pH 6.0, where growth stunts severely)) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Beet (Beta vulgaris): Prefers loose, friable, well-drained loam or sandy loam free of crusting with an optimal soil pH of 6.2–7.0 (beets are highly sensitive to acidic soils below pH 6.0, where growth stunts severely). topic: Beet Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking) (Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum)
problem_name: Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking)
causal_agent: Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum
affected_plant_parts: Taproot tip (young seedlings) and mature taproot periderm/cortex
growth_stage: Seedling taproot elongation (Forking) and mid-to-late root sizing (Cavity Spot)
season: Cool, wet, poorly drained soil conditions
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture, compacted beds, or delayed harvest in wet autumn soils
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Two distinct syndromes caused by the same soil-borne Pythium species: (1) Cavity Spot on mature carrots/parsnips: small, sunken, elliptical, horizontal (crosswise) greyish-brown to dark craters/cavities (1/8 to 1/2 inch wide) scattered along the side of an otherwise normal-sized taproot where the outer skin collapses over a shallow subsurface pocket; (2) Pythium Root Dieback: when Pythium kills the delicate apical meristem tip of a 1-to-3-week-old seedling taproot, the root loses apical dominance and splits into multiple 'forked', 'stubbed', or 'fanged' roots.
symptom_keywords: sunken horizontal elliptical pits on carrot root, crosswise root cavities, forked fanged taproots, stubbed stunted carrots, completely healthy green tops
symptom_progression: In spring, Pythium zoospores nip the young primary root tip causing forking; later in summer/autumn, infections along the secondary root emergence sites of the maturing taproot form sunken horizontal cavities under the periderm.
distinguishing_features: Cavity Spot is distinguished by horizontal (crosswise) elliptical sunken lesions with tattered skin margins and no insect tunnels inside (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots leave winding rust-colored tunnels filled with frass).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot tunnels, Root-Knot Nematode (round bead-like galls on lateral roots), Streptomyces Common Scab (raised corky warts in dry alkaline soil)
risk_factors: Poorly drained or compacted soils, over-irrigation, high soil nitrogen, growing carrots repeatedly in the same bed, and leaving mature carrots in wet soil too long in autumn.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate (59–68°F), wet soils.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oomycetes surviving as thick-walled oospores in soil and spreading via swimming zoospores in saturated soil pores.
management_actions: Harvest carrots and parsnips promptly once they reach marketable maturity rather than holding them in wet fall beds; avoid overwatering once roots size up.
prevention_actions: Grow carrots and parsnips on deep (10–12 inch) raised beds for rapid drainage; maintain soil pH around 6.5–6.8; plant Cavity-Spot-tolerant carrot hybrids (such as 'Bolero' or 'Napoli'); rotate out of umbellifers for 3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Beet (taproot tip (young seedlings) and mature taproot periderm/cortex) weekly during cool, wet, poorly drained soil conditions (55–70°F (13–21°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking) from Carrot Rust Fly Maggot tunnels, Root-Knot Nematode (round bead-like galls on lateral roots), Streptomyces Common Scab (raised corky warts in dry alkaline soil).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (mars root appearance and causes severe taproot forking)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–70°F (13–21°C) and high soil moisture, compacted beds, or delayed harvest in wet autumn soils.
host_range: Documented on Beet (Beta vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Parsnip, Beet, Radish, Turnip).

Distinguishing features: Cavity Spot is distinguished by horizontal (crosswise) elliptical sunken lesions with tattered skin margins and no insect tunnels inside (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots leave winding rust-colored tunnels filled with frass). Favored by cool-to-moderate (59–68°f), wet soils. (55–70°F (13–21°C)). topic: Beet Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.
recommended_observations: Scout Beet (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cercospora Leaf Spot from Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (ruins marketable leaves on Swiss chard and spinach and weakens beet, carrot, and pepper plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh) and warm summer rains or overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Beet (Beta vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beet, Swiss chard, Spinach, Amaranth, Carrot, Celery, Parsley, Pepper).
knowledge_text: Beet (Beta vulgaris) Cercospora Leaf Spot is a fungal disease caused by Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes). Symptoms on beet (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves. Distinguishing features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches). Favored by warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°f) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness. (75–90°F (24–32°C)). Management and prevention: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants. Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.

topic: Beet Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato (Streptomyces scabies)
problem_name: Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato
causal_agent: Streptomyces scabies (Common Scab - filamentous bacterium) and Rhizoctonia solani (Black Scurf)
affected_plant_parts: Underground tubers, stolons, stems, and swollen storage roots
growth_stage: Tuber initiation and early bulking (first 3–5 weeks after stolon tips swell)
season: Warm, dry soil conditions during early summer tuber set

topic: Beet Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury

favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.

management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.

topic: Beet Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Beet (Beta vulgaris): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Beet (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Beet (Beta vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).

topic: Beet (Beta vulgaris) Boron (B) Deficiency ('Black Spot' / Internal Corky Rings & Crown Heart Rot): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Boron (B) Deficiency ('Black Spot' / Internal Corky Rings & Crown Heart Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy beet taproot interior/surface and youngest central crown leaves
growth_stage: Mid-to-late taproot bulking
season: Cool season (direct sow in spring 3–4 weeks before last frost, and in late summer 8–10 weeks before first fall frost)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 60–70°F (15–21°C); high heat (>85°F) combined with drought causes alternating white and red internal rings ('zoning') and woody texture; prolonged cold (<45°F for 2+ weeks) on young plants can induce bolting

visible_symptoms: Youngest central heart leaves turn dark red-black, twisted, and die back ('heart rot'), while the enlarging taproot develops hard, dry, black or dark-brown corky necrotic zones arranged in concentric rings inside the root flesh ('internal black spot') and rough, cracked, black cankered patches on the outer root shoulder.
symptom_keywords: beet, boron (b) deficiency, immobile in phloem in most garden crops (transported passively via xylem transpiration), fleshy beet taproot interior/surface and youngest central crown leaves, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Apical meristems, young expanding heart leaves, fleshy pith of stems and storage roots, floral buds, and developing curds or fruits. Boron deficiency arrests meristematic growth in the crown bud and cambial rings of the beet root, producing dead corky internal pockets and surface cracks.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Immobile in phloem in most garden crops (transported passively via xylem transpiration). Dry, hard, black corky pockets inside the concentric cambial rings of the beet root along with dead central heart leaves are diagnostic of Boron deficiency (beats have one of the highest boron requirements of any garden vegetable).
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Beet.
risk_factors: Leached sandy soils low in organic matter, alkaline or recently over-limed soils (pH > 7.0) where boric acid adsorbs onto clay/hydroxide surfaces, or prolonged summer drought that halts mass-flow transport of boric acid (H3BO3) to roots.

growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather

topic: Sweet potato Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs Management
problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests
causal_agent: Cylas formicarius (Sweetpotato Weevil), Conoderus / Melanotus / Limonius spp. (Wireworms - Click Beetle larvae), and Phyllophaga / Popillia / Cyclocephala spp. (White Grubs - Scarab Beetle larvae)
affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod).
host_range: Documented on Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas, Convolvulaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet potato, Potato, Carrot, Beet, Radish, Turnip, Parsnip, Onion).

topic: Sweet potato Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Sweet potato (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).
severity_or_impact: High (causes direct sap depletion, sooty mold, Squash Silverleaf, irregular tomato ripening, and transmits Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus and Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas, Convolvulaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).
