topic: Lettuce Downy Mildew (Pseudoperonospora cubensis)
problem_name: Downy Mildew
causal_agent: Pseudoperonospora cubensis (Cucurbits); Peronospora destructor (Alliums); Peronospora farinosa f. sp. spinaciae (Spinach); Bremia lactucae (Lettuce); Hyaloperonospora brassicae (Brassicas); Peronospora belbahrii (Basil); Peronospora viciae (Peas); Plasmopara viticola (Grape)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves (upper chlorotic lesions and lower sporangiophore growth); shoots and young clusters in grape
growth_stage: Vegetative rosette/vine growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-warm, wet, humid, overcast weather with heavy morning dew
temperature_range: 58–75°F (14–24°C) (up to 82°F for cucurbit and basil downy mildew)
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>85–95% RH) and minimum 4–6 hours of free leaf wetness from dew, fog, or rain
visible_symptoms: On Lettuce (Lactuca sativa): Upper leaf surface develops bright yellow (or pale greenish-yellow in watermelon/basil) angular blotches strictly bounded and squared-off by the leaf veins (giving a 'checkerboard' or 'stained-glass' appearance in cucumber, lettuce, spinach, and basil); on the corresponding UNDERSIDE of the leaf during humid mornings, a diagnostic velvety purplish-gray, violet-brown, or dark gray-black fuzzy down of sporangia develops; leaves rapidly turn necrotic brown, curl upward, and die ('wildfire' canopy collapse).
symptom_keywords: angular yellow leaf spots bounded by veins, purplish-gray fuzzy growth on leaf underside, checkerboard yellow blotches, upward curling brown dead leaves
symptom_progression: Wind-borne sporangia germinate in morning dew films; angular yellow blotches appear in 4–7 days and rapidly coalesce into necrotic brown sheets that crisp the mid-canopy leaves while leaving petioles standing upright.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Powdery Mildew by angular vein-delimited yellow spots on the upper leaf surface and dark purplish-gray/violet-black fuzzy sporulation restricted strictly to the LOWER leaf surface (in Basil Downy Mildew, dark gray-purple fuzz underneath yellow vein-bounded leaf zones is often mistaken for nitrogen deficiency!).
similar_conditions: Powdery Mildew, Angular Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans), Nitrogen/Magnesium Deficiency, Alternaria Leaf Blight
risk_factors: Late-summer plantings (when airborne cucurbit downy mildew sporangia arrive on storm fronts), overhead irrigation, night/evening watering, and dense shaded foliage.
favorable_conditions: Overcast, humid weather with night/morning temperatures of 58–75°F and heavy dew or fog.
transmission_or_spread: Airborne sporangia travel hundreds of miles on wind currents (cucurbit downy mildew moves northward annually from frost-free overwintering zones; basil downy mildew can also be seed-borne; spinach/brassica/grape/allium species overwinter as oospores in debris).
management_actions: Water strictly in the early morning via drip irrigation so leaves never stay wet overnight; remove infected leaves early; check regional forecasts (cdm.ipmpipe.org) and apply copper or targeted oomycete fungicides preventatively when risky weather occurs.
prevention_actions: Plant downy-mildew-resistant (DMR) cultivars (e.g., DMR cucumbers 'DMR 401'/'Bristol', resistant spinach races, 'Prospera'/'Rutgers Devotion' basil); trellis vines and space widely in full sun for rapid morning dew evaporation.

topic: Lettuce Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Lettuce (Lactuca sativa): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').
symptom_keywords: fuzzy brownish-gray mold, dusty spore masses, stem pruning wound canker, blossom blight, berry gray rot, ghost spot rings on tomato
symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.

risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.
recommended_observations: Scout Lettuce (senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits) weekly during cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) from Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight.
severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, brambles, grapes, and high-tunnel tomatoes (major pre- and post-harvest fruit loss)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh), fog, rain, and poor air circulation.
host_range: Documented on Lettuce (Lactuca sativa, Asteraceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Grape, Blueberry).

topic: Lettuce Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce (Septoria apiicola)
problem_name: Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce
causal_agent: Septoria apiicola (Celery/Parsley Late Blight) and Septoria lactucae (Lettuce Septoria Leaf Spot)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (stalks)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% RH)
visible_symptoms: On Lettuce (Lactuca sativa): Small, chlorotic yellow flecks on older outer leaves that expand into irregular-to-circular reddish-brown or tan necrotic spots (1/8 to 1/2 inch) heavily peppered with dozens of tiny, dark-brown to black, pinhead-sized pycnidia (spore-fruiting bodies) visible even before the tissue dies; on celery and parsley, lesions spread onto the fleshy petioles (stalks) and coalesce to blight and scorch entire outer leaves.
symptom_keywords: tan-brown leaf spots peppered with tiny black pycnidia dots, blighted celery stalks, outer leaf scorching, yellow-haloed spots
symptom_progression: Seed-borne or debris-borne pycnidia extrude gelatinous tendrils (cirrhi) of spores when wet; rain and sprinklers splash spores across rows, blighting foliage every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified under a hand lens by the numerous tiny black pycnidia dots embedded directly inside the tan/brown leaf and petiole spots (distinguishing it from Cercospora Leaf Spot, which has larger ashy-gray spots WITHOUT black pycnidia dots, and Bacterial Leaf Spot, which has dark greasy water-soaked spots without pycnidia).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii)
risk_factors: Infected seed (primary source in celery and parsley!), overhead watering, working in beds when foliage is wet, and <2-year rotations.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate temperatures (60–75°F) with frequent rain or sprinkler wetting.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne (spores survive up to 2 years in celery seed coats) and residue-borne; spread by rain splash, sprinklers, workers, and tools.
management_actions: Use drip irrigation only and never walk through or harvest parsley, celery, or lettuce while foliage is wet; strip and destroy spotted outer leaves.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed or treat celery/parsley seed with hot water (118–122°F / 48–50°C for 30 minutes) or use 3-year-old celery seed (after 3 years in storage, seed-borne Septoria fungi die out while celery seed remains viable!); rotate Apiaceae and Lettuce crops for 2–3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Lettuce (leaves and petioles (stalks)) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce from Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (renders celery stalks, parsley bunches, and romaine lettuce unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% rh).

topic: Lettuce Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) (Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae)
problem_name: Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV)
causal_agent: Orthotospovirus tomatomaculae (Tomato spotted wilt virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young upper leaves, shoot terminals, stems, and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Late spring through summer when thrips vectors migrate
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction
visible_symptoms: On Lettuce (Lactuca sativa): Purpling, bronzing (metallic copper cast), and downward curling of young upper leaves accompanied by dark necrotic flecks or ringspots; dark brown necrotic streaks along petioles and terminal stems causing one-sided shoot tip dieback; on ripening tomato and pepper fruit, striking concentric yellow, orange, and green ringspots, marbled blotches, and raised bumps.
symptom_keywords: bronzing of upper leaves, concentric ringspots on fruit, necrotic stem streaks, terminal shoot dieback, stunted rosette, purple leaf veins
symptom_progression: Transmitted by adult thrips that acquired the virus as larvae; young terminal leaves bronze and develop necrotic specks, growth stunts severely, and fruits develop diagnostic target-like yellow/red ringspots.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by metallic bronzing and dark flecks on YOUNG upper leaves (unlike Early Blight on older lower leaves) and vivid yellow/orange concentric ringspots on ripening fruit.
similar_conditions: Early Blight, Tobacco/Tomato Mosaic Virus, Cucumber Mosaic Virus, Phosphorus Deficiency purpling
risk_factors: Abundant western flower thrips or tobacco thrips populations, nearby flowering weeds (chickweed, dandelion, spiny amaranth, buttercup) acting as virus reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather favoring thrips generation turnover and weed dry-down that drives thrips onto garden crops.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently and exclusively by thrips (especially Western flower thrips Frankliniella occidentalis and Tobacco thrips F. fusca); only larval thrips can acquire the virus by feeding on an infected plant, and emerging adults transmit it for life (not seed-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants so larval thrips cannot develop on them and spread virus to neighboring plants; use UV-reflective silver mulch to repel incoming adult thrips.
prevention_actions: Plant TSWV-resistant cultivars (carrying the Sw-5 gene in tomato, e.g., 'Amelia', 'Crista', 'Bella Rosa', 'Mountain Glory', or Tsw gene in pepper); eliminate winter/spring broadleaf weeds in a 30-ft perimeter around the garden BEFORE planting.

severity_or_impact: High (severely stunts plants and renders ringed fruit unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm, dry weather that accelerates thrips vector reproduction.
host_range: Documented on Lettuce (Lactuca sativa, Asteraceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Lettuce, Spinach, Celery, Beans).

topic: Coriander Black Swallowtail Caterpillar Management
problem_name: Black Swallowtail Caterpillar (Parsleyworm) and Carrot Weevil
causal_agent: Papilio polyxenes (Black Swallowtail / Parsleyworm) and Listronotus oregonensis (Carrot Weevil)
affected_plant_parts: Feathery foliage and flower umbels (Parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (Carrot Weevil)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through umbel flowering and root bulking
season: Late spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Coriander (Coriandrum sativum): Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail Caterpillar): young caterpillars are tiny black, saddle-backed larvae with a white band across the middle (mimicking bird droppings!), which molt into large (2-inch), smooth, bright-green caterpillars banded across each segment with black stripes dotted with bright yellow-orange spots; when poked, the caterpillar everts a bright orange, Y-shaped fleshy horn (osmeterium) from behind its head that emits a pungent citrus-terpene scent to deter birds; Carrot Weevil: small (1/4 inch) coppery-brown snout beetles chew small oval cavities in celery/carrot petioles to lay eggs, and legless creamy-white C-shaped grubs with amber-brown heads tunnel zig-zag cavities across the UPPER one-third and crown shoulder of carrot, parsnip, and celery roots.
symptom_keywords: green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley, orange Y-shaped horn behind head when poked, young black caterpillar with white saddle mimicking bird dropping, zig-zag tunnels in upper crown shoulder of carrot root
symptom_progression: Black Swallowtail butterflies lay single round yellow eggs on feathery umbellifer tips; Carrot Weevils walk from overwintering grassy borders in spring to lay eggs in young petioles at the 3–4 true-leaf stage.
distinguishing_features: Parsleyworm is a prized native butterfly larva unmistakable for its green-black-and-yellow bands and reversible orange Y-shaped osmeterium horn; Carrot Weevil larvae have a distinct amber-brown head capsule and tunnel in the UPPER third/crown of the carrot root (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots are headless and tunnel in the LOWER two-thirds of the root!).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms
risk_factors: Uncovered carrot/celery beds adjacent to last year's carrot patch (for Carrot Weevil).
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days from May through September.
transmission_or_spread: Swallowtail butterflies fly on the wing; Carrot Weevils rarely fly and walk primarily along the ground from overwintering borders.
management_actions: For Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail): because Papilio polyxenes transforms into the magnificent native Eastern Black Swallowtail butterfly and rarely kills established plants, most gardeners simply plant 2–3 extra dill, fennel, or parsley plants as a dedicated 'butterfly nursery' and gently move caterpillars onto those extra plants rather than spraying! For Carrot Weevil: place wooden wooden-slat Boivin traps baited with carrot slices along bed borders at the 2-leaf stage or cover carrot/celery beds with insect netting.
prevention_actions: Rotate carrots, celery, and parsnips away from last year's umbellifer bed so walking Carrot Weevils cannot easily reach young seedlings; remove all cull carrots at harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Coriander (feathery foliage and flower umbels (parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (carrot weevil)) twice weekly during late spring through autumn (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley to distinguish Black Swallowtail Caterpillar from Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms.
severity_or_impact: Low to Moderate for Parsleyworm (beneficial pollinator butterfly); Moderate to High for Carrot Weevil
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and warm sunny spring and summer weather.

symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.

topic: Coriander Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Coriander (Coriandrum sativum): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.
recommended_observations: Scout Coriander (phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures) weekly during mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Aster Yellows from Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High on carrots, lettuce, and celery (infected roots and heads are bitter and inedible)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement.
host_range: Documented on Coriander (Coriandrum sativum, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Celery, Lettuce, Spinach, Parsley, Coriander, Dill, Parsnip).

topic: Coriander Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce (Septoria apiicola)
problem_name: Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce
causal_agent: Septoria apiicola (Celery/Parsley Late Blight) and Septoria lactucae (Lettuce Septoria Leaf Spot)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (stalks)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% RH)
visible_symptoms: On Coriander (Coriandrum sativum): Small, chlorotic yellow flecks on older outer leaves that expand into irregular-to-circular reddish-brown or tan necrotic spots (1/8 to 1/2 inch) heavily peppered with dozens of tiny, dark-brown to black, pinhead-sized pycnidia (spore-fruiting bodies) visible even before the tissue dies; on celery and parsley, lesions spread onto the fleshy petioles (stalks) and coalesce to blight and scorch entire outer leaves.
symptom_keywords: tan-brown leaf spots peppered with tiny black pycnidia dots, blighted celery stalks, outer leaf scorching, yellow-haloed spots
symptom_progression: Seed-borne or debris-borne pycnidia extrude gelatinous tendrils (cirrhi) of spores when wet; rain and sprinklers splash spores across rows, blighting foliage every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified under a hand lens by the numerous tiny black pycnidia dots embedded directly inside the tan/brown leaf and petiole spots (distinguishing it from Cercospora Leaf Spot, which has larger ashy-gray spots WITHOUT black pycnidia dots, and Bacterial Leaf Spot, which has dark greasy water-soaked spots without pycnidia).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii)
risk_factors: Infected seed (primary source in celery and parsley!), overhead watering, working in beds when foliage is wet, and <2-year rotations.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate temperatures (60–75°F) with frequent rain or sprinkler wetting.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne (spores survive up to 2 years in celery seed coats) and residue-borne; spread by rain splash, sprinklers, workers, and tools.
management_actions: Use drip irrigation only and never walk through or harvest parsley, celery, or lettuce while foliage is wet; strip and destroy spotted outer leaves.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed or treat celery/parsley seed with hot water (118–122°F / 48–50°C for 30 minutes) or use 3-year-old celery seed (after 3 years in storage, seed-borne Septoria fungi die out while celery seed remains viable!); rotate Apiaceae and Lettuce crops for 2–3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Coriander (leaves and petioles (stalks)) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce from Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (renders celery stalks, parsley bunches, and romaine lettuce unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% rh).
host_range: Documented on Coriander (Coriandrum sativum, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Celery, Parsley, Coriander, Dill, Lettuce, Artichoke).

topic: Coriander (Coriandrum sativum) Thermal Scorch & Rapid Heat Exhaustion of Coriander (Cilantro): Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management
problem_name: Thermal Scorch & Rapid Heat Exhaustion of Coriander (Cilantro)
affected_plant_parts: Basal and cauline leaves
growth_stage: Temperatures above 80–85°F
season: Cool season (direct sow in early spring, and in late summer/autumn for best prolonged leafy cilantro harvest)
temperature_range: Optimal vegetative cilantro growth 50–70°F (10–21°C); warm temperatures above 75–80°F and long days rapidly trigger bolting and a shift to finely divided feathery stem leaves with altered flavor
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Basal leaves turn reddish-purple or yellow at the margins, wilt during midday sun, and the entire plant bolts into feathery stems within days.
symptom_keywords: coriander, thermal scorch & rapid heat exhaustion of coriander (cilantro), heat stress, thermal leaf scorch, midday wilting, stomatal closure, heat-arrested growth, leaf rolling
symptom_progression: Warm soil (>75°F) and hot air trigger immediate vegetative senescence and floral transition.
distinguishing_features: Reddish-yellow basal leaves and immediate bolting in warm weather.
similar_conditions: Pseudomonas bacterial leaf spot.
risk_factors: Multi-day heat waves above 90–100°F accompanied by warm nights (>72–75°F), intense solar radiation, dry winds, and bare unmulched soil.
favorable_conditions: Multi-day heat waves above 90–100°F accompanied by warm nights (>72–75°F), intense solar radiation, dry winds, and bare unmulched soil.
management_actions: Install 30–40% woven shade cloth over hoops to lower canopy temperatures by 6–10°F, irrigate deeply in the early morning before heat peaks, and apply 2–3 inches of straw or organic mulch to cool the root zone.
prevention_actions: Select heat-tolerant cultivars, time cool-season plantings for spring and autumn windows, mulch beds early, and avoid fertilizer salt buildup prior to summer heat waves.
recommended_observations: Correlate symptom onset across Coriander and neighboring garden plants with recent weather extremes (heat, frost, wind, hail, flooding, drought) or nearby herbicide/fertilizer applications, and inspect new growth for recovery.
severity_or_impact: Prevents summer cilantro leaf production without shade and cooling.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Cool-season fast-growing annual herb grown for fresh leaves ('cilantro') and aromatic dry seeds ('coriander', Coriandrum sativum). Optimal thermal regime: Optimal vegetative cilantro growth 50–70°F (10–21°C); warm temperatures above 75–80°F and long days rapidly trigger bolting and a shift to finely divided feathery stem leaves with altered flavor.
host_range: Coriander (Coriandrum sativum, family Apiaceae) and physiologically similar herb crops.
knowledge_text: Thermal Scorch & Rapid Heat Exhaustion of Coriander (Cilantro) on Coriander (Coriandrum sativum, family Apiaceae) is an abiotic environmental stress caused by prolonged high ambient temperatures (>90–95°f / 32–35°c) and high vapor pressure deficit exceeding crop thermal optima. topic: Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) Molybdenum (Mo) Deficiency (Impaired Nitrogenase & Nitrate Reductase Chlorosis): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Molybdenum (Mo) Deficiency (Impaired Nitrogenase & Nitrate Reductase Chlorosis)
affected_plant_parts: Trifoliate leaves, stems, and Rhizobium root nodules
growth_stage: Vegetative growth and flowering in acidic soils
season: Cool to mild season (direct sow in spring after hard frosts pass, or in autumn in mild-winter climates)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 60–80°F (15–27°C); tolerates light frost; excessive heat and humidity shorten vegetative phase
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Because molybdenum is the catalytic core of both symbiotic nitrogenase in root nodules and plant nitrate reductase, fenugreek plants in acidic soils (pH < 5.6) turn uniformly pale yellowish-green with upward-cupped, marginal-scorched leaflets and small, greenish-white (inactive) root nodules instead of healthy pink leghemoglobin-rich nodules.
symptom_keywords: fenugreek, molybdenum (mo) deficiency, moderately mobile to immobile (essential cofactor for nitrate reductase and rhizobium nitrogenase enzymes), trifoliate leaves, stems, and rhizobium root nodules, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Young expanding central leaves (whiptail deformation in Brassicas) or whole-plant pale chlorosis and marginal leaf burn from unreduced nitrate accumulation. General pale chlorosis and marginal leaflet burn progress across the foliage as nitrogen fixation and nitrate assimilation stall.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Moderately mobile to immobile (essential cofactor for nitrate reductase and Rhizobium nitrogenase enzymes). Inactive pale-green/white root nodules combined with marginal nitrate scorch in acidic soil distinguish Mo deficiency from simple lack of Rhizobium meliloti inoculation.
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Fenugreek.
risk_factors: Strongly acidic soils (pH < 5.5)—unlike all other micronutrients, molybdenum (MoO4 2-) availability drops sharply as soil pH decreases because molybdate ions bind tightly to iron and aluminum oxides in acid soils.
favorable_conditions: Strongly acidic soils (pH < 5.5)—unlike all other micronutrients, molybdenum (MoO4 2-) availability drops sharply as soil pH decreases because molybdate ions bind tightly to iron and aluminum oxides in acid soils.
management_actions: Apply a foliar spray or transplant drench of sodium molybdate or ammonium molybdate (at trace extension rates, e.g., 0.5–1 oz per acre or dilute foliar solution), and lime acidic soil to raise pH above 6.2 to release native soil molybdenum.
prevention_actions: Test soil pH before planting Brassicas, cucurbits, and legumes, and apply agricultural limestone to maintain soil pH between 6.2 and 6.8, which naturally restores molybdate availability without needing trace-element salts.

topic: Amaranth Armyworms Management
problem_name: Armyworms (Beet, Yellowstriped, Fall, and Southern Armyworms)
causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. Beet Armyworm is olive-green with a prominent black spot on the thorax above the second pair of true legs; Yellowstriped Armyworm is velvety gray-black with two bright yellow-orange dorsal stripes and black triangular markings; Fall Armyworm has a prominent white inverted 'Y' suture on its dark head capsule and four black dots arranged in a square on the 8th abdominal segment.
symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.

topic: Amaranth Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)

affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering
risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.
management_actions: On Spinach, Swiss Chard, and Beets: flip leaves twice weekly to rub off the neat rows of chalk-white eggs on the underside BEFORE they hatch, and pinch/clip off any mined blotch leaves immediately (note: contact sprays like soapcannot reach maggots hidden inside the leaf epidermis, though spinosad and azadirachtin/neem have translaminar activity that penetrates into mines!); on Tomatoes, Beans, and Cucurbits, simply avoid broad-spectrum sprays so native Diglyphus parasitic wasps naturally suppress serpentine mines.
prevention_actions: Cover spinach, Swiss chard, and beet beds with floating row covers or fine insect netting from seeding through harvest (in beds rotated away from last year's chenopods); eradicate lambsquarters (Chenopodium album) weeds around the garden.
recommended_observations: Scout Amaranth (interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis) twice weekly during spring through autumn (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves to distinguish Leafminers from Cercospora Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Tuta absoluta (Tomato Leafminer moth), Frost Blistering.
severity_or_impact: High on spinach, Swiss chard, and beet greens (blotch mines ruin edible leaves); Low to Moderate on fruiting crops unless natural enemies are killed
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and mild-to-warm weather.
host_range: Documented on Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Spinach, Swiss chard, Beet, Amaranth, Lettuce, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Amaranth Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained loam or sandy loam; adapts to moderately poor soils once established
management_actions: Prepare a well-drained loam or sandy loam; adapts to moderately poor soils once established adjusted to pH 6.0–7.0 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Amaranth to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Amaranth Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.
recommended_observations: Scout Amaranth (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cercospora Leaf Spot from Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (ruins marketable leaves on Swiss chard and spinach and weakens beet, carrot, and pepper plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh) and warm summer rains or overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beet, Swiss chard, Spinach, Amaranth, Carrot, Celery, Parsley, Pepper).

prevention_actions: Base fertilizer rates on a soil test and maintain soil pH at 6.0–7.0 to keep macronutrients and micronutrients bioavailable; avoid over-application of soluble nitrogen salts which can burn roots or skew vegetative-to-reproductive balance.
recommended_observations: Monitor shoot vigor, leaf color on both older lower leaves (mobile nutrients N, P, K, Mg) and new upper leaves (immobile nutrients Fe, Ca, B, Zn, Mn), and fruit/root set.

topic: Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor) Drought Stress (Leaf Flagging, Stunted Stems & Early Panicle Hardening): Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management
problem_name: Drought Stress (Leaf Flagging, Stunted Stems & Early Panicle Hardening)
affected_plant_parts: Ovate leaves and succulent stems
growth_stage: Vegetative leafy harvest stage
season: Warm season (sow after last spring frost when soil temperature reaches at least 65–70°F)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); C4 photosynthesis thrives in intense summer heat where cool-season greens bolt; killed by frost
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Although C4 amaranth is relatively drought-hardy for survival, soil moisture deficit causes leaves to wilt at midday, remain small and leathery, and triggers early woody stem lignification and seed head emergence.
symptom_keywords: amaranth, drought stress (leaf flagging, stunted stems & early panicle hardening), drought stress, moisture deficit, wilting, marginal leaf firing, fibrous woody tissue, premature abscission
symptom_progression: Moisture stress shifts C4 carbon partitioning from tender leaf expansion to early seed panicle formation.
distinguishing_features: Midday flagging and rapid stem hardening in dry soil.
similar_conditions: Nitrogen deficiency.
risk_factors: Extended rain-free periods, coarse sandy soils with low water-holding capacity, shallow compacted root zones, high weed competition, and hot dry winds.
favorable_conditions: Extended rain-free periods, coarse sandy soils with low water-holding capacity, shallow compacted root zones, high weed competition, and hot dry winds.
management_actions: Irrigate deeply and slowly at the base of plants using drip tape or soaker hoses to wet the top 8–12 inches of soil, and apply 2–3 inches of organic mulch to halt surface evaporation.
prevention_actions: Amend garden soils with 2–3 inches of compost annually to increase available water capacity, install drip irrigation on timers, control weeds early, and mulch thoroughly.
recommended_observations: Correlate symptom onset across Amaranth and neighboring garden plants with recent weather extremes (heat, frost, wind, hail, flooding, drought) or nearby herbicide/fertilizer applications, and inspect new growth for recovery.
severity_or_impact: Ruins tenderness of vegetable amaranth greens.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Warm-season frost-sensitive C4 annual grown for colorful nutritious leaves and/or pseudocereal grain (Amaranthus tricolor, A. cruentus, A. hypochondriacus). Optimal thermal regime: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); C4 photosynthesis thrives in intense summer heat where cool-season greens bolt; killed by frost.
host_range: Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor, family Amaranthaceae) and physiologically similar leafy green/grain crops.
knowledge_text: Drought Stress (Leaf Flagging, Stunted Stems & Early Panicle Hardening) on Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor, family Amaranthaceae) is an abiotic environmental stress caused by prolonged soil water deficit exceeding root extraction capacity and inducing abscisic acid (aba) stomatal closure and leaf senescence. topic: Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor) Short-Day / Stress-Induced Premature Flowering of Leafy Amaranth: Physiological Mechanism, Diagnosis & Prevention
problem_name: Short-Day / Stress-Induced Premature Flowering of Leafy Amaranth
affected_plant_parts: Terminal and axillary dense floral spikes (panicles) and main stem
growth_stage: Vegetative leafy harvest stage
season: Warm season (sow after last spring frost when soil temperature reaches at least 65–70°F)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); C4 photosynthesis thrives in intense summer heat where cool-season greens bolt; killed by frost
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Leafy vegetable amaranth prematurely stops producing broad tender leaves, the main stem hardens and becomes fibrous, and dense bristly green or red floral panicles emerge at the shoot apex and leaf axils.
symptom_keywords: amaranth, short-day / stress-induced premature flowering of leafy amaranth, bolting, premature flowering, seed stalk elongation, bitter leaves, pithy woody root, vernalization

risk_factors: Cold spells below 45–50°F lasting 1–3 weeks on juvenile biennial transplants (cabbage, onion, celery, beet, carrot), or long summer daylengths and temperatures above 78–85°F on cool-season leafy greens and radishes.
favorable_conditions: Cold spells below 45–50°F lasting 1–3 weeks on juvenile biennial transplants (cabbage, onion, celery, beet, carrot), or long summer daylengths and temperatures above 78–85°F on cool-season leafy greens and radishes.

prevention_actions: Select slow-bolt / heat-tolerant cultivars, time plantings for the correct photoperiod and temperature window, avoid chilling young biennial transplants below 50°F for extended periods, and prevent drought or root-bound stress.

knowledge_text: Short-Day / Stress-Induced Premature Flowering of Leafy Amaranth in Amaranth (Amaranthus tricolor, family Amaranthaceae) is a non-infectious physiological disorder caused by vernalization by prolonged cool temperatures (35–50°f) or long-day photoperiod (>13–14 hours) combined with high ambient heat. Visual symptoms: Leafy vegetable amaranth prematurely stops producing broad tender leaves, the main stem hardens and becomes fibrous, and dense bristly green or red floral panicles emerge at the shoot apex and leaf axils. Progression: Triggered by short photoperiods, root-bound crowding, or drought/nitrogen stress. Distinguishing features: Early emergence of dense bristly terminal flower spikes and rapid stem woodiness. Favorable conditions: Cold spells below 45–50°F lasting 1–3 weeks on juvenile biennial transplants (cabbage, onion, celery, beet, carrot), or long summer daylengths and temperatures above 78–85°F on cool-season leafy greens and radishes. Management and prevention: Harvest bolted leafy greens or root crops immediately at the first sign of central stem elongation before bitterness and lignification peak; pinch flower spikes on culinary herbs like basil to prolong vegetative leaf production. Select slow-bolt / heat-tolerant cultivars, time plantings for the correct photoperiod and temperature window, avoid chilling young biennial transplants below 50°F for extended periods, and prevent drought or root-bound stress.

topic: Onion Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Onion (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Onion (Allium cepa, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Onion Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Onion (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.

Visible signs and feeding damage on onion (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots. growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)

topic: Onion Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Onion (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Onion (Allium cepa, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Onion Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Loose, friable, fertile, well-drained sandy loam or silt loam; compacted clay restricts bulb expansion (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a loose, friable, fertile, well-drained sandy loam or silt loam; compacted clay restricts bulb expansion adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Onion to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Onion Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Onion (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) from Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.
host_range: Documented on Onion (Allium cepa, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Onion Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.
recommended_observations: Scout Onion (phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures) weekly during mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Aster Yellows from Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High on carrots, lettuce, and celery (infected roots and heads are bitter and inedible)

topic: Onion Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)

growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding

symptom_progression: Fungus enters root tips or nematode wounds and colonizes xylem vessels; lower leaves yellow and wilt unilaterally, progressing upward until entire shoots brown, collapse, and die without soft stem rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity

transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.
management_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants including roots immediately; do not compost infected stems; solarize soil in hot sunny climates; maintain soil pH near 6.5–7.0 using agricultural lime and use nitrate-nitrogen rather than ammonium-nitrogen.

topic: Onion Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)

causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea

management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.

topic: Onion Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)

causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
