topic: Onion White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums (Sclerotium cepivorum)
problem_name: White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums
causal_agent: Sclerotium cepivorum (White Rot), Botrytis allii (Neck Rot), and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae (Basal Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck
growth_stage: Mid-spring bulb enlargement through harvest and post-harvest curing/storage
season: Cool-to-moderate spring (White Rot: 50–68°F) or warm summer/storage (Basal/Neck Rot: 70–85°F)
humidity_conditions: Moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing
visible_symptoms: On Onion (Allium cepa): Above ground: premature yellowing, tip dieback, and wilting of older leaves progressing to collapse of the top fan; Below ground: in White Rot, a fluffy snow-white mycelial mat covers the basal plate and lower bulb studded with thousands of poppy-seed-sized (0.5 mm) spherical jet-black sclerotia; in Fusarium Basal Rot, the basal plate turns pinkish-brown and spongy with decayed roots; in Botrytis Neck Rot, sunken gray water-soaked decay softens the bulb neck during storage with gray mold and black sclerotia between scales.
symptom_keywords: fluffy white mycelium on bulb base, tiny black poppy-seed sclerotia, rotted basal plate, premature top yellowing and dieback, spongy sunken bulb neck in storage
symptom_progression: Root exudates (alkyl cysteines) uniquely produced only by Allium species stimulate dormant soil sclerotia to germinate and rot the roots and basal plate; Neck Rot enters through uncured moist neck cuts at harvest.
distinguishing_features: White Rot is distinguished by the crust of tiny (0.5 mm) uniform round black poppy-seed-like sclerotia embedded in white mycelium at the bulb base; Botrytis Neck Rot starts at the TOP neck of stored bulbs when tops were cut too green or cured poorly.
similar_conditions: Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot
risk_factors: Planting non-certified culinary grocery-store garlic cloves (major pathway introducing White Rot to home gardens!), short Allium rotations, harvesting in wet weather, and failing to cure bulbs thoroughly.
favorable_conditions: Cool moist spring soils (50–68°F) for White Rot; warm soils (75–85°F) for Fusarium Basal Rot; wet harvest weather for Botrytis Neck Rot.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotium cepivorum sclerotia survive in soil for 15–20+ years even without an Allium host; spreads via infected seed garlic cloves, onion sets, and contaminated soil.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag infected bulbs plus surrounding soil; stop all irrigation 2–3 weeks before onion/garlic harvest and cure harvested bulbs thoroughly at 75–85°F with strong airflow for 2–3 weeks until necks are tight and bone-dry before trimming.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL RULE: NEVER plant grocery-store garlic or uncertified sets—plant only certified disease-free seed garlic and onion sets; rotate Allium family crops on a minimum 4-year cycle.
recommended_observations: Scout Onion (roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring (white rot: 50–68°f) or warm summer/storage (basal/neck rot: 70–85°f) (50–80°F (10–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums from Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot.
severity_or_impact: Critical (White Rot permanently contaminates garden beds against all Alliums for 15–20 years; Neck Rot ruins stored bulbs)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–80°F (10–27°C) and moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing.
host_range: Documented on Onion (Allium cepa, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives).

topic: Garlic Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.

problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests
causal_agent: Cylas formicarius (Sweetpotato Weevil), Conoderus / Melanotus / Limonius spp. (Wireworms - Click Beetle larvae), and Phyllophaga / Popillia / Cyclocephala spp. (White Grubs - Scarab Beetle larvae)
affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod).

topic: Garlic Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Garlic (inner leaf folds/necks (alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods) twice weekly during hot, dry late spring and summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect for silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks to distinguish Thrips from Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering.
severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Garlic (Allium sativum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Garlic Routine Garden Maintenance, Pruning, Support, and Weed Management
growth_stage: Established vegetative growth through harvest
management_actions: Mulch heavily with 4 inches of weed-free straw in fall to suppress weeds and prevent frost heaving; on hardneck cultivars, snap or cut off the curling flower stalk ('garlic scape') as soon as it forms a loop in late spring—leaving the scape on reduces bulb yield by 20–30%
prevention_actions: Cultivate shallowly around plants to avoid severing surface feeder roots, keep mulch pulled slightly back from direct stem contact where crown rot is a risk, and sanitize pruning tools between plants.
recommended_observations: Check Garlic weekly for structural support needs, weed competition, mulch depth, and pollinator activity.

topic: Garlic Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained, loose, fertile loam or sandy loam amended with aged compost; rots in waterlogged winter clay (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a well-drained, loose, fertile loam or sandy loam amended with aged compost; rots in waterlogged winter clay adjusted to pH 6.0–7.0 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Garlic to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Garlic Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Garlic (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) from Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.

topic: Garlic Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.

topic: Garlic Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)

causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola

growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Small water-soaked translucent spots around wounds, insect holes, sunscald patches, or hollow stems that rapidly expand within 24–72 hours into a wet, slimy, mushy, cream-to-tan liquified collapse of the fleshy parenchyma tissue (while the outer epidermis remains intact like a water-filled bag until broken), accompanied by an unmistakable, putrid, foul fishy/sulfurous stench (in brassicas, onions, and potatoes); in Potato Blackleg, an inky jet-black slimy decay rises from the decaying seed piece up the lower 4–8 inches of the green stem, yellowing and rolling upper leaves.
symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak

favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.
prevention_actions: Control insect pests (cabbageworms, root maggots, borers) that create entry wounds; select domed broccoli cultivars that shed rainwater; plant whole uncut certified seed potatoes or cure cut seed pieces at 55–60°F and 85% RH for 3–5 days before planting in warmed (>50°F) well-drained soil.

topic: Garlic Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.
host_range: Documented on Garlic (Allium sativum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Asparagus, Sweet corn, Onion).

topic: Garlic Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii)
problem_name: Southern Blight
causal_agent: Agroathelia rolfsii (syn. Sclerotium rolfsii)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth and fruiting during hot summer weather
season: Hot, humid summer months
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Sudden, permanent daytime and nighttime wilting of the entire plant without prior leaf yellowing; inspection of the stem right at the soil line reveals a dark brown water-soaked cortical rot girdling the collar, covered by a conspicuous fan-like mat of coarse, pure-white fungal mycelium studded with numerous round (1–2 mm) mustard-seed-like sclerotia that turn from white to tan to reddish-brown.
symptom_keywords: white fan-like fungal mat at soil line, mustard-seed sclerotia, stem collar rot, sudden permanent wilting, southern stem blight
symptom_progression: Fungus attacks the outer stem cortex at the warm, moist soil surface, rapidly girdling the stem within days and causing total above-ground wilt while producing hundreds of tan-brown sclerotia on the rotted collar and soil.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the bright white fan-like mycelial webbing at the base of the stem at the soil line and the 1–2 mm spherical tan-to-reddish-brown mustard-seed-like sclerotia.
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt
risk_factors: Undecomposed organic mulch or crop residue piled directly against stems, acidic soils (pH 3.5–6.5), and hot rainy summer weather.
favorable_conditions: High temperatures (85–95°F) with moist, well-aerated surface soil and decaying organic matter at the stem collar.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotia survive in upper soil layers and plant debris, floating on irrigation/rain water and carried on soil and transplants.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag the infected plant PLUS a 6-inch radius of surrounding topsoil containing sclerotia and dispose in trash; keep mulch pulled 2–3 inches back from direct contact with plant stems.
prevention_actions: Deep-turn or bury surface crop residues >6 inches deep (sclerotia cannot germinate without oxygen at depth); amend acidic soils with lime/calcium; rotate with less susceptible monocots (sweet corn); solarize beds in summer.
recommended_observations: Scout Garlic (lower stem collar at the soil line, crown, roots, and fruits/tubers touching soil) weekly during hot, humid summer months (85–95°F (29–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Southern Blight from Sclerotinia White Mold (produces much larger, irregular black sclerotia in cool weather), Phytophthora Crown Rot, Fusarium/Bacterial Wilt.
severity_or_impact: High in warm southern/subtropical gardens (rapidly kills girdled plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 85–95°F (29–35°C) and high soil moisture and high humidity at the soil surface following summer rains.
host_range: Documented on Garlic (Allium sativum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Watermelon).

topic: Garlic White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums (Sclerotium cepivorum)
problem_name: White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums
causal_agent: Sclerotium cepivorum (White Rot), Botrytis allii (Neck Rot), and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae (Basal Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck
growth_stage: Mid-spring bulb enlargement through harvest and post-harvest curing/storage
season: Cool-to-moderate spring (White Rot: 50–68°F) or warm summer/storage (Basal/Neck Rot: 70–85°F)
humidity_conditions: Moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing
visible_symptoms: On Garlic (Allium sativum): Above ground: premature yellowing, tip dieback, and wilting of older leaves progressing to collapse of the top fan; Below ground: in White Rot, a fluffy snow-white mycelial mat covers the basal plate and lower bulb studded with thousands of poppy-seed-sized (0.5 mm) spherical jet-black sclerotia; in Fusarium Basal Rot, the basal plate turns pinkish-brown and spongy with decayed roots; in Botrytis Neck Rot, sunken gray water-soaked decay softens the bulb neck during storage with gray mold and black sclerotia between scales.
symptom_keywords: fluffy white mycelium on bulb base, tiny black poppy-seed sclerotia, rotted basal plate, premature top yellowing and dieback, spongy sunken bulb neck in storage
symptom_progression: Root exudates (alkyl cysteines) uniquely produced only by Allium species stimulate dormant soil sclerotia to germinate and rot the roots and basal plate; Neck Rot enters through uncured moist neck cuts at harvest.
distinguishing_features: White Rot is distinguished by the crust of tiny (0.5 mm) uniform round black poppy-seed-like sclerotia embedded in white mycelium at the bulb base; Botrytis Neck Rot starts at the TOP neck of stored bulbs when tops were cut too green or cured poorly.
similar_conditions: Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot
risk_factors: Planting non-certified culinary grocery-store garlic cloves (major pathway introducing White Rot to home gardens!), short Allium rotations, harvesting in wet weather, and failing to cure bulbs thoroughly.
favorable_conditions: Cool moist spring soils (50–68°F) for White Rot; warm soils (75–85°F) for Fusarium Basal Rot; wet harvest weather for Botrytis Neck Rot.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotium cepivorum sclerotia survive in soil for 15–20+ years even without an Allium host; spreads via infected seed garlic cloves, onion sets, and contaminated soil.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag infected bulbs plus surrounding soil; stop all irrigation 2–3 weeks before onion/garlic harvest and cure harvested bulbs thoroughly at 75–85°F with strong airflow for 2–3 weeks until necks are tight and bone-dry before trimming.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL RULE: NEVER plant grocery-store garlic or uncertified sets—plant only certified disease-free seed garlic and onion sets; rotate Allium family crops on a minimum 4-year cycle.
recommended_observations: Scout Garlic (roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring (white rot: 50–68°f) or warm summer/storage (basal/neck rot: 70–85°f) (50–80°F (10–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums from Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot.
severity_or_impact: Critical (White Rot permanently contaminates garden beds against all Alliums for 15–20 years; Neck Rot ruins stored bulbs)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–80°F (10–27°C) and moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing.
host_range: Documented on Garlic (Allium sativum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives).

affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Basil (Ocimum basilicum): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.
symptom_keywords: greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem, upward-moving bronzed papery leaves without webbing, stunted brittle downward-cupped terminal pepper shoots, rosetted distorted strawberry crown leaves, corky russeted fruit
symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).
distinguishing_features: Tomato Russet Mite is distinguished from Spider Mites by the complete absence of silk webbing or individual stipple dots and the greasy bronze-tan sheen on the lower stem; Broad Mite injury on pepper/strawberry terminal shoots mimics viral mosaic or 2,4-D herbicide drift, except leaf veins do not show Parallel 'strapping' and a 20x lens reveals tiny football-shaped eggs studded with rows of white polka-dot tubercles!
similar_conditions: 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites)
risk_factors: Warm weather, infested greenhouse transplants or strawberry crowns, and broad-spectrum insecticide use.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.
transmission_or_spread: Crawl between touching plants, blow on wind, or hitchhike phoretically on the legs of whiteflies and aphids (Broad Mite!).

prevention_actions: Purchase certified mite-free strawberry crowns and vegetable transplants; control whiteflies (which carry broad mites on their legs); rotate nightshades and destroy all volunteer solanaceous weeds (black nightshade, jimsonweed).

topic: Basil Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Basil (Ocimum basilicum): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Basil (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Basil (Ocimum basilicum, Lamiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Basil Routine Garden Maintenance, Pruning, Support, and Weed Management
growth_stage: Established vegetative growth through harvest
management_actions: Pinch out the central growing tip just above a pair of lateral leaf buds once plants are 6 inches tall and have 3–4 sets of true leaves, and pinch off flower buds as soon as they appear—allowing basil to flower halts leaf production and turns leaves bitter and woody
prevention_actions: Cultivate shallowly around plants to avoid severing surface feeder roots, keep mulch pulled slightly back from direct stem contact where crown rot is a risk, and sanitize pruning tools between plants.
recommended_observations: Check Basil weekly for structural support needs, weed competition, mulch depth, and pollinator activity.

knowledge_subtype: Soil Texture, pH, Drainage & Bed Preparation
topic: Basil Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Moist, fertile, well-drained loam or container mix rich in compost
management_actions: Prepare a moist, fertile, well-drained loam or container mix rich in compost adjusted to pH 6.0–7.0 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Basil to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Basil (Ocimum basilicum): Prefers moist, fertile, well-drained loam or container mix rich in compost with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–7.0. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Basil Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Basil (Ocimum basilicum): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury
risk_factors: Abundant perennial weeds (pokeweed, milkweed, chickweed, white cockle, nightshade, bindweed) harboring CMV near the garden and migrating winged aphids.
favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored non-persistently (stylet-borne) by >80 species of aphids (especially Green peach aphid Myzus persicae and Melon aphid Aphis gossypii); aphids acquire and transmit the virus in just 10–60 seconds of test probing (so insecticides cannot kill aphids fast enough to prevent transmission!).
management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.
recommended_observations: Scout Basil (young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits) weekly during late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) from Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stunting and deformed, warty, unmarketable fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal.
host_range: Documented on Basil (Ocimum basilicum, Lamiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cucumber, Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Melon, Watermelon, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Basil Fusarium Wilt (Fusarium oxysporum)
problem_name: Fusarium Wilt
causal_agent: Fusarium oxysporum (host-specific formae speciales: f. sp. lycopersici, melongenae, tuberosi, niveum, melonis, cucumerinum, conglutinans, cepae, pisi, phaseoli, spinaciae, basilici, cubense)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through flowering and fruit/organ fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil pH and root-knot nematode feeding
visible_symptoms: On Basil (Ocimum basilicum): Bright yellowing (chlorosis) and drooping of older lower leaves—classically starting on ONLY ONE SIDE of a leaf, one branch, or one side of the plant ('one-sided flagging')—which wilts during warm afternoons and eventually fails to recover at night; slicing the lower main stem or petiole lengthwise reveals a diagnostic reddish-brown to dark-brown discoloration of the water-conducting vascular ring while the central pith remains healthy.
symptom_keywords: one-sided yellowing, unilateral wilting, vascular browning, reddish-brown xylem ring, lower leaf yellowing, daytime wilting, stunted growth
symptom_progression: Fungus enters root tips or nematode wounds and colonizes xylem vessels; lower leaves yellow and wilt unilaterally, progressing upward until entire shoots brown, collapse, and die without soft stem rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity
risk_factors: Acidic sandy soils (pH <6.0), root-knot nematode infestations creating root entry wounds, high ammonium-nitrogen fertilization, and replanting susceptible cultivars in infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm soil temperatures (80–90°F) and moisture stress during fruiting.
transmission_or_spread: Long-lived thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) persist in soil for 5–10+ years and spread via contaminated transplants, soil on tools/shoes, and infected seed.
management_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants including roots immediately; do not compost infected stems; solarize soil in hot sunny climates; maintain soil pH near 6.5–7.0 using agricultural lime and use nitrate-nitrogen rather than ammonium-nitrogen.
prevention_actions: Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'F', 'FF', or 'FFF' for Races 1, 2, 3 in tomato; Fusarium-resistant watermelon, melon, cabbage 'Yellows Resistant', pea, basil, and banana cultivars); control root-knot nematodes; practice 4–6 year crop rotations.
recommended_observations: Scout Basil (roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)) weekly during warm summer growing season (80–90°F (27–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Fusarium Wilt from Verticillium Wilt (favors cooler 68–75°F temps), Bacterial Wilt (Ralstonia/Erwinia - rapid green wilt with bacterial streaming), Southern Blight, Walnut Toxicity.
severity_or_impact: High (lethal systemic vascular wilt; soil remains infested for many years)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–90°F (27–32°C) and warm soil temperatures; aggravated by low soil ph and root-knot nematode feeding.
host_range: Documented on Basil (Ocimum basilicum, Lamiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Eggplant, Pepper, Potato, Watermelon, Melon, Cucumber, Pumpkin).

Symptoms on basil (roots, crown, and water-conducting xylem vascular system (manifesting as foliar yellowing and wilting)): Bright yellowing (chlorosis) and drooping of older lower leaves—classically starting on ONLY ONE SIDE of a leaf, one branch, or one side of the plant ('one-sided flagging')—which wilts during warm afternoons and eventually fails to recover at night; slicing the lower main stem or petiole lengthwise reveals a diagnostic reddish-brown to dark-brown discoloration of the water-conducting vascular ring while the central pith remains healthy. Distinguishing features: Distinguished by classic one-sided yellowing of leaflets/shoots, warm-weather peak (80–90°F), dark reddish-brown vascular discoloration inside the lower stem, and absence of bacterial streaming ooze (unlike Bacterial Wilt). Favored by warm soil temperatures (80–90°f) and moisture stress during fruiting. (80–90°F (27–32°C)). Plant resistant cultivars (designated 'F', 'FF', or 'FFF' for Races 1, 2, 3 in tomato; Fusarium-resistant watermelon, melon, cabbage 'Yellows Resistant', pea, basil, and banana cultivars); control root-knot nematodes; practice 4–6 year crop rotations.

topic: Basil Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Basil (Ocimum basilicum): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').
symptom_keywords: fuzzy brownish-gray mold, dusty spore masses, stem pruning wound canker, blossom blight, berry gray rot, ghost spot rings on tomato
symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.

causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Mint (Mentha spicata): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)

topic: Mint Verticillium Wilt (Verticillium dahliae)
problem_name: Verticillium Wilt
causal_agent: Verticillium dahliae (and Verticillium albo-atrum)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/tuber enlargement
season: Cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: Moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand
visible_symptoms: On Mint (Mentha spicata): V-shaped yellow chlorotic blotches developing at the margins and tips of older lower leaflets that soon turn brown and necrotic with a yellow halo; leaves wilt during the heat of the day (often affecting one side of a leaf or branch first); outer older leaves on strawberry crowns turn brown and collapse while inner leaves remain green initially; light tan-to-brown streaking is visible in the vascular tissue near the base of the stem.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesion on leaf margin, lower leaf wilting, light tan vascular streaking, outer crown collapse, stunting, midday flagging
symptom_progression: Microsclerotia germinate near root exudates, invade root cortex and xylem, and slowly plug water transport; plants become chronically stunted with progressive lower-leaf V-necrosis and reduced fruit size.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by characteristic V-shaped marginal yellow-and-brown fan lesions at leaflet tips, cooler temperature optimum (68–78°F vs 80–90°F for Fusarium wilt), and lighter tan vascular discoloration restricted closer to the lower stem.
similar_conditions: Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot
risk_factors: Planting susceptible crops (such as strawberry, raspberry, or eggplant) in soil where tomato, potato, pepper, or eggplant grew within the preceding 3–4 years; root-lesion nematode feeding.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild soil temperatures (68–78°F) in spring followed by warm summer transpiration stress.
transmission_or_spread: Survives in soil for 8–10+ years as microscopic dark resting bodies (microsclerotia) across a wide host range of >300 broadleaf crops and weeds (nightshades, lambsquarters, pigweed).
management_actions: Remove infected plants and roots; maintain even irrigation and balanced potassium nutrition to help moderately tolerant plants mature fruit; solarize infested garden beds under clear plastic for 6 weeks in midsummer.
prevention_actions: Plant Verticillium-resistant cultivars ('V' designation in tomatoes); NEVER plant strawberries, brambles, or eggplants where nightshade family crops grew in the past 4 years; rotate with non-host grasses, sweet corn, or brassicas (broccoli residue biofumigation reduces microsclerotia).
recommended_observations: Scout Mint (roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather (68–78°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Verticillium Wilt from Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes chronic stunting, defoliation, and plant death in highly susceptible hosts like eggplant, potato, and strawberry)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–78°F (20–25°C) and moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand.
host_range: Documented on Mint (Mentha spicata, Lamiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Eggplant, Potato, Pepper, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Watermelon).

growth_stage: Vegetative growth in dry beds or containers
season: Spring to autumn (plant divisions, cuttings, or transplants in spring or early fall)

symptom_progression: Mint evolved along stream banks and lacks stomatal drought conservation, rapidly desiccating when topsoil dries.

similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Mint.

topic: Parsley Black Swallowtail Caterpillar Management
problem_name: Black Swallowtail Caterpillar (Parsleyworm) and Carrot Weevil
causal_agent: Papilio polyxenes (Black Swallowtail / Parsleyworm) and Listronotus oregonensis (Carrot Weevil)
affected_plant_parts: Feathery foliage and flower umbels (Parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (Carrot Weevil)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through umbel flowering and root bulking
season: Late spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Parsley (Petroselinum crispum): Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail Caterpillar): young caterpillars are tiny black, saddle-backed larvae with a white band across the middle (mimicking bird droppings!), which molt into large (2-inch), smooth, bright-green caterpillars banded across each segment with black stripes dotted with bright yellow-orange spots; when poked, the caterpillar everts a bright orange, Y-shaped fleshy horn (osmeterium) from behind its head that emits a pungent citrus-terpene scent to deter birds; Carrot Weevil: small (1/4 inch) coppery-brown snout beetles chew small oval cavities in celery/carrot petioles to lay eggs, and legless creamy-white C-shaped grubs with amber-brown heads tunnel zig-zag cavities across the UPPER one-third and crown shoulder of carrot, parsnip, and celery roots.
symptom_keywords: green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley, orange Y-shaped horn behind head when poked, young black caterpillar with white saddle mimicking bird dropping, zig-zag tunnels in upper crown shoulder of carrot root
symptom_progression: Black Swallowtail butterflies lay single round yellow eggs on feathery umbellifer tips; Carrot Weevils walk from overwintering grassy borders in spring to lay eggs in young petioles at the 3–4 true-leaf stage.
distinguishing_features: Parsleyworm is a prized native butterfly larva unmistakable for its green-black-and-yellow bands and reversible orange Y-shaped osmeterium horn; Carrot Weevil larvae have a distinct amber-brown head capsule and tunnel in the UPPER third/crown of the carrot root (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots are headless and tunnel in the LOWER two-thirds of the root!).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms
risk_factors: Uncovered carrot/celery beds adjacent to last year's carrot patch (for Carrot Weevil).
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days from May through September.
transmission_or_spread: Swallowtail butterflies fly on the wing; Carrot Weevils rarely fly and walk primarily along the ground from overwintering borders.
management_actions: For Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail): because Papilio polyxenes transforms into the magnificent native Eastern Black Swallowtail butterfly and rarely kills established plants, most gardeners simply plant 2–3 extra dill, fennel, or parsley plants as a dedicated 'butterfly nursery' and gently move caterpillars onto those extra plants rather than spraying! For Carrot Weevil: place wooden wooden-slat Boivin traps baited with carrot slices along bed borders at the 2-leaf stage or cover carrot/celery beds with insect netting.
prevention_actions: Rotate carrots, celery, and parsnips away from last year's umbellifer bed so walking Carrot Weevils cannot easily reach young seedlings; remove all cull carrots at harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsley (feathery foliage and flower umbels (parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (carrot weevil)) twice weekly during late spring through autumn (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley to distinguish Black Swallowtail Caterpillar from Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms.
severity_or_impact: Low to Moderate for Parsleyworm (beneficial pollinator butterfly); Moderate to High for Carrot Weevil
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and warm sunny spring and summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Parsley (Petroselinum crispum, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Parsley, Dill, Fennel, Coriander, Celery, Carrot, Parsnip).

topic: Parsley Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Parsley (Petroselinum crispum): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsley (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) from Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.
host_range: Documented on Parsley (Petroselinum crispum, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).
knowledge_text: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits). Symptoms on parsley (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks. Distinguishing features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins). Favored by warm temperatures (70–85°f) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness. (70–85°F (21–29°C)). Management and prevention: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading. topic: Parsley Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Parsley (Petroselinum crispum): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.

topic: Parsley Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)

topic: Parsley Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce (Septoria apiicola)
problem_name: Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce
causal_agent: Septoria apiicola (Celery/Parsley Late Blight) and Septoria lactucae (Lettuce Septoria Leaf Spot)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (stalks)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% RH)
visible_symptoms: On Parsley (Petroselinum crispum): Small, chlorotic yellow flecks on older outer leaves that expand into irregular-to-circular reddish-brown or tan necrotic spots (1/8 to 1/2 inch) heavily peppered with dozens of tiny, dark-brown to black, pinhead-sized pycnidia (spore-fruiting bodies) visible even before the tissue dies; on celery and parsley, lesions spread onto the fleshy petioles (stalks) and coalesce to blight and scorch entire outer leaves.
symptom_keywords: tan-brown leaf spots peppered with tiny black pycnidia dots, blighted celery stalks, outer leaf scorching, yellow-haloed spots
symptom_progression: Seed-borne or debris-borne pycnidia extrude gelatinous tendrils (cirrhi) of spores when wet; rain and sprinklers splash spores across rows, blighting foliage every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified under a hand lens by the numerous tiny black pycnidia dots embedded directly inside the tan/brown leaf and petiole spots (distinguishing it from Cercospora Leaf Spot, which has larger ashy-gray spots WITHOUT black pycnidia dots, and Bacterial Leaf Spot, which has dark greasy water-soaked spots without pycnidia).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii)
risk_factors: Infected seed (primary source in celery and parsley!), overhead watering, working in beds when foliage is wet, and <2-year rotations.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate temperatures (60–75°F) with frequent rain or sprinkler wetting.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne (spores survive up to 2 years in celery seed coats) and residue-borne; spread by rain splash, sprinklers, workers, and tools.
management_actions: Use drip irrigation only and never walk through or harvest parsley, celery, or lettuce while foliage is wet; strip and destroy spotted outer leaves.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed or treat celery/parsley seed with hot water (118–122°F / 48–50°C for 30 minutes) or use 3-year-old celery seed (after 3 years in storage, seed-borne Septoria fungi die out while celery seed remains viable!); rotate Apiaceae and Lettuce crops for 2–3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsley (leaves and petioles (stalks)) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce from Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (renders celery stalks, parsley bunches, and romaine lettuce unmarketable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% rh).
host_range: Documented on Parsley (Petroselinum crispum, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Celery, Parsley, Coriander, Dill, Lettuce, Artichoke).

growth_stage: Heat waves above 90°F
season: Cool season (sow or transplant in early spring 3–4 weeks before last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones)

topic: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) Vernalization-Induced Second-Year / Cold-Shock Bolting of Parsley: Physiological Mechanism, Diagnosis & Prevention

growth_stage: Spring after overwintering or prolonged cold shock on transplants

favorable_conditions: Cold spells below 45–50°F lasting 1–3 weeks on juvenile biennial transplants (cabbage, onion, celery, beet, carrot), or long summer daylengths and temperatures above 78–85°F on cool-season leafy greens and radishes.

prevention_actions: Select slow-bolt / heat-tolerant cultivars, time plantings for the correct photoperiod and temperature window, avoid chilling young biennial transplants below 50°F for extended periods, and prevent drought or root-bound stress.
