knowledge_text: Vernalization-Induced Second-Year / Cold-Shock Bolting of Parsley in Parsley (Petroselinum crispum, family Apiaceae) is a non-infectious physiological disorder caused by vernalization by prolonged cool temperatures (35–50°f) or long-day photoperiod (>13–14 hours) combined with high ambient heat. Visual symptoms: The dense tuft of curled or flat trifoliate leaves sends up a tall (2–3 ft), round, hollow, branched flowering stem bearing flat greenish-yellow compound umbels; remaining leaves turn coarse, pale, and bitter. Progression: As a biennial, overwintered crowns or spring transplants exposed to prolonged <45°F temperatures shift irreversibly to reproductive flowering. Distinguishing features: Tall round hollow stem topped by greenish-yellow umbels. Favorable conditions: Cold spells below 45–50°F lasting 1–3 weeks on juvenile biennial transplants (cabbage, onion, celery, beet, carrot), or long summer daylengths and temperatures above 78–85°F on cool-season leafy greens and radishes. Management and prevention: Harvest bolted leafy greens or root crops immediately at the first sign of central stem elongation before bitterness and lignification peak; pinch flower spikes on culinary herbs like basil to prolong vegetative leaf production. Select slow-bolt / heat-tolerant cultivars, time plantings for the correct photoperiod and temperature window, avoid chilling young biennial transplants below 50°F for extended periods, and prevent drought or root-bound stress.

topic: Strawberry Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm Management
problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents
visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin.
symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.
distinguishing_features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters).
similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.
prevention_actions: Plant early-maturing sweet corn cultivars as early in spring as soil temperature allows to harvest before peak late-summer moth flights; select sweet corn hybrids with tight, long husk extensions beyond the ear tip; encourage Trichogramma egg-parasitoid wasps and Orius minute pirate bugs (which eat earworm eggs on silks).
recommended_observations: Scout Strawberry (sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear to distinguish Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm from European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm.
severity_or_impact: High (the #1 insect pest of sweet corn and a destructive borer in tomatoes, peppers, beans, and okra)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm weather and southerly summer wind currents.
host_range: Documented on Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea).
knowledge_text: Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa) Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm is a chewing caterpillar pest caused by Helicoverpa zea. Visible signs and feeding damage on strawberry (sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin. Distinguishing features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters). topic: Strawberry Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites Management
problem_name: Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites (Tomato Russet Mite, Broad Mite, and Cyclamen Mite)
causal_agent: Aculops lycopersici (Tomato Russet Mite), Polyphagotarsonemus latus (Broad Mite), and Phytonemus pallidus (Cyclamen Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.
symptom_keywords: greasy bronze-tan lower tomato stem, upward-moving bronzed papery leaves without webbing, stunted brittle downward-cupped terminal pepper shoots, rosetted distorted strawberry crown leaves, corky russeted fruit
symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).

similar_conditions: 2,4-D / Dicamba Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Viruses, Boron/Calcium Deficiency (no bronze stem sheen or dotted eggs), Two-Spotted Spider Mite (has webbing and visible 8-legged mites)
risk_factors: Warm weather, infested greenhouse transplants or strawberry crowns, and broad-spectrum insecticide use.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.
transmission_or_spread: Crawl between touching plants, blow on wind, or hitchhike phoretically on the legs of whiteflies and aphids (Broad Mite!).
management_actions: Apply wettable/micronized sulfur (highly effective against Eriophyid russet and broad mites, provided air temperature is below 85–90°F to avoid sulfur burn) or abamectin/horticultural oil early; rogue severely rosetted plants; clean and sanitize tomato stakes and cages at season's end.
prevention_actions: Purchase certified mite-free strawberry crowns and vegetable transplants; control whiteflies (which carry broad mites on their legs); rotate nightshades and destroy all volunteer solanaceous weeds (black nightshade, jimsonweed).

severity_or_impact: High (often misdiagnosed as blight or virus until lower foliage is completely bronzed or terminal buds abort)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and high humidity inside dense crowns (broad/cyclamen mites) or warm dry summer weather (tomato russet mite).
host_range: Documented on Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Strawberry, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon).

topic: Strawberry Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.
recommended_observations: Scout Strawberry (seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes) twice weekly during cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights (45–75°F (7–24°C)); inspect for ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries to distinguish Slugs and Garden Snails from Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime).
severity_or_impact: High in cool, wet climates and on seedlings, lettuce, brassicas, and strawberries
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–75°F (7–24°C) and high humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds.
host_range: Documented on Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Lettuce, Spinach, Swiss chard, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy).

topic: Strawberry Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Strawberry (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Strawberry Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs Management
problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests
causal_agent: Cylas formicarius (Sweetpotato Weevil), Conoderus / Melanotus / Limonius spp. (Wireworms - Click Beetle larvae), and Phyllophaga / Popillia / Cyclocephala spp. (White Grubs - Scarab Beetle larvae)
affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).
recommended_observations: Scout Strawberry (underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds) twice weekly during spring planting through autumn harvest (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil to distinguish Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs from Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod).
host_range: Documented on Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet potato, Potato, Carrot, Beet, Radish, Turnip, Parsnip, Onion).

topic: Strawberry Tarnished Plant Bug Management

topic: Strawberry Angular Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans)
problem_name: Angular Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Pseudomonas syringae pv. lachrymans (Cucurbits) and Xanthomonas fragariae (Strawberry)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, petioles, stems, blossoms, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through fruiting
season: Cool-to-warm, rainy, windy spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, driving rain, overhead irrigation, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): Small, water-soaked, translucent angular spots on leaves strictly bounded by fine leaf veins; under humid mornings, glistening milky-white droplets of bacterial exudate ooze from the lower surface of the lesions and dry into a thin, shiny, white crust or film; on cucurbits, tan necrotic spot centers soon dry out, tear, and fall away, leaving ragged angular 'shot-holes'; on cucumber/squash fruits, small circular water-soaked spots turn chalky white and crack, allowing soft-rot bacteria inside.
symptom_keywords: vein-bounded water-soaked angular spots, shiny white dried bacterial film on leaf underside, ragged angular shot-holes, chalky cracked fruit spots
symptom_progression: Seed- or debris-borne bacteria splash onto leaves; lesions expand up to vein boundaries, dry, and drop out as ragged holes while fruit lesions open pathways for belly/soft rot.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Cucurbit Downy Mildew by the shiny white dried bacterial crust on the underside of lesions (rather than purplish-gray fuzzy sporangia) and by the dry centers dropping out to leave ragged angular holes.
similar_conditions: Downy Mildew (yellow angular spots with purplish-gray fuzz underneath, no shot-holes or white crust), Anthracnose, Belly Rot
risk_factors: Contaminated seed, overhead sprinklers, working in cucumber or strawberry beds when foliage is wet, and short crop rotations.
favorable_conditions: Rainy weather at 68–80°F with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne (cucurbits) or crown-borne on nursery transplants (strawberry); spread rapidly down rows by splashing rain, sprinklers, hands, and harvest containers.
management_actions: Never cultivate, weed, or harvest cucumbers, squash, or strawberries when leaves are wet; switch to drip irrigation; apply fixed copper sprays early if bacterial spotting starts.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed and angular-leaf-spot-resistant cucumber hybrids; rotate cucurbits out of affected beds for 2–3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Strawberry (leaves, petioles, stems, blossoms, and fruit surfaces) weekly during cool-to-warm, rainy, windy spring and early summer weather (65–82°F (18–28°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Angular Leaf Spot from Downy Mildew (yellow angular spots with purplish-gray fuzz underneath, no shot-holes or white crust), Anthracnose, Belly Rot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (defoliates vines and predisposes cucumber fruits to soft rot)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–82°F (18–28°C) and high humidity, driving rain, overhead irrigation, or heavy dew.

topic: Strawberry Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.)
problem_name: Anthracnose
causal_agent: Colletotrichum spp. (C. coccodes on Solanaceae; C. orbiculare on Cucurbits; C. lindemuthianum on Beans; C. acutatum / C. gloeosporioides on Fruits)

topic: Strawberry Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits

symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.

growth_stage: Any stage after soil saturation or heavy rainfall
season: Warm, rainy summer weather or poorly drained wet soils

topic: Strawberry Verticillium Wilt (Verticillium dahliae)

causal_agent: Verticillium dahliae (and Verticillium albo-atrum)

growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/tuber enlargement

visible_symptoms: On Strawberry (Fragaria x ananassa): V-shaped yellow chlorotic blotches developing at the margins and tips of older lower leaflets that soon turn brown and necrotic with a yellow halo; leaves wilt during the heat of the day (often affecting one side of a leaf or branch first); outer older leaves on strawberry crowns turn brown and collapse while inner leaves remain green initially; light tan-to-brown streaking is visible in the vascular tissue near the base of the stem.

symptom_progression: Microsclerotia germinate near root exudates, invade root cortex and xylem, and slowly plug water transport; plants become chronically stunted with progressive lower-leaf V-necrosis and reduced fruit size.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by characteristic V-shaped marginal yellow-and-brown fan lesions at leaflet tips, cooler temperature optimum (68–78°F vs 80–90°F for Fusarium wilt), and lighter tan vascular discoloration restricted closer to the lower stem.
similar_conditions: Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Early Blight, Potassium/Magnesium Deficiency, Phytophthora Crown Rot
risk_factors: Planting susceptible crops (such as strawberry, raspberry, or eggplant) in soil where tomato, potato, pepper, or eggplant grew within the preceding 3–4 years; root-lesion nematode feeding.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild soil temperatures (68–78°F) in spring followed by warm summer transpiration stress.
transmission_or_spread: Survives in soil for 8–10+ years as microscopic dark resting bodies (microsclerotia) across a wide host range of >300 broadleaf crops and weeds (nightshades, lambsquarters, pigweed).
management_actions: Remove infected plants and roots; maintain even irrigation and balanced potassium nutrition to help moderately tolerant plants mature fruit; solarize infested garden beds under clear plastic for 6 weeks in midsummer.
prevention_actions: Plant Verticillium-resistant cultivars ('V' designation in tomatoes); NEVER plant strawberries, brambles, or eggplants where nightshade family crops grew in the past 4 years; rotate with non-host grasses, sweet corn, or brassicas (broccoli residue biofumigation reduces microsclerotia).

visible_symptoms: Strawberry is the single most salt-sensitive fruit crop (yield drops above soil ECe 1.0 dS/m): older and middle trifoliate leaves develop a sharp, dry, reddish-brown to dark-brown necrotic scorch around the serrated leaflet margins ('salt burn'), plants are stunted, and runner/berry size shrinks.
symptom_keywords: strawberry, salinity & chloride marginal leaf burn of strawberry, salinity stress, salt injury, fertilizer burn, marginal leaf scorch, osmotic stunting, necrotic leaf tips
symptom_progression: Sodium and chloride ions accumulate in the transpirational stream at the serrated leaf margins until toxic concentrations kill marginal mesophyll cells.
distinguishing_features: Crisp brown necrotic scorching around all serration tips of mature leaves across the bed, correlated with high EC or heavy fertilizer application.
similar_conditions: Potassium deficiency (leaves a green triangle at the leaflet base and affects mainly fruiting plants); Leaf scorch fungus (irregular purple blotches across the blade).
risk_factors: Arid/semi-arid regions with saline well water, heavy applications of high-salt-index synthetic fertilizers or raw poultry/feedlot manure near roots, or un-leached high tunnels and containers.
favorable_conditions: Arid/semi-arid regions with saline well water, heavy applications of high-salt-index synthetic fertilizers or raw poultry/feedlot manure near roots, or un-leached high tunnels and containers.
management_actions: Leach the root zone deeply with low-salt fresh water (applying 2–4 inches of slow irrigation where drainage permits) to flush soluble salts below the active root zone, and stop all fertilizer applications.
prevention_actions: Test soil and irrigation water EC, place banded fertilizers at least 2–3 inches beside and below seeds/roots, use low-salt-index slow-release or organic fertilizers, and periodically flush high-tunnel soils.

topic: Grape Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs Management
problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.

topic: Grape Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.

severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)

topic: Grape Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Grape (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Grape (Vitis vinifera, Vitaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Grape Black Rot of Grape (Guignardia bidwellii)
problem_name: Black Rot of Grape
causal_agent: Guignardia bidwellii (anamorph Phyllosticta ampelicida)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, shoots, tendrils, petioles, and developing berries
growth_stage: 1-inch shoot growth through bloom and berry veraison (berries become resistant once sugar accumulation/veraison begins!)
season: Warm, rainy, humid late spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Rain events keeping leaves/berries wet for 6–12+ hours
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): On leaves: circular reddish-brown to tan spots (1/8 to 1/4 inch) with a narrow dark-brown border and a diagnostic ring of tiny black pimple-like pycnidia just inside the outer margin; On green berries (from pea-size until veraison): a small pale whitish dot rapidly enlarges into a mahogany-brown sunken band that engulfs the entire berry within 48 hours, shriveling it within a week into a hard, wrinkled, coal-black 'mummy' studded with black pycnidia.
symptom_keywords: circular tan leaf spots with ring of black dots, shriveled hard coal-black raisin mummies on grape cluster, mahogany berry rot
symptom_progression: Overwintered mummies on the trellis and ground shoot ascospores during spring rains, infecting young leaves and tendrils first; conidia from leaf spots and hanging mummies then wash directly onto young green berries during the critical 4–5 week window after bloom.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the ring of tiny black pycnidia dots inside circular tan leaf spots and the transformation of green grapes into rock-hard, wrinkled, coal-black mummies (unlike Botrytis bunch rot, which occurs on ripe sugary grapes with fuzzy gray mold).
similar_conditions: Botrytis Bunch Rot (affects ripe berries after veraison with fuzzy gray mold), Downy Mildew, Powdery Mildew, Anthracnose ('bird's-eye' spots)
risk_factors: Leaving old shriveled black grape mummies hanging on trellis wires or in old tendrils during winter pruning, dense shaded canopies, and rainy post-bloom weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm rains (70–85°F) during bloom and the 4 weeks immediately following bloom.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in mummified berries hanging in the trellis or lying on the ground and in cane lesions.
management_actions: During winter dormant pruning, meticulously remove EVERY old shriveled cluster mummy from the vines and trellis wires and bury or mulch fallen mummies on the ground (even a few hanging mummies left in the canopy will shower the clusters below with spores!); pull leaves around clusters after bloom for rapid drying.
prevention_actions: Select tolerant cultivars (such as muscadines Vitis rotundifolia or tolerant bunch grapes 'Norton'/'Cynthiana', 'Chambourcin'); apply protectant fungicides from immediate pre-bloom through 4 weeks post-bloom if wet weather occurs.
recommended_observations: Scout Grape (leaves, shoots, tendrils, petioles, and developing berries) weekly during warm, rainy, humid late spring and early summer (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Rot of Grape from Botrytis Bunch Rot (affects ripe berries after veraison with fuzzy gray mold), Downy Mildew, Powdery Mildew, Anthracnose ('bird's-eye' spots).
severity_or_impact: High to Critical in humid eastern/midwestern gardens (can turn 80–100% of a grape crop into hard black mummies before ripening)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and rain events keeping leaves/berries wet for 6–12+ hours.
host_range: Documented on Grape (Vitis vinifera, Vitaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape).

topic: Grape Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Grape (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Grape (Vitis vinifera, Vitaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).

topic: Grape Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').
symptom_keywords: fuzzy brownish-gray mold, dusty spore masses, stem pruning wound canker, blossom blight, berry gray rot, ghost spot rings on tomato
symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.
recommended_observations: Scout Grape (senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits) weekly during cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) from Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight.
severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, brambles, grapes, and high-tunnel tomatoes (major pre- and post-harvest fruit loss)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh), fog, rain, and poor air circulation.
host_range: Documented on Grape (Vitis vinifera, Vitaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Grape, Blueberry).

topic: Grape Pierce's Disease, Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot, and Eutypa Dieback of Grape (Xylella fastidiosa)
problem_name: Pierce's Disease, Phomopsis Cane and Leaf Spot, and Eutypa Dieback of Grape
causal_agent: Xylella fastidiosa (Pierce's Disease - bacterium), Phomopsis viticola (Phomopsis), and Eutypa lata (Eutypa Dieback)
affected_plant_parts: Xylem vascular vessels, canes, spurs, leaves, rachises, and berries
growth_stage: Budbreak and spring shoot elongation through late summer
season: Wet spring (Phomopsis/Eutypa) or warm mild-winter climates (Pierce's Disease)
humidity_conditions: Spring rain splash (Phomopsis) or xylem-feeding sharpshooter leafhopper activity (Pierce's Disease)
visible_symptoms: On Grape (Vitis vinifera): Pierce's Disease (late summer): leaf margins scorch yellow-to-red and dry brown in concentric zones while green 'islands' of tissue remain on maturing brown canes, clusters raisin prematurely, and uniquely, dead scorched leaf blades drop off the vine while the bare petioles ('matchsticks') remain firmly attached to the cane!; Phomopsis: tiny black necrotic spots with yellow halos on lower shoot leaves and elongated, sunken, black scabby cracks along the lowest 3–6 internodes of young green shoots, bleaching white with black speckles in winter; Eutypa Dieback: stunted spring shoots with small, cupped, tattered yellow leaves on one cordon arm and a dark V-shaped dead wedge in cross-section of the woody trunk.
symptom_keywords: scorched leaf margins with bare matchstick petioles left on cane, green islands on maturing cane bark, black scabby cracks on basal shoot internodes, V-shaped dead wood wedge in cordon
symptom_progression: In Pierce's Disease, sharpshooter insects inject Xylella bacteria directly into xylem water vessels, forming bacterial biofilm plugs that cause terminal water stress and 'matchstick' petiole drop in late summer; in Phomopsis, spring rain splashes spores from bleached spurs onto emerging basal shoot internodes.
distinguishing_features: Pierce's Disease is uniquely identified by 'matchsticks' (leaf blades abscising cleanly from the petiole tip while the petiole stays attached to the cane) plus patchy green-and-brown bark maturation.
similar_conditions: Black Rot, Downy Mildew, Potassium or Magnesium Deficiency (no matchstick petioles), Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Mild winters (allowing Xylella fastidiosa and glassy-winged/blue-green sharpshooters to survive in USDA Zones 7b–10), riparian/weedy vineyard borders, and large unsealed winter pruning wounds made during wet weather.
favorable_conditions: Mild winter climates and warm summers (Pierce's Disease); prolonged cool spring rains after budbreak (Phomopsis).
transmission_or_spread: Pierce's Disease is vectored by xylem-feeding sharpshooter leafhoppers and spittlebugs; Phomopsis splashes by rain from old spurs; Eutypa ascospores blow into large pruning wounds during rain.
management_actions: Prune out bleached/black-speckled Phomopsis spurs and dead Eutypa cordon arms during dry late-winter weather (cutting back to clean healthy white wood and painting large pruning cuts with wound sealant or boron/fungicide paste); rogue Pierce's-Disease-infected vines.
prevention_actions: In Pierce's Disease regions (Southeast US, Gulf Coast, Texas, low-elevation California), plant resistant muscadine grapes (Vitis rotundifolia) or PD-resistant bunch grape hybrids (such as 'Blanc du Bois', 'Black Spanish'/'Lenoir', 'Camminare Noir', 'Paseante Noir', 'Ambulo Blanc').

severity_or_impact: Critical for Pierce's Disease in warm winter zones; Moderate-to-High for Phomopsis and Eutypa in humid zones
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–85°F (15–29°C) and spring rain splash (phomopsis) or xylem-feeding sharpshooter leafhopper activity (pierce's disease).
host_range: Documented on Grape (Vitis vinifera, Vitaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape).

topic: Grape Nutrient Requirements and Fertilization Schedule
growth_stage: Pre-plant bed preparation, active vegetative growth, and reproductive/storage organ development
soil_ph: 5.5–6.5 for American/labrusca and muscadine grapes; 6.0–7.0 for European Vitis vinifera
management_actions: Moderate feeder; base applications on petiole tissue analysis; excessive nitrogen causes overly vigorous shaded canopies, poor fruit set, delayed cane hardening, and winter injury
prevention_actions: Base fertilizer rates on a soil test and maintain soil pH at 5.5–6.5 for American/labrusca and muscadine grapes; 6.0–7.0 for European Vitis vinifera to keep macronutrients and micronutrients bioavailable; avoid over-application of soluble nitrogen salts which can burn roots or skew vegetative-to-reproductive balance.
recommended_observations: Monitor shoot vigor, leaf color on both older lower leaves (mobile nutrients N, P, K, Mg) and new upper leaves (immobile nutrients Fe, Ca, B, Zn, Mn), and fruit/root set.

Maintain soil pH within 5.5–6.5 for American/labrusca and muscadine grapes; 6.0–7.0 for European Vitis vinifera to ensure optimal nutrient availability.

topic: Grape Harvest Readiness Indicators, Harvesting Method, and Storage

causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)

season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Citrus (Citrus sinensis): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.

symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.

transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.

prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.

topic: Citrus Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites Management
problem_name: Eriophyid and Tarsonemid Mites (Tomato Russet Mite, Broad Mite, and Cyclamen Mite)
causal_agent: Aculops lycopersici (Tomato Russet Mite), Polyphagotarsonemus latus (Broad Mite), and Phytonemus pallidus (Cyclamen Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Lower stems and lower leaves moving upward (Tomato Russet Mite) OR newest apical shoot tips, buds, and young fruit (Broad and Cyclamen Mites)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through flowering and fruit set
season: Warm-to-hot summer weather (Russet/Broad Mite) or cool humid spring/fall (Cyclamen Mite)
humidity_conditions: High humidity inside dense crowns (Broad/Cyclamen Mites) or warm dry summer weather (Tomato Russet Mite)
visible_symptoms: On Citrus (Citrus sinensis): Tomato Russet Mite: a greasy, bronze, russet-tan discoloration starting at the base of the main stem and lower petioles that moves steadily upward like a rising tide—lower leaves turn bronze-brown, papery, and dry up (WITHOUT wilting first and WITHOUT any silk webbing!), while stems become tan-russeted with fine surface cracks; Broad Mite (on Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Papaya, Citrus) & Cyclamen Mite (on Strawberry): toxic saliva injected into the newest unfolded crown leaves causes terminal shoots to become severely stunted, thickened, brittle, downward-cupped or crinkled, bronzed, and rosetted, with aborted flowers and corky russeted fruit.

symptom_progression: Microscopic mites (0.15–0.2 mm—invisible to the naked eye and requiring a 20x–30x lens!) reproduce every 4–7 days, either climbing upward from the stem base (Russet Mite) or hiding tightly inside unopened terminal buds (Broad/Cyclamen Mites).
distinguishing_features: Tomato Russet Mite is distinguished from Spider Mites by the complete absence of silk webbing or individual stipple dots and the greasy bronze-tan sheen on the lower stem; Broad Mite injury on pepper/strawberry terminal shoots mimics viral mosaic or 2,4-D herbicide drift, except leaf veins do not show Parallel 'strapping' and a 20x lens reveals tiny football-shaped eggs studded with rows of white polka-dot tubercles!

favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) for Russet and Broad Mites; cooler humid weather (60–75°F) for Cyclamen Mite.

topic: Citrus Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing / HLB) and Citrus Canker (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus)
problem_name: Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing / HLB) and Citrus Canker
causal_agent: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (HLB) and Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri (Citrus Canker)
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system (HLB), leaves, twigs, and fruits
growth_stage: Year-round during new vegetative shoot flushes and fruit development
season: Warm subtropical/tropical growing seasons
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring Asian citrus psyllid (HLB) or wind-driven summer rains (Citrus Canker)
visible_symptoms: On Citrus (Citrus sinensis): Huanglongbing (HLB): diagnostic ASYMMETRICAL ('blotchy mottle') yellow-and-green chlorosis on leaves where yellowing crosses veins irregularly and is NOT identical on the left and right halves of the leaf blade, accompanied by yellow corky veins, upright small 'rabbit-ear' leaves, twig dieback, and small, lopsided, curved fruits that stay green at the blossom/stylar end ('greening') with aborted dark-brown seeds and bitter, salty juice; Citrus Canker: raised, corky, crater-like tan-brown lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit surrounded by a distinct oily water-soaked margin and a bright yellow halo.
symptom_keywords: asymmetrical blotchy mottle on leaves, lopsided fruit staying green at bottom, aborted dark seeds, bitter citrus juice, raised corky craters with yellow halo
symptom_progression: In HLB, Asian citrus psyllids inject phloem-limited bacteria into new shoot flushes, progressively starving the roots and plugging sieve tubes over 1–3 years; in Canker, wind-blown rain splashes bacteria into stomata and thorn scratches.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION for HLB vs Nutrient (Zinc/Iron/Magnesium) Deficiency: Nutrient deficiencies produce SYMMETRICAL chlorosis (the left and right sides of the leaf blade across the midrib are mirror images), whereas HLB produces ASYMMETRICAL 'blotchy mottle' where yellow and green patches do not match across the midrib!
similar_conditions: Zinc, Iron, Manganese, or Magnesium Micronutrient Deficiency (symmetrical leaf patterns), Phytophthora Foot Rot, Citrus Scab
risk_factors: Presence of the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri), moving non-certified citrus plants or budwood, and citrus leafminer feeding galleries (which dramatically increase Citrus Canker infection).
favorable_conditions: Warm flushing periods attracting Asian citrus psyllids; tropical storms and wind-driven rain for Citrus Canker.
transmission_or_spread: HLB is vectored persistently by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) and by grafting infected budwood; Citrus Canker is spread by wind-driven rain splash and contaminated tools.
management_actions: Inspect new tender leaf flushes for adult Asian citrus psyllids (which feed tilted at a 45-degree angle with brown-mottled wings) and yellow-orange nymphs Producing waxy tubules; manage psyllids and citrus leafminers; provide optimal balanced micro-nutrient nutrition and low-stress irrigation.
prevention_actions: NEVER move citrus plants, cuttings, or curry leaf plants out of quarantined HLB/Canker areas; purchase only certified clean nursery stock grown in insect-proof screenhouses.
recommended_observations: Scout Citrus (phloem vascular system (hlb), leaves, twigs, and fruits) weekly during warm subtropical/tropical growing seasons (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Citrus Greening (Huanglongbing / HLB) and Citrus Canker from Zinc, Iron, Manganese, or Magnesium Micronutrient Deficiency (symmetrical leaf patterns), Phytophthora Foot Rot, Citrus Scab.
severity_or_impact: Critical (HLB is the most devastating disease of citrus worldwide; systemic and incurable)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and warm weather favoring asian citrus psyllid (hlb) or wind-driven summer rains (citrus canker).
host_range: Documented on Citrus (Citrus sinensis, Rutaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Citrus, Lemon, Lime).

topic: Citrus (Citrus sinensis) High-Temperature 'June Drop' (Physiological Fruitlet Abscission) of Citrus: Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management
problem_name: High-Temperature 'June Drop' (Physiological Fruitlet Abscission) of Citrus
affected_plant_parts: Pea-to-walnut-sized green citrus fruitlets and young leaves
growth_stage: Late spring / early summer heat spikes (>95–100°F)
season: Spring planting after all danger of frost in USDA Zones 9–11 (or year-round in large containers moved indoors in winter in colder zones)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 70–90°F (21–32°C); vegetative growth ceases below 55°F (quiescence); mature sweet orange/mandarin trees tolerate brief dips to 26–28°F, while ripe fruit freezes at 27–28°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Young green citrus fruitlets (0.5–1.5 inches in diameter) turn dull yellowish-green from the stylar end, separate cleanly at the calyx button disk, and rain down from the tree in large numbers while young flush leaves curl inward like boats.
symptom_keywords: citrus, high-temperature 'june drop' (physiological fruitlet abscission) of citrus, heat stress, thermal leaf scorch, midday wilting, stomatal closure, heat-arrested growth, leaf rolling
symptom_progression: While some post-bloom physiological drop is normal adjustment of crop load, sudden late-spring heat waves (>95–100°F) create severe carbohydrate and water competition between leaves and fruitlets, triggering massive ethylene-mediated abscission.
distinguishing_features: Clean separation of small green fruitlets at the calyx disk during hot weather without black fungal lesions inside the button.
similar_conditions: Post-bloom fruit drop (Colletotrichum acutatum—leaves persistent enlarged orange-brown calyx 'buttons' attached to twigs).
risk_factors: Multi-day heat waves above 90–100°F accompanied by warm nights (>72–75°F), intense solar radiation, dry winds, and bare unmulched soil.
favorable_conditions: Multi-day heat waves above 90–100°F accompanied by warm nights (>72–75°F), intense solar radiation, dry winds, and bare unmulched soil.
management_actions: Install 30–40% woven shade cloth over hoops to lower canopy temperatures by 6–10°F, irrigate deeply in the early morning before heat peaks, and apply 2–3 inches of straw or organic mulch to cool the root zone.
prevention_actions: Select heat-tolerant cultivars, time cool-season plantings for spring and autumn windows, mulch beds early, and avoid fertilizer salt buildup prior to summer heat waves.
recommended_observations: Correlate symptom onset across Citrus and neighboring garden plants with recent weather extremes (heat, frost, wind, hail, flooding, drought) or nearby herbicide/fertilizer applications, and inspect new growth for recovery.
severity_or_impact: Excessive heat-induced June drop can strip 60–90% of the developing crop on Navel oranges and mandarins.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Subtropical/tropical broadleaf evergreen woody perennial fruit tree (Citrus sinensis sweet orange, C. reticulata mandarin/tangerine, C. paradisi grapefruit). topic: Citrus (Citrus sinensis) Salinity & Chloride Bronzing / Tip Burn of Citrus: Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management
problem_name: Salinity & Chloride Bronzing / Tip Burn of Citrus
affected_plant_parts: Mature older leaves
growth_stage: Mid-to-late summer in saline soil or water
season: Spring planting after all danger of frost in USDA Zones 9–11 (or year-round in large containers moved indoors in winter in colder zones)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 70–90°F (21–32°C); vegetative growth ceases below 55°F (quiescence); mature sweet orange/mandarin trees tolerate brief dips to 26–28°F, while ripe fruit freezes at 27–28°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.

symptom_progression: Chloride and sodium ions accumulate in transpiring mature leaves when irrigation water EC exceeds 1.5–2.0 dS/m.
distinguishing_features: Tip and marginal brown scorch on older leaves without yellow halos or raised corky pustules.
similar_conditions: Citrus canker; Potassium deficiency.
