prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Mango to verify soil pH (5.5–7.5) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Mango (Mangifera indica): Prefers well-drained sandy, gravelly, limestone, or loamy soil; tolerates low-fertility soils but rots in flooded clay with an optimal soil pH of 5.5–7.5. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Mango Nutrient Requirements and Fertilization Schedule

management_actions: CRITICAL: mature bearing mango trees require VERY LOW nitrogen and high potassium plus calcium, magnesium, boron, zinc, and iron; excessive nitrogen causes vegetative flushes instead of flowers and induces physiological 'soft nose' / 'spongy tissue' internal fruit breakdown
prevention_actions: Base fertilizer rates on a soil test and maintain soil pH at 5.5–7.5 to keep macronutrients and micronutrients bioavailable; avoid over-application of soluble nitrogen salts which can burn roots or skew vegetative-to-reproductive balance.
recommended_observations: Monitor shoot vigor, leaf color on both older lower leaves (mobile nutrients N, P, K, Mg) and new upper leaves (immobile nutrients Fe, Ca, B, Zn, Mn), and fruit/root set.

topic: Mango (Mangifera indica) Chilling Injury of Mango Inflorescences, Flush & Fruit: Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management
problem_name: Chilling Injury of Mango Inflorescences, Flush & Fruit
affected_plant_parts: Floral panicles, tender copper-red vegetative flushes, and fruit skin
growth_stage: Temperatures between 34°F and 50°F (1–10°C)
season: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring or early summer in frost-free USDA Zones 10–11
temperature_range: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); requires dry cool-to-mild winter weather (50–60°F nights) to check vegetative flushes and induce floral panicles; young trees are killed below 29–30°F and mature trees damaged below 25–27°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Non-freezing temperatures below 45–50°F during winter/spring bloom blister and blacken tender floral panicles, cause embryo abortion (producing small seedless 'nubbin' mangoes), scorch young vegetative flushes, and cause grayish-brown skin scald on fruit stored below 50–55°F.
symptom_keywords: mango, chilling injury of mango inflorescences, flush & fruit, chilling injury, cold shock, water-soaked leaves, membrane leakage, surface pitting, cold-stunted growth
symptom_progression: Pollen tube growth and fertilized mango embryos abort when night temperatures fall below 48–50°F during bloom.
distinguishing_features: Aborted black floral spikelets and small seedless 'haden-nubbin' fruits following <50°F bloom nights.
similar_conditions: Mango anthracnose and powdery mildew on panicles.
risk_factors: Setting warm-season transplants outdoors too early in spring when soil is below 58–60°F and nights drop into the 40s°F, or storing harvested warm-season fruits below 50–55°F.
favorable_conditions: Setting warm-season transplants outdoors too early in spring when soil is below 58–60°F and nights drop into the 40s°F, or storing harvested warm-season fruits below 50–55°F.
management_actions: Cover chilled field plants with spunbonded floating row covers or cloches overnight, withhold heavy watering while cold roots cannot absorb water, and store chilling-sensitive produce above 52–55°F.
prevention_actions: Wait to transplant warm-season vegetables until soil temperature at 4-inch depth reaches 60–65°F and night air stays above 55°F; pre-warm beds with black plastic mulch.
recommended_observations: Correlate symptom onset across Mango and neighboring garden plants with recent weather extremes (heat, frost, wind, hail, flooding, drought) or nearby herbicide/fertilizer applications, and inspect new growth for recovery.
severity_or_impact: Causes heavy blossom loss and high proportions of small seedless nubbin fruit.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Tropical broadleaf evergreen woody perennial fruit tree (Mangifera indica). Optimal thermal regime: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); requires dry cool-to-mild winter weather (50–60°F nights) to check vegetative flushes and induce floral panicles; young trees are killed below 29–30°F and mature trees damaged below 25–27°F.
host_range: Mango (Mangifera indica, family Anacardiaceae) and physiologically similar fruit crops.
knowledge_text: Chilling Injury of Mango Inflorescences, Flush & Fruit on Mango (Mangifera indica, family Anacardiaceae) is an abiotic environmental stress caused by non-freezing chilling temperatures (33–54°f / 1–12°c) disrupting cell membrane lipid fluidity and chloroplast function in warm-season/tropical crops. Visual symptoms: Non-freezing temperatures below 45–50°F during winter/spring bloom blister and blacken tender floral panicles, cause embryo abortion (producing small seedless 'nubbin' mangoes), scorch young vegetative flushes, and cause grayish-brown skin scald on fruit stored below 50–55°F. Progression: Pollen tube growth and fertilized mango embryos abort when night temperatures fall below 48–50°F during bloom. Distinguishing features: Aborted black floral spikelets and small seedless 'haden-nubbin' fruits following <50°F bloom nights. Predisposing conditions: Setting warm-season transplants outdoors too early in spring when soil is below 58–60°F and nights drop into the 40s°F, or storing harvested warm-season fruits below 50–55°F. Management and prevention: Cover chilled field plants with spunbonded floating row covers or cloches overnight, withhold heavy watering while cold roots cannot absorb water, and store chilling-sensitive produce above 52–55°F. Wait to transplant warm-season vegetables until soil temperature at 4-inch depth reaches 60–65°F and night air stays above 55°F; pre-warm beds with black plastic mulch.

topic: Mango (Mangifera indica) Zinc (Zn) Deficiency ('Little-Leaf' Rosetting & Leaf Blade Distortion): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Zinc (Zn) Deficiency ('Little-Leaf' Rosetting & Leaf Blade Distortion)
affected_plant_parts: Young terminal vegetative flushes and floral panicles
growth_stage: Post-harvest vegetative flushes and panicle emergence
season: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring or early summer in frost-free USDA Zones 10–11
temperature_range: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); requires dry cool-to-mild winter weather (50–60°F nights) to check vegetative flushes and induce floral panicles; young trees are killed below 29–30°F and mature trees damaged below 25–27°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Terminal flush internodes are drastically shortened so that small, narrow, thickened, brittle leaves cluster in an upright 'little-leaf' rosette; leaf blades bend or twist with yellow interveinal blotches and bronzed necrotic margins, and floral panicles emerge small and deformed.
symptom_keywords: mango, zinc (zn) deficiency, immobile in phloem (required for auxin/iaa synthesis and internode elongation), young terminal vegetative flushes and floral panicles, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Young terminal shoots, apical leaf whorls, and newly expanding leaves. Develops on alkaline/calcareous limestone soils or after heavy phosphorus fertilization.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Immobile in phloem (required for auxin/IAA synthesis and internode elongation). Thickened, brittle, narrow rosetted leaves with yellow interveinal blotches and green veins distinguish Zinc deficiency from Fungal mango malformation (which produces compact witches'-brooms of green vegetative buds without interveinal chlorosis).
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Mango.
risk_factors: Calcareous or high-pH soils (pH > 7.0), sandy soils low in organic matter or leveled subsoils exposed during grading, cold wet spring soils, or excessive soil phosphorus levels (phosphorus-induced zinc tie-up in roots and soil).
favorable_conditions: Calcareous or high-pH soils (pH > 7.0), sandy soils low in organic matter or leveled subsoils exposed during grading, cold wet spring soils, or excessive soil phosphorus levels (phosphorus-induced zinc tie-up in roots and soil).
management_actions: Apply a foliar spray of zinc sulfate, zinc chelate (Zn-EDTA), or neutralized zinc spray to emerging spring foliage flashes, or incorporate zinc sulfate into the root zone.
prevention_actions: Avoid excessive phosphorus fertilization on high-P soils, maintain soil pH between 6.0 and 6.8, incorporate compost to preservemycorrhizal colonization (which strongly aids Zn uptake), and use dormant or post-bloom foliar zinc sprays in perennial orchards.
recommended_observations: Inspect whether symptoms initiate on older lower foliage vs. youngest upper leaves/meristems on Mango, verify soil pH (optimal for Mango: 5.5–7.5) and soil moisture, and confirm with a soil or plant tissue test.
severity_or_impact: Severely reduces panicle fruit set and stunts canopy renewal flushes.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Tropical broadleaf evergreen woody perennial fruit tree (Mangifera indica). Optimal thermal regime: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); requires dry cool-to-mild winter weather (50–60°F nights) to check vegetative flushes and induce floral panicles; young trees are killed below 29–30°F and mature trees damaged below 25–27°F.

topic: Mango (Mangifera indica) Spongy Tissue & Internal Pulp Breakdown ('Jelly Seed') of Mango: Physiological Mechanism, Diagnosis & Prevention
problem_name: Spongy Tissue & Internal Pulp Breakdown ('Jelly Seed') of Mango
affected_plant_parts: Internal mesocarp pulp surrounding the stone (endocarp)
growth_stage: Physiological maturation and ripening on the tree
season: Plant container-grown grafted trees in spring or early summer in frost-free USDA Zones 10–11
temperature_range: Optimal growth 75–95°F (24–35°C); requires dry cool-to-mild winter weather (50–60°F nights) to check vegetative flushes and induce floral panicles; young trees are killed below 29–30°F and mature trees damaged below 25–27°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Externally the mango fruit looks completely normal and healthy, but slicing the ripe fruit reveals either (1) Spongy tissue—a pale yellowish-white, unripe, sour, spongy-to-corky patch with air pockets in the lower mesocarp; or (2) Jelly seed / Soft nose—over-ripe, translucent, jelly-like breakdown of the flesh around the stone or beak.
symptom_keywords: mango, spongy tissue & internal pulp breakdown ('jelly seed') of mango, hollow heart, internal brown spot, blackheart, internal cavitation, star-shaped hollow center, pith separation
symptom_progression: Spongy tissue is triggered by convective heat radiation from bare soil inactivating ripening enzymes (amylase/invertase) in the lower flesh; jelly seed is linked to low fruit Calcium relative to Nitrogen/Potassium.
distinguishing_features: Internal pale spongy sour zone or jelly-like periseed breakdown inside an externally spotless mango without mango seed weevil larvae.
similar_conditions: Mango seed weevil (Sternochetus mangiferae); Anthracnose.
risk_factors: Wide plant spacing, excessive nitrogen fertilization, and sudden heavy irrigation or warm weather following a cool/dry spell during rapid tuber, melon, or stem bulking (or >90°F soil/storage hypoxia for blackheart).
favorable_conditions: Wide plant spacing, excessive nitrogen fertilization, and sudden heavy irrigation or warm weather following a cool/dry spell during rapid tuber, melon, or stem bulking (or >90°F soil/storage hypoxia for blackheart).
management_actions: Maintain uniform irrigation and harvest on time before oversize bulking; sort out hollow or internally discolored produce by specific gravity or sampling before long-term storage.
prevention_actions: Use closer in-row plant spacing to moderate individual unit growth rate, split nitrogen applications, maintain consistent soil moisture, and ensure adequate soil drainage and storage ventilation.
recommended_observations: Examine the exact anatomical position of symptoms on Mango (Internal mesocarp pulp surrounding the stone (endocarp)), review recent irrigation, temperature, pollination, and fertility logs, and confirm absence of fungal fruiting bodies or insect larvae.
severity_or_impact: Causes up to 30% hidden internal rejection in susceptible cultivars (such as Alphonso and Tommy Atkins).
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Tropical broadleaf evergreen woody perennial fruit tree (Mangifera indica). knowledge_text: Spongy Tissue & Internal Pulp Breakdown ('Jelly Seed') of Mango in Mango (Mangifera indica, family Anacardiaceae) is a non-infectious physiological disorder caused by abrupt surge in parenchyma cell enlargement outpacing central pith division or internal oxygen depletion (hypoxia). Visual symptoms: Externally the mango fruit looks completely normal and healthy, but slicing the ripe fruit reveals either (1) Spongy tissue—a pale yellowish-white, unripe, sour, spongy-to-corky patch with air pockets in the lower mesocarp; or (2) Jelly seed / Soft nose—over-ripe, translucent, jelly-like breakdown of the flesh around the stone or beak. Progression: Spongy tissue is triggered by convective heat radiation from bare soil inactivating ripening enzymes (amylase/invertase) in the lower flesh; jelly seed is linked to low fruit Calcium relative to Nitrogen/Potassium. Distinguishing features: Internal pale spongy sour zone or jelly-like periseed breakdown inside an externally spotless mango without mango seed weevil larvae. Favorable conditions: Wide plant spacing, excessive nitrogen fertilization, and sudden heavy irrigation or warm weather following a cool/dry spell during rapid tuber, melon, or stem bulking (or >90°F soil/storage hypoxia for blackheart). Management and prevention: Maintain uniform irrigation and harvest on time before oversize bulking; sort out hollow or internally discolored produce by specific gravity or sampling before long-term storage. Use closer in-row plant spacing to moderate individual unit growth rate, split nitrogen applications, maintain consistent soil moisture, and ensure adequate soil drainage and storage ventilation.

problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes

distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.

topic: Apple Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.

similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.

topic: Apple Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies Management
problem_name: Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies
problem_category: Fruit-Scarring & Internal Larval Pest of Stone and Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Conotrachelus nenuphar (Plum Curculio) and Rhagoletis cingulata / Rhagoletis fausta / Rhagoletis indifferens (Cherry Fruit Flies)
affected_plant_parts: Immature newly set fruits (petal fall / shuck split) and ripening cherries
growth_stage: Petal fall / shuck split through harvest
season: Spring (Plum Curculio) and early summer as cherries turn yellow-red (Cherry Fruit Fly)
humidity_conditions: Warm (>70°F) humid spring days and nights following rain
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Plum Curculio: a small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), rough-backed, brownish-black snout weevil with grey-white flecks and four prominent humps on its wing covers that emerges at petal fall / shuck split; the female chews a small hole in the tiny green fruitlet, inserts an egg, and then cuts a diagnostic crescent-shaped (D-shaped / half-moon) slit right underneath the egg so the rapidly expanding fruit flesh will not crush her egg! In apples and pears, the fruit expansion usually crushes the larva anyway, leaving a raised, corky, D-shaped fan scar on the mature apple skin; in plums, peaches, cherries, and blueberries, the legless, curved, yellowish-white grub with a brown head tunnels to the pit, causing clear gummy sap droplets to ooze from the crescent scar and causing premature fruit drop or ripe wormy fruit; Cherry Fruit Fly: legless white maggots (no head capsule!) feed around the pit of ripe red cherries without external deformity until sunken soft spots and exit holes appear.
symptom_keywords: crescent-shaped half-moon scar on young green plum peach or apple, gummy clear sap droplet oozing from crescent cut, rough humpbacked brown snout weevil playing dead when tapped, legless grub with brown head next to peach or plum pit, headless white maggot inside ripe cherry
symptom_progression: Overwintered Plum Curculio adults walk/fly from woodlots into fruit trees during bloom and attack fruitlets for 3–5 weeks after petal fall whenever temperatures exceed 70°F; Cherry Fruit Flies emerge from soil just as early cherries show the first blush of yellow-pink color.
distinguishing_features: Plum Curculio is unmistakably identified by the signature crescent-shaped (half-moon) oviposition scar cut into the skin of young apples, plums, peaches, and cherries; inside ripe cherries, Plum Curculio larva has a distinct brown head capsule and curved C-shape, whereas Cherry Fruit Fly maggot is headless and cone-shaped.
similar_conditions: Tarnished Plant Bug / Stink Bug Catfacing (sunken dimples without a crescent-shaped flap cut), Hail Scars, Codling Moth
risk_factors: Fruit trees planted adjacent to deciduous woodlots, hedgerows, or brush piles (where Plum Curculio adults overwinter in leaf litter) and uncollected dropped stone fruits.
favorable_conditions: Spring days reaching 70–75°F+ or warm nights (>60°F) right after petal fall / shuck split.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded border litter and migrate into trees in spring; mature larvae exit fallen fruit to pupate 1–2 inches deep in the soil.
management_actions: Lay a light-colored sheet on the ground under plum, peach, and apple branches in the cool early morning for the 3 weeks after petal fall and sharply tap limbs with a padded stick—Plum Curculio adults fold their legs, play dead ('thanatosis'), and drop onto the sheet looking like bits of bark or bird droppings so you can collect and destroy them; spray kaolin clay (Surround—keep a white coat on fruitlets from petal fall for 4 weeks) or spinosad (for Cherry Fruit Fly, hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate as soon as cherries turn yellow-blush).
prevention_actions: Pick up and dispose of all 'June drop' fruitlets under plum, peach, cherry, and apple trees every 2 days in May/June before curculio grubs crawl out into the soil; prune trees open (Plum Curculio strongly prefers cool, dark, dense interior canopies).

severity_or_impact: Critical east of the Rocky Mountains (the #1 early-season insect pest of plums, peaches, cherries, and apples)

host_range: Documented on Apple (Malus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Plum, Peach, Cherry, Apple, Pear, Blueberry).

topic: Apple Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.
recommended_observations: Scout Apple (flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles) twice weekly during early spring through autumn (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips to distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug from Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs.

topic: Apple Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam; wet poorly drained clay promotes Phytophthora crown and collar rot (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry)
management_actions: Prepare a deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam; wet poorly drained clay promotes phytophthora crown and collar rot adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Apple to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Apple (Malus domestica): Prefers deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam; wet poorly drained clay promotes phytophthora crown and collar rot with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.
source_name: Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden
evidence_notes: Soil texture, drainage, and pH requirements verified against Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden and UC Statewide IPM Program (UC ANR).

topic: Apple Apple and Pear Scab (Venturia inaequalis)
problem_name: Apple and Pear Scab
causal_agent: Venturia inaequalis (Apple Scab) and Venturia pirina (Pear Scab)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, blossoms, pedicels, and developing fruits (plus young twigs in pear)
growth_stage: Green tip through petal fall and early summer fruit sizing
season: Cool, rainy spring weather
humidity_conditions: Rain events keeping leaves wet for 6–18+ hours (governed by the Mills Table of temperature x wetting duration)
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Velvety, olive-green to radiating sooty-black circular spots with feathery/indistinct margins on young leaves, causing leaves to pucker, yellow, and drop prematurely in early summer; on fruits, olive-black velvety spots mature into sunken, dark-brown corky, scabby lesions that restrict skin expansion on one side, causing the growing apple or pear to deform and crack open.
symptom_keywords: olive-green velvety leaf spots, corky black scabby fruit lesions, cracked deformed apples, feathery spot margins, premature early-summer leaf drop
symptom_progression: Overwintered pseudothecia in fallen autumn leaves forcefully shoot ascospores into the air during spring rains from green tip through 2–3 weeks after petal fall; primary leaf lesions then produce secondary conidia that splash onto fruit all summer.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the velvety olive-green-to-black spots with feathery margins on young spring leaves and dark corky scabs on fruit (unlike Sooty Blotch/Flyspeck, which appears late in summer strictly as superficial smudges/dots on the waxy fruit cuticle without deforming the skin).
similar_conditions: Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck, Cedar-Apple Rust (bright orange-yellow spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (Black Rot), Fire Blight
risk_factors: Susceptible cultivars (such as 'McIntosh', 'Cortland', 'Fuji', 'Gala', 'Bartlett'), un-raked fallen autumn leaf litter under trees, and frequent spring rains.
favorable_conditions: Spring rain events at 55–75°F lasting 6–12+ hours (Mills Infection Periods).
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in fallen infected leaves on the orchard floor (and in twig lesions in Pear Scab), releasing wind-borne ascospores in spring rain and splashing conidia in summer.
management_actions: Rake and destroy (or shred with a lawnmower and spray with 5% urea solution in late autumn) all fallen apple and pear leaves to eliminate 80–90% of overwintering ascospore inoculum; prune trees annually to open the canopy for rapid drying.
prevention_actions: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars carrying the Vf (Rvi6) gene (such as 'Liberty', 'Enterprise', 'GoldRush', 'Pristine', 'CrimsonCrisp', 'Freedom', 'Williams' Pride') and scab-resistant pears.
recommended_observations: Scout Apple (leaves, blossoms, pedicels, and developing fruits (plus young twigs in pear)) weekly during cool, rainy spring weather (55–75°F (13–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Apple and Pear Scab from Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck, Cedar-Apple Rust (bright orange-yellow spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (Black Rot), Fire Blight.
severity_or_impact: High (the #1 fungal disease of apples in humid regions; causes heavy defoliation and scabby cracked fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–75°F (13–24°C) and rain events keeping leaves wet for 6–18+ hours (governed by the mills table of temperature x wetting duration).
host_range: Documented on Apple (Malus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear).

topic: Apple Bitter Rot, Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Sooty Blotch / Flyspeck of Pome Fruits (Colletotrichum gloeosporioides / acutatum)
problem_name: Bitter Rot, Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Sooty Blotch / Flyspeck of Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides / acutatum (Bitter Rot), Botryosphaeria obtusa (Black Rot / Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Peltaster / Schizothyrium complex (Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening fruits, leaves, fruiting spurs, and woody limbs
growth_stage: Petal fall through late-summer fruit maturation and harvest
season: Warm-to-hot, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High summer humidity (>80% RH) and warm afternoon thunderstorms
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Bitter Rot: sunken, circular brown saucer-like rot spots on summer-ripening apples that develop concentric rings of creamy salmon-pink slimy spore masses in humid weather and penetrate toward the core in a diagnostic V-shaped cone when the apple is sliced in half (unlike Black Rot/White Rot which rot downward in a cylindrical core); Black Rot: 'frogeye leaf spots' (circular purple-bordered spots with tan centers on leaves), reddish-brown limb cankers, and firm black fruit rot with concentric brown-and-black bands and only ONE spot per fruit; Sooty Blotch & Flyspeck: superficial dull olive-black cloudy smudges and clusters of 10–50 tiny shiny black dots strictly on the waxy outer cuticle of late-season apples (peels or rubs off with no underlying rot!).
symptom_keywords: sunken saucer fruit rot with salmon-pink spore rings, V-shaped cone rot toward apple core, frogeye tan-centered leaf spots, superficial sooty smudges and tiny black flyspecks on skin
symptom_progression: Fungi overwinter in dead fire-blighted twigs, mummified fruitlets left from thinning, and bark cankers, splashing onto developing apples during hot humid summer storms.
distinguishing_features: Slice the rotted apple in half through the lesion: Bitter Rot forms a clean V-shaped cone pointing toward the core with salmon-pink slimy spore rings on the surface, whereas Black Rot forms a cylinder of firm black leathery rot; Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck are 100% cosmetic surface blemishes on the wax cuticle.
similar_conditions: Apple Scab (rough corky cracked skin lesions starting in spring), Brown Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit (small sunken physiological spots concentrated at calyx end with spongy brown flecks under skin)
risk_factors: Dead twigs (especially old Fire Blight strikes), unremoved fruit mummies, retained thinned fruitlets hanging in clusters, and dense humid tree canopies.
favorable_conditions: Hot, humid summer weather (77–90°F) with frequent rain showers.
transmission_or_spread: Rain-splashed conidia and wind-borne ascospores from dead twigs, limb cankers, and mummified fruits.
management_actions: Prune out all dead wood, cankers, and old Fire Blight strikes during winter; remove all mummified apples and hand-thinned fruitlets from the tree (do not leave thinned fruitlets lodged in spurs!); prune for open summer airflow (Sooty Blotch/Flyspeck apples are completely safe to eat after washing/peeling!).
prevention_actions: Maintain open-canopy pruning, thin fruit clusters to single apples, and apply summer protectant sprays in hot humid regions.
recommended_observations: Scout Apple (ripening fruits, leaves, fruiting spurs, and woody limbs) weekly during warm-to-hot, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bitter Rot, Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Sooty Blotch / Flyspeck of Pome Fruits from Apple Scab (rough corky cracked skin lesions starting in spring), Brown Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit (small sunken physiological spots concentrated at calyx end with spongy brown flecks under skin).
severity_or_impact: High for Bitter Rot and Black Rot in warm humid summers; Low/Cosmetic for Sooty Blotch & Flyspeck
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high summer humidity (>80% rh) and warm afternoon thunderstorms.
host_range: Documented on Apple (Malus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear).

topic: Apple Cedar-Apple Rust and Quince/Hawthorn Rust (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae)
problem_name: Cedar-Apple Rust and Quince/Hawthorn Rust
causal_agent: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae (Cedar-Apple Rust) and Gymnosporangium clavipes (Quince Rust)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, petioles, and fruits (and twigs in Quince Rust)
growth_stage: Pink bud through 4 weeks after petal fall
season: Warm spring rains
humidity_conditions: Spring rain wetting eastern red cedar galls for 4–8+ hours
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Bright, vivid yellow-to-orange circular spots (1/8 to 1/2 inch) on the upper surface of apple leaves (dotted with tiny black pycnia in the center) that develop clusters of cup-like, fringed, tubular projections (aecia) on the underside of the leaf and on the blossom end of deformed fruits in midsummer; heavy infection causes mid-season leaf yellowing and drop.
symptom_keywords: bright orange-yellow leaf spots, fringed tubular cups on leaf underside, orange blossom-end fruit spots, gelatinous orange horns on red cedar
symptom_progression: After spring rain swells brown woody galls on nearby Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana) into bright orange gelatinous tentacles, wind-borne basidiospores blow onto young apple leaves and fruit within 1–2 miles.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the brilliant neon yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface and the star-like clusters of fringed tubular aecia cups on the lower leaf surface in summer.
similar_conditions: Apple Scab (olive-black velvety spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (brown circular spots with gray centers)
risk_factors: Growing susceptible apple cultivars ('Golden Delicious', 'Rome', 'Jonathan', 'Ginger Gold') within 0.5–2 miles of Eastern Red Cedar or ornamental junipers.
favorable_conditions: Spring rains at 55–75°F while apples are between pink bud and 3 weeks post-petal-fall.
transmission_or_spread: Heteroecious rust requiring two alternate hosts to complete its 2-year lifecycle: Juniperus species (Eastern red cedar) and Rosaceae pome fruits (apple, crabapple, pear, quince, hawthorn); does NOT spread from apple leaf to apple leaf!
management_actions: Remove brown spherical galls from ornamental junipers/red cedars on your property in late winter before orange gelatinous horns emerge; apply protectant fungicides from pink bud through 3 weeks after petal fall on susceptible cultivars.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars (such as 'Liberty', 'Enterprise', 'Freedom', 'Redfree', 'William's Pride', 'Honeycrisp').
recommended_observations: Scout Apple (leaves, petioles, and fruits (and twigs in quince rust)) weekly during warm spring rains (55–75°F (13–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cedar-Apple Rust and Quince/Hawthorn Rust from Apple Scab (olive-black velvety spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (brown circular spots with gray centers).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (defoliates susceptible cultivars and disfigures fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–75°F (13–24°C) and spring rain wetting eastern red cedar galls for 4–8+ hours.
host_range: Documented on Apple (Malus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear).

Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the brilliant neon yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface and the star-like clusters of fringed tubular aecia cups on the lower leaf surface in summer. topic: Apple Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Apple (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Apple (Malus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).

Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!). Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.

topic: Apple Fire Blight (Erwinia amylovora)
problem_name: Fire Blight
causal_agent: Erwinia amylovora
affected_plant_parts: Blossoms, fruiting spurs, succulent terminal shoots, branches, rootstock crowns, and immature fruit
growth_stage: Spring bloom through active early-summer shoot elongation
season: Warm, humid spring bloom and early-summer thunderstorms/hail
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>60%), warm rain, heavy dew, or hail/wind storms during bloom and shoot growth
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Blossoms suddenly wilt, turn water-soaked, and shrivel dark brown-to-black ('blossom blight'); infection moves into succulent young shoots which wilt and bend over at the tip into a diagnostic inverted J-hook ('shepherd's crook') while dead blackened leaves and shriveled mummified fruitlets remain stubbornly attached to the branch as if scorched by a blowtorch; during humid weather, milky-to-amber sticky droplets of bacterial ooze bead on blighted stems and dark sunken branch cankers.
symptom_keywords: shepherd's crook shoot tip, scorched black leaves clinging to branch, blighted black blossoms, amber bacterial ooze droplets, sunken bark canker
symptom_progression: Bacteria multiply on flower stigmas during warm (>65°F) wet bloom and invade nectaries, racing down spurs into shoots and scaffold limbs (especially fast in pear and dwarf M.9/M.26 apple rootstocks).
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the 'shepherd's crook' bent shoot tips, scorched black leaves that do NOT drop off the dead twig, and amber bacterial ooze droplets.
similar_conditions: Pear Psylla Honeydew Sooty Mold, Twig Borer/Oriental Fruit Moth Flagging (has entry hole/larva in twig), Winter Freeze Dieback
risk_factors: Highly susceptible cultivars ('Bartlett'/'Bosc' pear; 'Gala', 'Fuji', 'Jonathan', 'Honeycrisp', 'Granny Smith' apple), excessive nitrogen fertilization or heavy winter pruning that forces lush succulent water sprouts, and hailstorms.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–82°F optimal, >65°F threshold) during open bloom accompanied by rain or high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters at the margins of sunken holdover bark cankers; in spring, insects (bees, flies, ants) and splashing rain carry oozing bacteria to open blossoms and tender shoot tips.
management_actions: Prune out blighted 'shepherd's crook' shoots during dry weather by cutting at least 12 inches BELOW the lowest visible bark discoloration, dipping pruning loppers in 70% rubbing alcohol or 10% bleach between EVERY cut (never prune in wet weather!); remove all rootstock suckers.
prevention_actions: Plant fire-blight-resistant pear cultivars ('Harrow Delight', 'Harrow Sweet', 'Moonglow', 'Potomac', 'Warren') and resistant apple rootstocks ('Geneva' series G.11, G.41, G.935 instead of susceptible M.9/M.26); keep nitrogen fertilization low so shoot growth stays moderate.
recommended_observations: Scout Apple (blossoms, fruiting spurs, succulent terminal shoots, branches, rootstock crowns, and immature fruit) weekly during warm, humid spring bloom and early-summer thunderstorms/hail (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Fire Blight from Pear Psylla Honeydew Sooty Mold, Twig Borer/Oriental Fruit Moth Flagging (has entry hole/larva in twig), Winter Freeze Dieback.
severity_or_impact: Critical (can kill entire pear trees and dwarf apple trees in a single season)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and high humidity (>60%), warm rain, heavy dew, or hail/wind storms during bloom and shoot growth.
host_range: Documented on Apple (Malus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear, Raspberry, Blackberry).

Plant fire-blight-resistant pear cultivars ('Harrow Delight', 'Harrow Sweet', 'Moonglow', 'Potomac', 'Warren') and resistant apple rootstocks ('Geneva' series G.11, G.41, G.935 instead of susceptible M.9/M.26); keep nitrogen fertilization low so shoot growth stays moderate.

topic: Apple Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot (Phytophthora capsici)
problem_name: Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot
causal_agent: Phytophthora capsici (on Solanaceae, Cucurbits, Legumes); Phytophthora cactorum / P. fragariae (on Strawberry/Apple); Phytophthora cinnamomi / P. nicotianae (on Avocado, Citrus, Papaya, Blueberry, Rosemary, Sage)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown/collar (foot rot/gummosis), stems, leaves, and fruit ('buckeye rot' on tomato; white yeast-like powder on squash/pepper/watermelon)
growth_stage: Any stage after soil saturation or heavy rainfall
season: Warm, rainy summer weather or poorly drained wet soils
humidity_conditions: Saturated, waterlogged, or flooded soil (>24 hours of standing water) and splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Apple (Malus domestica): Dark brown-to-black water-soaked lesion girdling the stem base/crown right above the soil line ('black shank' in pepper/squash; 'red stele' reddish-pink central root core in strawberry; 'foot rot/gummosis' cracking bark and oozing gum at graft union in citrus; feeder root blackening and canopy dieback in avocado/blueberry/rosemary), causing rapid permanent wilting; on pepper, cucurbit, and eggplant fruits, dark water-soaked blotches rapidly covered in a diagnostic dusting of white, yeast-like or powdered-sugar-like sporangia (on green tomato fruit touching soil, smooth brown 'buckeye rot' target rings).

symptom_progression: Swimming zoospores released in saturated soil chemotactically swim to roots and crowns, rotting the root system and stem collar within days and splashing onto low-hanging fruits.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished in pepper and cucurbits by the dark black basal stem girdling ('black shank') and the tight, flat, powdered-sugar-like white coating of sporangia on rotting fruit (unlike fluffy tall cottony Pythium or white fan-like Southern Blight with mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight, Pythium Cottony Leak, Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Sclerotinia White Mold
risk_factors: Poorly drained clay soils, low spots where rainwater puddles, over-irrigation, planting crowns/graft unions too deeply, and short rotations between peppers, eggplants, tomatoes, and cucurbits.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) combined with heavy rainfall or waterlogged soil.
transmission_or_spread: Thick-walled oospores survive in soil for 5–10+ years; motile biflagellate zoospores swim through soil water films and spread in surface runoff and ponded irrigation water.
management_actions: Immediately remove infected plants and rotting fruits; improve surface drainage and never overwater; on citrus and fruit trees, keep mulch 6–12 inches away from the trunk and ensure the graft union is 4–6 inches above soil; on avocado, apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) and maintain a 6-inch coarse leaf/woodchip mulch mat.

severity_or_impact: Critical (causes rapid plant death after heavy rains and persistent soil infestation)

affected_plant_parts: Spur/shoot leaves and maturing fruit
growth_stage: Heat domes exceeding 95–105°F
season: Plant dormant bare-root trees in early spring as soon as soil can be worked (or late autumn in mild Zones 7–8)

favorable_conditions: Multi-day heat waves above 90–100°F accompanied by warm nights (>72–75°F), intense solar radiation, dry winds, and bare unmulched soil.

topic: Apple (Malus domestica) Boron (B) Deficiency (Internal Cork, Drought Spot & Shoot Dieback / Rosetting): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Boron (B) Deficiency (Internal Cork, Drought Spot & Shoot Dieback / Rosetting)
affected_plant_parts: Developing apple fruit flesh/skin and terminal woody shoots
growth_stage: Post-bloom fruit cell division through maturation and spring budbreak
season: Plant dormant bare-root trees in early spring as soon as soil can be worked (or late autumn in mild Zones 7–8)
temperature_range: Requires 500–1,000 winter chill hours (32–45°F) depending on cultivar (low-chill cultivars like 'Anna' and 'Dorsett Golden' need only 150–300 hours); winter-hardy to -25°F to -35°F; open spring blossoms are killed at 25–28°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Inside the apple fruit, large irregular brown, dry, spongy-to-corky necrotic zones form deep in the cortex around the core ('internal cork'), causing bumpy, deformed fruit that drop early, or russeted cracked surface lesions ('external drought spot'); on branches, terminal buds fail to break properly in spring, forming witches'-broom rosettes and dieback with inner bark measles.
symptom_keywords: apple, boron (b) deficiency, immobile in phloem in most garden crops (transported passively via xylem transpiration), developing apple fruit flesh/skin and terminal woody shoots, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Apical meristems, young expanding heart leaves, fleshy pith of stems and storage roots, floral buds, and developing curds or fruits. Internal cork initiates 2–6 weeks after petal fall during rapid cell division, especially in dry springs on sandy or high-pH soils.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Immobile in phloem in most garden crops (transported passively via xylem transpiration). Deep internal corky brown zones around the core developing early in the season (coupled with spring terminal bud dieback) distinguish Boron internal cork from Calcium bitter pit (which forms small shallow pits just under the skin near the calyx end late in the season).
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Apple.
risk_factors: Leached sandy soils low in organic matter, alkaline or recently over-limed soils (pH > 7.0) where boric acid adsorbs onto clay/hydroxide surfaces, or prolonged summer drought that halts mass-flow transport of boric acid (H3BO3) to roots.
favorable_conditions: Leached sandy soils low in organic matter, alkaline or recently over-limed soils (pH > 7.0) where boric acid adsorbs onto clay/hydroxide surfaces, or prolonged summer drought that halts mass-flow transport of boric acid (H3BO3) to roots.
management_actions: Apply a carefully measured dilute boron application (Solubor or household borax at strictly calibrated low rates—roughly 1 to 2 lb actual B per acre, or 1 level tablespoon borax dissolved in 3–5 gallons of water per 100 sq ft) to the soil or as a pre-heading foliar spray. WARNING: Boron has a very narrow margin between deficiency and severe phytotoxicity.
prevention_actions: Maintain soil organic matter with compost, avoid over-liming above pH 6.8, maintain uniform soil moisture during rapid stem/root expansion, and test soil boron before supplementing on Brassicas, root crops, and celery.

topic: Apple (Malus domestica) Calcium (Ca) Deficiency (Shoot Tip Dieback & Fruit Cork / Bitter Pit Complex): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Calcium (Ca) Deficiency (Shoot Tip Dieback & Fruit Cork / Bitter Pit Complex)
affected_plant_parts: Young terminal shoot leaves and developing/stored apple fruit cortex
growth_stage: Mid-summer shoot extension through fruit maturation and storage
season: Plant dormant bare-root trees in early spring as soon as soil can be worked (or late autumn in mild Zones 7–8)
temperature_range: Requires 500–1,000 winter chill hours (32–45°F) depending on cultivar (low-chill cultivars like 'Anna' and 'Dorsett Golden' need only 150–300 hours); winter-hardy to -25°F to -35°F; open spring blossoms are killed at 25–28°F
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Under severe tree deficiency, young terminal shoot leaves roll upward with chlorotic and brown ragged margins; much more commonly, localized fruit calcium deficiency causes small, sunken, dark-green-to-brown bitter corky pits in the outer flesh concentrated near the calyx end of the apple.
symptom_keywords: apple, calcium (ca) deficiency, strictly immobile in phloem (transported exclusively upward via xylem transpiration stream), young terminal shoot leaves and developing/stored apple fruit cortex, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Youngest expanding upper leaves, enclosed heart leaves, apical meristems, root tips, and low-transpiring developing fruits or storage tissues. Vigorous vegetative shoots outcompete low-transpiring apples for xylem calcium during cell expansion; corky pits develop in late summer on the tree or after 1–2 months in cold storage.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Strictly immobile in phloem (transported exclusively upward via xylem transpiration stream). Sunken dark pits underlain by dry, spongy, brown corky tissue just beneath the skin at the calyx end (without fungal decay or insect tunnels) are diagnostic of Calcium deficiency / bitter pit.
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Apple.
risk_factors: Fluctuating soil moisture (drought alternating with heavy watering), high relative humidity or enclosed leaf morphology suppressing xylem transpiration into inner leaves/fruits, acidic unlimed soils (pH < 5.5), high soil salinity, or excess ammonium (NH4+), potassium (K+), or magnesium (Mg2+) competing for root uptake.
favorable_conditions: Fluctuating soil moisture (drought alternating with heavy watering), high relative humidity or enclosed leaf morphology suppressing xylem transpiration into inner leaves/fruits, acidic unlimed soils (pH < 5.5), high soil salinity, or excess ammonium (NH4+), potassium (K+), or magnesium (Mg2+) competing for root uptake.
management_actions: Regulate soil moisture immediately with consistent irrigation and organic mulch; apply foliar calcium sprays (calcium chloride or calcium nitrate at 3–5 lb/100 gal or labeled home-garden rate) directly onto young expanding leaves and developing fruit clusters, and side-dress with calcium nitrate or gypsum.
prevention_actions: Lime acidic soils to pH 6.2–6.8 using calcitic limestone or apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) where pH is already optimal, use nitrate-N rather than ammonium-N fertilizers, avoid pruning feeder roots during cultivation, and maintain steady soil moisture.
recommended_observations: Inspect whether symptoms initiate on older lower foliage vs. youngest upper leaves/meristems on Apple, verify soil pH (optimal for Apple: 6.0–6.8) and soil moisture, and confirm with a soil or plant tissue test.
severity_or_impact: Causes major pre-harvest and post-harvest fruit loss in susceptible cultivars (such as Honeycrisp, Granny Smith, and Baldwin).
geographic_or_climate_notes: Crop adaptation: Cool-temperate deciduous woody perennial pome fruit tree (Malus domestica). topic: Pear Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs Management
problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.

topic: Pear Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot Management
problem_name: Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot
problem_category: Internal Fruit-Boring Pest of Tree Fruits
causal_agent: Cydia pomonella (Codling Moth), Grapholita molesta (Oriental Fruit Moth), and Rhagoletis pomonella (Apple Maggot / 'Railroad Worm')
affected_plant_parts: Internal fruit core/seeds (Codling Moth), fruit flesh (Apple Maggot), and tender spring shoot tips + fruit (Oriental Fruit Moth)
growth_stage: Petal fall through harvest
season: May through September
humidity_conditions: Warm dusk temperatures (>60°F) for moth egg-laying; summer rains for Apple Maggot fly emergence
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Codling Moth ('the worm in the apple'): a pinkish-white caterpillar (1/2 to 3/4 inch) with a brown head bores through the side or blossom calyx cup straight to the center core of apples, pears, and walnuts to eat the seeds, pushing a pile of coarse, reddish-brown, sawdust-like frass out of the entry hole ('frass plug'); Oriental Fruit Moth: in spring, first-generation pinkish larvae bore 2–4 inches down into the tender terminal shoot tips of peach, nectarine, plum, and apple trees, causing the top 3–4 leaves of new shoots to wilt and flag brown ('shoot flagging'), while summer generations bore into ripening peaches (often right down the stem channel without leaving an obvious external hole!); Apple Maggot ('Railroad Worm'): small black flies with distinctive dark 'F'-shaped wing bands puncture apple skin in summer, and legless white maggots chew brown, winding, thread-like trails all through the apple flesh, making the fruit lumpy and dimpled.

similar_conditions: Plum Curculio (crescent-shaped corky scar on young fruit skin), Fire Blight (scorched shepherd's crook without a larva burrow inside the twig)

topic: Pear Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla Management
problem_name: Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla
problem_category: Wood-Boring Moth & Sap-Feeding Psyllid Pests of Fruit Trees
causal_agent: Synanthedon exitiosa (Peachtree Borer), Synanthedon pictipes (Lesser Peachtree Borer), and Cacopsylla pyricola (Pear Psylla)
affected_plant_parts: Lower trunk at and 2–3 inches below the soil line (Peachtree Borer), upper scaffold limb wounds/cankers (Lesser Peachtree Borer), and pear leaves/fruits (Pear Psylla)
growth_stage: Perennial woody trunk/limbs and summer foliage
season: Summer egg-laying with year-round larval feeding (Borers); early spring through autumn (Pear Psylla)
humidity_conditions: Warm summer days for clearwing moth flight; lush nitrogen-stimulated pear shoots for Pear Psylla
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Peachtree Borer: masses of thick, amber-to-clear, jelly-like gum MIXED WITH coarse reddish-brown sawdust-like insect frass and empty brown pupal skins protruding at the base of the trunk right at the soil line of peach, plum, and cherry trees; beneath the bark, 1-inch-long creamy-white caterpillars with dark-brown heads tunnel through the cambium around the root collar, girdling and killing young trees and causing older trees to yellow and die back on one side (Lesser Peachtree Borer causes identical frass-filled gummosis higher up on scaffold branch crotches and cankers); Pear Psylla: tiny (2 mm) cicada-like reddish-brown winged adults and flat, yellowish-green-to-brown wingpad nymphs submerged inside droplets of sticky clear honeydew on pear leaves and shoots, causing black sooty mold russeting on pears and sudden blackened leaf blotches ('psylla shock').

symptom_progression: Day-flying metallic blue-black clearwing moths (females have a bright orange band across the abdomen) lay eggs on the lower trunk from June through September; larvae tunnel under the bark all autumn, winter, and spring.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION for Stone Fruit Gummosis: Amber gum oozing from a peach, plum, or cherry trunk that is CLEAR and free of sawdust/frass is caused by abiotic injury, Cytospora fungus, or Bacterial Canker; gum that contains gritty brown sawdust-like frass particles and cast skins at the soil line is Peachtree Borer!
similar_conditions: Bacterial Canker / Cytospora Canker (clear amber gum WITHOUT brown insect sawdust/frass), Crown Gall, Fire Blight (on Pear)
risk_factors: String-trimmer or lawnmower bark wounds at the base of stone fruit trunks, volcano mulching piled against the bark, winter sunscald cracks, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer on pear trees (which pushes succulent water sprouts favored by Pear Psylla).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer months (June–September).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying diurnal clearwing moths attracted to wounded or stressed stone fruit bark; Pear Psylla overwinters as adults in bark crevices.
management_actions: For Peachtree Borer: inspect the trunk base at the soil line in spring and autumn, carefully probe active frass-filled gum holes with a flexible wire to puncture the larva under the bark, or apply beneficial entomopathogenic nematodes (Steinernema carpocapsae) as a moist drench around the lower trunk in late summer/spring; for Pear Psylla: apply a delayed-dormant horticultural oil spray in early spring just before buds open to deter egg-laying on pear twigs, and wash honeydew off leaves with insecticidal soap.
prevention_actions: Keep mulch pulled back 4–6 inches from the trunk base of peach, plum, and cherry trees (never pile mulch against the bark!), protect trunks with breathable white tree guards against string-trimmers and winter sunscald, and whitewash south-west trunks with 50:50 water-diluted white interior latex paint; summer-prune upright water sprouts out of pear trees.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm summer days for clearwing moth flight; lush nitrogen-stimulated pear shoots for pear psylla.

topic: Pear Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies Management
problem_name: Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies
problem_category: Fruit-Scarring & Internal Larval Pest of Stone and Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Conotrachelus nenuphar (Plum Curculio) and Rhagoletis cingulata / Rhagoletis fausta / Rhagoletis indifferens (Cherry Fruit Flies)
affected_plant_parts: Immature newly set fruits (petal fall / shuck split) and ripening cherries
growth_stage: Petal fall / shuck split through harvest
season: Spring (Plum Curculio) and early summer as cherries turn yellow-red (Cherry Fruit Fly)
humidity_conditions: Warm (>70°F) humid spring days and nights following rain
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Plum Curculio: a small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), rough-backed, brownish-black snout weevil with grey-white flecks and four prominent humps on its wing covers that emerges at petal fall / shuck split; the female chews a small hole in the tiny green fruitlet, inserts an egg, and then cuts a diagnostic crescent-shaped (D-shaped / half-moon) slit right underneath the egg so the rapidly expanding fruit flesh will not crush her egg! In apples and pears, the fruit expansion usually crushes the larva anyway, leaving a raised, corky, D-shaped fan scar on the mature apple skin; in plums, peaches, cherries, and blueberries, the legless, curved, yellowish-white grub with a brown head tunnels to the pit, causing clear gummy sap droplets to ooze from the crescent scar and causing premature fruit drop or ripe wormy fruit; Cherry Fruit Fly: legless white maggots (no head capsule!) feed around the pit of ripe red cherries without external deformity until sunken soft spots and exit holes appear.
symptom_keywords: crescent-shaped half-moon scar on young green plum peach or apple, gummy clear sap droplet oozing from crescent cut, rough humpbacked brown snout weevil playing dead when tapped, legless grub with brown head next to peach or plum pit, headless white maggot inside ripe cherry
symptom_progression: Overwintered Plum Curculio adults walk/fly from woodlots into fruit trees during bloom and attack fruitlets for 3–5 weeks after petal fall whenever temperatures exceed 70°F; Cherry Fruit Flies emerge from soil just as early cherries show the first blush of yellow-pink color.
distinguishing_features: Plum Curculio is unmistakably identified by the signature crescent-shaped (half-moon) oviposition scar cut into the skin of young apples, plums, peaches, and cherries; inside ripe cherries, Plum Curculio larva has a distinct brown head capsule and curved C-shape, whereas Cherry Fruit Fly maggot is headless and cone-shaped.
similar_conditions: Tarnished Plant Bug / Stink Bug Catfacing (sunken dimples without a crescent-shaped flap cut), Hail Scars, Codling Moth
risk_factors: Fruit trees planted adjacent to deciduous woodlots, hedgerows, or brush piles (where Plum Curculio adults overwinter in leaf litter) and uncollected dropped stone fruits.
favorable_conditions: Spring days reaching 70–75°F+ or warm nights (>60°F) right after petal fall / shuck split.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded border litter and migrate into trees in spring; mature larvae exit fallen fruit to pupate 1–2 inches deep in the soil.
management_actions: Lay a light-colored sheet on the ground under plum, peach, and apple branches in the cool early morning for the 3 weeks after petal fall and sharply tap limbs with a padded stick—Plum Curculio adults fold their legs, play dead ('thanatosis'), and drop onto the sheet looking like bits of bark or bird droppings so you can collect and destroy them; spray kaolin clay (Surround—keep a white coat on fruitlets from petal fall for 4 weeks) or spinosad (for Cherry Fruit Fly, hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate as soon as cherries turn yellow-blush).
prevention_actions: Pick up and dispose of all 'June drop' fruitlets under plum, peach, cherry, and apple trees every 2 days in May/June before curculio grubs crawl out into the soil; prune trees open (Plum Curculio strongly prefers cool, dark, dense interior canopies).

severity_or_impact: Critical east of the Rocky Mountains (the #1 early-season insect pest of plums, peaches, cherries, and apples)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–85°F (15–29°C) and warm (>70°f) humid spring days and nights following rain.
host_range: Documented on Pear (Pyrus communis, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Plum, Peach, Cherry, Apple, Pear, Blueberry).

causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)

topic: Pear Apple and Pear Scab (Venturia inaequalis)
problem_name: Apple and Pear Scab
causal_agent: Venturia inaequalis (Apple Scab) and Venturia pirina (Pear Scab)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, blossoms, pedicels, and developing fruits (plus young twigs in pear)
growth_stage: Green tip through petal fall and early summer fruit sizing
season: Cool, rainy spring weather
humidity_conditions: Rain events keeping leaves wet for 6–18+ hours (governed by the Mills Table of temperature x wetting duration)
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Velvety, olive-green to radiating sooty-black circular spots with feathery/indistinct margins on young leaves, causing leaves to pucker, yellow, and drop prematurely in early summer; on fruits, olive-black velvety spots mature into sunken, dark-brown corky, scabby lesions that restrict skin expansion on one side, causing the growing apple or pear to deform and crack open.
symptom_keywords: olive-green velvety leaf spots, corky black scabby fruit lesions, cracked deformed apples, feathery spot margins, premature early-summer leaf drop
symptom_progression: Overwintered pseudothecia in fallen autumn leaves forcefully shoot ascospores into the air during spring rains from green tip through 2–3 weeks after petal fall; primary leaf lesions then produce secondary conidia that splash onto fruit all summer.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the velvety olive-green-to-black spots with feathery margins on young spring leaves and dark corky scabs on fruit (unlike Sooty Blotch/Flyspeck, which appears late in summer strictly as superficial smudges/dots on the waxy fruit cuticle without deforming the skin).
similar_conditions: Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck, Cedar-Apple Rust (bright orange-yellow spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (Black Rot), Fire Blight
risk_factors: Susceptible cultivars (such as 'McIntosh', 'Cortland', 'Fuji', 'Gala', 'Bartlett'), un-raked fallen autumn leaf litter under trees, and frequent spring rains.
favorable_conditions: Spring rain events at 55–75°F lasting 6–12+ hours (Mills Infection Periods).
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in fallen infected leaves on the orchard floor (and in twig lesions in Pear Scab), releasing wind-borne ascospores in spring rain and splashing conidia in summer.
management_actions: Rake and destroy (or shred with a lawnmower and spray with 5% urea solution in late autumn) all fallen apple and pear leaves to eliminate 80–90% of overwintering ascospore inoculum; prune trees annually to open the canopy for rapid drying.
prevention_actions: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars carrying the Vf (Rvi6) gene (such as 'Liberty', 'Enterprise', 'GoldRush', 'Pristine', 'CrimsonCrisp', 'Freedom', 'Williams' Pride') and scab-resistant pears.
recommended_observations: Scout Pear (leaves, blossoms, pedicels, and developing fruits (plus young twigs in pear)) weekly during cool, rainy spring weather (55–75°F (13–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Apple and Pear Scab from Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck, Cedar-Apple Rust (bright orange-yellow spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (Black Rot), Fire Blight.
severity_or_impact: High (the #1 fungal disease of apples in humid regions; causes heavy defoliation and scabby cracked fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–75°F (13–24°C) and rain events keeping leaves wet for 6–18+ hours (governed by the mills table of temperature x wetting duration).
host_range: Documented on Pear (Pyrus communis, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear).
