topic: Pear Bitter Rot, Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Sooty Blotch / Flyspeck of Pome Fruits (Colletotrichum gloeosporioides / acutatum)
problem_name: Bitter Rot, Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Sooty Blotch / Flyspeck of Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides / acutatum (Bitter Rot), Botryosphaeria obtusa (Black Rot / Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Peltaster / Schizothyrium complex (Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening fruits, leaves, fruiting spurs, and woody limbs
growth_stage: Petal fall through late-summer fruit maturation and harvest
season: Warm-to-hot, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High summer humidity (>80% RH) and warm afternoon thunderstorms
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Bitter Rot: sunken, circular brown saucer-like rot spots on summer-ripening apples that develop concentric rings of creamy salmon-pink slimy spore masses in humid weather and penetrate toward the core in a diagnostic V-shaped cone when the apple is sliced in half (unlike Black Rot/White Rot which rot downward in a cylindrical core); Black Rot: 'frogeye leaf spots' (circular purple-bordered spots with tan centers on leaves), reddish-brown limb cankers, and firm black fruit rot with concentric brown-and-black bands and only ONE spot per fruit; Sooty Blotch & Flyspeck: superficial dull olive-black cloudy smudges and clusters of 10–50 tiny shiny black dots strictly on the waxy outer cuticle of late-season apples (peels or rubs off with no underlying rot!).
symptom_keywords: sunken saucer fruit rot with salmon-pink spore rings, V-shaped cone rot toward apple core, frogeye tan-centered leaf spots, superficial sooty smudges and tiny black flyspecks on skin
symptom_progression: Fungi overwinter in dead fire-blighted twigs, mummified fruitlets left from thinning, and bark cankers, splashing onto developing apples during hot humid summer storms.
distinguishing_features: Slice the rotted apple in half through the lesion: Bitter Rot forms a clean V-shaped cone pointing toward the core with salmon-pink slimy spore rings on the surface, whereas Black Rot forms a cylinder of firm black leathery rot; Sooty Blotch and Flyspeck are 100% cosmetic surface blemishes on the wax cuticle.
similar_conditions: Apple Scab (rough corky cracked skin lesions starting in spring), Brown Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit (small sunken physiological spots concentrated at calyx end with spongy brown flecks under skin)
risk_factors: Dead twigs (especially old Fire Blight strikes), unremoved fruit mummies, retained thinned fruitlets hanging in clusters, and dense humid tree canopies.
favorable_conditions: Hot, humid summer weather (77–90°F) with frequent rain showers.
transmission_or_spread: Rain-splashed conidia and wind-borne ascospores from dead twigs, limb cankers, and mummified fruits.
management_actions: Prune out all dead wood, cankers, and old Fire Blight strikes during winter; remove all mummified apples and hand-thinned fruitlets from the tree (do not leave thinned fruitlets lodged in spurs!); prune for open summer airflow (Sooty Blotch/Flyspeck apples are completely safe to eat after washing/peeling!).
prevention_actions: Maintain open-canopy pruning, thin fruit clusters to single apples, and apply summer protectant sprays in hot humid regions.
recommended_observations: Scout Pear (ripening fruits, leaves, fruiting spurs, and woody limbs) weekly during warm-to-hot, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bitter Rot, Black Rot (Frogeye Leaf Spot), and Sooty Blotch / Flyspeck of Pome Fruits from Apple Scab (rough corky cracked skin lesions starting in spring), Brown Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit (small sunken physiological spots concentrated at calyx end with spongy brown flecks under skin).
severity_or_impact: High for Bitter Rot and Black Rot in warm humid summers; Low/Cosmetic for Sooty Blotch & Flyspeck
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high summer humidity (>80% rh) and warm afternoon thunderstorms.
host_range: Documented on Pear (Pyrus communis, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear).

Favored by hot, humid summer weather (77–90°f) with frequent rain showers. (75–90°F (24–32°C)). Management and prevention: Prune out all dead wood, cankers, and old Fire Blight strikes during winter; remove all mummified apples and hand-thinned fruitlets from the tree (do not leave thinned fruitlets lodged in spurs!); prune for open summer airflow (Sooty Blotch/Flyspeck apples are completely safe to eat after washing/peeling!). topic: Pear Cedar-Apple Rust and Quince/Hawthorn Rust (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae)
problem_name: Cedar-Apple Rust and Quince/Hawthorn Rust
causal_agent: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae (Cedar-Apple Rust) and Gymnosporangium clavipes (Quince Rust)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, petioles, and fruits (and twigs in Quince Rust)
growth_stage: Pink bud through 4 weeks after petal fall
season: Warm spring rains
humidity_conditions: Spring rain wetting eastern red cedar galls for 4–8+ hours
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Bright, vivid yellow-to-orange circular spots (1/8 to 1/2 inch) on the upper surface of apple leaves (dotted with tiny black pycnia in the center) that develop clusters of cup-like, fringed, tubular projections (aecia) on the underside of the leaf and on the blossom end of deformed fruits in midsummer; heavy infection causes mid-season leaf yellowing and drop.
symptom_keywords: bright orange-yellow leaf spots, fringed tubular cups on leaf underside, orange blossom-end fruit spots, gelatinous orange horns on red cedar
symptom_progression: After spring rain swells brown woody galls on nearby Eastern Red Cedar (Juniperus virginiana) into bright orange gelatinous tentacles, wind-borne basidiospores blow onto young apple leaves and fruit within 1–2 miles.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the brilliant neon yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface and the star-like clusters of fringed tubular aecia cups on the lower leaf surface in summer.
similar_conditions: Apple Scab (olive-black velvety spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (brown circular spots with gray centers)
risk_factors: Growing susceptible apple cultivars ('Golden Delicious', 'Rome', 'Jonathan', 'Ginger Gold') within 0.5–2 miles of Eastern Red Cedar or ornamental junipers.
favorable_conditions: Spring rains at 55–75°F while apples are between pink bud and 3 weeks post-petal-fall.
transmission_or_spread: Heteroecious rust requiring two alternate hosts to complete its 2-year lifecycle: Juniperus species (Eastern red cedar) and Rosaceae pome fruits (apple, crabapple, pear, quince, hawthorn); does NOT spread from apple leaf to apple leaf!
management_actions: Remove brown spherical galls from ornamental junipers/red cedars on your property in late winter before orange gelatinous horns emerge; apply protectant fungicides from pink bud through 3 weeks after petal fall on susceptible cultivars.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant apple cultivars (such as 'Liberty', 'Enterprise', 'Freedom', 'Redfree', 'William's Pride', 'Honeycrisp').
recommended_observations: Scout Pear (leaves, petioles, and fruits (and twigs in quince rust)) weekly during warm spring rains (55–75°F (13–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cedar-Apple Rust and Quince/Hawthorn Rust from Apple Scab (olive-black velvety spots), Frogeye Leaf Spot (brown circular spots with gray centers).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (defoliates susceptible cultivars and disfigures fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–75°F (13–24°C) and spring rain wetting eastern red cedar galls for 4–8+ hours.
host_range: Documented on Pear (Pyrus communis, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear).

topic: Pear Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Pear (Pyrus communis): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Pear (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Pear (Pyrus communis, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).
knowledge_text: Pear (Pyrus communis) Crown Gall is a bacterial disease caused by Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall). problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.

topic: Peach Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot Management
problem_name: Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot
problem_category: Internal Fruit-Boring Pest of Tree Fruits
causal_agent: Cydia pomonella (Codling Moth), Grapholita molesta (Oriental Fruit Moth), and Rhagoletis pomonella (Apple Maggot / 'Railroad Worm')
affected_plant_parts: Internal fruit core/seeds (Codling Moth), fruit flesh (Apple Maggot), and tender spring shoot tips + fruit (Oriental Fruit Moth)
growth_stage: Petal fall through harvest
season: May through September
humidity_conditions: Warm dusk temperatures (>60°F) for moth egg-laying; summer rains for Apple Maggot fly emergence
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Codling Moth ('the worm in the apple'): a pinkish-white caterpillar (1/2 to 3/4 inch) with a brown head bores through the side or blossom calyx cup straight to the center core of apples, pears, and walnuts to eat the seeds, pushing a pile of coarse, reddish-brown, sawdust-like frass out of the entry hole ('frass plug'); Oriental Fruit Moth: in spring, first-generation pinkish larvae bore 2–4 inches down into the tender terminal shoot tips of peach, nectarine, plum, and apple trees, causing the top 3–4 leaves of new shoots to wilt and flag brown ('shoot flagging'), while summer generations bore into ripening peaches (often right down the stem channel without leaving an obvious external hole!); Apple Maggot ('Railroad Worm'): small black flies with distinctive dark 'F'-shaped wing bands puncture apple skin in summer, and legless white maggots chew brown, winding, thread-like trails all through the apple flesh, making the fruit lumpy and dimpled.
symptom_keywords: pinkish-white caterpillar with brown head inside apple core, pile of coarse reddish-brown sawdust frass pushed out of hole in apple, brown winding railroad trails throughout apple flesh, wilted flagging terminal shoot tips on peach in spring
symptom_progression: Codling Moth and Oriental Fruit Moth overwinter as cocoons under loose trunk bark and emerge around apple bloom (Codling Moth eggs hatch at ~250 Degree Days base 50°F after biofix); Apple Maggot flies emerge from soil from late June through August.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the two main 'apple worms': Codling Moth is a caterpillar WITH a brown head and legs that tunnels straight to the seed core and pushes coarse brown frass out the hole; Apple Maggot is a headless, legless white fly maggot that leaves thin, winding brown 'railroad tracks' throughout the white flesh without tunneling to the core or pushing out frass.
similar_conditions: Plum Curculio (crescent-shaped corky scar on young fruit skin), Fire Blight (scorched shepherd's crook without a larva burrow inside the twig)
risk_factors: Uncared-for wild apple, crabapple, or hawthorn trees nearby, uncollected fallen 'drop' apples under trees, and failure to thin apple clusters to single fruits (touching apples give Codling Moth larvae leverage to bore in!).
favorable_conditions: Calm, warm evenings (>60°F at dusk) after petal fall.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths and maggot flies fly between neighboring backyard fruit trees and wild crabapples/hawthorns.
management_actions: NON-CHEMICAL BAGGING & TRAPPING FOR HOME ORCHARDS: (1) Fruit Bagging: when thinned apples/pears are 1/2 to 3/4 inch wide (about 3 weeks after petal fall), slip small zip-top sandwich bags (with bottom corners snipped for drainage), Japanese paper fruit bags, or nylon footies over individual fruits—this produces 100% worm-free apples without sprays! (2) Red Sphere Traps: hang 3–6 sticky-coated dark-red spheres per apple tree in June–August to trap egg-laying Apple Maggot flies; (3) wrap corrugated cardboard trunk bands around apple trunks in June and August to trap and destroy pupating Codling Moth cocoons; (4) spray Cydia pomonella granulovirus (CpGV—a 100% selective biological virus for Codling Moth), spinosad, or kaolin clay timed at 250 DD after bloom.
prevention_actions: Pick up and remove all fallen 'June drop' and wormy apples/peaches every 2–3 days before larvae exit the fruit into the soil or trunk bark; thin apples to 1 fruit per cluster; prune out flagged Oriental Fruit Moth shoot tips on peaches in spring before the larva exits.

severity_or_impact: Critical on apples, pears, and peaches (can infest 60–100% of unmanaged backyard apples)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm dusk temperatures (>60°f) for moth egg-laying; summer rains for apple maggot fly emergence.
host_range: Documented on Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry, Walnut).

topic: Peach Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies Management
problem_name: Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies
problem_category: Fruit-Scarring & Internal Larval Pest of Stone and Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Conotrachelus nenuphar (Plum Curculio) and Rhagoletis cingulata / Rhagoletis fausta / Rhagoletis indifferens (Cherry Fruit Flies)
affected_plant_parts: Immature newly set fruits (petal fall / shuck split) and ripening cherries
growth_stage: Petal fall / shuck split through harvest
season: Spring (Plum Curculio) and early summer as cherries turn yellow-red (Cherry Fruit Fly)
humidity_conditions: Warm (>70°F) humid spring days and nights following rain
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Plum Curculio: a small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), rough-backed, brownish-black snout weevil with grey-white flecks and four prominent humps on its wing covers that emerges at petal fall / shuck split; the female chews a small hole in the tiny green fruitlet, inserts an egg, and then cuts a diagnostic crescent-shaped (D-shaped / half-moon) slit right underneath the egg so the rapidly expanding fruit flesh will not crush her egg! distinguishing_features: Plum Curculio is unmistakably identified by the signature crescent-shaped (half-moon) oviposition scar cut into the skin of young apples, plums, peaches, and cherries; inside ripe cherries, Plum Curculio larva has a distinct brown head capsule and curved C-shape, whereas Cherry Fruit Fly maggot is headless and cone-shaped.
similar_conditions: Tarnished Plant Bug / Stink Bug Catfacing (sunken dimples without a crescent-shaped flap cut), Hail Scars, Codling Moth
risk_factors: Fruit trees planted adjacent to deciduous woodlots, hedgerows, or brush piles (where Plum Curculio adults overwinter in leaf litter) and uncollected dropped stone fruits.
favorable_conditions: Spring days reaching 70–75°F+ or warm nights (>60°F) right after petal fall / shuck split.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded border litter and migrate into trees in spring; mature larvae exit fallen fruit to pupate 1–2 inches deep in the soil.
management_actions: Lay a light-colored sheet on the ground under plum, peach, and apple branches in the cool early morning for the 3 weeks after petal fall and sharply tap limbs with a padded stick—Plum Curculio adults fold their legs, play dead ('thanatosis'), and drop onto the sheet looking like bits of bark or bird droppings so you can collect and destroy them; spray kaolin clay (Surround—keep a white coat on fruitlets from petal fall for 4 weeks) or spinosad (for Cherry Fruit Fly, hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate as soon as cherries turn yellow-blush).

topic: Peach Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.

severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).

topic: Peach Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

management_actions: Train to an Open-Center ('vase-shaped') system with 3–4 main scaffold limbs radiating at 45 degrees and NO central leader so sunlight penetrates the entire interior; prune heavily every late winter/early spring (removing 40–50% of wood) because peaches bear fruit EXCLUSIVELY on 1-year-old reddish-brown shoots grown the previous summer; thin heavy fruit sets 4–6 weeks after bloom so remaining peaches are spaced 6–8 inches apart
prevention_actions: Cultivate shallowly around plants to avoid severing surface feeder roots, keep mulch pulled slightly back from direct stem contact where crown rot is a risk, and sanitize pruning tools between plants.
recommended_observations: Check Peach weekly for structural support needs, weed competition, mulch depth, and pollinator activity.

knowledge_subtype: Soil Texture, pH, Drainage & Bed Preparation
topic: Peach Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Deep, very well-drained sandy loam or gravelly loam; peach roots are extremely sensitive to waterlogging and root asphyxiation in heavy clay (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a deep, very well-drained sandy loam or gravelly loam; peach roots are extremely sensitive to waterlogging and root asphyxiation in heavy clay adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Peach to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Peach (Prunus persica): Prefers deep, very well-drained sandy loam or gravelly loam; peach roots are extremely sensitive to waterlogging and root asphyxiation in heavy clay with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.
secondary_source_name: Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden
evidence_notes: Soil texture, drainage, and pH requirements verified against University of Maryland Extension (HGIC) and Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden.

topic: Peach Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits (Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae)
problem_name: Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits
causal_agent: Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae (Bacterial Canker) and Wilsonomyces carpophilus (Coryneum Blight / Shot Hole)
affected_plant_parts: Dormant buds, twigs, scaffold limbs, trunk bark, leaves, and fruit
growth_stage: Autumn leaf drop through winter dormancy and spring budbreak
season: Cool, wet autumn, winter, and early spring weather
humidity_conditions: Rainy autumn/winter/spring weather and freeze-thaw cycles
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Bacterial Canker: sunken, dark, water-soaked elliptical cankers on branches and trunks that ooze copious amounts of thick, amber-to-orange gummy sap ('gummosis') in spring and emit a distinct sour, fermented beer-like odor when the dead brown inner bark is sliced open; whole spurs, buds, or scaffold limbs fail to leaf out or suddenly wilt and die in spring; on leaves, small circular purple-brown spots dry up and fall out leaving 'shot-holes'; Coryneum Blight (Fungal Shot Hole): small reddish-purple spots with tan centers on buds, twigs (forming concentric gummy twig cankers), leaves (falling out as shot-holes), and raised rough purple-scabby spots on peach/apricot fruit.
symptom_keywords: amber gummy sap oozing from bark cankers, sour fermented bark odor, circular leaf spots dropping out as shot-holes, dead dormant buds, purple scabby fruit spots
symptom_progression: Pseudomonas bacteria colonize leaf scars in autumn rain and ice-nucleate inside dormant buds/bark during winter freezes; in spring, cankers girdle branches and ooze gum.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Cytospora/Leucostoma Perennial Canker and Peach Tree Borer by: (1) Bacterial Canker produces a sour odor under the bark and lacks insect sawdust/frass inside the gum (unlike Peach Tree Borer at the soil line, which mixes dark sawdust frass into the gum), and (2) Coryneum Blight kills dormant winter buds with tiny gummy twig lesions.
similar_conditions: Peach Tree Borer (gum at trunk base mixed with brown insect frass/sawdust), Cytospora Perennial Canker, Nitrogen Toxicity / X-Disease
risk_factors: Pruning stone fruit trees in autumn or mid-winter during cold wet weather (major mistake!), sandy acidic soils infested with ring nematodes (Mesocriconema xenoplax), and freeze injury.
favorable_conditions: Cool, wet autumn and early-spring rains (50–65°F) combined with winter freeze events.
transmission_or_spread: Epiphytic bacteria and fungal spores wash by rain into autumn leaf scars, dormant buds, and winter pruning wounds.
management_actions: CRITICAL STONE FRUIT PRUNING RULE: NEVER prune peach, plum, or cherry trees in autumn or mid-winter! Delay all pruning until late spring (pink bud to bloom) or dry summer after harvest when wounds heal rapidly and bacterial activity is low; prune out cankered limbs several inches below discolored bark during dry weather.
prevention_actions: Apply a fixed copper spray at autumn leaf drop (to protect fresh leaf scars) and again at late-winter delayed dormancy before bud swell; lime acidic soils and avoid drought stress.
recommended_observations: Scout Peach (dormant buds, twigs, scaffold limbs, trunk bark, leaves, and fruit) weekly during cool, wet autumn, winter, and early spring weather (45–70°F (7–21°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits from Peach Tree Borer (gum at trunk base mixed with brown insect frass/sawdust), Cytospora Perennial Canker, Nitrogen Toxicity / X-Disease.
severity_or_impact: High (shortens tree lifespan and causes 'peach tree short life' and cherry limb dieback)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–70°F (7–21°C) and rainy autumn/winter/spring weather and freeze-thaw cycles.
host_range: Documented on Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Peach, Plum, Cherry).

Management and prevention: CRITICAL STONE FRUIT PRUNING RULE: NEVER prune peach, plum, or cherry trees in autumn or mid-winter! topic: Peach Bacterial Spot (Xanthomonas spp.)
problem_name: Bacterial Spot
causal_agent: Xanthomonas spp. (X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri on Solanaceae; X. arboricola pv. pruni on Stone Fruits; X. cucurbitae on Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves, stems, petioles, pedicels, blossoms, and developing green fruit
growth_stage: Seedling transplant stage through fruit maturation
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, driving rain, wind-blown mist, and overhead irrigation
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), irregular, greasy water-soaked dark brown-to-black spots on leaves that often develop yellow halos, coalesce into ragged necrotic blotches, and cause severe defoliation (especially in pepper, or 'shot-hole' drop-out in peach/plum leaves); on green tomato and pepper fruit, small water-soaked blisters enlarge into raised, scabby, corky brown-to-black warts (1/8–1/4 inch) with sunken centers.
symptom_keywords: greasy water-soaked leaf spots, raised scabby fruit spots, corky fruit warts, yellow leaf halo, shot-hole leaves, blossom drop, defoliation
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter through stomata and hydathodes or wind/sand wounds; foliar spots multiply rapidly after summer thunderstorms, causing heavy leaf drop and sunscald of exposed scabby fruit.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished on fruit by raised, rough, scabby brown spots without white halos (whereas Bacterial Canker produces 'bird's-eye' spots with flat white halos and Septoria rarely spots fruit); on leaves, lesions look greasy on the underside and lack fungal pycnidia or concentric target rings.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Speck (prefers cooler <75°F weather and tiny <1 mm superficial black fruit specks), Bacterial Canker, Septoria Leaf Spot, Early Blight
risk_factors: Contaminated seed or commercial transplants, working in wet gardens, overhead watering, and warm driving rainstorms.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–86°F) with frequent rain, high humidity, and wind-driven water splash.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and transplant-borne; survives briefly on crop residue and volunteer plants, spreading rapidly from plant to plant via splashing rain and human contact with wet foliage.
management_actions: Never handle, prune, or harvest plants when leaves are wet; use drip irrigation; apply fixed copper + mancozeb or biological bactericides preventatively when warm rainy weather is forecast; remove heavily infected early transplants.
prevention_actions: Purchase certified pathogen-free seed (or hot-water treat seed at 122°F/50°C for 25 minutes) and disease-resistant pepper cultivars (carrying Bs1, Bs2, Bs3, Bs4 resistance genes); rotate away from host crops for 2–3 years; mulch beds to reduce splash.
recommended_observations: Scout Peach (leaves, stems, petioles, pedicels, blossoms, and developing green fruit) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer weather (75–86°F (24–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Spot from Bacterial Speck (prefers cooler <75°F weather and tiny <1 mm superficial black fruit specks), Bacterial Canker, Septoria Leaf Spot, Early Blight.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe defoliation in peppers and tomatoes and unmarketable scabby/cracked fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–86°F (24–30°C) and high humidity, driving rain, wind-blown mist, and overhead irrigation.
host_range: Documented on Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Peach, Plum, Cherry).
knowledge_text: Peach (Prunus persica) Bacterial Spot is a bacterial disease caused by Xanthomonas spp. (X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri on Solanaceae; X. arboricola pv. pruni on Stone Fruits; X. cucurbitae on Cucurbits). Distinguishing features: Distinguished on fruit by raised, rough, scabby brown spots without white halos (whereas Bacterial Canker produces 'bird's-eye' spots with flat white halos and Septoria rarely spots fruit); on leaves, lesions look greasy on the underside and lack fungal pycnidia or concentric target rings. Favored by warm temperatures (75–86°f) with frequent rain, high humidity, and wind-driven water splash. (75–86°F (24–30°C)). Management and prevention: Never handle, prune, or harvest plants when leaves are wet; use drip irrigation; apply fixed copper + mancozeb or biological bactericides preventatively when warm rainy weather is forecast; remove heavily infected early transplants. Purchase certified pathogen-free seed (or hot-water treat seed at 122°F/50°C for 25 minutes) and disease-resistant pepper cultivars (carrying Bs1, Bs2, Bs3, Bs4 resistance genes); rotate away from host crops for 2–3 years; mulch beds to reduce splash.
secondary_source_name: Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden
evidence_notes: Host-specific disease relationship (Peach - Bacterial Spot), symptoms, and IPM controls verified via University of Maryland Extension (HGIC) and Utah State University Extension Yard and Garden.

topic: Peach Black Knot of Plum and Cherry (Apiosporina morbosa)
problem_name: Black Knot of Plum and Cherry
causal_agent: Apiosporina morbosa
affected_plant_parts: Twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs
growth_stage: Spring shoot elongation through perennial woody growth (2-year lifecycle)
season: Wet spring weather for infection; visible year-round (especially in dormant winter)
humidity_conditions: Spring rain wetting emerging green shoots
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Elongated, rough, coal-black, hard, warty, charcoal-like cylindrical swellings ('knots', 1 to 12+ inches long) encasing twigs and branches; first-year knots start in late summer as subtle olive-green velvety corky swellings that rupture the bark, then turn hard, rough, and jet-black in their second summer/winter, gradually girdling and killing the branch beyond the knot.
symptom_keywords: coal-black warty branch swellings, charcoal-like twig galls, rough black cylindrical knots on plum branches, girdled dead limbs
symptom_progression: Ascospores ejected from 2-year-old knots during spring rains infect succulent new green twigs; soft olive-green swellings appear the first autumn and harden into rough jet-black spore-releasing knots the second year.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hard, rough, coal-black tar-like woody knots wrapped around plum and cherry twigs.
similar_conditions: Crown Gall (occurs at roots/crown base), Bacterial Canker (sunken gummy bark lesions rather than raised black knots)
risk_factors: Nearby wild cherry or wild plum trees (especially chokecherry Prunus virginiana and black cherry P. serotina) harboring black knots in woodlots/hedgerows, and susceptible plum cultivars ('Stanley', 'Damson', 'Shiro').
favorable_conditions: Rainy spring weather between budbreak and shuck split at 55–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Wind- and rain-borne ascospores discharged from 2-year-old black knots in spring.
management_actions: PRUNE OUT KNOTS IN WINTER: during late-winter dormancy (before March bud swell when spores are released), prune out all knotted branches by cutting at least 4–6 inches BELOW the visible swelling (as internal fungal mycelium extends several inches beyond the knot), sterilize loppers with 70% alcohol between cuts, and burn or bag/trash the pruned knots immediately (disconnected knots left on the ground still shoot spores!).
prevention_actions: Remove wild plum and chokecherry trees within 500 ft of the garden; plant resistant plum cultivars ('President'); inspect trees every winter.
recommended_observations: Scout Peach (twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs) weekly during wet spring weather for infection; visible year-round (especially in dormant winter) (55–77°F (13–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Knot of Plum and Cherry from Crown Gall (occurs at roots/crown base), Bacterial Canker (sunken gummy bark lesions rather than raised black knots).
severity_or_impact: High on plums and cherries (unchecked knots girdle scaffold limbs and ruin the entire tree within a few years)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–77°F (13–25°C) and spring rain wetting emerging green shoots.
host_range: Documented on Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Plum, Cherry, Peach).
knowledge_text: Peach (Prunus persica) Black Knot of Plum and Cherry is a fungal disease caused by Apiosporina morbosa. Symptoms on peach (twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs): Elongated, rough, coal-black, hard, warty, charcoal-like cylindrical swellings ('knots', 1 to 12+ inches long) encasing twigs and branches; first-year knots start in late summer as subtle olive-green velvety corky swellings that rupture the bark, then turn hard, rough, and jet-black in their second summer/winter, gradually girdling and killing the branch beyond the knot. Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the hard, rough, coal-black tar-like woody knots wrapped around plum and cherry twigs. Favored by rainy spring weather between budbreak and shuck split at 55–77°f. (55–77°F (13–25°C)). Management and prevention: PRUNE OUT KNOTS IN WINTER: during late-winter dormancy (before March bud swell when spores are released), prune out all knotted branches by cutting at least 4–6 inches BELOW the visible swelling (as internal fungal mycelium extends several inches beyond the knot), sterilize loppers with 70% alcohol between cuts, and burn or bag/trash the pruned knots immediately (disconnected knots left on the ground still shoot spores!). Remove wild plum and chokecherry trees within 500 ft of the garden; plant resistant plum cultivars ('President'); inspect trees every winter.
evidence_notes: Host-specific disease relationship (Peach - Black Knot of Plum and Cherry), symptoms, and IPM controls verified via University of Maryland Extension (HGIC) and University of Wisconsin-Madison Extension Horticulture.

topic: Peach Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Monilinia fructicola)
problem_name: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits
causal_agent: Monilinia fructicola (and Monilinia laxa)
affected_plant_parts: Blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits
growth_stage: Spring bloom and final 3 weeks of fruit ripening through post-harvest
season: Warm, wet, humid spring bloom and summer harvest periods
humidity_conditions: High humidity and rain or prolonged wetness during bloom and fruit ripening
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Blossom & Twig Blight: open spring flowers suddenly turn brown, wither, and cling to the twig inside a drop of amber gum, girdling the fruiting twig; Fruit Rot: small circular light-brown soft spots on ripening peaches, plums, or cherries that expand across the entire fruit within 24–48 hours and erupt in concentric tufts of dusty tan-to-ash-gray conidia spores; rotted fruits shrivel into wrinkled, hard black/gray 'mummies' that hang on the tree through winter.
symptom_keywords: soft brown fruit rot, dusty tan-gray spore tufts on fruit, shriveled hanging fruit mummies, blighted gummy blossoms, twig dieback
symptom_progression: Spring spores from overwintered mummies infect blossoms and twigs; as fruits ripen and sugar rises in summer, secondary conidia invade through microscopic cuticle cracks or insect wounds (plum curculio, oriental fruit moth, Japanese beetle, stink bugs), rotting whole crops in days.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the rapid, firm-yet-soft brown decay covered in powdery tan/buff-gray spore tufts (unlike black Rhizopus rot whiskers) and the shriveled mummified fruits hanging on branches.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Rot (black coarse mold whiskers in storage), Bacterial Spot, Anthracnose, Botrytis Gray Mold
risk_factors: Leaving mummified fruits hanging in trees or lying on the ground over winter, unharvested overripe fruit, insect feeding punctures, fruit cracking from rain, and dense unpruned canopies.
favorable_conditions: Warm (70–80°F), rainy, or humid weather during spring bloom and the final 3 weeks before harvest.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in hanging and fallen fruit mummies and twig cankers; conidia and ascospores spread by wind, rain splash, and fruit-feeding insects.
management_actions: SANITATION IS PARAMOUNT: pick up and destroy all fallen fruit during summer and remove every single shriveled mummy from the tree and ground during winter pruning; thin fruits so they do not touch each other in clusters; control plum curculio and oriental fruit moth whose feeding holes let brown rot in.
prevention_actions: Prune peach, plum, and cherry trees to an open center for sunlight and rapid drying; harvest fruit promptly as it matures.
recommended_observations: Scout Peach (blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits) weekly during warm, wet, humid spring bloom and summer harvest periods (68–80°F (20–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Brown Rot of Stone Fruits from Rhizopus Rot (black coarse mold whiskers in storage), Bacterial Spot, Anthracnose, Botrytis Gray Mold.
severity_or_impact: Critical (the most destructive disease of peaches, plums, and cherries; can rot 50–100% of ripening fruit in wet summers)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–80°F (20–27°C) and high humidity and rain or prolonged wetness during bloom and fruit ripening.
host_range: Documented on Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Peach, Plum, Cherry).
knowledge_text: Peach (Prunus persica) Brown Rot of Stone Fruits is a fungal disease caused by Monilinia fructicola (and Monilinia laxa). Symptoms on peach (blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits): Blossom & Twig Blight: open spring flowers suddenly turn brown, wither, and cling to the twig inside a drop of amber gum, girdling the fruiting twig; Fruit Rot: small circular light-brown soft spots on ripening peaches, plums, or cherries that expand across the entire fruit within 24–48 hours and erupt in concentric tufts of dusty tan-to-ash-gray conidia spores; rotted fruits shrivel into wrinkled, hard black/gray 'mummies' that hang on the tree through winter. Management and prevention: SANITATION IS PARAMOUNT: pick up and destroy all fallen fruit during summer and remove every single shriveled mummy from the tree and ground during winter pruning; thin fruits so they do not touch each other in clusters; control plum curculio and oriental fruit moth whose feeding holes let brown rot in. Prune peach, plum, and cherry trees to an open center for sunlight and rapid drying; harvest fruit promptly as it matures.

topic: Peach Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Peach (Prunus persica): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Peach (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Peach (Prunus persica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).
knowledge_text: Peach (Prunus persica) Crown Gall is a bacterial disease caused by Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall). Symptoms on peach (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness. Distinguishing features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!). Favored by warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding. (68–86°F (20–30°C)). Management and prevention: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking. Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.

topic: Plum Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs Management
problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Asian Citrus Psyllid vectors fatal HLB; Scales and Mealybugs weaken branches and coat fruit in sooty mold)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–92°F (20–33°C) and warm, humid growing conditions.
host_range: Documented on Plum (Prunus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Citrus, Lemon, Lime, Avocado, Mango, Guava, Papaya, Banana).

topic: Plum Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot Management
problem_name: Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot
problem_category: Internal Fruit-Boring Pest of Tree Fruits
causal_agent: Cydia pomonella (Codling Moth), Grapholita molesta (Oriental Fruit Moth), and Rhagoletis pomonella (Apple Maggot / 'Railroad Worm')
affected_plant_parts: Internal fruit core/seeds (Codling Moth), fruit flesh (Apple Maggot), and tender spring shoot tips + fruit (Oriental Fruit Moth)
growth_stage: Petal fall through harvest
season: May through September
humidity_conditions: Warm dusk temperatures (>60°F) for moth egg-laying; summer rains for Apple Maggot fly emergence
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Codling Moth ('the worm in the apple'): a pinkish-white caterpillar (1/2 to 3/4 inch) with a brown head bores through the side or blossom calyx cup straight to the center core of apples, pears, and walnuts to eat the seeds, pushing a pile of coarse, reddish-brown, sawdust-like frass out of the entry hole ('frass plug'); Oriental Fruit Moth: in spring, first-generation pinkish larvae bore 2–4 inches down into the tender terminal shoot tips of peach, nectarine, plum, and apple trees, causing the top 3–4 leaves of new shoots to wilt and flag brown ('shoot flagging'), while summer generations bore into ripening peaches (often right down the stem channel without leaving an obvious external hole!); Apple Maggot ('Railroad Worm'): small black flies with distinctive dark 'F'-shaped wing bands puncture apple skin in summer, and legless white maggots chew brown, winding, thread-like trails all through the apple flesh, making the fruit lumpy and dimpled.
symptom_keywords: pinkish-white caterpillar with brown head inside apple core, pile of coarse reddish-brown sawdust frass pushed out of hole in apple, brown winding railroad trails throughout apple flesh, wilted flagging terminal shoot tips on peach in spring
symptom_progression: Codling Moth and Oriental Fruit Moth overwinter as cocoons under loose trunk bark and emerge around apple bloom (Codling Moth eggs hatch at ~250 Degree Days base 50°F after biofix); Apple Maggot flies emerge from soil from late June through August.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the two main 'apple worms': Codling Moth is a caterpillar WITH a brown head and legs that tunnels straight to the seed core and pushes coarse brown frass out the hole; Apple Maggot is a headless, legless white fly maggot that leaves thin, winding brown 'railroad tracks' throughout the white flesh without tunneling to the core or pushing out frass.
similar_conditions: Plum Curculio (crescent-shaped corky scar on young fruit skin), Fire Blight (scorched shepherd's crook without a larva burrow inside the twig)
risk_factors: Uncared-for wild apple, crabapple, or hawthorn trees nearby, uncollected fallen 'drop' apples under trees, and failure to thin apple clusters to single fruits (touching apples give Codling Moth larvae leverage to bore in!).
favorable_conditions: Calm, warm evenings (>60°F at dusk) after petal fall.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths and maggot flies fly between neighboring backyard fruit trees and wild crabapples/hawthorns.
management_actions: NON-CHEMICAL BAGGING & TRAPPING FOR HOME ORCHARDS: (1) Fruit Bagging: when thinned apples/pears are 1/2 to 3/4 inch wide (about 3 weeks after petal fall), slip small zip-top sandwich bags (with bottom corners snipped for drainage), Japanese paper fruit bags, or nylon footies over individual fruits—this produces 100% worm-free apples without sprays! (2) Red Sphere Traps: hang 3–6 sticky-coated dark-red spheres per apple tree in June–August to trap egg-laying Apple Maggot flies; (3) wrap corrugated cardboard trunk bands around apple trunks in June and August to trap and destroy pupating Codling Moth cocoons; (4) spray Cydia pomonella granulovirus (CpGV—a 100% selective biological virus for Codling Moth), spinosad, or kaolin clay timed at 250 DD after bloom.
prevention_actions: Pick up and remove all fallen 'June drop' and wormy apples/peaches every 2–3 days before larvae exit the fruit into the soil or trunk bark; thin apples to 1 fruit per cluster; prune out flagged Oriental Fruit Moth shoot tips on peaches in spring before the larva exits.

severity_or_impact: Critical on apples, pears, and peaches (can infest 60–100% of unmanaged backyard apples)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm dusk temperatures (>60°f) for moth egg-laying; summer rains for apple maggot fly emergence.
host_range: Documented on Plum (Prunus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry, Walnut).

topic: Plum Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla Management
problem_name: Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla
problem_category: Wood-Boring Moth & Sap-Feeding Psyllid Pests of Fruit Trees
causal_agent: Synanthedon exitiosa (Peachtree Borer), Synanthedon pictipes (Lesser Peachtree Borer), and Cacopsylla pyricola (Pear Psylla)
affected_plant_parts: Lower trunk at and 2–3 inches below the soil line (Peachtree Borer), upper scaffold limb wounds/cankers (Lesser Peachtree Borer), and pear leaves/fruits (Pear Psylla)
growth_stage: Perennial woody trunk/limbs and summer foliage
season: Summer egg-laying with year-round larval feeding (Borers); early spring through autumn (Pear Psylla)
humidity_conditions: Warm summer days for clearwing moth flight; lush nitrogen-stimulated pear shoots for Pear Psylla
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Peachtree Borer: masses of thick, amber-to-clear, jelly-like gum MIXED WITH coarse reddish-brown sawdust-like insect frass and empty brown pupal skins protruding at the base of the trunk right at the soil line of peach, plum, and cherry trees; beneath the bark, 1-inch-long creamy-white caterpillars with dark-brown heads tunnel through the cambium around the root collar, girdling and killing young trees and causing older trees to yellow and die back on one side (Lesser Peachtree Borer causes identical frass-filled gummosis higher up on scaffold branch crotches and cankers); Pear Psylla: tiny (2 mm) cicada-like reddish-brown winged adults and flat, yellowish-green-to-brown wingpad nymphs submerged inside droplets of sticky clear honeydew on pear leaves and shoots, causing black sooty mold russeting on pears and sudden blackened leaf blotches ('psylla shock').
symptom_keywords: thick amber jelly gum mixed with brown sawdust frass at base of peach trunk, creamy white caterpillar under bark at soil line, brown pupal skins sticking out of trunk base, day-flying blue-black wasp-mimic clearwing moth, pear leaves dripping honeydew with black leaf blotches
symptom_progression: Day-flying metallic blue-black clearwing moths (females have a bright orange band across the abdomen) lay eggs on the lower trunk from June through September; larvae tunnel under the bark all autumn, winter, and spring.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION for Stone Fruit Gummosis: Amber gum oozing from a peach, plum, or cherry trunk that is CLEAR and free of sawdust/frass is caused by abiotic injury, Cytospora fungus, or Bacterial Canker; gum that contains gritty brown sawdust-like frass particles and cast skins at the soil line is Peachtree Borer!
similar_conditions: Bacterial Canker / Cytospora Canker (clear amber gum WITHOUT brown insect sawdust/frass), Crown Gall, Fire Blight (on Pear)
risk_factors: String-trimmer or lawnmower bark wounds at the base of stone fruit trunks, volcano mulching piled against the bark, winter sunscald cracks, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer on pear trees (which pushes succulent water sprouts favored by Pear Psylla).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer months (June–September).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying diurnal clearwing moths attracted to wounded or stressed stone fruit bark; Pear Psylla overwinters as adults in bark crevices.
management_actions: For Peachtree Borer: inspect the trunk base at the soil line in spring and autumn, carefully probe active frass-filled gum holes with a flexible wire to puncture the larva under the bark, or apply beneficial entomopathogenic nematodes (Steinernema carpocapsae) as a moist drench around the lower trunk in late summer/spring; for Pear Psylla: apply a delayed-dormant horticultural oil spray in early spring just before buds open to deter egg-laying on pear twigs, and wash honeydew off leaves with insecticidal soap.
prevention_actions: Keep mulch pulled back 4–6 inches from the trunk base of peach, plum, and cherry trees (never pile mulch against the bark!), protect trunks with breathable white tree guards against string-trimmers and winter sunscald, and whitewash south-west trunks with 50:50 water-diluted white interior latex paint; summer-prune upright water sprouts out of pear trees.
recommended_observations: Scout Plum (lower trunk at and 2–3 inches below the soil line (peachtree borer), upper scaffold limb wounds/cankers (lesser peachtree borer), and pear leaves/fruits (pear psylla)) twice weekly during summer egg-laying with year-round larval feeding (borers); early spring through autumn (pear psylla) (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for thick amber jelly gum mixed with brown sawdust frass at base of peach trunk to distinguish Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla from Bacterial Canker / Cytospora Canker (clear amber gum WITHOUT brown insect sawdust/frass), Crown Gall, Fire Blight (on Pear).
severity_or_impact: Critical on peach, plum, cherry, and pear (Peachtree Borer can girdle and kill young stone fruit trees in 1–2 seasons)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm summer days for clearwing moth flight; lush nitrogen-stimulated pear shoots for pear psylla.

topic: Plum Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies Management

affected_plant_parts: Immature newly set fruits (petal fall / shuck split) and ripening cherries
growth_stage: Petal fall / shuck split through harvest
season: Spring (Plum Curculio) and early summer as cherries turn yellow-red (Cherry Fruit Fly)
humidity_conditions: Warm (>70°F) humid spring days and nights following rain
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Plum Curculio: a small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), rough-backed, brownish-black snout weevil with grey-white flecks and four prominent humps on its wing covers that emerges at petal fall / shuck split; the female chews a small hole in the tiny green fruitlet, inserts an egg, and then cuts a diagnostic crescent-shaped (D-shaped / half-moon) slit right underneath the egg so the rapidly expanding fruit flesh will not crush her egg! risk_factors: Fruit trees planted adjacent to deciduous woodlots, hedgerows, or brush piles (where Plum Curculio adults overwinter in leaf litter) and uncollected dropped stone fruits.
favorable_conditions: Spring days reaching 70–75°F+ or warm nights (>60°F) right after petal fall / shuck split.
