topic: Plum Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Plum (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).

topic: Plum Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

topic: Plum Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained loam, sandy loam, or clay loam (plums tolerate slightly heavier soils than peaches when grafted on Myrobalan or Mariana rootstocks) (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)

topic: Plum Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits (Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae)
problem_name: Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits
causal_agent: Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae (Bacterial Canker) and Wilsonomyces carpophilus (Coryneum Blight / Shot Hole)
affected_plant_parts: Dormant buds, twigs, scaffold limbs, trunk bark, leaves, and fruit
growth_stage: Autumn leaf drop through winter dormancy and spring budbreak
season: Cool, wet autumn, winter, and early spring weather
humidity_conditions: Rainy autumn/winter/spring weather and freeze-thaw cycles

topic: Plum Bacterial Spot (Xanthomonas spp.)
problem_name: Bacterial Spot
causal_agent: Xanthomonas spp. (X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri on Solanaceae; X. arboricola pv. pruni on Stone Fruits; X. cucurbitae on Cucurbits)

season: Warm, rainy, humid summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, driving rain, wind-blown mist, and overhead irrigation

topic: Plum Black Knot of Plum and Cherry (Apiosporina morbosa)
problem_name: Black Knot of Plum and Cherry
causal_agent: Apiosporina morbosa
affected_plant_parts: Twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs
growth_stage: Spring shoot elongation through perennial woody growth (2-year lifecycle)
season: Wet spring weather for infection; visible year-round (especially in dormant winter)
humidity_conditions: Spring rain wetting emerging green shoots
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Elongated, rough, coal-black, hard, warty, charcoal-like cylindrical swellings ('knots', 1 to 12+ inches long) encasing twigs and branches; first-year knots start in late summer as subtle olive-green velvety corky swellings that rupture the bark, then turn hard, rough, and jet-black in their second summer/winter, gradually girdling and killing the branch beyond the knot.
symptom_keywords: coal-black warty branch swellings, charcoal-like twig galls, rough black cylindrical knots on plum branches, girdled dead limbs
symptom_progression: Ascospores ejected from 2-year-old knots during spring rains infect succulent new green twigs; soft olive-green swellings appear the first autumn and harden into rough jet-black spore-releasing knots the second year.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hard, rough, coal-black tar-like woody knots wrapped around plum and cherry twigs.
similar_conditions: Crown Gall (occurs at roots/crown base), Bacterial Canker (sunken gummy bark lesions rather than raised black knots)
risk_factors: Nearby wild cherry or wild plum trees (especially chokecherry Prunus virginiana and black cherry P. serotina) harboring black knots in woodlots/hedgerows, and susceptible plum cultivars ('Stanley', 'Damson', 'Shiro').
favorable_conditions: Rainy spring weather between budbreak and shuck split at 55–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Wind- and rain-borne ascospores discharged from 2-year-old black knots in spring.
management_actions: PRUNE OUT KNOTS IN WINTER: during late-winter dormancy (before March bud swell when spores are released), prune out all knotted branches by cutting at least 4–6 inches BELOW the visible swelling (as internal fungal mycelium extends several inches beyond the knot), sterilize loppers with 70% alcohol between cuts, and burn or bag/trash the pruned knots immediately (disconnected knots left on the ground still shoot spores!).
prevention_actions: Remove wild plum and chokecherry trees within 500 ft of the garden; plant resistant plum cultivars ('President'); inspect trees every winter.
recommended_observations: Scout Plum (twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs) weekly during wet spring weather for infection; visible year-round (especially in dormant winter) (55–77°F (13–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Knot of Plum and Cherry from Crown Gall (occurs at roots/crown base), Bacterial Canker (sunken gummy bark lesions rather than raised black knots).
severity_or_impact: High on plums and cherries (unchecked knots girdle scaffold limbs and ruin the entire tree within a few years)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–77°F (13–25°C) and spring rain wetting emerging green shoots.
host_range: Documented on Plum (Prunus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Plum, Cherry, Peach).

topic: Plum Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Monilinia fructicola)
problem_name: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits
causal_agent: Monilinia fructicola (and Monilinia laxa)
affected_plant_parts: Blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits
growth_stage: Spring bloom and final 3 weeks of fruit ripening through post-harvest
season: Warm, wet, humid spring bloom and summer harvest periods
humidity_conditions: High humidity and rain or prolonged wetness during bloom and fruit ripening
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Blossom & Twig Blight: open spring flowers suddenly turn brown, wither, and cling to the twig inside a drop of amber gum, girdling the fruiting twig; Fruit Rot: small circular light-brown soft spots on ripening peaches, plums, or cherries that expand across the entire fruit within 24–48 hours and erupt in concentric tufts of dusty tan-to-ash-gray conidia spores; rotted fruits shrivel into wrinkled, hard black/gray 'mummies' that hang on the tree through winter.
symptom_keywords: soft brown fruit rot, dusty tan-gray spore tufts on fruit, shriveled hanging fruit mummies, blighted gummy blossoms, twig dieback
symptom_progression: Spring spores from overwintered mummies infect blossoms and twigs; as fruits ripen and sugar rises in summer, secondary conidia invade through microscopic cuticle cracks or insect wounds (plum curculio, oriental fruit moth, Japanese beetle, stink bugs), rotting whole crops in days.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the rapid, firm-yet-soft brown decay covered in powdery tan/buff-gray spore tufts (unlike black Rhizopus rot whiskers) and the shriveled mummified fruits hanging on branches.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Rot (black coarse mold whiskers in storage), Bacterial Spot, Anthracnose, Botrytis Gray Mold
risk_factors: Leaving mummified fruits hanging in trees or lying on the ground over winter, unharvested overripe fruit, insect feeding punctures, fruit cracking from rain, and dense unpruned canopies.
favorable_conditions: Warm (70–80°F), rainy, or humid weather during spring bloom and the final 3 weeks before harvest.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in hanging and fallen fruit mummies and twig cankers; conidia and ascospores spread by wind, rain splash, and fruit-feeding insects.
management_actions: SANITATION IS PARAMOUNT: pick up and destroy all fallen fruit during summer and remove every single shriveled mummy from the tree and ground during winter pruning; thin fruits so they do not touch each other in clusters; control plum curculio and oriental fruit moth whose feeding holes let brown rot in.
prevention_actions: Prune peach, plum, and cherry trees to an open center for sunlight and rapid drying; harvest fruit promptly as it matures.
recommended_observations: Scout Plum (blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits) weekly during warm, wet, humid spring bloom and summer harvest periods (68–80°F (20–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Brown Rot of Stone Fruits from Rhizopus Rot (black coarse mold whiskers in storage), Bacterial Spot, Anthracnose, Botrytis Gray Mold.
severity_or_impact: Critical (the most destructive disease of peaches, plums, and cherries; can rot 50–100% of ripening fruit in wet summers)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–80°F (20–27°C) and high humidity and rain or prolonged wetness during bloom and fruit ripening.
host_range: Documented on Plum (Prunus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Peach, Plum, Cherry).

topic: Plum Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Plum (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Plum (Prunus domestica, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).

topic: Plum Peach Leaf Curl (Taphrina deformans)
problem_name: Peach Leaf Curl
causal_agent: Taphrina deformans
affected_plant_parts: Emerging spring leaves, tender shoots, and occasionally blossoms/fruitlets
growth_stage: Spring bud swell and leaf emergence
season: Cool, wet early spring weather
humidity_conditions: Rain or prolonged dampness as dormant leaf buds swell and scales separate
visible_symptoms: On Plum (Prunus domestica): Newly emerging spring leaves become severely thickened, puckered, curled, crisp/brittle, and twisted, turning striking shades of pink, scarlet-red, or pale yellowish-green; soon a dusty greyish-white bloom of naked asci spores covers the blistered upper leaf surface, after which affected leaves turn brown, shrivel, and drop in late spring/early summer, forcing the tree to expend energy growing a second flush of leaves.
symptom_keywords: thickened puckered red-and-yellow curled leaves, blistered brittle spring leaves, dusty white bloom on distorted leaves, early-summer defoliation
symptom_progression: Yeast-like blastospores overwintering under bud scales wash onto embryonic leaves during cool spring rains right as buds swell; once leaves emerge and turn red/puckered, the fungus is already inside and fungicides can no longer cure that year's leaves.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on peach and nectarine in spring by the thick, fleshy, red-and-yellow puckered leaves (unlike Aphid leaf curling, where leaves remain thin and green with live aphids and sticky honeydew inside the curl).
similar_conditions: Green Peach Aphid / Leaf Curl Plum Aphid (thin green curled leaves with aphids inside), Frost Crinkling, Herbicide Drift
risk_factors: Cool, rainy spring weather during bud swell and failure to apply a dormant fungicide before buds swell.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (50–62°F) with rain wetting swelling buds; fungal infection stops once temperatures exceed 79–85°F in summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as yeast-like conidia/blastospores lodged in bark crevices and between dormant bud scales, washing into opening buds with rain.

growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.

topic: Sweet corn Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm Management
problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin.
symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.
distinguishing_features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters).
similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.
prevention_actions: Plant early-maturing sweet corn cultivars as early in spring as soil temperature allows to harvest before peak late-summer moth flights; select sweet corn hybrids with tight, long husk extensions beyond the ear tip; encourage Trichogramma egg-parasitoid wasps and Orius minute pirate bugs (which eat earworm eggs on silks).

severity_or_impact: High (the #1 insect pest of sweet corn and a destructive borer in tomatoes, peppers, beans, and okra)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm weather and southerly summer wind currents.
host_range: Documented on Sweet corn (Zea mays, Poaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Beans, Cowpea, Soybean, Pea).

topic: Sweet corn Cucumber Beetles Management
problem_name: Cucumber Beetles (Striped and Spotted Cucumber Beetles)
causal_agent: Acalymma vittatum (Striped Cucumber Beetle) and Diabrotica undecimpunctata howardi (Spotted Cucumber Beetle / Southern Corn Rootworm)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence through flowering and fruiting
season: Spring transplant/emergence through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oblong bright-yellow-green beetles with either three jet-black longitudinal stripes down the wing covers (Striped Cucumber Beetle) or twelve black spots (Spotted Cucumber Beetle); overwintered adults swarm emerging cucurbit cotyledons and young transplants in spring, chewing ragged holes through leaves, girdling tender stems, congregating inside open yellow cucurbit blossoms (chewing anthers/pistils and reducing fruit set), scarring the underside and rind of melons/pumpkins, and transmitting the fatal bacterium Erwinia tracheiphila (Bacterial Wilt); white brown-headed larvae feed underground on cucurbit, corn, and bean roots.
symptom_keywords: yellow beetle with three black stripes, yellow-green beetle with twelve black spots, chewed cucurbit cotyledons and stems, beetles packed inside squash blossoms, scarred pumpkin rinds, sudden bacterial wilt
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge when spring temperatures exceed 55–65°F, attracted strongly by cucurbitacin bitter compounds in emerging cucurbit seedlings; females lay orange-yellow eggs in soil cracks at the stem base, producing root-feeding larvae and a mid-summer second adult generation.
distinguishing_features: Striped Cucumber Beetle has 3 sharp black stripes on a yellow back with a black head and black abdomen underside (unlike Western Corn Rootworm, which has blurred stripes and a yellow abdomen); Spotted Cucumber Beetle is yellow-green with 12 black spots (unlike beneficial Pink Spotted Lady Beetles, which are pink/reddish-orange with spots on the thorax too).
similar_conditions: Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles
risk_factors: Uncovered spring cucurbit seedlings, cultivars high in cucurbitacins, and bacterial wilt reservoirs.
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny spring days (>60°F) during seedling emergence and bloom.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded field borders and weedy garden debris, flying into cucurbit beds as soon as seedlings crack the soil.
management_actions: Keep cucurbit seedlings and transplants completely covered under floating row covers or insect netting sealed at the edges from the day of planting until female flowers open (then remove covers for bee pollination); hand-vacuum beetles out of open squash blossoms early in the morning; apply kaolin clay (Surround) particle film or botanical pyrethrin/spinosad/neem sprays in the evening when bees are not inside flowers (squash blossoms close by afternoon!).
prevention_actions: Transplant robust 3-to-4-week-old cucurbit starts rather than direct-seeding in high-pressure gardens; plant a perimeter trap crop of 'Blue Hubbard' squash (which has extreme cucurbitacin levels that lure 85–90% of cucumber beetles away from cucumbers and melons!); mulch with straw to encourage wolf spiders and ground beetles.
recommended_observations: Scout Sweet corn (cotyledons, young seedlings, leaves, stems, open blossoms, silk channels, roots (larvae), and fruit rinds) twice weekly during spring transplant/emergence through autumn (60–90°F (15–32°C)); inspect for yellow beetle with three black stripes to distinguish Cucumber Beetles from Western Corn Rootworm, Flea Beetles (much smaller and jump), Beneficial Lady Beetles.
severity_or_impact: Critical on cucumbers, melons, and squash (both from direct seedling destruction and as the sole vector of Bacterial Wilt)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm spring and summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Sweet corn (Zea mays, Poaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Bottle gourd, Bitter gourd).

topic: Sweet corn Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)

growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils

symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.

transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.

topic: Sweet corn Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.

severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Sweet corn (Zea mays, Poaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Sweet corn Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Sweet corn (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Sweet corn (Zea mays, Poaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Sweet corn Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Sweet corn (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Sweet corn (Zea mays, Poaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

problem_name: Sweetpotato Weevil, Wireworms, and White Grubs
problem_category: Subterranean Root- and Tuber-Feeding Beetle Pests

affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Sweetpotato Weevil: slender, ant-like snout beetles (1/4 inch / 6 mm) with a metallic dark-blue head and wing covers and a bright brick-red thorax and legs; legless white grubs tunnel extensively through crowns and fleshy sweet potato storage roots, packing winding tunnels with dark bitter frass and triggering the sweet potato to synthesize toxic sesquiterpenes (ipomeamarone) that give the entire root a terribly bitter, turpentine-like flavor and odor making it completely inedible even in un-tunneled parts!; Wireworms: hard-bodied, shiny, cylindrical, wire-like yellow-to-coppery-brown larvae (1/2 to 1.5 inches long) with 3 pairs of short thoracic legs that bore clean, round, straight-walled 'drill holes' (1–2 mm wide) deep into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, carrots, beets, and germinating corn seeds; White Grubs: plump, C-shaped creamy-white larvae with brown heads, 6 prominent legs, and a dark raster end that chew large wide gouges out of potatoes, carrots, and strawberry roots.
symptom_keywords: ant-like metallic blue-and-red snout weevil, frass-filled tunnels inside sweet potato with bitter turpentine taste, hard shiny yellow-brown wire-like worm boring clean drill holes in potato and carrot, C-shaped white scarab grub chewing wide gouges in tubers and strawberry roots
symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! For Sweetpotato Weevil, hill soil 2–3 inches deep over developing sweet potato roots so soil cracks do not expose roots to egg-laying females, and destroy infested roots immediately.
prevention_actions: Never plant potatoes, sweet potatoes, carrots, strawberries, or corn in the first year after breaking grassy sod (grow tomatoes, squash, beans, or brassicas first, or solarize/clean-cultivate the sod in summer); in Sweetpotato Weevil quarantine zones (Gulf Coast, South Florida, coastal South), use only certified weevil-free slips cut above the soil line and eradicate wild morning glories (Ipomoea spp.).

severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Sweetpotato Weevil renders entire roots bitterly toxic; Wireworms and White Grubs ruin tubers and kill strawberry crowns)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod).
host_range: Documented on Sweet corn (Zea mays, Poaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet potato, Potato, Carrot, Beet, Radish, Turnip, Parsnip, Onion).

topic: Sweet corn Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam or silt loam (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt); drainage: Good Drainage)
management_actions: Prepare a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or silt loam adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Sweet corn to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Sweet corn (Zea mays): Prefers deep, fertile, well-drained loam or silt loam with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Sweet corn Corn Smut (Common Smut) and Northern Corn Leaf Blight (Ustilago maydis)
problem_name: Corn Smut (Common Smut) and Northern Corn Leaf Blight
causal_agent: Ustilago maydis (Common Smut) and Exserohilum turcicum (Northern Corn Leaf Blight)
affected_plant_parts: Ears/kernels, tassels, nodal buds, stalks, and leaves
growth_stage: Vegetative whorl through silking and ear fill
season: Warm summer growing season
humidity_conditions: Dry hot weather followed by rain/hail or detasseling/cultivation wounds (Smut); heavy dew/rain (NCLB)
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Common Smut: conspicuous, swollen, tumor-like fleshy galls (1 to 6+ inches across) on corn ears (replacing individual kernels), tassels, or stalk nodes that are initially covered in a glistening, silvery-white membrane ('huitlacoche' when young and tender) before darkening and rupturing to release a greasy-to-powdery mass of millions of sooty olive-black teliospores; Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB): long (1 to 6 inch), elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan necrotic lesions on lower-to-upper leaf blades.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white swollen kernel galls, black sooty spore masses on corn ear, huitlacoche, long cigar-shaped gray-tan leaf lesions
symptom_progression: Smut sporidia enter unpollinated silk channels or hail/insect/cultivation wounds on meristematic tissue, swelling into silvery-white galls within 10–14 days; NCLB conidia splash onto lower leaves and work upward.
distinguishing_features: Common Smut is unmistakable due to the large silvery-white galls filled with black spores on ears and tassels; NCLB is distinguished by its large (2–6 inch) boat- or cigar-shaped gray-tan leaf lesions.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm feeding at ear tip, Stewart's Bacterial Wilt (long pale-green-to-tan streaks with wavy margins along veins vectored by corn flea beetles)
risk_factors: Hail, wind, or cultivation damage to stalks, poor pollination (leaving silks receptive longer), high nitrogen levels, and sweet corn monoculture.
favorable_conditions: Hot dry weather interrupted by thunderstorm showers (Smut); moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with heavy dew (NCLB).
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in soil and corn debris as black teliospores (Smut) or conidia/mycelia (NCLB), carried by wind and splashing rain.
management_actions: Cut off and remove silvery-white smut galls BEFORE the membrane ruptures and releases black spores into the garden soil (note: intact young silvery-white ear galls are a prized edible culinary delicacy known as 'huitlacoche' or Mexican truffle!).
prevention_actions: Plant resistant sweet corn hybrids (carrying Ht genes for NCLB); avoid mechanical injury to stalks during weeding; plant in 4+ row blocks for rapid complete silk pollination; avoid excessive nitrogen.
recommended_observations: Scout Sweet corn (ears/kernels, tassels, nodal buds, stalks, and leaves) weekly during warm summer growing season (65–80°F (NCLB); 78–93°F (Common Smut)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Corn Smut (Common Smut) and Northern Corn Leaf Blight from Corn Earworm feeding at ear tip, Stewart's Bacterial Wilt (long pale-green-to-tan streaks with wavy margins along veins vectored by corn flea beetles).
severity_or_impact: Moderate (disfigures infected ears, though young smut galls are edible)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (NCLB); 78–93°F (Common Smut) and dry hot weather followed by rain/hail or detasseling/cultivation wounds (smut); heavy dew/rain (nclb).

topic: Sweet corn Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Sweet corn (Zea mays): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.

topic: Sweet corn Nutrient Requirements and Fertilization Schedule
growth_stage: Pre-plant bed preparation, active vegetative growth, and reproductive/storage organ development
management_actions: Heavy nitrogen, phosphorus, and zinc feeder; apply starter phosphorus at planting, side-dress with nitrogen when plants are knee-high (V6, 12–18 inches tall), and again when tassel is in the whorl

topic: Asparagus Asparagus Beetles Management
problem_name: Asparagus Beetles (Common and Spotted Asparagus Beetles)
causal_agent: Crioceris asparagi (Common Asparagus Beetle) and Crioceris duodecimpunctata (Spotted Asparagus Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Emerging spring spears, summer fern cladodes (needles), bark, and red berries
growth_stage: Spring spear harvest through summer fern growth
season: Spring emergence through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis): Two closely related 1/4-inch (6 mm) oblong beetles strictly specific to asparagus: (1) Common Asparagus Beetle has a metallic bluish-black head and wing covers marked with 6 large cream-colored patches bordered in bright red; females glue rows of conspicuous dark-brown/black oblong eggs standing upright on end like little pegs along emerging spears and ferns (staining spears with black specks and causing spears to bend into crooked 'shepherd's crooks' where beetles chew one side), while plump, olive-gray, humpbacked slug-like larvae with black heads strip the green needles/bark off summer ferns, turning the fern canopy bleached tan and starving the underground crown; (2) Spotted Asparagus Beetle is reddish-orange with 12 black spots whose orange larvae feed exclusively inside the round red asparagus berries.
symptom_keywords: rows of dark black peg-like eggs standing upright on asparagus spears, bluish-black beetle with 6 cream spots and red border, reddish-orange beetle with 12 black spots, plump olive-gray slug-like larvae stripping asparagus ferns
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from hollow old fern stubs just as the first spring spears poke through the soil, chewing spears and laying rows of dark upright eggs that hatch in 3–8 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on asparagus by the comb-like rows of dark-brown peg-like eggs glued perpendicular to the spears and ferns, accompanied by the distinctive cream-spotted blue-black or 12-spotted orange beetles.
similar_conditions: Beneficial Lady Beetles (rounded dome shape rather than narrow oblong neck, and lay yellow-orange eggs), Cutworms (chew spears at night from the soil without laying black peg eggs)
risk_factors: Leaving old dead hollow asparagus fern stalks standing over winter and leaving volunteer seedling asparagus around the garden.
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>60°F) during spring spear harvest and summer fern growth.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter inside hollow dead asparagus stems and under bark/mulch right in the asparagus patch.
management_actions: During spring harvest, pick spears cleanly every 1–2 days (harvesting spears before the dark peg-like eggs have 4–7 days to hatch removes the eggs from the garden—and eggs wipe off easily with a damp cloth!); in summer, handpick beetles/larvae into soapy water in the cool morning or spray spinosad/pyrethrin/neem on ferns if >10% of ferns are infested, while conserving the tiny metallic-green parasitic wasp Tetrastichus asparagi.
prevention_actions: Cut down and remove all dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter before spring spears emerge to eliminate overwintering beetle shelter; plant all-male hybrid asparagus cultivars (such as 'Jersey Knight', 'Millennium'), which do not produce seed berries for Spotted Asparagus Beetle larvae.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (scars spring spears and defoliates summer ferns, weakening next year's spear yield)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny spring and summer weather.

topic: Asparagus Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Asparagus (ripening soft-skinned berries (swd), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (japanese beetle), and grape clusters (grape berry moth)) twice weekly during mid-june through autumn frost (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking to distinguish Spotted Wing Drosophila from Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer).
severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis, Asparagaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Asparagus Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Deep, well-drained sandy loam or loam completely free of perennial weeds before planting (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter, Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
soil_ph: 6.5–7.5 (asparagus thrives in neutral pH and performs poorly in acidic soils below 6.0)
management_actions: Prepare a deep, well-drained sandy loam or loam completely free of perennial weeds before planting adjusted to pH 6.5–7.5 (asparagus thrives in neutral pH and performs poorly in acidic soils below 6.0) based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Asparagus to verify soil pH (6.5–7.5 (asparagus thrives in neutral pH and performs poorly in acidic soils below 6.0)) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis): Prefers deep, well-drained sandy loam or loam completely free of perennial weeds before planting with an optimal soil pH of 6.5–7.5 (asparagus thrives in neutral pH and performs poorly in acidic soils below 6.0). Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Asparagus Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Asparagus (Asparagus officinalis): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Asparagus (upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods) weekly during moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity (65–80°F (18–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) from Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.

topic: Okra Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm Management
problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin.
symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.
distinguishing_features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters).
similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.
prevention_actions: Plant early-maturing sweet corn cultivars as early in spring as soil temperature allows to harvest before peak late-summer moth flights; select sweet corn hybrids with tight, long husk extensions beyond the ear tip; encourage Trichogramma egg-parasitoid wasps and Orius minute pirate bugs (which eat earworm eggs on silks).

severity_or_impact: High (the #1 insect pest of sweet corn and a destructive borer in tomatoes, peppers, beans, and okra)
