topic: Okra Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.

topic: Okra Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Okra (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, Malvaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Okra Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.

severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, Malvaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Okra Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.

topic: Okra Whiteflies Management
problem_name: Whiteflies (Silverleaf and Greenhouse Whiteflies)
causal_agent: Bemisia tabaci (Silverleaf / Sweetpotato Whitefly) and Trialeurodes vaporariorum (Greenhouse Whitefly)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits
growth_stage: Transplant establishment through fruiting
season: Warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Tiny (1–1.5 mm), snow-white, powdery-winged moth-like adults flutter up in a cloud from the undersides of leaves when plants are shaken; on lower leaf undersides, flat, oval, translucent-greenish to yellow scale-like nymphs ('crawlers' and pupae) suck phloem sap, excreting copious sticky honeydew that coats leaves and fruits in black sooty mold; on Zucchini/Squash, Bemisia tabaci nymph feeding injects systemic compounds that turn the upper surface of new leaves a brilliant metallic silver ('Squash Silverleaf') and blanches fruit pale; on Tomato, feeding causes irregular blotchy fruit ripening with hard white internal tissue.
symptom_keywords: cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken, translucent oval scale-like nymphs under leaves, sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, silver upper squash leaves, irregular blotchy tomato ripening
symptom_progression: Females lay tiny oblong eggs in arcs on undersides of young leaves; first-instar crawlers settle into immobile scale-like nymphs that complete development in 18–28 days in warm weather.
distinguishing_features: Greenhouse whitefly adults hold their wings flat/roof-like and their pupae have a fringe of glassy wax filaments around a straight-sided cake-shaped body; Silverleaf whitefly adults hold wings tent-like tighter to the body with a slight gap showing the yellow abdomen, and their pupae are dome-shaped without a marginal wax fringe.
similar_conditions: Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly)
risk_factors: Purchasing infested greenhouse transplants, warm dry late-summer weather, excessive nitrogen, and broad-spectrum sprays that wipe out Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus parasitic wasps.
favorable_conditions: Hot weather (80–90°F) and dry conditions or greenhouse cultivation.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-assisted flight of adults over short distances and long-distance movement on infested nursery transplants and ornamentals (poinsettia, hibiscus, lantana).
management_actions: Hang yellow sticky cards at canopy height to monitor and trap adults; vacuum or wash leaf undersides early in the morning when adults are cool and sluggish; spray insecticidal soap, neem oil, or Beauveria bassiana thoroughly on leaf undersides every 5–7 days; release Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus parasitoids in greenhouses.
prevention_actions: Inspect the undersides of all vegetable and herb transplants with a hand lens before bringing them into the garden; use UV-reflective silver mulch and fine 50-mesh insect exclusion screens; remove crop residues promptly after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Okra (undersides of leaves (adults on upper canopy leaves; immobile scale-like nymphs on lower leaves) and fruits) twice weekly during warm summer and autumn seasons (and year-round in greenhouses or frost-free zones) (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for cloud of tiny white moth-like insects when shaken to distinguish Whiteflies from Aphids (pear-shaped wingless colonies with cornicles), Leafhoppers (wedge-shaped insects that hop sideways), Powdery Mildew (fungal coating, does not fly).
severity_or_impact: High (causes direct sap depletion, sooty mold, Squash Silverleaf, irregular tomato ripening, and transmits Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus and Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm, dry-to-moderate weather and protected high-tunnel environments.
host_range: Documented on Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, Malvaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Sweet potato, Cucumber, Melon, Watermelon, Squash).

topic: Okra Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained sandy loam or loam; intolerant of wet, waterlogged soils (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt); drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a well-drained sandy loam or loam; intolerant of wet, waterlogged soils adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Okra to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Prefers well-drained sandy loam or loam; intolerant of wet, waterlogged soils with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Okra Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus and Choanephora Wet Rot (Bhendi yellow vein mosaic begomovirus)
problem_name: Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus and Choanephora Wet Rot
causal_agent: Bhendi yellow vein mosaic begomovirus (OYVMV) and Choanephora cucurbitarum (Blossom Blight / Wet Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Leaf veins, blades, blossoms, and young developing pods/fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through daily flowering and pod/fruit set
season: Hot, humid summer and monsoon/late-summer seasons
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>85% RH), frequent summer rains, or surging silverleaf whitefly populations
visible_symptoms: On Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus): Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus (OYVMV): a striking, vivid network of bright canary-yellow veins and veinlets enclosing small islands of green tissue across the leaf blade (or turning entire upper leaves solid yellow-cream), accompanied by stunted plants and small, pale yellowish-green, hard, fibrous pods; Choanephora Wet Rot (on Okra pods, Squash/Zucchini blossoms-and-fruits, Cowpea pods, and Pepper shoots): fading spent flowers fail to drop off the tip of the young pod or squash and quickly erupt in a dense beard of metallic whisker-like fungal stalks topped with tiny shiny black pinheads ('pins stuck in a pincushion'), rotting the attached blossom end of the young okra pod or squash into a soft watery brown mush.
symptom_keywords: vivid canary-yellow vein network on okra leaf, pale yellow fibrous okra pods, whiskers with shiny black pinheads on blossom end of young squash or okra pod, soft wet blossom-end rot
symptom_progression: Whiteflies transmit OYVMV persistently into phloem veins; Choanephora invades senescing day-old flower petals stuck to the tip of young okra pods or summer squash during humid rainy weather and grows into the fruit tip.
distinguishing_features: OYVMV is unmistakable due to the brilliant yellow net-like clearing of every major and minor leaf vein; Choanephora Wet Rot is distinguished from physiological Blossom-End Rot by the fuzzy whisker-like stalks tipped with tiny black pinhead sporangia covering the decaying blossom end!
similar_conditions: Blossom-End Rot (dry sunken leathery black patch from calcium/water stress WITHOUT whiskers or black pinheads), Iron/Magnesium Deficiency (yellow BETWEEN veins while veins stay green—the exact opposite of Yellow Vein Mosaic!)
risk_factors: High populations of silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) for OYVMV; dense canopies, overhead watering, and high humidity keeping spent flower petals stuck to young fruit tips for Choanephora.
favorable_conditions: Hot, humid weather (80–95°F) with whiteflies (OYVMV) or summer rain showers (Choanephora).
transmission_or_spread: OYVMV is transmitted persistently by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci (not seed-borne); Choanephora spores are spread by wind, rain splash, and flower-visiting bees/beetles.
management_actions: Rogue OYVMV-infected okra plants early and manage whiteflies with insecticidal soap or yellow sticky traps; for Choanephora Wet Rot, gently pluck spent wilted flower corollas off the tips of young squash and okra pods during humid rainy spells and harvest pods every 1–2 days.
prevention_actions: Plant OYVMV-resistant okra hybrids; space okra and summer squash generously for rapid morning sun drying of blossoms.
recommended_observations: Scout Okra (leaf veins, blades, blossoms, and young developing pods/fruits) weekly during hot, humid summer and monsoon/late-summer seasons (78–95°F (26–35°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Okra Yellow Vein Mosaic Virus and Choanephora Wet Rot from Blossom-End Rot (dry sunken leathery black patch from calcium/water stress WITHOUT whiskers or black pinheads), Iron/Magnesium Deficiency (yellow BETWEEN veins while veins stay green—the exact opposite of Yellow Vein Mosaic!).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (OYVMV stunts pod yield by 50–80%; Choanephora rots young squash and okra pods in wet summers)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 78–95°F (26–35°C) and high humidity (>85% rh), frequent summer rains, or surging silverleaf whitefly populations.
host_range: Documented on Okra (Abelmoschus esculentus, Malvaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Okra, Squash, Zucchini, Cowpea, Pepper, Eggplant).

growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/tuber enlargement
season: Cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather

causal_agent: Papilio polyxenes (Black Swallowtail / Parsleyworm) and Listronotus oregonensis (Carrot Weevil)
affected_plant_parts: Feathery foliage and flower umbels (Parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (Carrot Weevil)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through umbel flowering and root bulking
season: Late spring through autumn

visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail Caterpillar): young caterpillars are tiny black, saddle-backed larvae with a white band across the middle (mimicking bird droppings!), which molt into large (2-inch), smooth, bright-green caterpillars banded across each segment with black stripes dotted with bright yellow-orange spots; when poked, the caterpillar everts a bright orange, Y-shaped fleshy horn (osmeterium) from behind its head that emits a pungent citrus-terpene scent to deter birds; Carrot Weevil: small (1/4 inch) coppery-brown snout beetles chew small oval cavities in celery/carrot petioles to lay eggs, and legless creamy-white C-shaped grubs with amber-brown heads tunnel zig-zag cavities across the UPPER one-third and crown shoulder of carrot, parsnip, and celery roots.
symptom_keywords: green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley, orange Y-shaped horn behind head when poked, young black caterpillar with white saddle mimicking bird dropping, zig-zag tunnels in upper crown shoulder of carrot root
symptom_progression: Black Swallowtail butterflies lay single round yellow eggs on feathery umbellifer tips; Carrot Weevils walk from overwintering grassy borders in spring to lay eggs in young petioles at the 3–4 true-leaf stage.
distinguishing_features: Parsleyworm is a prized native butterfly larva unmistakable for its green-black-and-yellow bands and reversible orange Y-shaped osmeterium horn; Carrot Weevil larvae have a distinct amber-brown head capsule and tunnel in the UPPER third/crown of the carrot root (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots are headless and tunnel in the LOWER two-thirds of the root!).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms
risk_factors: Uncovered carrot/celery beds adjacent to last year's carrot patch (for Carrot Weevil).
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days from May through September.
transmission_or_spread: Swallowtail butterflies fly on the wing; Carrot Weevils rarely fly and walk primarily along the ground from overwintering borders.
management_actions: For Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail): because Papilio polyxenes transforms into the magnificent native Eastern Black Swallowtail butterfly and rarely kills established plants, most gardeners simply plant 2–3 extra dill, fennel, or parsley plants as a dedicated 'butterfly nursery' and gently move caterpillars onto those extra plants rather than spraying! prevention_actions: Rotate carrots, celery, and parsnips away from last year's umbellifer bed so walking Carrot Weevils cannot easily reach young seedlings; remove all cull carrots at harvest.

topic: Celery Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Celery (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Celery Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils

symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.

transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.

topic: Celery Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.

severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Celery Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.

severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Celery Spider Mites Management
problem_name: Spider Mites (Two-Spotted Spider Mite and European Red Mite)
causal_agent: Tetranychus urticae (Two-Spotted Spider Mite) and Panonychus ulmi (European Red Mite)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)
growth_stage: Mid-summer vegetative growth through fruit maturation
season: Hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather
humidity_conditions: Low relative humidity (<50% RH), drought stress, and dusty conditions
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Thousands of microscopic pinpoint pale-yellow or whitish-green flecking dots ('stippling') on the upper surface of leaves as mites pierce individual mesophyll cells and suck out chlorophyll; as feeding intensifies, leaves turn bronze, coppery-yellow, or rusty-brown, become dry and papery, and drop prematurely (exposing fruits to sunscald); under a 10x hand lens on the lower leaf surface, tiny (0.4 mm) 8-legged oval greenish-yellow mites with two dark side spots (or brick-red mites in European Red Mite), spherical translucent pearl-like eggs, and fine silken webbing are visible.
symptom_keywords: fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling, bronzed coppery leaves, fine silken webbing under leaves, tiny moving dots on white paper tap test, premature scorching in hot dry weather
symptom_progression: Overwintered females in weeds or bark crevices lay spherical eggs under leaves; at 85–90°F, eggs hatch and mature into adults in just 5–7 days, exploding exponentially during hot dry spells.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'white paper tap test': tap a stippled bronzed leaf over a sheet of white paper—spider mites appear as tiny specks the size of a period that slowly walk across the paper and leave a green/red streak when crushed, accompanied by fine silk webbing on the leaf underside (unlike Thrips, which are elongated/cigar-shaped and leave shiny black fecal specks without webbing).
similar_conditions: Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch
risk_factors: Hot dry weather (>85°F), drought-stressed plants, dusty garden paths/roads (dust coats leaves and kills predatory mites), and applications of carbaryl (Sevin), pyrethroids, or imidacloprid (which kill predatory mites and hormonally stimulate spider mite egg-laying!).
favorable_conditions: Hot (85–95°F), dry, dusty weather.
transmission_or_spread: Mites 'balloon' on wind currents trailing a strand of silk, crawl from drying roadside weeds, or ride on clothing and tools.
management_actions: Hose down the undersides of plants with a forceful spray of cool water every 2–3 days during hot dry spells to dislodge mites, break up webbing, and raise humidity; apply insecticidal soap or horticultural/neem oil thoroughly to leaf undersides (avoiding sulfur or oils when temperatures exceed 85–90°F); release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
prevention_actions: Keep plants deeply watered during heat waves (drought-stressed leaves have higher soluble sugars/amino acids that fuel mite outbreaks); wet down dusty garden paths; never apply broad-spectrum pyrethroids or carbaryl for other pests.
recommended_observations: Scout Celery (undersides of leaves (starting on older lower/inner leaves and moving upward)) twice weekly during hot, dry mid-to-late summer weather (80–95°F (27–35°C)); inspect for fine yellow pinpoint leaf stippling to distinguish Spider Mites from Thrips (silver streaks with shiny black fecal dots, no silk webbing), Russet Mites (microscopic 4-legged wedge mites with greasy bronzing and no webbing), Ozone/Air Pollution Stipple, Drought Scorch.
severity_or_impact: High in hot dry summers (can defoliate tomatoes, beans, melons, eggplants, and strawberries within 2 weeks)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 80–95°F (27–35°C) and low relative humidity (<50% rh), drought stress, and dusty conditions.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Celery Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, peaches, celery, beans, tomatoes, and pomegranates
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed.

knowledge_text: Celery (Apium graveolens) Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs is a sap-feeding true bug pest caused by Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs). topic: Celery Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.
recommended_observations: Scout Celery (phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures) weekly during mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Aster Yellows from Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High on carrots, lettuce, and celery (infected roots and heads are bitter and inedible)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Celery, Lettuce, Spinach, Parsley, Coriander, Dill, Parsnip).

topic: Celery Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)
problem_name: Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg
causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits
growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Small water-soaked translucent spots around wounds, insect holes, sunscald patches, or hollow stems that rapidly expand within 24–72 hours into a wet, slimy, mushy, cream-to-tan liquified collapse of the fleshy parenchyma tissue (while the outer epidermis remains intact like a water-filled bag until broken), accompanied by an unmistakable, putrid, foul fishy/sulfurous stench (in brassicas, onions, and potatoes); in Potato Blackleg, an inky jet-black slimy decay rises from the decaying seed piece up the lower 4–8 inches of the green stem, yellowing and rolling upper leaves.
symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak
risk_factors: Insect feeding wounds (cabbageworms, onion/cabbage maggots, corn borers, slugs), harvesting bruising, washing vegetables in warm unchlorinated water, boron/calcium deficiency (hollow stem), and dome-less flat broccoli heads holding rainwater.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.
prevention_actions: Control insect pests (cabbageworms, root maggots, borers) that create entry wounds; select domed broccoli cultivars that shed rainwater; plant whole uncut certified seed potatoes or cure cut seed pieces at 55–60°F and 85% RH for 3–5 days before planting in warmed (>50°F) well-drained soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Celery (fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits) weekly during warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg from Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (destroys marketable cabbage/broccoli heads, peppers, and stored potatoes, carrots, and onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Potato, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy, Chinese cabbage, Lettuce).

topic: Celery Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.
recommended_observations: Scout Celery (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cercospora Leaf Spot from Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (ruins marketable leaves on Swiss chard and spinach and weakens beet, carrot, and pepper plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh) and warm summer rains or overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beet, Swiss chard, Spinach, Amaranth, Carrot, Celery, Parsley, Pepper).

topic: Celery Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) (Cucumovirus CMV)
problem_name: Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV)
causal_agent: Cucumovirus CMV (Cucumber mosaic virus)
affected_plant_parts: Young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through fruiting
season: Late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate
humidity_conditions: Weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal
visible_symptoms: On Celery (Apium graveolens): Prominent yellow-and-green mosaic mottling, vein clearing, downward leaf curling, rugose wrinkling, and severe stunting of young apical leaves (in tomato, leaflets often narrow into extreme 'shoestring' or 'rat-tail' threads; in spinach, called 'spinach blight' with bright yellow inward-curled inner leaves that die); cucurbit and pepper fruits are small, distorted, knobby/warty, and mottled with pale yellow-green and dark-green islands ('color break') with bitter flavor.
symptom_keywords: green and yellow mosaic leaves, warty bumpy mottled cucumbers, shoestring tomato leaves, stunted vine tips, spinach blight yellow heart
symptom_progression: Transmitted within seconds by probing winged aphids; newly emerging leaves 7–14 days later show mosaic mottling and rugosity, internodes rosette, and all subsequent fruits are bumpy and color-broken.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by warty, pale-and-dark-green mottled cucurbit fruits and multi-crop host range (>1,200 species); in tomato, CMV shoestringing is even more thread-like than ToMV and is accompanied by nearby aphid activity rather than tobacco/pruning spread.
similar_conditions: Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury
risk_factors: Abundant perennial weeds (pokeweed, milkweed, chickweed, white cockle, nightshade, bindweed) harboring CMV near the garden and migrating winged aphids.
favorable_conditions: Mild spring weather building aphid numbers on weeds followed by warm dry weather driving winged aphids into vegetable beds.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored non-persistently (stylet-borne) by >80 species of aphids (especially Green peach aphid Myzus persicae and Melon aphid Aphis gossypii); aphids acquire and transmit the virus in just 10–60 seconds of test probing (so insecticides cannot kill aphids fast enough to prevent transmission!).
management_actions: Immediately pull and bag CMV-infected plants so aphids cannot spread the virus down the row; control perennial weeds around the garden.
prevention_actions: Plant CMV-resistant cultivars (widely available in cucumber, zucchini/squash, spinach, pepper, and bean); lay UV-reflective silver mulch or floating row covers over young cucurbits and peppers to deter landing winged aphids; eradicate pokeweed and chickweed near beds.
recommended_observations: Scout Celery (young expanding leaves, shoot tips, flowers, and developing fruits) weekly during late spring through autumn when winged aphids migrate (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV) from Zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV), Watermelon Mosaic Virus (WMV), Papaya Ringspot Virus (PRSV-W), Herbicide Drift, Broad Mite injury.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stunting and deformed, warty, unmarketable fruit)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and weather favoring spring weed growth followed by dry-down that triggers winged aphid dispersal.
host_range: Documented on Celery (Apium graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cucumber, Squash, Zucchini, Pumpkin, Melon, Watermelon, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Celery White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation

distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.

problem_name: Armyworms (Beet, Yellowstriped, Fall, and Southern Armyworms)
causal_agent: Spodoptera exigua (Beet Armyworm), Spodoptera ornithogalli (Yellowstriped Armyworm), Spodoptera frugiperda (Fall Armyworm), and Spodoptera eridania (Southern Armyworm)
affected_plant_parts: Whorl leaves (Sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and fruiting
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Clusters of dozens of tiny Newly hatched caterpillars skeletonize the underside of leaves inside a delicate web ('windowpane' feeding where only the translucent upper epidermis remains intact); as smooth-skinned caterpillars grow to 1.25–1.5 inches, they disperse to chew large ragged holes in leaves, bore into cabbage/lettuce hearts and sweet corn whorls (leaving ragged 'shot-hole' rows packed with wet sawdust-like frass), or gouge shallow surface scars on tomato and pepper fruits. Beet Armyworm is olive-green with a prominent black spot on the thorax above the second pair of true legs; Yellowstriped Armyworm is velvety gray-black with two bright yellow-orange dorsal stripes and black triangular markings; Fall Armyworm has a prominent white inverted 'Y' suture on its dark head capsule and four black dots arranged in a square on the 8th abdominal segment.
symptom_keywords: fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves, windowpane skeletonized leaf patches by gregarious young larvae, white inverted Y on caterpillar head, black thoracic spot on olive-green worm, ragged frass-filled sweet corn whorl
symptom_progression: Female moths lay masses of 50–150 eggs covered in a fuzzy blanket of tan/white scales from her abdomen on leaf undersides; hatching larvae feed gregariously as a skeletonizing 'army' for 4–6 days before scattering across the plant.
distinguishing_features: Unlike solitary Corn Earworms or Loopers, Armyworms lay fuzzy scale-covered egg masses of 50–150 eggs, so young larvae feed in crowded groups creating translucent 'windowpane' patches on leaves; Fall Armyworm has the unmistakable white inverted 'Y' on its head.
similar_conditions: Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms
risk_factors: Late-summer/fall plantings of sweet corn, greens, brassicas, and tomatoes when southern moth migrations peak, and weedy pigweed/lambsquarters borders.
favorable_conditions: Warm late-summer and fall weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Migratory nocturnal moths fly northward every summer from overwintering zones in South Florida, South Texas, and tropical regions.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for fuzzy tan/white scale-covered egg masses and crush or clip them off before they hatch; spray Bacillus thuringiensis aizawai (Bt aizawai is substantially more effective against Spodoptera armyworms than Bt kurstaki!) or spinosad while caterpillars are small (<1/2 inch) and windowpaning.
prevention_actions: Keep beds free of pigweed (Amaranthus) and lambsquarters (preferred egg-laying hosts for Beet Armyworm); cover fall brassica and leafy green plantings with floating row covers.
recommended_observations: Scout Swiss chard (whorl leaves (sweet corn), foliage, crowns, and fruit surfaces) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for fuzzy tan hair-covered egg masses under leaves to distinguish Armyworms from Corn Earworm (lays single eggs, no fuzzy egg masses or windowpaning), Cabbage Looper (walks with an inchworm arch), Cutworms.
severity_or_impact: High in late summer and fall
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–92°F (24–33°C) and warm-to-hot late summer and autumn weather.
host_range: Documented on Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Sweet corn, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Sweet potato, Beet, Swiss chard).

topic: Swiss chard Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Swiss chard (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).
