topic: Swiss chard Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.
recommended_observations: Scout Swiss chard (undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins) twice weekly during late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations) (70–90°F (21–32°C)); inspect for wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying to distinguish Leafhoppers from Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus.
severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)

topic: Swiss chard Leafminers Management
problem_name: Leafminers (Vegetable, Serpentine, and Spinach/Beet Leafminers)
causal_agent: Liriomyza sativae (Vegetable Leafminer), Liriomyza trifolii (American Serpentine Leafminer), and Pegomya hyoscyami (Spinach / Beet Leafminer)
affected_plant_parts: Interior mesophyll tissue between the upper and lower leaf epidermis
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative harvest
season: Spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Mild-to-warm weather
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Two distinct leaf-mining patterns eaten between the intact upper and lower skins of the leaf by legless fly maggots: (1) Serpentine Leafminers (Liriomyza spp. on Tomato, Beans, Cucurbits, Lettuce, Celery, Onion): narrow, winding, white-to-translucent snake-like trails ('serpentine mines') with a thin central trail of black frass that gradually widen as the tiny (2 mm) bright-yellow maggot grows inside; (2) Spinach/Beet Leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami on Spinach, Swiss Chard, Beet, Amaranth): small serpentine tracks quickly expand into large, pale tan-to-white, translucent blister-like blotches ('blotch mines') across the leaf blade containing 1–5 creamy-white maggots (6–8 mm) and dark frass pellets visible when held up to the light; underside of beet/chard/spinach leaves shows neat rows of 3–8 tiny, chalk-white cylindrical eggs glued side-by-side.
symptom_keywords: winding white snake-like serpentine trails in leaves, large pale papery blotch blisters in spinach and Swiss chard leaves, rows of tiny chalk-white eggs under beet and chard leaves, tiny yellow or white maggot inside leaf skin
symptom_progression: Adult Liriomyza flies (tiny 2 mm black-and-yellow flies) puncture leaves to feed and insert single eggs inside the leaf, whereas gray Pegomya flies glue neat rows of 3–8 white oblong eggs on the underside of spinach/chard/beet leaves; maggots mine inside the leaf for 1–2 weeks before dropping to the soil to pupate.
distinguishing_features: Hold the leaf up to the sun: a Leafminer blotch or serpentine trail is hollow between the two intact papery skins of the leaf and contains a visible yellow or white maggot and dark frass specs inside (unlike Fungal Leaf Spots or Downy Mildew, where the tissue is solid rather than a hollow two-ply blister).

risk_factors: Broad-spectrum insecticide sprays (pyrethroids, carbamates, organophosphates) which kill the tiny native parasitic wasps (Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica) that normally parasitize 80–95% of Liriomyza leafminers, plus lambsquarters weeds (primary wild host of Spinach/Beet Leafminer).
favorable_conditions: Spring and early summer for Spinach/Beet Leafminer; warm summer weather for Serpentine Leafminers.
transmission_or_spread: Adult flies emerge from puparia in soil and fly to susceptible crops or ride on greenhouse transplants.
management_actions: On Spinach, Swiss Chard, and Beets: flip leaves twice weekly to rub off the neat rows of chalk-white eggs on the underside BEFORE they hatch, and pinch/clip off any mined blotch leaves immediately (note: contact sprays like soapcannot reach maggots hidden inside the leaf epidermis, though spinosad and azadirachtin/neem have translaminar activity that penetrates into mines!); on Tomatoes, Beans, and Cucurbits, simply avoid broad-spectrum sprays so native Diglyphus parasitic wasps naturally suppress serpentine mines.

topic: Swiss chard Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.

topic: Swiss chard Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, peaches, celery, beans, tomatoes, and pomegranates
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed.
host_range: Documented on Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Amaranthaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Peach, Plum, Apple, Pear, Beans).

topic: Swiss chard Cercospora Leaf Spot (Cercospora beticola)
problem_name: Cercospora Leaf Spot
causal_agent: Cercospora beticola (Beet/Chard/Spinach); Cercospora carotae (Carrot); Cercospora apii (Celery); Cercospora capsici ('Frogeye' on Pepper); Cercospora melongenae (Eggplant); Cercospora citrullina (Cucurbits); Cercospora arachidicola / kikuchii / sojina (Legumes)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative rosette/canopy growth through harvest
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH) and warm summer rains or overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves.
symptom_keywords: frogeye leaf spots, ash-gray center with reddish-purple border, circular tan spots with maroon rim, outer leaf scorching, petiole lesions
symptom_progression: Conidia splash from debris or weeds onto outer leaves; circular gray-centered spots expand and merge during warm wet spells, blighting outer leaves and weakened carrot/celery petioles.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches).
similar_conditions: Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot
risk_factors: Planting beet, Swiss chard, and spinach successively in the same bed, warm rainy weather, overhead irrigation, and crowded rows.
favorable_conditions: Warm-to-hot temperatures (75–90°F) with high humidity and night/morning leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as stromata in infected crop residue, weed hosts (lambsquarters, pigweed), and on seed; conidia splash by rain and wind.
management_actions: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants.
prevention_actions: Practice a 3-year crop rotation separating Chenopodioideae/Amaranthaceae (beet, chard, spinach, amaranth) and Apiaceae (carrot, celery, parsley); space rows for airflow; use disease-free seed and tolerant beet/chard cultivars.
recommended_observations: Scout Swiss chard (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer weather (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cercospora Leaf Spot from Alternaria Leaf Spot, Septoria Leaf Spot, Bacterial Leaf Spot, Ramularia Leaf Spot, Phoma Leaf Spot.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (ruins marketable leaves on Swiss chard and spinach and weakens beet, carrot, and pepper plants)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh) and warm summer rains or overhead watering.

Symptoms on swiss chard (leaves and petioles (and calyces/fruit stems in pepper and pomegranate)): Numerous small (1/8 to 1/4 inch / 2–5 mm), circular spots with characteristic pale ash-gray to tan centers and distinct reddish-purple, dark-brown, or maroon borders ('frogeye' appearance, especially conspicuous on beet, Swiss chard, spinach, and pepper leaves); under humid conditions, tiny dark clusters of conidiophores make the gray center look finely peppered; as spots multiply and coalesce, older outer leaves turn yellow, scorch brown, and collapse while the plant pushes new central leaves. Distinguishing features: Distinguished by the uniform circular 'frogeye' lesions with pale ash-gray centers and sharply defined reddish-purple or dark-brown rims (on Carrots, Cercospora carotae attacks younger faster-growing leaves earlier in summer with circular tan-centered spots, whereas Alternaria dauci attacks older leaves with dark irregular blotches). Management and prevention: Promptly harvest or clip and remove spotted outer leaves on Swiss chard and beets; use drip irrigation; apply copper or Bacillus biofungicides if heavy spotting threatens young plants. topic: Brussels sprouts Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.

severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Brussels sprouts Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Brussels sprouts (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Brussels sprouts Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).
recommended_observations: Scout Brussels sprouts (cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of potato, sweetpotato, and striped flea beetles)) twice weekly during spring through mid-summer (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves to distinguish Flea Beetles from Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass).
severity_or_impact: High on seedlings and young eggplant, radish, bok choy, arugula, turnip, and mustard greens
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny, dry spring weather.
host_range: Documented on Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Eggplant, Potato, Tomato, Pepper, Radish, Turnip, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Brussels sprouts Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).

causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.

favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.

topic: Brussels sprouts Black Rot of Crucifers (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris)
problem_name: Black Rot of Crucifers
causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
affected_plant_parts: Leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots
growth_stage: Seedling stage through heading and root maturity
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Diagnostic V-shaped bright yellow (chlorotic) blotches initiating at the leaf margins (with the point of the 'V' directed inward toward the midrib) that turn tan-brown and papery dry; holding the V-shaped lesion up to the light reveals a network of jet-blackened veins inside the yellow/tan wedge; slicing the petiole or main stem crosswise shows a black-brown vascular ring; infected cabbage and cauliflower heads often develop secondary foul-smelling bacterial soft rot.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesions on leaf margin, blackened veins inside yellow wedge, black vascular ring in stem, marginal leaf blight
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter water pores (hydathodes) along the leaf edges inside morning guttation droplets, moving inward down the xylem veins to form V-shaped wedges and eventually invading the main stem vascular system.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Alternaria Leaf Spot and Downy Mildew by the classic V-shaped yellow marginal wedges with jet-black veins inside the lesion (Verticillium Wilt also causes V-shaped marginal yellowing, but lacks the crisp jet-black vein network inside the leaf blade and occurs in cooler weather).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins)
risk_factors: Saved or untreated brassica seed, infected transplants, cruciferous weeds, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and working in wet beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–86°F) with heavy morning dew/guttation and splashing rain.
transmission_or_spread: Primarily seed-borne (even 1 infected seed in 10,000 can cause an epidemic in transplant trays); survives up to 2 years in unrotted brassica stalks and spreads by splashing water and equipment.
management_actions: Remove infected plants early; never work in brassica beds when leaves are wet with morning dew or guttation droplets; use drip irrigation; copper sprays offer only limited suppression once established.
prevention_actions: Plant certified pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed (122°F/50°C for 25 minutes for cabbage/broccoli/brussels sprouts; 15 minutes for cauliflower/kale/turnip/bok choy) and black-rot-tolerant cultivars; rotate out of all Brassicaceae for 3 years; chop and bury brassica stalks immediately after harvest so they decompose.
recommended_observations: Scout Brussels sprouts (leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather (77–86°F (25–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Rot of Crucifers from Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins).
severity_or_impact: High (most destructive bacterial disease of brassicas worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–86°F (25–30°C) and high humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Brussels sprouts Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.
recommended_observations: Scout Brussels sprouts (taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)) weekly during warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils (68–77°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Clubroot from Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (persists in soil for up to 20 years and prevents marketable head or root formation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (ph <6.5).
host_range: Documented on Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Brussels sprouts White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum)
problem_name: White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot)
causal_agent: Sclerotinia sclerotiorum (and Sclerotinia minor)
affected_plant_parts: Main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots
growth_stage: Flowering, canopy closure, and pod/head maturation
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours)
visible_symptoms: On Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera): Water-soaked pale-brown lesions at stem nodes, branch axils (where spent flower petals lodge), or the crown base (in lettuce/cabbage/carrot) that bleached to bone-white or tan papery dry rot ('timber rot'); lesions quickly become covered in a thick, fluffy, pure cottony-white mycelial mat in which large (1/8 to 1/2 inch), hard, coal-black irregular resting bodies (sclerotia, resembling rat droppings) form both on the surface and inside the hollow stem pith.
symptom_keywords: cottony pure white mold, hard black sclerotia inside stem, bleached white woody stem, lettuce drop, watery soft pod rot
symptom_progression: Airborne ascospores colonize senescing flower petals first, using the petal as an energy base to invade healthy stems and pods, girdling stems so upper foliage wilts and dies.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the fluffy pure-white cottony mycelium and large (3–10 mm) irregular coal-black sclerotia inside hollowed-out bleached stems or under rotted crowns (unlike Southern Blight, which occurs in hot 85–95°F weather and forms tiny 1–2 mm round tan-brown mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak
risk_factors: Dense, lush, over-fertilized canopies that trap moisture, narrow row spacing, overhead irrigation during bloom, and planting after susceptible broadleaf crops.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-mild temperatures (60–75°F) with overcast skies and continuous canopy wetness during flowering.
transmission_or_spread: Hard black sclerotia survive in soil for 5–8+ years; in cool moist weather, sclerotia in the top 2 inches of soil germinate to form tiny tan cup-shaped mushrooms (apothecia) that eject wind-borne ascospores onto blossoms.
management_actions: Immediately rogue and bag infected plants before black sclerotia drop to the soil; prune lower leaves and widen plant spacing to allow sunlight and breeze to dry the lower canopy and soil surface.
prevention_actions: Rotate with non-host grasses or sweet corn for 4–5 years; use drip irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen that creates lodging and dense canopies; biological control with Coniothyrium minitans degrades sclerotia in soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Brussels sprouts (main stems, branch crotches, petioles, crowns (lettuce drop), pods, and storage roots) weekly during cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Mold (Sclerotinia Stem & Timber Rot) from Southern Blight (Agroathelia rolfsii), Gray Mold (Botrytis cinerea - gray dusty spores), Pythium Cottony Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (causes severe stem girdling in beans/tomatoes, head drop in lettuce/cabbage, and storage rot in carrots)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and continuous high canopy humidity, fog, mist, or prolonged wetness (>16–48 hours).
host_range: Documented on Brussels sprouts (Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Soybean, Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant).

topic: Collards Aphids Management
problem_name: Aphids (Green Peach, Melon, Potato, Pea, Bean, and Cabbage Aphids)
causal_agent: Myzus persicae (Green Peach Aphid), Aphis gossypii (Melon/Cotton Aphid), Macrosiphum euphorbiae (Potato Aphid), Acyrthosiphon pisum (Pea Aphid), Aphis fabae (Black Bean Aphid), and Brevicoryne brassicae (Cabbage Aphid)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems
growth_stage: Seedling through vegetative growth and flowering
season: Spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer)
humidity_conditions: Moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants)
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Dense colonies of small (1–3 mm), soft-bodied, pear-shaped insects (green, yellow, pink, black, or waxy gray depending on species) clustered on the undersides of leaves and tender growing tips, recognizable by the pair of tailpipe-like cornicles projecting from the rear abdomen; feeding causes downward leaf curling, puckering, distortion of shoot tips, yellowing, and stunting, accompanied by shiny sticky 'honeydew' excrement on lower leaves that becomes coated in black sooty mold and tiny white cast skins (exuviae); ants frequently patrol stems to tend aphids for honeydew.
symptom_keywords: soft pear-shaped insects under leaves, curled puckered shoot tips, sticky shiny honeydew, black sooty mold, white cast skins, ants tending stems
symptom_progression: Winged females (alates) land on succulent new shoots and give live birth parthenogenetically to nymphs that mature in 7–10 days, building dense colonies and transmitting non-persistent plant viruses within seconds of probing.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the pear-shaped soft bodies with two rear cornicles ('tailpipes'), clusters of white shed exoskeletons stuck in sticky honeydew on leaf undersides, and downward-cupped leaves that remain green and soft (unlike viral mosaic or herbicide drift where no insects/cast skins are present).
similar_conditions: Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves)
risk_factors: Over-fertilization with high soluble nitrogen (which creates lush amino-acid-rich sap that accelerates aphid reproduction), broad-spectrum pyrethroid/carbamate insecticide sprays that kill ladybugs and parasitic wasps, ant tending, and greenhouse/indoors transplant carryover.
favorable_conditions: Mild temperatures (65–80°F) without heavy rainstorms, combined with lush nitrogen-rich shoot growth.
transmission_or_spread: Winged alate aphids disperse on wind currents from overwintering weeds, woody hosts (Prunus, Euonymus), or neighboring crops; ants also move aphids between plants.
management_actions: Blast colonies off sturdy plants with a sharp morning stream of water; conserve natural enemies (lady beetles, lacewing larvae, syrphid fly maggots, and Aphidius/Diaeretiella braconid wasps that turn aphids into tan papery 'mummies'); spray potassium salts of fatty acids (insecticidal soap) or horticultural/neem oil directly onto leaf undersides.
prevention_actions: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer; use reflective silver mulch to repel winged aphids from young cucurbits, tomatoes, and peppers; plant insectary flowers (sweet alyssum, dill, coriander, yarrow) to attract hoverflies and lacewings; control honeydew-farming ants.
recommended_observations: Scout Collards (undersides of young leaves, succulent shoot tips, flower buds, and stems) twice weekly during spring through autumn (peaking in mild spring and early summer) (60–82°F (15–28°C)); inspect for soft pear-shaped insects under leaves to distinguish Aphids from Whiteflies (tiny white moth-like insects that flutter up when disturbed), Spider Mites (fine webbing and bronze stippling), Peach Leaf Curl (thick red fleshy leaves).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (direct stunting plus primary vector of CMV, PVY, PRSV, ZYMV, WMV, and BCMV)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–82°F (15–28°C) and moderate humidity and dry weather (heavy driving rain washes aphids off plants).
host_range: Documented on Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Potato, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin).

topic: Collards Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Collards (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Collards Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Collards (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Collards Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.

severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Collards Stink Bugs Management
problem_name: Stink Bugs (Brown Marmorated, Southern Green, Green, and Harlequin Bugs)
causal_agent: Halyomorpha halys (Brown Marmorated Stink Bug - BMSB), Nezara viridula (Southern Green Stink Bug), Chinavia hilaris (Green Stink Bug), and Murgantia histrionica (Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
affected_plant_parts: Developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for Harlequin Bug on Brassicas)
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/pod/nut development through harvest
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Shield-shaped true bugs (1/2 to 5/8 inch long) that pierce fruits, pods, and seeds with needle-like stylets and inject digestive enzymes: on Tomato, Pepper, & Okra, feeding leaves pinpoint punctures surrounded by pale yellow-to-white blotches ('cloudy spot') on the skin backed underneath by dry, white, spongy/corky flesh; on Peach, Apple, & Pear, feeding causes sunken dimples ('catfacing') with corky brown flesh underneath; on Beans, Cowpeas, & Soybeans, feeding shrivels seeds and prevents pod drop ('stay-green'); on Brassicas (Kale, Collards, Cabbage, Broccoli), the striking black-and-bright-orange/red Harlequin Bug lays clusters of 12 white-and-black striped barrel-shaped eggs ('miniature beer kegs') and sucks sap from leaves, leaving white-and-yellow fan-shaped blotches that turn brown and wither.
symptom_keywords: shield-shaped green or brown bug, white bands on antennae of brown stink bug, cloudy yellow-white spots on ripe tomato and pepper skin, white spongy corky tissue under fruit skin, catfaced dimpled peaches and apples, black-and-orange harlequin bug with striped barrel eggs on kale
symptom_progression: Overwintered adults emerge in spring and lay tight clusters of 12–30 barrel-shaped eggs on leaf undersides; 5 nymphal instars and adults feed heavily on high-protein seeds, pods, and ripening fruits from July through September.
distinguishing_features: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug is identified by alternating light-and-dark bands on its antennae and along the flared rear edge of its abdomen (distinguishing it from beneficial predatory Rough Stink Bugs and Spined Soldier Bugs, which have pointed shoulder spines or thick piercing beaks); Harlequin Bug is unmistakable with its glossy black-and-fiery-orange shield and two-row clusters of black-and-white striped barrel eggs. Note: cloudy white spongy spots under tomato/pepper skin are Stink Bug feeding, NOT a fungal disease!
similar_conditions: Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface)
risk_factors: Weedy borders (especially mustard weeds for Harlequin Bug, and tree-of-heaven Ailanthus, paulownia, pokeweed, and wild blackberry for BMSB), wooded edges, and unnetted fruiting beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer and early autumn weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying adults move from wild border trees, weeds, and maturing field crops directly onto ripening garden fruits and pods.
management_actions: Handpick adults, nymphs, and barrel-shaped egg clusters in the cool early morning by knocking them into a bucket of soapy water; cover high-value tomato, pepper, bean, and brassica beds with fine insect netting; vacuum Harlequin bugs off kale/collards.
prevention_actions: Plant a perimeter trap crop of early-maturing cowpeas/soybeans, sweet corn, or sunflowers (for green/brown stink bugs) or 'Cleome' spider flower / mustard greens (for Harlequin Bug) to intercept immigrating adults before they reach main crops; mow weedy borders BEFORE weeds go to seed.
recommended_observations: Scout Collards (developing fruits, pods, kernels/nuts, and leaves (for harlequin bug on brassicas)) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (70–92°F (21–33°C)); inspect for shield-shaped green or brown bug to distinguish Stink Bugs from Spined Soldier Bug (beneficial predator with sharp shoulder spines), Blossom-End Rot, Calcium Bitter Pit on Apple (concentrated at blossom end rather than upper/outer fruit surface).
severity_or_impact: High (causes widespread 'cloudy spot' on tomatoes/peppers, catfacing on peaches/apples, shriveled beans/pecans, and severe scorching of kale/collards)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–92°F (21–33°C) and warm, sunny summer weather.

knowledge_subtype: Soil Texture, pH, Drainage & Bed Preparation
topic: Collards Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Fertile, moist, well-drained loam or sandy loam (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage)
management_actions: Prepare a fertile, moist, well-drained loam or sandy loam adjusted to pH 6.0–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Collards to verify soil pH (6.0–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Prefers fertile, moist, well-drained loam or sandy loam with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Collards Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Collards (older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) from Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes unmarketable brown rot on broccoli/cauliflower heads and weakens carrot/onion tops)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew.
host_range: Documented on Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).
