topic: Collards Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.
recommended_observations: Scout Collards (taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)) weekly during warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils (68–77°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Clubroot from Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (persists in soil for up to 20 years and prevents marketable head or root formation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (ph <6.5).
host_range: Documented on Collards (Brassica oleracea var. viridis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) Botanical Identification and Growth Habit
season: Cool season (plant in spring or, ideally, late summer/early fall as shortening days and cooling temperatures prevent premature bolting)
sunlight_requirement: Full sun to partial shade (5–8 hours daily)
normal_appearance: Cool-season fast-maturing Asian biennial leafy vegetable grown as an annual (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis). Compact upright cluster of thick, succulent white or pale-green spoon-shaped petioles topped by dark green rounded leaf blades (6–14 inches tall). Growth form: Erect (growth rate: Rapid). Healthy bok choy forms a neat, bulbous-based upright rosette of smooth, glossy, dark green rounded-obovate leaf blades with entire margins supported by wide, thick, crisp, spoon-shaped ivory-white ('pak choi') or jade-green ('Shanghai bok choy') petioles.
recommended_observations: Verify species identity (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, family Brassicaceae), growth habit (Compact upright cluster of thick, succulent white or pale-green spoon-shaped petioles topped by dark green rounded leaf blades (6–14 inches tall)), and expected seasonal adaptation before garden layout planning.
geographic_or_climate_notes: Lifecycle: Cool-season fast-maturing Asian biennial leafy vegetable grown as an annual (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis). Optimal growth 55–70°F (13–21°C); very sensitive to vernalization—exposure of seedlings to <50°F for 1–2 weeks followed by lengthening spring days triggers rapid bolting.
knowledge_text: Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) is a leafy green in the Brassicaceae family grown as a cool-season fast-maturing asian biennial leafy vegetable grown as an annual (brassica rapa subsp. chinensis). Growth form: Erect (growth rate: Rapid). topic: Bok choy Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.
prevention_actions: Cover cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and bok choy beds immediately after planting with lightweight floating row covers or fine insect netting (since brassicas are harvested for leaves/heads/roots and require NO insect pollination, netting can stay on until harvest and blocks 100% of butterflies and moths!); conserve Cotesia rubecula and Diadegma insulare parasitic wasps.
recommended_observations: Scout Bok choy (outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts) twice weekly during spring through late autumn (55–85°F (13–29°C)); inspect for ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves to distinguish Cabbageworms from Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails).
severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Bok choy Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).
recommended_observations: Scout Bok choy (cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of potato, sweetpotato, and striped flea beetles)) twice weekly during spring through mid-summer (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves to distinguish Flea Beetles from Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass).
severity_or_impact: High on seedlings and young eggplant, radish, bok choy, arugula, turnip, and mustard greens
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–88°F (15–31°C) and warm, sunny, dry spring weather.
host_range: Documented on Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Eggplant, Potato, Tomato, Pepper, Radish, Turnip, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Bok choy Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Bok choy (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.

topic: Bok choy Slugs and Garden Snails Management
problem_name: Slugs and Garden Snails
causal_agent: Deroceras reticulatum (Gray Field Slug), Arion spp., and Cornu aspersum (Brown Garden Snail)
affected_plant_parts: Seedlings, low-hanging outer leaves, inner cabbage/lettuce heads, ripe strawberries, and low-hanging tomatoes
growth_stage: Seedling emergence through leafy and fruit harvest
season: Cool, wet spring and autumn weather and rainy summer nights
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain, heavy night dew, and moist mulched beds
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Large, ragged, irregular holes with smooth rasped edges chewed in the center and margins of leaves (unlike caterpillars and beetles, which can only occur when temperature permits, slugs feed even at 40–50°F in cool wet spring weather!), completely severed young bean, lettuce, and brassica seedlings, and deep, clean-walled cavities rasped into ripening strawberries and low-hanging tomatoes; the unmistakable calling card left on damaged leaves, fruits, and surrounding soil is a glistening, iridescent, silvery-white dried mucus trail ('slime trail').
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in leaves and ripe strawberries, glistening silvery-white dried slime trails on leaves and soil, hollowed cavities in ripe strawberries and low tomatoes, nocturnal soft-bodied gray or tan slugs under boards and mulch
symptom_progression: Hermaphroditic slugs and snails lay clusters of 20–50 translucent, pearl-like spherical eggs under damp mulch, stones, and soil clods; they hide in cool damp shelters by day and glide out on a ribbon of mucus at night or on rainy days to rasp plant tissue with their toothed radula.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably distinguished from Caterpillar, Earwig, or Beetle chewing by the glistening silvery dried slime trails left across the leaf surface and soil, plus night inspection with a flashlight.
similar_conditions: Cutworms, Cabbageworms (leave dark-green frass pellets rather than silvery slime trails), Earwigs, Birds (peck V-shaped holes in strawberries during daytime)
risk_factors: Thick wet organic mulch (straw, leaves, woodchips) piled right against young seedlings in wet spring weather, overhead evening watering (which keeps soil damp all night), weedy bed edges, and wooden raised-bed corners.
favorable_conditions: Cool, cloudy, rainy nights and mornings (50–70°F).
transmission_or_spread: Crawl locally from damp mulched borders, compost piles, and transported nursery pots.
management_actions: Switch strictly to morning watering so the soil surface is dry by nightfall; scatter OMRI-listed Iron Phosphate (ferric phosphate) bait pellets lightly around beds in the evening after rain (Iron Phosphate causes slugs to immediately stop feeding and Crawl underground to die, and is safe around pets, birds, and wildlife—avoid toxic metaldehyde baits!); sink shallow saucers or yogurt cups rim-level into the soil filled with stale beer or a yeast-sugar-water mixture to drown slugs overnight; handpick at night with a headlamp.
prevention_actions: Wait to apply thick straw mulch until late spring after seedlings are sturdy and soils warm up; wrap a 2-to-3-inch-wide strip of copper foil/mesh tape around the top rim of raised beds or pots (copper reacts with slug mucus to deliver a mild deterrent electric shock); encourage ground beetles, toads, and garter snakes.

topic: Bok choy Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)
problem_name: Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot)
causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.
symptom_keywords: concentric target leaf spots, dark sooty spore coating, brown head rot on broccoli and cauliflower, purple blotch on onion leaves, scorched carrot tops
symptom_progression: Spores splash or blow onto older lower leaves first, forming target-ringed spots covered in dark olive-black velvety conidia in humid weather, then spreading to heads, curds, or leaf collars.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).
similar_conditions: Black Rot (V-shaped marginal wedges), Downy Mildew, Cercospora Leaf Blight (circular tan spots on young carrot leaves vs dark irregular spots on older leaves in Alternaria)
risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.

topic: Bok choy Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg (Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum)
problem_name: Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg
causal_agent: Pectobacterium carotovorum, Pectobacterium atrosepticum (Potato Blackleg), and Dickeya dianthicola
affected_plant_parts: Fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits
growth_stage: Late maturity, harvest, and post-harvest storage (or spring emergence for Potato Blackleg)
season: Warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage
humidity_conditions: Free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Small water-soaked translucent spots around wounds, insect holes, sunscald patches, or hollow stems that rapidly expand within 24–72 hours into a wet, slimy, mushy, cream-to-tan liquified collapse of the fleshy parenchyma tissue (while the outer epidermis remains intact like a water-filled bag until broken), accompanied by an unmistakable, putrid, foul fishy/sulfurous stench (in brassicas, onions, and potatoes); in Potato Blackleg, an inky jet-black slimy decay rises from the decaying seed piece up the lower 4–8 inches of the green stem, yellowing and rolling upper leaves.
symptom_keywords: wet slimy mushy tissue collapse, foul putrid fishy odor, inky jet-black lower potato stem, water-soaked broccoli head rot, slimy rotted core
symptom_progression: Pectolytic enzymes secreted by bacteria dissolve the calcium pectate middle lamella cementing plant cells together, turning crisp heads, roots, or tubers into foul-smelling liquid mush within 2–3 days in warm wet conditions.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rapid conversion of firm plant tissue into a wet, slimy, cream-to-black liquid mush accompanied by a foul, putrid odor (unlike fungal rots which usually remain firmer or covered in visible cottony/powdery mold).
similar_conditions: Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak
risk_factors: Insect feeding wounds (cabbageworms, onion/cabbage maggots, corn borers, slugs), harvesting bruising, washing vegetables in warm unchlorinated water, boron/calcium deficiency (hollow stem), and dome-less flat broccoli heads holding rainwater.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–90°F) with a film of free water over a wound or lenticel.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous in soil, surface water, plant debris, and on seed tubers; spread by splashing rain, cutting knives, washing water, and root-feeding maggot flies.
management_actions: Harvest vegetables during cool dry weather and handle gently to prevent bruising; never wash storage crops (potatoes, onions, garlic, winter squash, cabbage) before storing; immediately chill harvested leafy/crucifer crops to 32–40°F.
prevention_actions: Control insect pests (cabbageworms, root maggots, borers) that create entry wounds; select domed broccoli cultivars that shed rainwater; plant whole uncut certified seed potatoes or cure cut seed pieces at 55–60°F and 85% RH for 3–5 days before planting in warmed (>50°F) well-drained soil.
recommended_observations: Scout Bok choy (fleshy heads, curds, crowns, stems, storage roots, bulbs, tubers, and fruits) weekly during warm, wet weather and high-temperature poorly ventilated storage (75–90°F (24–32°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Soft Rot and Blackleg from Sclerotinia White Mold (snow-white cottony mold with hard black sclerotia and no foul odor), Botrytis Gray Mold, Pythium Leak.
severity_or_impact: High (destroys marketable cabbage/broccoli heads, peppers, and stored potatoes, carrots, and onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and free water films on wounded tissues, waterlogged soils, or wet harvest conditions.
host_range: Documented on Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Potato, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Bok choy, Chinese cabbage, Lettuce).

topic: Bok choy Black Rot of Crucifers (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris)
problem_name: Black Rot of Crucifers
causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
affected_plant_parts: Leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots
growth_stage: Seedling stage through heading and root maturity
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Diagnostic V-shaped bright yellow (chlorotic) blotches initiating at the leaf margins (with the point of the 'V' directed inward toward the midrib) that turn tan-brown and papery dry; holding the V-shaped lesion up to the light reveals a network of jet-blackened veins inside the yellow/tan wedge; slicing the petiole or main stem crosswise shows a black-brown vascular ring; infected cabbage and cauliflower heads often develop secondary foul-smelling bacterial soft rot.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesions on leaf margin, blackened veins inside yellow wedge, black vascular ring in stem, marginal leaf blight
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter water pores (hydathodes) along the leaf edges inside morning guttation droplets, moving inward down the xylem veins to form V-shaped wedges and eventually invading the main stem vascular system.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Alternaria Leaf Spot and Downy Mildew by the classic V-shaped yellow marginal wedges with jet-black veins inside the lesion (Verticillium Wilt also causes V-shaped marginal yellowing, but lacks the crisp jet-black vein network inside the leaf blade and occurs in cooler weather).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins)
risk_factors: Saved or untreated brassica seed, infected transplants, cruciferous weeds, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and working in wet beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–86°F) with heavy morning dew/guttation and splashing rain.
transmission_or_spread: Primarily seed-borne (even 1 infected seed in 10,000 can cause an epidemic in transplant trays); survives up to 2 years in unrotted brassica stalks and spreads by splashing water and equipment.
management_actions: Remove infected plants early; never work in brassica beds when leaves are wet with morning dew or guttation droplets; use drip irrigation; copper sprays offer only limited suppression once established.
prevention_actions: Plant certified pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed (122°F/50°C for 25 minutes for cabbage/broccoli/brussels sprouts; 15 minutes for cauliflower/kale/turnip/bok choy) and black-rot-tolerant cultivars; rotate out of all Brassicaceae for 3 years; chop and bury brassica stalks immediately after harvest so they decompose.

severity_or_impact: High (most destructive bacterial disease of brassicas worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–86°F (25–30°C) and high humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Bok choy Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.
recommended_observations: Scout Bok choy (taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)) weekly during warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils (68–77°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Clubroot from Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (persists in soil for up to 20 years and prevents marketable head or root formation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (ph <6.5).
host_range: Documented on Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

growth_stage: Summer heat (>85–90°F)

humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.

topic: Bok choy (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) Calcium (Ca) Deficiency (Heart Leaf Tipburn): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Calcium (Ca) Deficiency (Heart Leaf Tipburn)
affected_plant_parts: Youngest inner heart leaves and tender white/green petioles
growth_stage: Rapid mid-to-late rosette growth
season: Cool season (plant in spring or, ideally, late summer/early fall as shortening days and cooling temperatures prevent premature bolting)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 55–70°F (13–21°C); very sensitive to vernalization—exposure of seedlings to <50°F for 1–2 weeks followed by lengthening spring days triggers rapid bolting
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Margins and tips of the tender young central heart leaves turn water-soaked, then dry into dark brown-to-black papery ribbons while the leaf blade puckers because the dead margin cannot expand with the rest of the leaf.
symptom_keywords: bok choy, calcium (ca) deficiency, strictly immobile in phloem (transported exclusively upward via xylem transpiration stream), youngest inner heart leaves and tender white/green petioles, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Youngest expanding upper leaves, enclosed heart leaves, apical meristems, root tips, and low-transpiring developing fruits or storage tissues. Rapidly progresses during warm days with high humidity or uneven watering in rich soils.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Strictly immobile in phloem (transported exclusively upward via xylem transpiration stream). Blackened crinkled margins strictly on the youngest inner heart leaves while outer leaves remain spotless.
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Bok choy.
risk_factors: Fluctuating soil moisture (drought alternating with heavy watering), high relative humidity or enclosed leaf morphology suppressing xylem transpiration into inner leaves/fruits, acidic unlimed soils (pH < 5.5), high soil salinity, or excess ammonium (NH4+), potassium (K+), or magnesium (Mg2+) competing for root uptake.
favorable_conditions: Fluctuating soil moisture (drought alternating with heavy watering), high relative humidity or enclosed leaf morphology suppressing xylem transpiration into inner leaves/fruits, acidic unlimed soils (pH < 5.5), high soil salinity, or excess ammonium (NH4+), potassium (K+), or magnesium (Mg2+) competing for root uptake.
management_actions: Regulate soil moisture immediately with consistent irrigation and organic mulch; apply foliar calcium sprays (calcium chloride or calcium nitrate at 3–5 lb/100 gal or labeled home-garden rate) directly onto young expanding leaves and developing fruit clusters, and side-dress with calcium nitrate or gypsum.
prevention_actions: Lime acidic soils to pH 6.2–6.8 using calcitic limestone or apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) where pH is already optimal, use nitrate-N rather than ammonium-N fertilizers, avoid pruning feeder roots during cultivation, and maintain steady soil moisture.
recommended_observations: Inspect whether symptoms initiate on older lower foliage vs. youngest upper leaves/meristems on Bok choy, verify soil pH (optimal for Bok choy: 6.0–7.0) and soil moisture, and confirm with a soil or plant tissue test.
severity_or_impact: Destroys visual appeal and invites Pectobacterium bacterial soft rot into the crown.

prevention_actions: Select slow-bolt / heat-tolerant cultivars, time plantings for the correct photoperiod and temperature window, avoid chilling young biennial transplants below 50°F for extended periods, and prevent drought or root-bound stress.

topic: Kohlrabi Cabbageworms Management
problem_name: Cabbageworms (Imported Cabbageworm, Cabbage Looper, and Diamondback Moth)
causal_agent: Pieris rapae (Imported Cabbageworm), Trichoplusia ni (Cabbage Looper), and Plutella xylostella (Diamondback Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Outer wrapper leaves, inner heads, broccoli/cauliflower curds, and growing hearts
growth_stage: Seedling through heading and harvest
season: Spring through late autumn
humidity_conditions: All humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall
visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): Ragged circular-to-irregular holes chewed through brassica leaves and heads, accompanied by abundant wet dark-green pellets of caterpillar frass accumulating in leaf axils and staining cauliflower/broccoli curds; THREE distinct caterpillar species frequently co-occur: (1) Imported Cabbageworm: velvety, sluggish, matte-green caterpillar (1.25 inches) with a faint yellow stripe down the back that blends perfectly with leaf veins, produced by the familiar daytime white butterfly with 1–2 black wing spots; (2) Cabbage Looper: smooth pale-green caterpillar (1.5 inches) with thin white side stripes and only 3 pairs of rear prolegs, causing it to arch its back into a loop ('inchworm') as it walks; (3) Diamondback Moth larva: small (1/3 inch), spindle-shaped pale-green caterpillar tapered at both ends that wriggles violently backward and drops on a silk thread when touched, chewing small 'windowpane' holes.
symptom_keywords: ragged holes in cabbage and kale leaves, velvety green caterpillar, looping inchworm green caterpillar, small wriggling spindle-shaped larva, wet dark-green frass pellets in broccoli head, white butterflies fluttering in daytime
symptom_progression: Day-flying white Pieris butterflies lay single bullet-shaped yellow eggs standing upright on leaf undersides (while nocturnal Looper and Diamondback moths lay flat round eggs); larvae feed for 2–3 weeks, boring into developing heads and contaminating broccoli florets with pupae and frass.
distinguishing_features: Easy field identification of the 3 brassica caterpillars: Imported Cabbageworm is velvety and sluggish (from white daytime butterflies); Cabbage Looper arches its middle into a loop like an inchworm; Diamondback Moth larva is tiny (<3/8 inch), pointed at both ends, and thrashing/wriggling violently when poked.
similar_conditions: Cross-Striped Cabbageworm (bluish-gray with black cross-stripes feeding in groups), Flea Beetles (tiny 1-2 mm 'shot-holes'), Slugs (silvery slime trails)
risk_factors: Uncovered brassica beds, mustard-family weeds (shepherd's purse, yellow rocket, wild mustard), and continuous planting of cole crops without row covers.
favorable_conditions: Mild-to-warm days (60–85°F) from early spring through late autumn frost.
transmission_or_spread: Adult white cabbage butterflies (daytime) and looper/diamondback moths (nighttime) are attracted from long distances by mustard-oil glucosinolate volatiles released by brassica leaves.
management_actions: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt—a selective biological stomach poison that kills ONLY feeding caterpillars and is 100% safe for bees, ladybugs, and humans, with 0-day pre-harvest interval!) or spinosad every 7–10 days when white butterflies or young larvae are seen; add a drop of liquid castile soap/spreader-sticker so spray adheres to waxy cabbage leaves; soak harvested broccoli heads in salted cold water for 20 minutes to float out hidden worms.

severity_or_impact: High (the primary pest complex of all Brassica crops worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–85°F (13–29°C) and all humidity levels across spring, summer, and fall.
host_range: Documented on Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Mustard greens, Bok choy).

topic: Kohlrabi Cutworms Management
problem_name: Cutworms (Black, Variegated, Granulate, and Dingy Cutworms)
causal_agent: Agrotis ipsilon (Black Cutworm), Peridroma saucia (Variegated Cutworm), and Feltia subterranea (Granulate Cutworm)
affected_plant_parts: Seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears
growth_stage: Seedling emergence and first 2–3 weeks after transplanting
season: Spring and early summer
humidity_conditions: Moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils
visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): Healthy young vegetable transplants or newly emerged seedlings are found toppled over flat on the ground in the morning, cleanly severed ('felled like a miniature tree') right at or just below the soil line, often with the wilted green top pulled slightly into a small burrow hole; when you scratch 1–2 inches into the loose soil around the base of the severed stem, you uncover a plump, greasy-looking, dull gray, brown, or black caterpillar (1 to 2 inches long) that immediately curls into a tight C-shape when disturbed; climbing cutworms (Variegated Cutworm) also climb asparagus spears (causing crooked 'butt-chewed' ferns) and tomato vines.
symptom_keywords: seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight, toppled wilted transplant, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled in C-shape in soil near stem base
symptom_progression: Overwintering larvae or spring-hatched caterpillars hide 1–2 inches beneath soil clods during the day and emerge at night to wrap around tender seedling stems and chew through them; a single large cutworm can sever 3–5 seedlings in a single row before pupating.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the clean overnight severing of the stem at the soil surface and finding the plump, greasy gray-brown caterpillar curled into a tight C-ring in the top inch of soil next to the freshly cut plant (unlike Damping-Off, where the stem is thin, dark, and shriveled rather than chewed off).
similar_conditions: Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem)
risk_factors: Turning under winter cover crops, sod, or spring weeds (Especially chickweed and curled dock) less than 2–3 weeks before planting (starving caterpillars already on the dying weeds immediately attack the new vegetable transplants!).
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-warm moist spring nights in beds with recent weed growth or surface debris.
transmission_or_spread: Nocturnal owlet moths (Noctuidae) lay eggs on low-growing spring weeds, cover crops, and damp soil.
management_actions: Place a 3-inch-tall protective 'cutworm collar' (made from a toilet-paper cardboard tube, paper cup with bottom removed, or aluminum foil strip) around the stem of every tomato, pepper, eggplant, and brassica transplant at planting, pushing the collar 1 inch into the soil and leaving 2 inches above ground; scratch the soil around freshly cut plants in the morning to find and crush the culprit caterpillar.
prevention_actions: Till under winter cover crops and spring weeds at least 2–3 weeks BEFORE planting or transplanting so resident cutworms starve or pupate before your crop goes in; keep garden borders free of winter chickweed.
recommended_observations: Scout Kohlrabi (seedling stems right at or just below the soil line, and low-hanging leaves/fruits or emerging asparagus spears) twice weekly during spring and early summer (55–80°F (13–27°C)); inspect for seedling stem cleanly chewed off at soil line overnight to distinguish Cutworms from Damping-Off (pinched dark rotting stem without chewing marks), Slugs (leave silvery dried slime trails), Birds/Rabbits (clip upper cotyledons/leaves rather than soil-line stem).
severity_or_impact: High during the first 2 weeks after emergence/transplanting (can wipe out entire rows of transplants overnight)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–80°F (13–27°C) and moist, weedy, or high-residue spring soils.
host_range: Documented on Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards).

topic: Kohlrabi Flea Beetles Management
problem_name: Flea Beetles (Crucifer, Striped, Potato, Eggplant, Palestriped, and Corn Flea Beetles)
causal_agent: Phyllotreta cruciferae (Crucifer Flea Beetle), Phyllotreta striolata (Striped Flea Beetle), Epitrix fuscula (Eggplant Flea Beetle), Epitrix cucumeris (Potato Flea Beetle), Systena blanda (Palestriped Flea Beetle), and Chaetocnema pulicaria (Corn Flea Beetle)
affected_plant_parts: Cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of Potato, Sweetpotato, and Striped Flea Beetles)
growth_stage: Cotyledon emergence and first 3–4 weeks after transplanting (most critical)
season: Spring through mid-summer
humidity_conditions: Warm, sunny, dry spring weather
visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): Numerous tiny (1–2 mm), round, shallow pits and perforations chewed into cotyledons and leaves, making the foliage look as though it has been blasted with fine buckshot ('shot-holing'); tiny (1/16 to 1/8 inch / 1.5–3 mm) shiny black, metallic blue-green, bronze, or yellow-striped beetles with enlarged muscular hind femora leap explosively like fleas when approached; on young brassica, radish, and beet seedlings, heavy feeding desiccates and kills the plant; on Sweet Corn, Corn Flea Beetles leave white scratch tracks parallel to veins and transmit Stewart's Bacterial Wilt; underground thread-like white larvae chew tiny winding grooves and shallow pimply tunnels into potato tubers, sweet potatoes, radishes, and turnips.
symptom_keywords: hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves, shot-hole riddled eggplant and radish leaves, tiny shiny black jumping beetles, fine winding surface tracks on sweet potato and radish roots
symptom_progression: Overwintered adult beetles emerge from grassy/weedy borders on the first warm (>60°F) sunny days of spring and swarm young seedlings; females lay eggs in soil around host roots, producing a second summer generation in July.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hundreds of tiny (1–2 mm) round 'shot-holes' peppered across eggplant, potato, radish, bok choy, and brassica leaves, combined with the tiny shiny beetles that jump like fleas when touched.
similar_conditions: Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass)
risk_factors: Direct-seeded spring brassicas/radishes and newly set eggplant/potato plants grown without floating row covers during warm dry spring weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm (>65°F), sunny, calm spring days.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as adults in soil and leaf litter along garden edges, flying and hopping onto host crops in spring.
management_actions: COVER SUSCEPTIBLE CROPS IMMEDIATELY AT PLANTING: drape lightweight floating row covers or fine mesh insect netting over eggplant, radish, bok choy, mustard greens, turnip, and brassica beds the moment seeds are sown or transplants are set, burying the edges in soil (note: avoid rotating susceptible crops into a bed that had flea-beetle-infested crops last year before putting row covers on, or beetles emerging from the soil inside will be trapped under the cover!); apply spinosad, kaolin clay, or pyrethrin/neem sprays if uncovered seedlings show >10–20% shot-holing.
prevention_actions: Set out sturdy, larger transplants whenever possible so plants outgrow early spring feeding; plant a fast-growing trap crop of 'Giant Red Mustard', 'Pac Choi', or radish along the bed perimeter 10 days before main brassicas or eggplants; keep soil moist with frequent light overhead watering in spring (flea beetles dislike wet foliage).
recommended_observations: Scout Kohlrabi (cotyledons, young leaves, and underground tubers/storage roots (larvae of potato, sweetpotato, and striped flea beetles)) twice weekly during spring through mid-summer (60–88°F (15–31°C)); inspect for hundreds of tiny buckshot holes in leaves to distinguish Flea Beetles from Shot-Hole Fungal/Bacterial Diseases (larger spots with yellow/purple halos on fruit trees), Imported Cabbageworm (larger ragged holes with green frass).
severity_or_impact: High on seedlings and young eggplant, radish, bok choy, arugula, turnip, and mustard greens

visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil

distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).

risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).

prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.

topic: Kohlrabi Alternaria Leaf Spot and Head Rot (Dark Leaf Spot) (Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae)

causal_agent: Alternaria brassicicola and Alternaria brassicae (Brassicas); Alternaria dauci (Carrot); Alternaria porri (Alliums); Alternaria cucumerina (Cucurbits)
affected_plant_parts: Older lower leaves, petioles, broccoli/cauliflower heads, carrot tops, and onion/garlic leaves ('purple blotch')
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through head/bulb/root maturity
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer and fall weather
humidity_conditions: Extended leaf wetness (>9–12 hours) from rain, fog, or heavy dew
visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): On Brassicas & Cucurbits: circular dark brown-to-black target-like spots (1/8 to 1 inch) with concentric rings and yellow halos on older leaves, plus sunken brown-black velvety rot on broccoli domes and cauliflower curds; On Carrots (Alternaria dauci): dark brown-to-black irregular lesions with yellow borders on older feathery leaflet margins that make carrot tops look scorched by fire and snap off during pulling; On Alliums (Alternaria porri 'Purple Blotch'): water-soaked pale lesions on tubular leaves that turn concentric purplish-brown with yellow streaks.

distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the concentric target rings and dark olive-black sooty spore fuzz in the lesion center (on Onion/Garlic, Purple Blotch forms zonate purple-brown lesions with yellow margins).

risk_factors: Infected seed, overwintered crop debris, crowded plantings, nitrogen deficiency on older leaves (especially in carrots and onions), and overhead irrigation.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (70–85°F) with frequent rain and prolonged leaf wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne and overwinters on crop debris and weeds, spreading via wind-borne and rain-splashed conidia.
management_actions: Remove infected lower leaves; maintain adequate nitrogen fertility on carrots and brassicas so older foliage stays vigorous; irrigate via drip in the morning; apply labeled protectant fungicides or copper/Bacillus biofungicides when wet weather occurs during heading.
prevention_actions: Use certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed; practice a 3-year crop rotation; space plants for good airflow and promptly bury crop residue after harvest.

topic: Kohlrabi Black Rot of Crucifers (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris)
problem_name: Black Rot of Crucifers
causal_agent: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris
affected_plant_parts: Leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots
growth_stage: Seedling stage through heading and root maturity
season: Warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering
visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): Diagnostic V-shaped bright yellow (chlorotic) blotches initiating at the leaf margins (with the point of the 'V' directed inward toward the midrib) that turn tan-brown and papery dry; holding the V-shaped lesion up to the light reveals a network of jet-blackened veins inside the yellow/tan wedge; slicing the petiole or main stem crosswise shows a black-brown vascular ring; infected cabbage and cauliflower heads often develop secondary foul-smelling bacterial soft rot.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesions on leaf margin, blackened veins inside yellow wedge, black vascular ring in stem, marginal leaf blight
symptom_progression: Bacteria enter water pores (hydathodes) along the leaf edges inside morning guttation droplets, moving inward down the xylem veins to form V-shaped wedges and eventually invading the main stem vascular system.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Alternaria Leaf Spot and Downy Mildew by the classic V-shaped yellow marginal wedges with jet-black veins inside the lesion (Verticillium Wilt also causes V-shaped marginal yellowing, but lacks the crisp jet-black vein network inside the leaf blade and occurs in cooler weather).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins)
risk_factors: Saved or untreated brassica seed, infected transplants, cruciferous weeds, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and working in wet beds.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (77–86°F) with heavy morning dew/guttation and splashing rain.
transmission_or_spread: Primarily seed-borne (even 1 infected seed in 10,000 can cause an epidemic in transplant trays); survives up to 2 years in unrotted brassica stalks and spreads by splashing water and equipment.
management_actions: Remove infected plants early; never work in brassica beds when leaves are wet with morning dew or guttation droplets; use drip irrigation; copper sprays offer only limited suppression once established.
prevention_actions: Plant certified pathogen-free or hot-water-treated seed (122°F/50°C for 25 minutes for cabbage/broccoli/brussels sprouts; 15 minutes for cauliflower/kale/turnip/bok choy) and black-rot-tolerant cultivars; rotate out of all Brassicaceae for 3 years; chop and bury brassica stalks immediately after harvest so they decompose.
recommended_observations: Scout Kohlrabi (leaf margins (hydathodes), leaf veins, petioles, vascular ring, heads, and storage roots) weekly during warm, humid, rainy summer and early autumn weather (77–86°F (25–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Rot of Crucifers from Verticillium Wilt, Alternaria Leaf Spot, Downy Mildew, Fusarium Yellows (one-sided yellowing with brown rather than jet-black veins).
severity_or_impact: High (most destructive bacterial disease of brassicas worldwide)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 77–86°F (25–30°C) and high humidity, heavy guttation/morning dew, driving rain, and overhead watering.
host_range: Documented on Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Kohlrabi Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae)
problem_name: Clubroot
causal_agent: Plasmodiophora brassicae
affected_plant_parts: Taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)
growth_stage: Seedling establishment through heading/root harvest
season: Warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (pH <6.5)
visible_symptoms: On Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes): Above ground: plants are stunted, outer leaves turn pale green-to-yellow or reddish-purple, and foliage flags/wilts during sunny afternoons before recovering partially at night; heads fail to form or stay small and loose; Below ground (diagnostic): roots are drastically distorted into massive, spindle-shaped, knobby, finger-like swollen galls ('clubs') up to several inches thick that eventually crack, turn brown, and decay from secondary soft-rot bacteria with a foul odor.
symptom_keywords: spindle-shaped swollen clubbed roots, finger-like root galls, daytime wilting in brassicas, stunted purple-yellow outer leaves, failure to head
symptom_progression: Resting spores germinate in acidic wet soil, releasing zoospores that infect root hairs and induce massive hyperplasia and hypertrophy (giant cells) in the root cortex, blocking water/nutrient uptake.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified on Brassicas by the massive spindle- and club-shaped root swellings (much larger and smoother than root-knot nematode bead galls, and lacking the hollow cavities of cabbage maggot tunnels).
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress
risk_factors: Acidic soils (pH below 6.5), poorly drained wet beds, brassica weeds (shepherd's purse, wild mustard, yellow rocket, pennycress), and importing infected bare-root transplants.
favorable_conditions: Moist, acidic soil (pH 5.0–6.5) at soil temperatures of 68–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Extremely long-lived resting spores survive in soil for 10–20 years and move on soil stuck to shoes, tillers, transplants, and surface water.
management_actions: Dig up and bag infected plants and clubbed roots carefully (never compost!); apply agricultural limestone (plus hydrated lime or calcium cyanamide where recommended by extension) to raise and maintain soil pH at 7.1–7.2, which strongly inhibits Plasmodiophora spore germination.
prevention_actions: Grow brassica transplants in sterile soilless mix; practice a 5–7 year rotation away from all Brassicaceae and eradicate mustard-family weeds; plant clubroot-resistant cultivars (such as 'Bilko', 'Kilaton', 'Tekila' cabbage; 'Emerald Jewel' broccoli) while maintaining soil pH at 6.8–7.2.
recommended_observations: Scout Kohlrabi (taproots and secondary fibrous roots (causing above-ground stunting and wilting)) weekly during warm spring and summer growing seasons in acidic soils (68–77°F (20–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Clubroot from Root-Knot Nematodes, Cabbage Maggot (tunnels + white legless maggots in roots), Hybrid Herbicide/Growth Regulator Galling, Drought Stress.
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (persists in soil for up to 20 years and prevents marketable head or root formation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–77°F (20–25°C) and high soil moisture (>70% field capacity) and acidic soil (ph <6.5).
host_range: Documented on Kohlrabi (Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes, Brassicaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Brussels sprouts, Collards, Bok choy, Kohlrabi).

topic: Leek Thrips Management
problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)
affected_plant_parts: Inner leaf folds/necks (Alliums), flower blossoms, terminal buds, young leaves, and developing fruits/pods
growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: Hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil)
visible_symptoms: On Leek (Allium ampeloprasum): Slender, minute (1–1.5 mm), cigar-shaped yellow, tan, or dark-brown insects with fringed wings that rasp-and-suck epidermal cells, leaving silvery-white to metallic-gray longitudinal streaks, patches, and scars across leaves (especially deep inside the tight central neck of onion, garlic, and leek leaves, where severe feeding turns the entire top fan silvery-white and curls tips downward); feeding patches are dotted with tiny, shiny jet-black specks of liquid fecal frass; in Cabbage, thrips cause rough bronze warty calluses ('edema/blisters') inside head wrapper leaves; in Strawberry, Pepper, Tomato, and Pea, flower feeding causes bronzed berries, scarred pods, or circular pale 'ghost spots' on fruit.
symptom_keywords: silvery-white longitudinal leaf streaks, tiny shiny black fecal specks on silver patches, silvered onion neck blades, bronze warty calluses inside cabbage head, scarred bronzed fruit and pods, slender cigar-shaped insects in flowers
symptom_progression: Females saw eggs into leaf/petal tissue; two larval instars feed in tight crevices or blossoms, then drop to the soil to pupate, completing a generation every 10–18 days in hot weather.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Spider Mites by: (1) silvery-gray metallic patches dotted with shiny black fecal droplets (and NO silk webbing), and (2) tapping blossoms or onion necks over a white card reveals slender, fast-moving, cigar-shaped yellow/brown insects rather than oval mites.
similar_conditions: Spider Mites (pinpoint stippling with silk webbing), Powdery Mildew, Downy Mildew, Genetic Silvering
risk_factors: Planting onions/garlic adjacent to alfalfa, clover, or small grain fields (which dump millions of migrating thrips when cut/harvested in early summer), drought stress, and broad-spectrum pyrethroid sprays.
favorable_conditions: Hot, dry summer weather (77–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne dispersal from drying hay/grain fields and weeds, and transport on infested onion transplants/sets or greenhouse bedding plants.
management_actions: Inspect tight inner onion/leek leaf axils and tap flowers onto a white index card; apply spinosad, neem oil, or insecticidal soap directed into the central neck of onions or onto foliage early in the morning (avoid spraying spinosad on open blossoms when bees are foraging); conserve predatory minute pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus) and predatory mites.
prevention_actions: Use UV-reflective silver plastic mulch around tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits to repel migrating flower thrips; overhead-irrigate onions occasionally during hot dry spells to wash thrips out of the neck; choose open-necked, glossy/yellow-green onion cultivars ('Sweet Spanish' types are more tolerant than tight-necked waxy blue-green types); remove cull onion piles.

severity_or_impact: High (reduces onion bulb size by 30–50% and vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus [TSWV] and Iris Yellow Spot Virus [IYSV])
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and hot, dry weather (heavy rain washes thrips from leaves and drowns pupae in soil).
host_range: Documented on Leek (Allium ampeloprasum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives, Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale).

topic: Leek Routine Garden Maintenance, Pruning, Support, and Weed Management
growth_stage: Established vegetative growth through harvest
management_actions: To produce a long, tender, white edible shank, transplant pencil-thick seedlings into 5-inch-deep holes poked with a dibble (just water them in without filling the hole with soil so the shaft blanches as it thickens) OR hill loose soil around the stems 2–3 times during summer (taking care not to throw soil down between the V-folded leaf bases where it causes gritty layers)
prevention_actions: Cultivate shallowly around plants to avoid severing surface feeder roots, keep mulch pulled slightly back from direct stem contact where crown rot is a risk, and sanitize pruning tools between plants.
recommended_observations: Check Leek weekly for structural support needs, weed competition, mulch depth, and pollinator activity.

topic: Leek Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Deep, loose, fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam amenable to trenching and hilling (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt); drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a deep, loose, fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam amenable to trenching and hilling adjusted to pH 6.0–7.0 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Leek to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Leek (Allium ampeloprasum): Prefers deep, loose, fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam amenable to trenching and hilling with an optimal soil pH of 6.0–7.0. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Leek Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Leek (Allium ampeloprasum): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.
recommended_observations: Scout Leek (upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods) weekly during moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity (65–80°F (18–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) from Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.
host_range: Documented on Leek (Allium ampeloprasum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Beans, Cowpea, Peas, Lentil, Chickpea, Asparagus, Sweet corn, Onion).

topic: Leek White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums (Sclerotium cepivorum)
problem_name: White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums
causal_agent: Sclerotium cepivorum (White Rot), Botrytis allii (Neck Rot), and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae (Basal Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck
growth_stage: Mid-spring bulb enlargement through harvest and post-harvest curing/storage
season: Cool-to-moderate spring (White Rot: 50–68°F) or warm summer/storage (Basal/Neck Rot: 70–85°F)
humidity_conditions: Moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing
visible_symptoms: On Leek (Allium ampeloprasum): Above ground: premature yellowing, tip dieback, and wilting of older leaves progressing to collapse of the top fan; Below ground: in White Rot, a fluffy snow-white mycelial mat covers the basal plate and lower bulb studded with thousands of poppy-seed-sized (0.5 mm) spherical jet-black sclerotia; in Fusarium Basal Rot, the basal plate turns pinkish-brown and spongy with decayed roots; in Botrytis Neck Rot, sunken gray water-soaked decay softens the bulb neck during storage with gray mold and black sclerotia between scales.
symptom_keywords: fluffy white mycelium on bulb base, tiny black poppy-seed sclerotia, rotted basal plate, premature top yellowing and dieback, spongy sunken bulb neck in storage
symptom_progression: Root exudates (alkyl cysteines) uniquely produced only by Allium species stimulate dormant soil sclerotia to germinate and rot the roots and basal plate; Neck Rot enters through uncured moist neck cuts at harvest.
distinguishing_features: White Rot is distinguished by the crust of tiny (0.5 mm) uniform round black poppy-seed-like sclerotia embedded in white mycelium at the bulb base; Botrytis Neck Rot starts at the TOP neck of stored bulbs when tops were cut too green or cured poorly.
similar_conditions: Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot
risk_factors: Planting non-certified culinary grocery-store garlic cloves (major pathway introducing White Rot to home gardens!), short Allium rotations, harvesting in wet weather, and failing to cure bulbs thoroughly.
favorable_conditions: Cool moist spring soils (50–68°F) for White Rot; warm soils (75–85°F) for Fusarium Basal Rot; wet harvest weather for Botrytis Neck Rot.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotium cepivorum sclerotia survive in soil for 15–20+ years even without an Allium host; spreads via infected seed garlic cloves, onion sets, and contaminated soil.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag infected bulbs plus surrounding soil; stop all irrigation 2–3 weeks before onion/garlic harvest and cure harvested bulbs thoroughly at 75–85°F with strong airflow for 2–3 weeks until necks are tight and bone-dry before trimming.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL RULE: NEVER plant grocery-store garlic or uncertified sets—plant only certified disease-free seed garlic and onion sets; rotate Allium family crops on a minimum 4-year cycle.
recommended_observations: Scout Leek (roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring (white rot: 50–68°f) or warm summer/storage (basal/neck rot: 70–85°f) (50–80°F (10–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums from Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot.
severity_or_impact: Critical (White Rot permanently contaminates garden beds against all Alliums for 15–20 years; Neck Rot ruins stored bulbs)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–80°F (10–27°C) and moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing.
host_range: Documented on Leek (Allium ampeloprasum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives).
