topic: Leek Nutrient Requirements and Fertilization Schedule
growth_stage: Pre-plant bed preparation, active vegetative growth, and reproductive/storage organ development
management_actions: Steady nitrogen and potassium requirement; side-dress with nitrogen every 3–4 weeks during spring and summer
prevention_actions: Base fertilizer rates on a soil test and maintain soil pH at 6.0–7.0 to keep macronutrients and micronutrients bioavailable; avoid over-application of soluble nitrogen salts which can burn roots or skew vegetative-to-reproductive balance.
recommended_observations: Monitor shoot vigor, leaf color on both older lower leaves (mobile nutrients N, P, K, Mg) and new upper leaves (immobile nutrients Fe, Ca, B, Zn, Mn), and fruit/root set.
knowledge_text: Nutrition and fertilizer management for Leek (Allium ampeloprasum): Steady nitrogen and potassium requirement; side-dress with nitrogen every 3–4 weeks during spring and summer. Maintain soil pH within 6.0–7.0 to ensure optimal nutrient availability.

topic: Chives Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Chives (Allium schoenoprasum): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Chives (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.

problem_name: Thrips (Western Flower Thrips, Onion Thrips, and Melon Thrips)
causal_agent: Frankliniella occidentalis (Western Flower Thrips), Thrips tabaci (Onion Thrips), and Thrips palmi (Melon Thrips)

growth_stage: Seedling through bulbing, flowering, and fruit set
season: Hot, dry late spring and summer weather

topic: Chives Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Chives (Allium schoenoprasum): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.
symptom_keywords: rusty-orange powdery pustules, cinnamon-brown blister spots, orange spore dust rubs off on fingers, dark brown late-season telia, premature leaf drop
symptom_progression: Wind-borne spores germinate in dew droplets; pale yellow flecks appear in 5 days and rupture into dusty orange-brown spore pustules in 7–10 days, repeating every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot/Blight (water-soaked flat spots, no orange spore powder), Downy Mildew, Spider Mite Bronzing
risk_factors: Dense plantings, shaded sites where morning dew lingers past mid-morning, overhead evening irrigation, and overwintered asparagus ferns, mint stems, or bean stakes.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (65–80°F) with cool dewy nights and humid mornings.
transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.
prevention_actions: Plant rust-resistant cultivars (available in snap/pole beans, sweet corn Rp-gene hybrids, and all-male asparagus); cut and destroy dead brown asparagus ferns in late winter and rake fallen fig leaves in autumn; space plants for airflow.

severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (causes severe defoliation in beans, figs, and garlic, and weakens asparagus crowns and mint stands)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–80°F (18–27°C) and high humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog.

topic: Chives White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums (Sclerotium cepivorum)
problem_name: White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums
causal_agent: Sclerotium cepivorum (White Rot), Botrytis allii (Neck Rot), and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae (Basal Rot)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck
growth_stage: Mid-spring bulb enlargement through harvest and post-harvest curing/storage
season: Cool-to-moderate spring (White Rot: 50–68°F) or warm summer/storage (Basal/Neck Rot: 70–85°F)
humidity_conditions: Moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing
visible_symptoms: On Chives (Allium schoenoprasum): Above ground: premature yellowing, tip dieback, and wilting of older leaves progressing to collapse of the top fan; Below ground: in White Rot, a fluffy snow-white mycelial mat covers the basal plate and lower bulb studded with thousands of poppy-seed-sized (0.5 mm) spherical jet-black sclerotia; in Fusarium Basal Rot, the basal plate turns pinkish-brown and spongy with decayed roots; in Botrytis Neck Rot, sunken gray water-soaked decay softens the bulb neck during storage with gray mold and black sclerotia between scales.
symptom_keywords: fluffy white mycelium on bulb base, tiny black poppy-seed sclerotia, rotted basal plate, premature top yellowing and dieback, spongy sunken bulb neck in storage
symptom_progression: Root exudates (alkyl cysteines) uniquely produced only by Allium species stimulate dormant soil sclerotia to germinate and rot the roots and basal plate; Neck Rot enters through uncured moist neck cuts at harvest.
distinguishing_features: White Rot is distinguished by the crust of tiny (0.5 mm) uniform round black poppy-seed-like sclerotia embedded in white mycelium at the bulb base; Botrytis Neck Rot starts at the TOP neck of stored bulbs when tops were cut too green or cured poorly.
similar_conditions: Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot
risk_factors: Planting non-certified culinary grocery-store garlic cloves (major pathway introducing White Rot to home gardens!), short Allium rotations, harvesting in wet weather, and failing to cure bulbs thoroughly.
favorable_conditions: Cool moist spring soils (50–68°F) for White Rot; warm soils (75–85°F) for Fusarium Basal Rot; wet harvest weather for Botrytis Neck Rot.
transmission_or_spread: Sclerotium cepivorum sclerotia survive in soil for 15–20+ years even without an Allium host; spreads via infected seed garlic cloves, onion sets, and contaminated soil.
management_actions: Immediately dig up and bag infected bulbs plus surrounding soil; stop all irrigation 2–3 weeks before onion/garlic harvest and cure harvested bulbs thoroughly at 75–85°F with strong airflow for 2–3 weeks until necks are tight and bone-dry before trimming.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL RULE: NEVER plant grocery-store garlic or uncertified sets—plant only certified disease-free seed garlic and onion sets; rotate Allium family crops on a minimum 4-year cycle.
recommended_observations: Scout Chives (roots, basal plate, underground bulb scales, and pseudostem neck) weekly during cool-to-moderate spring (white rot: 50–68°f) or warm summer/storage (basal/neck rot: 70–85°f) (50–80°F (10–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish White Rot and Neck/Basal Rot of Alliums from Onion Maggot (white legless maggots tunneling inside bulb base), Bulb Mites, Waterlogging Root Rot.
severity_or_impact: Critical (White Rot permanently contaminates garden beds against all Alliums for 15–20 years; Neck Rot ruins stored bulbs)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–80°F (10–27°C) and moist soil during bulbing or wet weather during harvest and incomplete curing.
host_range: Documented on Chives (Allium schoenoprasum, Amaryllidaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Onion, Garlic, Leek, Chives).

topic: Chives (Allium schoenoprasum) Sulfur (S) Deficiency: Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Sulfur (S) Deficiency
affected_plant_parts: Youngest emerging hollow scapes (leaves)
growth_stage: Continuous clump growth and post-cut regrowth
season: Early spring through late autumn (perennial in USDA Zones 3–9)
temperature_range: Optimal growth 55–75°F (13–24°C); extremely winter-hardy down to -35°F; one of the very first garden plants to emerge in early spring
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Newly emerging central hollow scapes turn uniformly pale yellowish-green, thin, and spindly with weak onion aroma after repeated cuttings in low-sulfur soil or potting media.
symptom_keywords: chives, sulfur (s) deficiency, immobile in phloem (structural component of cysteine, methionine, glucosinolates in brassicas, and alliin/allicin in alliums), youngest emerging hollow scapes (leaves), chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Youngest upper and central leaves first (uniform pale yellow-green coloration of both veins and lamina). Appears on the newest flush of shoots after harvesting when soluble sulfate is depleted.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Immobile in phloem (structural component of cysteine, methionine, glucosinolates in Brassicas, and alliin/allicin in Alliums). Uniform yellowing of newest emerging scapes while older outer blades stay green.
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Chives.
risk_factors: Coarse, well-drained sandy soils low in organic matter where sulfate (SO4 2-) leaches rapidly during heavy rain, cold spring soils with slow organic sulfur mineralization, and exclusive use of sulfur-free high-analysis synthetic fertilizers.
favorable_conditions: Coarse, well-drained sandy soils low in organic matter where sulfate (SO4 2-) leaches rapidly during heavy rain, cold spring soils with slow organic sulfur mineralization, and exclusive use of sulfur-free high-analysis synthetic fertilizers.
management_actions: Side-dress or water in a soluble sulfate source such as gypsum (calcium sulfate), Epsom salts (magnesium sulfate), potassium sulfate, or ammonium sulfate to rapidly supply plant-available SO4 2- ions.
prevention_actions: Incorporate organic compost or aged manure regularly, include sulfate-containing fertilizers (such as potassium sulfate or gypsum) in the fertility program for high-sulfur-demand Brassicas and Alliums, and mulch sandy beds.

knowledge_text: Sulfur (S) Deficiency in Chives (Allium schoenoprasum, family Amaryllidaceae): Sulfur (S) is immobile in phloem (structural component of cysteine, methionine, glucosinolates in brassicas, and alliin/allicin in alliums), so deficiency symptoms initiate on youngest upper and central leaves first (uniform pale yellow-green coloration of both veins and lamina). knowledge_text: Waterlogging & Crown Suffocation of Thyme on Thyme (Thymus vulgaris, family Lamiaceae) is an abiotic environmental stress caused by saturated soil pore space depleting root-zone oxygen (<2% o2), halting aerobic root respiration and triggering ethylene-mediated leaf epinasty. Visual symptoms: Stems turn dark brown at the base, tiny leaves turn gray-brown and mushy or drop off, and the entire cushion collapses outward from the center in soggy soil. Progression: Root hypoxia in cold wet winter soil or over-irrigated summer beds. Distinguishing features: Central cushion collapse and dark wet roots in poorly drained soil. Predisposing conditions: Heavy clay soils with poor internal drainage, compacted plow pans, low-lying garden depressions, excessive irrigation frequency, or torrential rainfall. Management and prevention: Cease irrigation immediately, open drainage trenches to draw standing water away from rows, lightly aerate crusted soil once surface dries, and avoid foot traffic on wet beds. Construct 6–10 inch raised beds amended with coarse organic compost, break up subsoil hardpans before planting, and use soil-moisture sensors to prevent over-watering.

topic: Dill Leafhoppers Management
problem_name: Leafhoppers (Potato Leafhopper, Beet Leafhopper, and Aster Leafhopper)
causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)
affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Dill (Anethum graveolens): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), slender, wedge-shaped pale lime-green or tan insects that fly away swiftly when plants are brushed and whose bright neon-green nymphs walk rapidly SIDEWAYS ('crab-like') across the underside of the leaf when flipped over! Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
symptom_keywords: wedge-shaped lime-green insect hopping and flying, neon-green nymphs walking sideways crab-like under leaf, V-shaped yellow tip burn and brown scorched leaf margins, hopperburn on potato and beans, curled dwarfed leaves with purple veins
symptom_progression: Potato and Aster Leafhoppers overwinter along the Gulf Coast and ride high-altitude warm spring storm fronts northward in May–June, often dumping into vegetable gardens whenever adjacent alfalfa hay fields are cut.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish 'Hopperburn' from Potassium Deficiency, Early Blight, or Drought Scorch by flipping over a yellowing V-tipped leaf and watching for the tiny (2–3 mm) bright lime-green wedge-shaped nymphs running rapidly SIDEWAYS across the leaf blade!
similar_conditions: Potassium Deficiency (marginal scorching without sideways-walking green nymphs), Early Blight, Herbicide Drift, Mosaic Virus
risk_factors: Planting potatoes, snap beans, eggplants, or strawberries near alfalfa or clover fields (cutting alfalfa forces millions of potato leafhoppers into neighboring gardens), and hot dry summer weather.
favorable_conditions: Warm, dry weather (75–90°F).
transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.
management_actions: Scout leaf undersides for sideways-running lime-green nymphs; cover susceptible bean, potato, carrot, and lettuce rows with lightweight floating row covers or insect netting; spray insecticidal soap, pyrethrin, neem, or kaolin clay (Surround) onto leaf undersides if nymphs exceed 1 per leaf on potatoes/beans.
prevention_actions: Plant pubescent (hairy-leaved) cultivars of beans and potatoes (dense hooked trichome hairs on leaves physically snag and deter leafhopper nymphs!); shade susceptible tomatoes and peppers lightly in arid Western regions to deter sun-loving Beet Leafhoppers.

severity_or_impact: High (Potato Leafhopper hopperburn can slash potato tuber and snap bean yields by 30–60% before gardeners realize an insect is the cause; Beet and Aster Leafhoppers transmit incurable systemic pathogens)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–90°F (21–32°C) and warm, dry summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Dill (Anethum graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Potato, Beans, Lima bean, Cowpea, Soybean, Eggplant, Tomato, Pepper).

topic: Dill Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Dill (Anethum graveolens): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Dill (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Dill (Anethum graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).

topic: Dill Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained, moderately fertile loam or sandy loam (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a well-drained, moderately fertile loam or sandy loam adjusted to pH 5.8–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Dill to verify soil pH (5.8–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.
knowledge_text: Soil requirements for Dill (Anethum graveolens): Prefers well-drained, moderately fertile loam or sandy loam with an optimal soil pH of 5.8–6.8. Good drainage and organic matter incorporation are essential for healthy root development and nutrient uptake.

topic: Dill Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Dill (Anethum graveolens): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.
recommended_observations: Scout Dill (phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures) weekly during mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Aster Yellows from Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High on carrots, lettuce, and celery (infected roots and heads are bitter and inedible)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement.
host_range: Documented on Dill (Anethum graveolens, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Celery, Lettuce, Spinach, Parsley, Coriander, Dill, Parsnip).

topic: Dill Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce (Septoria apiicola)
problem_name: Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce
causal_agent: Septoria apiicola (Celery/Parsley Late Blight) and Septoria lactucae (Lettuce Septoria Leaf Spot)
affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (stalks)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through harvest
season: Cool-to-moderate, wet, humid weather
humidity_conditions: Rain splash, overhead sprinkler irrigation, and heavy dew (>90% RH)
visible_symptoms: On Dill (Anethum graveolens): Small, chlorotic yellow flecks on older outer leaves that expand into irregular-to-circular reddish-brown or tan necrotic spots (1/8 to 1/2 inch) heavily peppered with dozens of tiny, dark-brown to black, pinhead-sized pycnidia (spore-fruiting bodies) visible even before the tissue dies; on celery and parsley, lesions spread onto the fleshy petioles (stalks) and coalesce to blight and scorch entire outer leaves.
symptom_keywords: tan-brown leaf spots peppered with tiny black pycnidia dots, blighted celery stalks, outer leaf scorching, yellow-haloed spots
symptom_progression: Seed-borne or debris-borne pycnidia extrude gelatinous tendrils (cirrhi) of spores when wet; rain and sprinklers splash spores across rows, blighting foliage every 10–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified under a hand lens by the numerous tiny black pycnidia dots embedded directly inside the tan/brown leaf and petiole spots (distinguishing it from Cercospora Leaf Spot, which has larger ashy-gray spots WITHOUT black pycnidia dots, and Bacterial Leaf Spot, which has dark greasy water-soaked spots without pycnidia).
similar_conditions: Cercospora Early Blight of Celery (ashy spots without black pycnidia), Bacterial Leaf Spot (Pseudomonas cichorii / syringae pv. apii)
risk_factors: Infected seed (primary source in celery and parsley!), overhead watering, working in beds when foliage is wet, and <2-year rotations.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate temperatures (60–75°F) with frequent rain or sprinkler wetting.
transmission_or_spread: Seed-borne (spores survive up to 2 years in celery seed coats) and residue-borne; spread by rain splash, sprinklers, workers, and tools.
management_actions: Use drip irrigation only and never walk through or harvest parsley, celery, or lettuce while foliage is wet; strip and destroy spotted outer leaves.

knowledge_text: Dill (Anethum graveolens) Septoria Leaf Spot of Apiaceae and Lettuce is a fungal disease caused by Septoria apiicola (Celery/Parsley Late Blight) and Septoria lactucae (Lettuce Septoria Leaf Spot). normal_appearance: Healthy dill plants have a single smooth, hollow, longitudinally striated glaucous blue-green stem with alternate, sheathing, 3-to-4-times pinnately decompound, soft, filiform (thread-like) feathery blue-green leaves. Extension morphological profile: Aromatic blue-green foliage have a delicate fern-like appearance. Leaves are compound and made up of two or more discrete leaflets. The underside of the leaf is not hairy or has few hairs. Leaves are highly aromatic when crushed and usually have the best flavor when the flowers first open. topic: Blueberry Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies Management
problem_name: Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies
problem_category: Fruit-Scarring & Internal Larval Pest of Stone and Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Conotrachelus nenuphar (Plum Curculio) and Rhagoletis cingulata / Rhagoletis fausta / Rhagoletis indifferens (Cherry Fruit Flies)
affected_plant_parts: Immature newly set fruits (petal fall / shuck split) and ripening cherries
growth_stage: Petal fall / shuck split through harvest
season: Spring (Plum Curculio) and early summer as cherries turn yellow-red (Cherry Fruit Fly)
humidity_conditions: Warm (>70°F) humid spring days and nights following rain
visible_symptoms: On Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum): Plum Curculio: a small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), rough-backed, brownish-black snout weevil with grey-white flecks and four prominent humps on its wing covers that emerges at petal fall / shuck split; the female chews a small hole in the tiny green fruitlet, inserts an egg, and then cuts a diagnostic crescent-shaped (D-shaped / half-moon) slit right underneath the egg so the rapidly expanding fruit flesh will not crush her egg! In apples and pears, the fruit expansion usually crushes the larva anyway, leaving a raised, corky, D-shaped fan scar on the mature apple skin; in plums, peaches, cherries, and blueberries, the legless, curved, yellowish-white grub with a brown head tunnels to the pit, causing clear gummy sap droplets to ooze from the crescent scar and causing premature fruit drop or ripe wormy fruit; Cherry Fruit Fly: legless white maggots (no head capsule!) feed around the pit of ripe red cherries without external deformity until sunken soft spots and exit holes appear.
symptom_keywords: crescent-shaped half-moon scar on young green plum peach or apple, gummy clear sap droplet oozing from crescent cut, rough humpbacked brown snout weevil playing dead when tapped, legless grub with brown head next to peach or plum pit, headless white maggot inside ripe cherry
symptom_progression: Overwintered Plum Curculio adults walk/fly from woodlots into fruit trees during bloom and attack fruitlets for 3–5 weeks after petal fall whenever temperatures exceed 70°F; Cherry Fruit Flies emerge from soil just as early cherries show the first blush of yellow-pink color.
distinguishing_features: Plum Curculio is unmistakably identified by the signature crescent-shaped (half-moon) oviposition scar cut into the skin of young apples, plums, peaches, and cherries; inside ripe cherries, Plum Curculio larva has a distinct brown head capsule and curved C-shape, whereas Cherry Fruit Fly maggot is headless and cone-shaped.
similar_conditions: Tarnished Plant Bug / Stink Bug Catfacing (sunken dimples without a crescent-shaped flap cut), Hail Scars, Codling Moth
risk_factors: Fruit trees planted adjacent to deciduous woodlots, hedgerows, or brush piles (where Plum Curculio adults overwinter in leaf litter) and uncollected dropped stone fruits.
favorable_conditions: Spring days reaching 70–75°F+ or warm nights (>60°F) right after petal fall / shuck split.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded border litter and migrate into trees in spring; mature larvae exit fallen fruit to pupate 1–2 inches deep in the soil.
management_actions: Lay a light-colored sheet on the ground under plum, peach, and apple branches in the cool early morning for the 3 weeks after petal fall and sharply tap limbs with a padded stick—Plum Curculio adults fold their legs, play dead ('thanatosis'), and drop onto the sheet looking like bits of bark or bird droppings so you can collect and destroy them; spray kaolin clay (Surround—keep a white coat on fruitlets from petal fall for 4 weeks) or spinosad (for Cherry Fruit Fly, hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate as soon as cherries turn yellow-blush).
prevention_actions: Pick up and dispose of all 'June drop' fruitlets under plum, peach, cherry, and apple trees every 2 days in May/June before curculio grubs crawl out into the soil; prune trees open (Plum Curculio strongly prefers cool, dark, dense interior canopies).

severity_or_impact: Critical east of the Rocky Mountains (the #1 early-season insect pest of plums, peaches, cherries, and apples)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–85°F (15–29°C) and warm (>70°f) humid spring days and nights following rain.
host_range: Documented on Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum, Ericaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Plum, Peach, Cherry, Apple, Pear, Blueberry).

topic: Blueberry Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.

severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and humid summer weather (swd activity pauses above 90°f in dry heat).
host_range: Documented on Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum, Ericaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Blueberry Routine Garden Maintenance, Pruning, Support, and Weed Management
growth_stage: Established vegetative growth through harvest
management_actions: Strip all flowers in Years 1–2; from Year 4 onward, prune annually in late winter by removing low sprawling growth, weak twiggy branches, and 1–2 of the oldest grey canes (>6 years old) at the crown so each bush maintains 8–12 healthy canes of mixed ages (berries form on 1-year-old reddish twig wood on 2-to-5-year-old canes)
prevention_actions: Cultivate shallowly around plants to avoid severing surface feeder roots, keep mulch pulled slightly back from direct stem contact where crown rot is a risk, and sanitize pruning tools between plants.
recommended_observations: Check Blueberry weekly for structural support needs, weed competition, mulch depth, and pollinator activity.

topic: Blueberry Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Moist, porous, well-drained sandy loam or peat-amended bed with high (>3–5%) acidic organic matter; blueberry roots completely lack root hairs and rely on ericoid mycorrhizal fungi that cannot function in heavy clay or alkaline soil (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, Loam (Silt), Sand; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry)
soil_ph: 4.5–5.5 (STRICTLY ACIDIC! Soil pH above 5.5 causes severe iron deficiency interveinal chlorosis on young leaves, stunted growth, and plant decline; test soil and amend with elemental sulfur 6–12 months before planting)
management_actions: Prepare a moist, porous, well-drained sandy loam or peat-amended bed with high (>3–5%) acidic organic matter; blueberry roots completely lack root hairs and rely on ericoid mycorrhizal fungi that cannot function in heavy clay or alkaline soil adjusted to pH 4.5–5.5 (STRICTLY ACIDIC! Soil pH above 5.5 causes severe iron deficiency interveinal chlorosis on young leaves, stunted growth, and plant decline; test soil and amend with elemental sulfur 6–12 months before planting) based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Blueberry to verify soil pH (4.5–5.5 (STRICTLY ACIDIC! topic: Blueberry Blueberry Mummy Berry and Phomopsis / Botryosphaeria Stem Blight (Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi)
problem_name: Blueberry Mummy Berry and Phomopsis / Botryosphaeria Stem Blight
causal_agent: Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi (Mummy Berry), Phomopsis vaccinii (Twig Blight), and Botryosphaeria dothidea (Stem Blight)
affected_plant_parts: Emerging leaf shoots, blossoms, ripening berries, twigs, and main woody canes
growth_stage: Budbreak and bloom through berry ripening
season: Cool wet spring (Mummy Berry/Phomopsis) and warm summer stress (Stem Blight)
humidity_conditions: Moist soil litter in spring and rain during budbreak and bloom
visible_symptoms: On Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum): Mummy Berry (two-stage lifecycle): Stage 1 (Shoot Blight) causes newly emerging spring leaves and shoot tips to suddenly wilt, turn chocolate-brown along the midrib, and droop like frost damage cleanly coated in buff-gray powdery conidia; Stage 2 (Fruit Mummification) occurs as bees carry those conidia into open flowers—infected berries grow normally until just before harvest when they turn salmon-pink/tan, shrivel into hard, ribbed, pumpkin-shaped gray-white 'mummies', and drop to the ground; Stem/Twig Blight: individual woody canes or crooked twig tips suddenly wilt in summer with dead reddish-brown leaves clinging to one side of the bush while adjacent canes stay green (slicing the cane reveals a brown wedge-shaped vascular discoloration).
symptom_keywords: pumpkin-shaped hard gray-white shriveled berry mummies, salmon-pink premature berries, droopy brown spring shoot blight, single dead cane with reddish leaves attached
symptom_progression: Overwintered berry mummies on the soil sprout tiny trumpet-shaped apothecia mushrooms at budbreak that shoot ascospores onto new leaves; bees are tricked by UV reflectance and sugar secretion on blighted shoots into carrying secondary spores straight into open blueberry blossoms!

affected_plant_parts: Undersides of leaves and phloem vascular veins
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through tuber/pod/fruit sizing
season: Late spring through summer (following warm southerly wind migrations)
humidity_conditions: Warm, dry summer weather

transmission_or_spread: Long-distance spring wind migration (Potato and Aster Leafhoppers) and local movement from drying rangeland/alfalfa.

topic: Raspberry Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.

severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth

topic: Raspberry Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

growth_stage: Established vegetative growth through harvest

management_actions: Prepare a deep, fertile, very well-drained sandy loam or loam; highly susceptible to phytophthora root rot in wet heavy clay adjusted to pH 5.8–6.5 based on a laboratory soil test. prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Raspberry to verify soil pH (5.8–6.5) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Raspberry Anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.)
problem_name: Anthracnose
causal_agent: Colletotrichum spp. (C. coccodes on Solanaceae; C. orbiculare on Cucurbits; C. lindemuthianum on Beans; C. acutatum / C. gloeosporioides on Fruits)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening and immature fruits, pods, leaves, petioles, and stems/canes
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit/pod maturation and post-harvest ripening
season: Warm, wet, humid summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>90%) and frequent splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Circular, sunken, water-soaked saucer-like lesions (1/4 to 1/2 inch across) on ripening or green fruits and bean pods that darken to brown or black with concentric rings of tiny black acervuli fruiting bodies; under warm humid conditions, the sunken centers exude sticky, gelatinous salmon-pink to orange spore masses; on cucurbit and bean leaves, reddish-brown to black angular or vein-delimited necrotic spots and elongated sunken stem/petiole cankers.
symptom_keywords: sunken circular fruit spots, salmon-pink sticky spore masses, concentric dark rings in sunken crater, dark vein-blackening on bean pods, tear-stain fruit streaks
symptom_progression: Spores splash onto green fruit or leaves, often establishing quiescent (latent) infections in green fruit skin that awaken and expand into sunken salmon-spored craters as the fruit ripens and softens.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by well-defined circular sunken ('thumbprint') craters on fruit and pods that produce slimy salmon-pink to orange conidial masses in humid weather.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Spot, Alternaria Black Mold, Phytophthora Fruit Rot, Cercospora Leaf Spot, Gummy Stem Blight
risk_factors: Fruits touching bare wet soil, overhead irrigation, saving seed from infected bean/cucurbit pods, and warm rainy weather during harvest.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–86°F) with frequent rainstorms and prolonged wetness.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters as microsclerotia or mycelium in crop residue, soil, and infected bean/cucurbit seeds; conidia are sticky and spread primarily by splashing rain, irrigation water, insects, and wet harvesting.
management_actions: Harvest ripe fruit promptly (do not allow overripe tomatoes, peppers, or berries to hang or rot on the ground); stake or trellis plants and mulch soil heavily with straw to prevent soil-to-fruit splash; never work in bean or cucurbit patches when foliage is wet; prune out dead twigs in mango/avocado/citrus canopies.
prevention_actions: Plant certified disease-free seed and anthracnose-resistant bean and cucurbit cultivars; practice a 3-year crop rotation; use drip irrigation.
recommended_observations: Scout Raspberry (ripening and immature fruits, pods, leaves, petioles, and stems/canes) weekly during warm, wet, humid summer weather (75–86°F (24–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Anthracnose from Bacterial Spot, Alternaria Black Mold, Phytophthora Fruit Rot, Cercospora Leaf Spot, Gummy Stem Blight.
severity_or_impact: High (primary cause of ripe fruit rot in tomatoes, peppers, strawberries, mangoes, papayas, avocados, and pod spots in beans)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–86°F (24–30°C) and high humidity (>90%) and frequent splashing rain.
host_range: Documented on Raspberry (Rubus idaeus, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Cucumber, Watermelon, Melon, Pumpkin, Squash).

topic: Raspberry Cane Blight, Spur Blight, and Anthracnose of Brambles (Elsinoe veneta)
problem_name: Cane Blight, Spur Blight, and Anthracnose of Brambles
causal_agent: Elsinoe veneta (Anthracnose), Didymella applanata (Spur Blight), and Leptosphaeria coniothyrium (Cane Blight)
affected_plant_parts: Primocanes, floricanes, lateral fruiting shoots, buds, and petioles
growth_stage: Spring primocane emergence through second-year floricane fruiting
season: Wet spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain splash, and dense un-thinned cane hedgerows
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Anthracnose: small purplish spots on young green primocanes that enlarge into sunken oval lesions (1/8–1/4 inch) with pale ash-gray centers and raised purple margins ('bird's-eye' cane spots) that crack bark and dry berries; Spur Blight (especially on red raspberry): chocolate-brown to purple V-shaped leaf blotches and dark purple-brown diamond patches surrounding lower buds on primocanes, causing those buds to fail to sprout fruiting laterals next spring; Cane Blight: dark brown-purple cankers spreading down from tipping/pruning wounds on canes, causing fruiting laterals to suddenly wilt and die before harvest.
symptom_keywords: purple sunken gray-centered cane spots, chocolate-purple patches around lower cane buds, sudden wilting of fruiting laterals on second-year canes, cracked cane bark
symptom_progression: Spores from old second-year floricanes splash onto tender emerging first-year primocanes in spring, damaging the vascular bark and buds needed for next summer's crop.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by discrete gray-centered purple-rimmed oval spots (Anthracnose), purple-brown patches centered at lower nodes/buds (Spur Blight), or dieback originating at pruning cuts (Cane Blight).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Phytophthora Root Rot (rotted roots and dark water-soaked crown base), Winter Cane Injury, Raspberry Cane Borer
risk_factors: Failure to prune out spent second-year floricanes after harvest, wide crowded hedgerows (>18 inches wide), overhead watering, and tipping canes right before rain.
favorable_conditions: Rainy spring and summer weather in crowded bramble rows.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters on infected 2-year-old canes and spent floricanes, splashing conidia and ascospores onto new green primocanes.
management_actions: Immediately after summer harvest finishes, cut all spent second-year floricanes flush to the ground and remove them from the patch; thin primocanes to 4–5 canes per linear foot in narrow (12–18 inch) trellised rows; perform summer tipping of primocanes only during dry sunny weather.
prevention_actions: Apply a single delayed-dormant liquid lime-sulfur or copper spray in early spring when buds show 1/4 to 1/2 inch of green tip; for fall-bearing primocane raspberries, mowing all canes to the ground every late winter virtually eliminates cane diseases.
recommended_observations: Scout Raspberry (primocanes, floricanes, lateral fruiting shoots, buds, and petioles) weekly during wet spring and summer weather (60–80°F (15–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cane Blight, Spur Blight, and Anthracnose of Brambles from Verticillium Wilt, Phytophthora Root Rot (rotted roots and dark water-soaked crown base), Winter Cane Injury, Raspberry Cane Borer.
severity_or_impact: High (severely reduces winter cane survival and second-year berry yield)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–80°F (15–27°C) and high humidity, rain splash, and dense un-thinned cane hedgerows.
host_range: Documented on Raspberry (Rubus idaeus, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry).

Distinguishing features: Distinguished by discrete gray-centered purple-rimmed oval spots (Anthracnose), purple-brown patches centered at lower nodes/buds (Spur Blight), or dieback originating at pruning cuts (Cane Blight). Favored by rainy spring and summer weather in crowded bramble rows. (60–80°F (15–27°C)). topic: Raspberry Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Raspberry (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Raspberry (Rubus idaeus, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).

topic: Raspberry Fire Blight (Erwinia amylovora)
problem_name: Fire Blight
causal_agent: Erwinia amylovora
affected_plant_parts: Blossoms, fruiting spurs, succulent terminal shoots, branches, rootstock crowns, and immature fruit
growth_stage: Spring bloom through active early-summer shoot elongation
season: Warm, humid spring bloom and early-summer thunderstorms/hail
humidity_conditions: High humidity (>60%), warm rain, heavy dew, or hail/wind storms during bloom and shoot growth
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Blossoms suddenly wilt, turn water-soaked, and shrivel dark brown-to-black ('blossom blight'); infection moves into succulent young shoots which wilt and bend over at the tip into a diagnostic inverted J-hook ('shepherd's crook') while dead blackened leaves and shriveled mummified fruitlets remain stubbornly attached to the branch as if scorched by a blowtorch; during humid weather, milky-to-amber sticky droplets of bacterial ooze bead on blighted stems and dark sunken branch cankers.
symptom_keywords: shepherd's crook shoot tip, scorched black leaves clinging to branch, blighted black blossoms, amber bacterial ooze droplets, sunken bark canker
symptom_progression: Bacteria multiply on flower stigmas during warm (>65°F) wet bloom and invade nectaries, racing down spurs into shoots and scaffold limbs (especially fast in pear and dwarf M.9/M.26 apple rootstocks).
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the 'shepherd's crook' bent shoot tips, scorched black leaves that do NOT drop off the dead twig, and amber bacterial ooze droplets.
similar_conditions: Pear Psylla Honeydew Sooty Mold, Twig Borer/Oriental Fruit Moth Flagging (has entry hole/larva in twig), Winter Freeze Dieback
risk_factors: Highly susceptible cultivars ('Bartlett'/'Bosc' pear; 'Gala', 'Fuji', 'Jonathan', 'Honeycrisp', 'Granny Smith' apple), excessive nitrogen fertilization or heavy winter pruning that forces lush succulent water sprouts, and hailstorms.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–82°F optimal, >65°F threshold) during open bloom accompanied by rain or high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters at the margins of sunken holdover bark cankers; in spring, insects (bees, flies, ants) and splashing rain carry oozing bacteria to open blossoms and tender shoot tips.
management_actions: Prune out blighted 'shepherd's crook' shoots during dry weather by cutting at least 12 inches BELOW the lowest visible bark discoloration, dipping pruning loppers in 70% rubbing alcohol or 10% bleach between EVERY cut (never prune in wet weather!); remove all rootstock suckers.
prevention_actions: Plant fire-blight-resistant pear cultivars ('Harrow Delight', 'Harrow Sweet', 'Moonglow', 'Potomac', 'Warren') and resistant apple rootstocks ('Geneva' series G.11, G.41, G.935 instead of susceptible M.9/M.26); keep nitrogen fertilization low so shoot growth stays moderate.
recommended_observations: Scout Raspberry (blossoms, fruiting spurs, succulent terminal shoots, branches, rootstock crowns, and immature fruit) weekly during warm, humid spring bloom and early-summer thunderstorms/hail (65–85°F (18–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Fire Blight from Pear Psylla Honeydew Sooty Mold, Twig Borer/Oriental Fruit Moth Flagging (has entry hole/larva in twig), Winter Freeze Dieback.
severity_or_impact: Critical (can kill entire pear trees and dwarf apple trees in a single season)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–85°F (18–29°C) and high humidity (>60%), warm rain, heavy dew, or hail/wind storms during bloom and shoot growth.
host_range: Documented on Raspberry (Rubus idaeus, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Apple, Pear, Raspberry, Blackberry).

topic: Raspberry Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').
symptom_keywords: fuzzy brownish-gray mold, dusty spore masses, stem pruning wound canker, blossom blight, berry gray rot, ghost spot rings on tomato
symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.
recommended_observations: Scout Raspberry (senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits) weekly during cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) from Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight.
severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, brambles, grapes, and high-tunnel tomatoes (major pre- and post-harvest fruit loss)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–75°F (15–24°C) and high relative humidity (>90% rh), fog, rain, and poor air circulation.
host_range: Documented on Raspberry (Rubus idaeus, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Eggplant, Strawberry, Raspberry, Blackberry, Grape, Blueberry).

topic: Raspberry Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot (Phytophthora capsici)
problem_name: Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot
causal_agent: Phytophthora capsici (on Solanaceae, Cucurbits, Legumes); Phytophthora cactorum / P. fragariae (on Strawberry/Apple); Phytophthora cinnamomi / P. nicotianae (on Avocado, Citrus, Papaya, Blueberry, Rosemary, Sage)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown/collar (foot rot/gummosis), stems, leaves, and fruit ('buckeye rot' on tomato; white yeast-like powder on squash/pepper/watermelon)
growth_stage: Any stage after soil saturation or heavy rainfall
season: Warm, rainy summer weather or poorly drained wet soils
humidity_conditions: Saturated, waterlogged, or flooded soil (>24 hours of standing water) and splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Raspberry (Rubus idaeus): Dark brown-to-black water-soaked lesion girdling the stem base/crown right above the soil line ('black shank' in pepper/squash; 'red stele' reddish-pink central root core in strawberry; 'foot rot/gummosis' cracking bark and oozing gum at graft union in citrus; feeder root blackening and canopy dieback in avocado/blueberry/rosemary), causing rapid permanent wilting; on pepper, cucurbit, and eggplant fruits, dark water-soaked blotches rapidly covered in a diagnostic dusting of white, yeast-like or powdered-sugar-like sporangia (on green tomato fruit touching soil, smooth brown 'buckeye rot' target rings).
symptom_keywords: black stem base collar rot, powdered-sugar white sporangia on fruit, buckeye rot on tomato, red stele root core in strawberry, citrus foot rot gummosis, avocado feeder root rot, sudden wilt after rain
symptom_progression: Swimming zoospores released in saturated soil chemotactically swim to roots and crowns, rotting the root system and stem collar within days and splashing onto low-hanging fruits.

management_actions: Remove infected plants and roots; maintain even irrigation and balanced potassium nutrition to help moderately tolerant plants mature fruit; solarize infested garden beds under clear plastic for 6 weeks in midsummer.

causal_agent: Empoasca fabae (Potato Leafhopper), Circulifer tenellus (Beet Leafhopper), and Macrosteles quadrilineatus (Aster Leafhopper)

Potato Leafhopper feeding injects toxic watery saliva that plugs phloem vascular bundles, causing classic 'Hopperburn' on Potato, Beans, Eggplant, Strawberry, and Apple: triangular yellow V-shaped chlorosis starting at the leaf tip and margins, followed by upward or downward rolling/cupping of the leaf blade and crisp reddish-brown scorching of the entire leaf edge as if burned by drought or fertilizer; Beet Leafhopper transmits Beet Curly Top Virus (causing dwarfed, tightly rolled upward leaves with swollen purple veins on tomato, pepper, bean, beet, and squash); Aster Leafhopper transmits Aster Yellows phytoplasma.
