topic: Blackberry Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.

topic: Blackberry Tarnished Plant Bug Management
problem_name: Tarnished Plant Bug (Lygus Bug) and Leaf-Footed Bugs
causal_agent: Lygus lineolaris (Tarnished Plant Bug) and Leptoglossus phyllopus / Leptoglossus zonatus (Leaf-Footed Bugs)
affected_plant_parts: Flower buds, open blossoms, developing berries/fruits (achene seeds on strawberry), pods, and tender shoot tips/petioles
growth_stage: Bud swell and bloom through fruit development
season: Early spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny weather, especially after nearby hay/alfalfa or weeds are mowed
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): Tarnished Plant Bug: small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), oval, brassy-brown mottled insects with a distinct yellow-Triangle ('Y') on the scutellum behind the head; adults and bright yellowish-green nymphs (with 5 black dots on the back) puncture flower buds and developing seeds—on Strawberry and Brambles, feeding on individual achenes (seeds) during bloom stops auxin hormone production in that part of the receptacle, resulting in severely 'buttoned', 'catfaced',nubbin berries with hard, seedy, woody green tips that never swell; on Celery and Lettuce, feeding causes brown sunken lesions along the inner petiole heart ('black joint'); Leaf-Footed Bugs: large (3/4 inch), elongated dark-brown bugs with flattened leaf-like expansions on their hind tibiae and a white zigzag band across the wings that swarm ripening tomatoes, pomegranates, peaches, and pecans in groups, leaving yellow cloudy spots and internal rot.
symptom_keywords: catfaced buttoned strawberry berries with hard seedy green tips, small brassy-brown bug with yellow triangle on back, green nymphs with five black dots, large brown bug with leaf-shaped hind legs and white wing band, celery petiole black joint
symptom_progression: Adults overwinter in weedy field borders and fly into gardens as soon as buds swell in spring; mowing nearby weeds or alfalfa forces mass migrations onto strawberries, peaches, and beans.
distinguishing_features: In Strawberry, distinguish Tarnished Plant Bug injury from Poor Pollination: Tarnished Plant Bug sucks individual achenes hollow, so the seeds in the deformed 'nubbin' tip are packed tightly together and straw-brown (whereas in Poor Pollination, the seeds at the tip are varying sizes and normal yellow-green!).
similar_conditions: Poor Bee Pollination / Frost Injury on Strawberry blossoms, Boron Deficiency, Stink Bugs
risk_factors: Weedy borders containing shepherd's purse, chickweed, pigweed, goldenrod, and fleabane, or mowing weedy areas right when strawberries, peaches, or beans are in bloom!
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days (>65°F) during bloom and fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Highly mobile flying adults moving between broadleaf weeds, forage legumes, and garden blossoms.
management_actions: Tap 10–20 strawberry flower clusters over a white saucer to count greenish nymphs; knock congregation of Leaf-Footed Bug nymphs (orange-red nymphs with black legs) and adults off tomatoes and pomegranates into soapy water; cover non-blooming celery/lettuce or everbearing strawberries with fine insect netting.
prevention_actions: CRITICAL MOWING RULE: NEVER mow weedy field borders, cover crops, or clover patches right when your strawberries, peaches, or snap beans are in bloom—mowing drives resident Tarnished Plant Bugs straight into your garden blossoms! Keep a clean mowed turf strip around strawberry beds from early spring onward.

topic: Blackberry Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained sandy loam or clay loam rich in organic matter (Extension soil texture tags: Clay, High Organic Matter, Loam (Silt), Shallow Rocky; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry)
management_actions: Prepare a well-drained sandy loam or clay loam rich in organic matter adjusted to pH 5.8–6.8 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Blackberry to verify soil pH (5.8–6.8) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Blackberry Cane Blight, Spur Blight, and Anthracnose of Brambles (Elsinoe veneta)
problem_name: Cane Blight, Spur Blight, and Anthracnose of Brambles
causal_agent: Elsinoe veneta (Anthracnose), Didymella applanata (Spur Blight), and Leptosphaeria coniothyrium (Cane Blight)
affected_plant_parts: Primocanes, floricanes, lateral fruiting shoots, buds, and petioles
growth_stage: Spring primocane emergence through second-year floricane fruiting
season: Wet spring and summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, rain splash, and dense un-thinned cane hedgerows
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): Anthracnose: small purplish spots on young green primocanes that enlarge into sunken oval lesions (1/8–1/4 inch) with pale ash-gray centers and raised purple margins ('bird's-eye' cane spots) that crack bark and dry berries; Spur Blight (especially on red raspberry): chocolate-brown to purple V-shaped leaf blotches and dark purple-brown diamond patches surrounding lower buds on primocanes, causing those buds to fail to sprout fruiting laterals next spring; Cane Blight: dark brown-purple cankers spreading down from tipping/pruning wounds on canes, causing fruiting laterals to suddenly wilt and die before harvest.
symptom_keywords: purple sunken gray-centered cane spots, chocolate-purple patches around lower cane buds, sudden wilting of fruiting laterals on second-year canes, cracked cane bark
symptom_progression: Spores from old second-year floricanes splash onto tender emerging first-year primocanes in spring, damaging the vascular bark and buds needed for next summer's crop.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by discrete gray-centered purple-rimmed oval spots (Anthracnose), purple-brown patches centered at lower nodes/buds (Spur Blight), or dieback originating at pruning cuts (Cane Blight).
similar_conditions: Verticillium Wilt, Phytophthora Root Rot (rotted roots and dark water-soaked crown base), Winter Cane Injury, Raspberry Cane Borer
risk_factors: Failure to prune out spent second-year floricanes after harvest, wide crowded hedgerows (>18 inches wide), overhead watering, and tipping canes right before rain.
favorable_conditions: Rainy spring and summer weather in crowded bramble rows.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters on infected 2-year-old canes and spent floricanes, splashing conidia and ascospores onto new green primocanes.
management_actions: Immediately after summer harvest finishes, cut all spent second-year floricanes flush to the ground and remove them from the patch; thin primocanes to 4–5 canes per linear foot in narrow (12–18 inch) trellised rows; perform summer tipping of primocanes only during dry sunny weather.
prevention_actions: Apply a single delayed-dormant liquid lime-sulfur or copper spray in early spring when buds show 1/4 to 1/2 inch of green tip; for fall-bearing primocane raspberries, mowing all canes to the ground every late winter virtually eliminates cane diseases.
recommended_observations: Scout Blackberry (primocanes, floricanes, lateral fruiting shoots, buds, and petioles) weekly during wet spring and summer weather (60–80°F (15–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cane Blight, Spur Blight, and Anthracnose of Brambles from Verticillium Wilt, Phytophthora Root Rot (rotted roots and dark water-soaked crown base), Winter Cane Injury, Raspberry Cane Borer.
severity_or_impact: High (severely reduces winter cane survival and second-year berry yield)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–80°F (15–27°C) and high humidity, rain splash, and dense un-thinned cane hedgerows.
host_range: Documented on Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry).

topic: Blackberry Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).

topic: Blackberry Fire Blight (Erwinia amylovora)

topic: Blackberry Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) (Botrytis cinerea)
problem_name: Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot)
causal_agent: Botrytis cinerea
affected_plant_parts: Senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits
growth_stage: Flowering through fruit ripening and post-harvest storage
season: Cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather
humidity_conditions: High relative humidity (>90% RH), fog, rain, and poor air circulation
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): V-shaped brown necrotic lesions on leaves (often starting where a dead blossom petal falls onto a wet leaf) and tan-brown elliptical stem cankers at pruning stubs covered in dense, dusty, velvety brownish-gray spore masses that puff like smoke when tapped; on berries (strawberry, raspberry, grape), soft light-brown blossom-end rot rapidly covered in fuzzy gray mold; on green tomato fruit, abortive infections leave diagnostic small pale-white halo rings ('ghost spots').
symptom_keywords: fuzzy brownish-gray mold, dusty spore masses, stem pruning wound canker, blossom blight, berry gray rot, ghost spot rings on tomato
symptom_progression: Fungus colonizes dying flower petals or fresh stem pruning wounds as a saprophyte first, then invades healthy adjacent fruit receptacles, stems, or leaves, producing millions of airborne conidia under cool humid conditions.
distinguishing_features: Readily identified by the characteristic velvety, mouse-gray-to-taupe fuzzy conidiophore turf on blighted blossoms, stems, and rotting berries, and pale white 'ghost spot' rings on tomato fruit.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight
risk_factors: Dense unpruned canopies, dead flower petals clinging to developing fruit, overhead watering, high humidity in high tunnels/greenhouses, and excessive nitrogen.
favorable_conditions: Cool temperatures (60–75°F) with relative humidity >90% and free moisture on blossoms or wounds for 6–12+ hours.
transmission_or_spread: Ubiquitous airborne conidia blown from decaying vegetation and overwintering sclerotia on crop debris.
management_actions: Harvest ripe berries every 1–2 days and immediately remove and discard any moldy or damaged fruit from the garden; prune and sucker only in dry sunny morning weather so stem wounds dry quickly; improve canopy ventilation.
prevention_actions: Space plants generously, use straw mulch beneath strawberries, orient rows with prevailing winds, avoid excess spring nitrogen (which creates lush shaded canopies), and irrigate strictly via drip lines.
recommended_observations: Scout Blackberry (senescing blossoms, pruning wounds on stems, leaves, and ripening/immature fruits) weekly during cool, damp, overcast spring, autumn, or high-tunnel weather (60–75°F (15–24°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Gray Mold (Botrytis Blight & Ghost Spot) from Rhizopus Soft Rot (coarse white whiskers with black pinhead sporangia and leaky mushy berries), Sclerotinia White Mold (cottony pure white mycelium + large black sclerotia), Late Blight.
severity_or_impact: High on strawberries, brambles, grapes, and high-tunnel tomatoes (major pre- and post-harvest fruit loss)

topic: Blackberry Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot (Phytophthora capsici)
problem_name: Phytophthora Blight and Crown/Root Rot
causal_agent: Phytophthora capsici (on Solanaceae, Cucurbits, Legumes); Phytophthora cactorum / P. fragariae (on Strawberry/Apple); Phytophthora cinnamomi / P. nicotianae (on Avocado, Citrus, Papaya, Blueberry, Rosemary, Sage)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, crown/collar (foot rot/gummosis), stems, leaves, and fruit ('buckeye rot' on tomato; white yeast-like powder on squash/pepper/watermelon)
growth_stage: Any stage after soil saturation or heavy rainfall
season: Warm, rainy summer weather or poorly drained wet soils
humidity_conditions: Saturated, waterlogged, or flooded soil (>24 hours of standing water) and splashing rain
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): Dark brown-to-black water-soaked lesion girdling the stem base/crown right above the soil line ('black shank' in pepper/squash; 'red stele' reddish-pink central root core in strawberry; 'foot rot/gummosis' cracking bark and oozing gum at graft union in citrus; feeder root blackening and canopy dieback in avocado/blueberry/rosemary), causing rapid permanent wilting; on pepper, cucurbit, and eggplant fruits, dark water-soaked blotches rapidly covered in a diagnostic dusting of white, yeast-like or powdered-sugar-like sporangia (on green tomato fruit touching soil, smooth brown 'buckeye rot' target rings).
symptom_keywords: black stem base collar rot, powdered-sugar white sporangia on fruit, buckeye rot on tomato, red stele root core in strawberry, citrus foot rot gummosis, avocado feeder root rot, sudden wilt after rain
symptom_progression: Swimming zoospores released in saturated soil chemotactically swim to roots and crowns, rotting the root system and stem collar within days and splashing onto low-hanging fruits.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished in pepper and cucurbits by the dark black basal stem girdling ('black shank') and the tight, flat, powdered-sugar-like white coating of sporangia on rotting fruit (unlike fluffy tall cottony Pythium or white fan-like Southern Blight with mustard-seed sclerotia).
similar_conditions: Southern Blight, Pythium Cottony Leak, Fusarium Wilt, Bacterial Wilt, Sclerotinia White Mold
risk_factors: Poorly drained clay soils, low spots where rainwater puddles, over-irrigation, planting crowns/graft unions too deeply, and short rotations between peppers, eggplants, tomatoes, and cucurbits.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–90°F) combined with heavy rainfall or waterlogged soil.
transmission_or_spread: Thick-walled oospores survive in soil for 5–10+ years; motile biflagellate zoospores swim through soil water films and spread in surface runoff and ponded irrigation water.
management_actions: Immediately remove infected plants and rotting fruits; improve surface drainage and never overwater; on citrus and fruit trees, keep mulch 6–12 inches away from the trunk and ensure the graft union is 4–6 inches above soil; on avocado, apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) and maintain a 6-inch coarse leaf/woodchip mulch mat.

severity_or_impact: Critical (causes rapid plant death after heavy rains and persistent soil infestation)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–90°F (24–32°C) and saturated, waterlogged, or flooded soil (>24 hours of standing water) and splashing rain.

topic: Blackberry Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust) (Uromyces appendiculatus)
problem_name: Rust (Bean, Pea, Asparagus, Corn, Allium, Mint & Fig Rust)
causal_agent: Uromyces appendiculatus (Bean); Uromyces viciae-fabae (Pea/Lentil); Puccinia asparagi (Asparagus); Puccinia sorghi (Sweet corn); Puccinia allii (Onion/Garlic/Leek/Chives); Puccinia menthae (Mint); Cerotelium fici (Fig)
affected_plant_parts: Upper and lower leaf surfaces, petioles, stems/spears/ferns, and occasionally pods
growth_stage: Mid-to-late vegetative growth through harvest
season: Moderate temperatures with heavy morning dew or high humidity
humidity_conditions: High humidity and 6–10+ hours of morning dew or fog
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): Numerous small (1–3 mm), raised, dusty, blister-like pustules (uredinia) erupting through the epidermis on both leaf surfaces (and stems/ferns in asparagus and mint) that release a rusty-orange, cinnamon-brown, or brick-red powder of urediniospores when rubbed with a finger, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo; in late season, pustules turn dark brown-to-black as overwintering teliospores form; heavily rusted leaves turn yellow, shrivel, and drop prematurely.

distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the discrete, raised, blister-like pustules that rupture the leaf cuticle and leave a rusty-orange or cinnamon-brown dust on fingers when rubbed.

transmission_or_spread: Obligate biotrophic fungi whose airborne urediniospores blow long distances on wind; autoecious species (bean, asparagus, mint, allium rusts) complete their entire lifecycle on the crop and overwinter as black teliospores on debris/crowns.
management_actions: Remove infected leaves or shear infected mint tops to the ground; apply wettable sulfur, neem oil, or labeled fungicides early when first pustules appear; water at the soil line in early morning.

topic: Blackberry Verticillium Wilt (Verticillium dahliae)
problem_name: Verticillium Wilt
causal_agent: Verticillium dahliae (and Verticillium albo-atrum)
affected_plant_parts: Roots, xylem vascular system, and lower-to-upper foliage
growth_stage: Flowering and fruit/tuber enlargement
season: Cool-to-moderate spring and early summer weather
humidity_conditions: Moist, cool soils followed by warm sunny days that increase transpirational demand
visible_symptoms: On Blackberry (Rubus fruticosus): V-shaped yellow chlorotic blotches developing at the margins and tips of older lower leaflets that soon turn brown and necrotic with a yellow halo; leaves wilt during the heat of the day (often affecting one side of a leaf or branch first); outer older leaves on strawberry crowns turn brown and collapse while inner leaves remain green initially; light tan-to-brown streaking is visible in the vascular tissue near the base of the stem.
symptom_keywords: V-shaped yellow lesion on leaf margin, lower leaf wilting, light tan vascular streaking, outer crown collapse, stunting, midday flagging
symptom_progression: Microsclerotia germinate near root exudates, invade root cortex and xylem, and slowly plug water transport; plants become chronically stunted with progressive lower-leaf V-necrosis and reduced fruit size.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by characteristic V-shaped marginal yellow-and-brown fan lesions at leaflet tips, cooler temperature optimum (68–78°F vs 80–90°F for Fusarium wilt), and lighter tan vascular discoloration restricted closer to the lower stem.

topic: Fig Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs Management
problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Fig (Ficus carica): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.
recommended_observations: Scout Fig (new tender leaf flushes (citrus psyllid & citrus leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (scales & mealybugs)) twice weekly during spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates) (68–92°F (20–33°C)); inspect for mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot to distinguish Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs from Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks).
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Asian Citrus Psyllid vectors fatal HLB; Scales and Mealybugs weaken branches and coat fruit in sooty mold)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–92°F (20–33°C) and warm, humid growing conditions.
host_range: Documented on Fig (Ficus carica, Moraceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Citrus, Lemon, Lime, Avocado, Mango, Guava, Papaya, Banana).

topic: Fig Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Fig (Ficus carica): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)
risk_factors: Late-season berries ripening from July through October (especially fall-bearing raspberries and thornless blackberries), unpicked overripe berries left on canes, shaded humid canopies, and wild bramble/honeysuckle/pokeweed borders.
favorable_conditions: Moderate temperatures (68–80°F) with high humidity.
transmission_or_spread: SWD flies disperse on wind and in transported fruit; Japanese Beetles emerge from turfgrass sod in June–July.
management_actions: HARVEST AND CHILL IMMEDIATELY FOR SWD: pick ripe raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries cleanly every 1–2 days (removing and bagging/solarizing any overripe or damaged berries) and immediately place harvested berries into the refrigerator at 33–38°F (cold storage halts SWD egg hatch and kills young maggots inside the berry!); for Japanese Beetles, knock congregating beetles off grape and raspberry leaves in the cool early morning into a bucket of soapy water (do NOT hang commercial Japanese Beetle pheromone/floral traps near your garden, as university research proves they attract 3–5x more beetles to surrounding plants than they catch!).
prevention_actions: Drape 80-gram fine insect exclusion netting (<1.0 x 0.6 mm mesh size) over blueberry bushes and raspberry/blackberry trellises right after pollination completes as berries begin turning pink; prune bramble rows narrow for sunlight and airflow.

severity_or_impact: Critical for late-summer raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, and cherries (SWD); Moderate to High for Japanese Beetle and Grape Berry Moth

host_range: Documented on Fig (Ficus carica, Moraceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Raspberry, Blackberry, Blueberry, Strawberry, Cherry, Grape, Plum, Peach).

topic: Fig Soil Type, pH Range, Drainage, and Preparation Requirements
soil_type: Well-drained loam, sandy loam, or clay loam amended with compost (Extension soil texture tags: High Organic Matter; drainage: Good Drainage, Moist)
management_actions: Prepare a well-drained loam, sandy loam, or clay loam amended with compost adjusted to pH 6.0–7.5 based on a laboratory soil test. Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost prior to planting to optimize soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
prevention_actions: Avoid compacted, poorly drained, or waterlogged soils that restrict root respiration and predispose roots to Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium rots; use raised beds where native drainage is poor.
recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Fig to verify soil pH (6.0–7.5) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Fig Crown Gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens)
problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Fig (Ficus carica): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.

topic: Fig Nutrient Requirements and Fertilization Schedule
growth_stage: Pre-plant bed preparation, active vegetative growth, and reproductive/storage organ development
management_actions: Very light nitrogen requirement on established in-ground trees (apply only if annual shoot growth is less than 12 inches); excessive nitrogen produces lush 5-ft shoots with few figs that fail to ripen before frost and suffer severe winter dieback
prevention_actions: Base fertilizer rates on a soil test and maintain soil pH at 6.0–7.5 to keep macronutrients and micronutrients bioavailable; avoid over-application of soluble nitrogen salts which can burn roots or skew vegetative-to-reproductive balance.
recommended_observations: Monitor shoot vigor, leaf color on both older lower leaves (mobile nutrients N, P, K, Mg) and new upper leaves (immobile nutrients Fe, Ca, B, Zn, Mn), and fruit/root set.
knowledge_text: Nutrition and fertilizer management for Fig (Ficus carica): Very light nitrogen requirement on established in-ground trees (apply only if annual shoot growth is less than 12 inches); excessive nitrogen produces lush 5-ft shoots with few figs that fail to ripen before frost and suffer severe winter dieback. problem_name: Late-Spring & Early-Autumn Freeze Dieback of Fig Wood
affected_plant_parts: One-year-old fruiting canes (breba wood), terminal buds, and main trunks
growth_stage: Late autumn (<20°F before hardening) or early spring (<25°F after bud swell)
season: Plant container-grown trees in spring after all danger of frost in USDA Zones 7–10 (or in large containers overwintered in an unheated garage in Zones 5–6)

symptom_keywords: fig, late-spring & early-autumn freeze dieback of fig wood, spring frost injury, freeze damage, blackened blossoms, water-soaked flaccid foliage, southwest winter sunscald, dieback
symptom_progression: Because fig wood has a wide spongy pith and breaks dormancy easily during warm late-winter spells, de-acclimated canes freeze rapidly at 15–22°F.
distinguishing_features: Dead, brittle, hollow-pith canes failing to leaf out in spring while vigorous suckers sprout from the surviving underground root crown.
similar_conditions: Phomopsis canker; Fig mosaic virus.
risk_factors: Clear, calm spring nights with radiational cooling in low-lying frost pockets after warm early-spring weather has triggered premature budbreak or emergence.
favorable_conditions: Clear, calm spring nights with radiational cooling in low-lying frost pockets after warm early-spring weather has triggered premature budbreak or emergence.
management_actions: Protect emerging plants or blooms before sunrise using floating row covers, frost blankets, or moist bare soil heat radiation; wait until new buds break after a freeze before pruning dead woody shoots.
prevention_actions: Plant orchards and frost-sensitive perennials on elevated slopes with cold-air drainage, avoid low frost pockets, paint tree trunks white to prevent winter southwest bark splitting, and plant after the local frost-free date.
recommended_observations: Correlate symptom onset across Fig and neighboring garden plants with recent weather extremes (heat, frost, wind, hail, flooding, drought) or nearby herbicide/fertilizer applications, and inspect new growth for recovery.
severity_or_impact: Eliminates the early summer breba crop and forces main-crop regrowth from basal suckers.

risk_factors: Leached sandy soils with low cation exchange capacity (CEC), heavy crop removal during peak fruit or tuber bulking, drought-restricted K+ diffusion in soil films, or excessive applications of competing cations (magnesium, calcium, or ammonium-N).

prevention_actions: Build soil potassium reserves based on soil testing prior to planting heavy-fruiting or root crops, avoid excessive ammonium or magnesium fertilization that antagonizes K+ uptake, and maintain uniform drip irrigation during fruit swell.

Fruit/seed profile: The infructescence is a ripened receptacle (syconium), not an ovary, that forms in late summer or fall on new wood. Sometimes a small second spring fruiting on new wood occurs. topic: Cherry Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs Management
problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.
recommended_observations: Scout Cherry (new tender leaf flushes (citrus psyllid & citrus leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (scales & mealybugs)) twice weekly during spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates) (68–92°F (20–33°C)); inspect for mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot to distinguish Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs from Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks).
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Asian Citrus Psyllid vectors fatal HLB; Scales and Mealybugs weaken branches and coat fruit in sooty mold)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–92°F (20–33°C) and warm, humid growing conditions.

topic: Cherry Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot Management
problem_name: Codling Moth, Oriental Fruit Moth, and Apple Maggot
problem_category: Internal Fruit-Boring Pest of Tree Fruits
causal_agent: Cydia pomonella (Codling Moth), Grapholita molesta (Oriental Fruit Moth), and Rhagoletis pomonella (Apple Maggot / 'Railroad Worm')
affected_plant_parts: Internal fruit core/seeds (Codling Moth), fruit flesh (Apple Maggot), and tender spring shoot tips + fruit (Oriental Fruit Moth)
growth_stage: Petal fall through harvest
season: May through September
humidity_conditions: Warm dusk temperatures (>60°F) for moth egg-laying; summer rains for Apple Maggot fly emergence
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Codling Moth ('the worm in the apple'): a pinkish-white caterpillar (1/2 to 3/4 inch) with a brown head bores through the side or blossom calyx cup straight to the center core of apples, pears, and walnuts to eat the seeds, pushing a pile of coarse, reddish-brown, sawdust-like frass out of the entry hole ('frass plug'); Oriental Fruit Moth: in spring, first-generation pinkish larvae bore 2–4 inches down into the tender terminal shoot tips of peach, nectarine, plum, and apple trees, causing the top 3–4 leaves of new shoots to wilt and flag brown ('shoot flagging'), while summer generations bore into ripening peaches (often right down the stem channel without leaving an obvious external hole!); Apple Maggot ('Railroad Worm'): small black flies with distinctive dark 'F'-shaped wing bands puncture apple skin in summer, and legless white maggots chew brown, winding, thread-like trails all through the apple flesh, making the fruit lumpy and dimpled.

similar_conditions: Plum Curculio (crescent-shaped corky scar on young fruit skin), Fire Blight (scorched shepherd's crook without a larva burrow inside the twig)

transmission_or_spread: Adult moths and maggot flies fly between neighboring backyard fruit trees and wild crabapples/hawthorns.

topic: Cherry Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla Management
problem_name: Peachtree Borer, Lesser Peachtree Borer, and Pear Psylla
problem_category: Wood-Boring Moth & Sap-Feeding Psyllid Pests of Fruit Trees
causal_agent: Synanthedon exitiosa (Peachtree Borer), Synanthedon pictipes (Lesser Peachtree Borer), and Cacopsylla pyricola (Pear Psylla)
affected_plant_parts: Lower trunk at and 2–3 inches below the soil line (Peachtree Borer), upper scaffold limb wounds/cankers (Lesser Peachtree Borer), and pear leaves/fruits (Pear Psylla)
growth_stage: Perennial woody trunk/limbs and summer foliage
season: Summer egg-laying with year-round larval feeding (Borers); early spring through autumn (Pear Psylla)
humidity_conditions: Warm summer days for clearwing moth flight; lush nitrogen-stimulated pear shoots for Pear Psylla
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Peachtree Borer: masses of thick, amber-to-clear, jelly-like gum MIXED WITH coarse reddish-brown sawdust-like insect frass and empty brown pupal skins protruding at the base of the trunk right at the soil line of peach, plum, and cherry trees; beneath the bark, 1-inch-long creamy-white caterpillars with dark-brown heads tunnel through the cambium around the root collar, girdling and killing young trees and causing older trees to yellow and die back on one side (Lesser Peachtree Borer causes identical frass-filled gummosis higher up on scaffold branch crotches and cankers); Pear Psylla: tiny (2 mm) cicada-like reddish-brown winged adults and flat, yellowish-green-to-brown wingpad nymphs submerged inside droplets of sticky clear honeydew on pear leaves and shoots, causing black sooty mold russeting on pears and sudden blackened leaf blotches ('psylla shock').
symptom_keywords: thick amber jelly gum mixed with brown sawdust frass at base of peach trunk, creamy white caterpillar under bark at soil line, brown pupal skins sticking out of trunk base, day-flying blue-black wasp-mimic clearwing moth, pear leaves dripping honeydew with black leaf blotches
symptom_progression: Day-flying metallic blue-black clearwing moths (females have a bright orange band across the abdomen) lay eggs on the lower trunk from June through September; larvae tunnel under the bark all autumn, winter, and spring.
distinguishing_features: CRITICAL DISTINCTION for Stone Fruit Gummosis: Amber gum oozing from a peach, plum, or cherry trunk that is CLEAR and free of sawdust/frass is caused by abiotic injury, Cytospora fungus, or Bacterial Canker; gum that contains gritty brown sawdust-like frass particles and cast skins at the soil line is Peachtree Borer!
similar_conditions: Bacterial Canker / Cytospora Canker (clear amber gum WITHOUT brown insect sawdust/frass), Crown Gall, Fire Blight (on Pear)
risk_factors: String-trimmer or lawnmower bark wounds at the base of stone fruit trunks, volcano mulching piled against the bark, winter sunscald cracks, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer on pear trees (which pushes succulent water sprouts favored by Pear Psylla).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer months (June–September).
transmission_or_spread: Strong-flying diurnal clearwing moths attracted to wounded or stressed stone fruit bark; Pear Psylla overwinters as adults in bark crevices.
management_actions: For Peachtree Borer: inspect the trunk base at the soil line in spring and autumn, carefully probe active frass-filled gum holes with a flexible wire to puncture the larva under the bark, or apply beneficial entomopathogenic nematodes (Steinernema carpocapsae) as a moist drench around the lower trunk in late summer/spring; for Pear Psylla: apply a delayed-dormant horticultural oil spray in early spring just before buds open to deter egg-laying on pear twigs, and wash honeydew off leaves with insecticidal soap.
prevention_actions: Keep mulch pulled back 4–6 inches from the trunk base of peach, plum, and cherry trees (never pile mulch against the bark!), protect trunks with breathable white tree guards against string-trimmers and winter sunscald, and whitewash south-west trunks with 50:50 water-diluted white interior latex paint; summer-prune upright water sprouts out of pear trees.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–90°F (15–32°C) and warm summer days for clearwing moth flight; lush nitrogen-stimulated pear shoots for pear psylla.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Peach, Plum, Cherry, Pear).

topic: Cherry Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies Management
problem_name: Plum Curculio and Cherry Fruit Flies
problem_category: Fruit-Scarring & Internal Larval Pest of Stone and Pome Fruits
causal_agent: Conotrachelus nenuphar (Plum Curculio) and Rhagoletis cingulata / Rhagoletis fausta / Rhagoletis indifferens (Cherry Fruit Flies)
affected_plant_parts: Immature newly set fruits (petal fall / shuck split) and ripening cherries
growth_stage: Petal fall / shuck split through harvest
season: Spring (Plum Curculio) and early summer as cherries turn yellow-red (Cherry Fruit Fly)
humidity_conditions: Warm (>70°F) humid spring days and nights following rain
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Plum Curculio: a small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), rough-backed, brownish-black snout weevil with grey-white flecks and four prominent humps on its wing covers that emerges at petal fall / shuck split; the female chews a small hole in the tiny green fruitlet, inserts an egg, and then cuts a diagnostic crescent-shaped (D-shaped / half-moon) slit right underneath the egg so the rapidly expanding fruit flesh will not crush her egg! In apples and pears, the fruit expansion usually crushes the larva anyway, leaving a raised, corky, D-shaped fan scar on the mature apple skin; in plums, peaches, cherries, and blueberries, the legless, curved, yellowish-white grub with a brown head tunnels to the pit, causing clear gummy sap droplets to ooze from the crescent scar and causing premature fruit drop or ripe wormy fruit; Cherry Fruit Fly: legless white maggots (no head capsule!) feed around the pit of ripe red cherries without external deformity until sunken soft spots and exit holes appear.
symptom_keywords: crescent-shaped half-moon scar on young green plum peach or apple, gummy clear sap droplet oozing from crescent cut, rough humpbacked brown snout weevil playing dead when tapped, legless grub with brown head next to peach or plum pit, headless white maggot inside ripe cherry
symptom_progression: Overwintered Plum Curculio adults walk/fly from woodlots into fruit trees during bloom and attack fruitlets for 3–5 weeks after petal fall whenever temperatures exceed 70°F; Cherry Fruit Flies emerge from soil just as early cherries show the first blush of yellow-pink color.
distinguishing_features: Plum Curculio is unmistakably identified by the signature crescent-shaped (half-moon) oviposition scar cut into the skin of young apples, plums, peaches, and cherries; inside ripe cherries, Plum Curculio larva has a distinct brown head capsule and curved C-shape, whereas Cherry Fruit Fly maggot is headless and cone-shaped.
similar_conditions: Tarnished Plant Bug / Stink Bug Catfacing (sunken dimples without a crescent-shaped flap cut), Hail Scars, Codling Moth
risk_factors: Fruit trees planted adjacent to deciduous woodlots, hedgerows, or brush piles (where Plum Curculio adults overwinter in leaf litter) and uncollected dropped stone fruits.
favorable_conditions: Spring days reaching 70–75°F+ or warm nights (>60°F) right after petal fall / shuck split.
transmission_or_spread: Adults overwinter in wooded border litter and migrate into trees in spring; mature larvae exit fallen fruit to pupate 1–2 inches deep in the soil.
management_actions: Lay a light-colored sheet on the ground under plum, peach, and apple branches in the cool early morning for the 3 weeks after petal fall and sharply tap limbs with a padded stick—Plum Curculio adults fold their legs, play dead ('thanatosis'), and drop onto the sheet looking like bits of bark or bird droppings so you can collect and destroy them; spray kaolin clay (Surround—keep a white coat on fruitlets from petal fall for 4 weeks) or spinosad (for Cherry Fruit Fly, hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate as soon as cherries turn yellow-blush).
prevention_actions: Pick up and dispose of all 'June drop' fruitlets under plum, peach, cherry, and apple trees every 2 days in May/June before curculio grubs crawl out into the soil; prune trees open (Plum Curculio strongly prefers cool, dark, dense interior canopies).

severity_or_impact: Critical east of the Rocky Mountains (the #1 early-season insect pest of plums, peaches, cherries, and apples)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 60–85°F (15–29°C) and warm (>70°f) humid spring days and nights following rain.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Plum, Peach, Cherry, Apple, Pear, Blueberry).

topic: Cherry Spotted Wing Drosophila Management
problem_name: Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), Japanese Beetle, and Grape Berry Moth
causal_agent: Drosophila suzukii (Spotted Wing Drosophila - SWD), Popillia japonica (Japanese Beetle), and Paralobesia viteana (Grape Berry Moth)
affected_plant_parts: Ripening soft-skinned berries (SWD), upper canopy leaves/silks/fruits (Japanese Beetle), and grape clusters (Grape Berry Moth)
growth_stage: Ripening fruit (SWD) and mid-summer vegetative/fruiting growth
season: Mid-June through autumn frost
humidity_conditions: Humid summer weather (SWD activity pauses above 90°F in dry heat)
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD): unlike common household vinegar/fruit flies that can only lay eggs in overripe rotting fruit, female SWD possess a heavily sclerotized, saw-toothed ovipositor that slices directly through the intact skin of healthy, firm, ripening raspberries, blackberries, blueberries, cherries, and late strawberries right on the bush! Within 2–3 days of harvest, healthy-looking berries suddenly soften, dimple, leak juice, and collapse from within as 1–10 tiny (2–3 mm) creamy-white headless maggots feed inside; Japanese Beetle: 3/8-inch metallic green beetles with coppery-brown wing covers and 5 white hair tufts along each side skeletonize upper-canopy grape, raspberry, bean, basil, and fruit tree leaves into lacework and clip sweet corn silks; Grape Berry Moth: small greenish-purple caterpillars web together grape florets/berries and bore into ripening grapes, leaving webbed red/purple-stained clusters.
symptom_keywords: healthy ripe raspberries and blueberries collapsing soft and leaky within days of picking, tiny white maggots floating out of berries in salt water test, small tan vinegar fly with dark spot on male wingtip, metallic green-and-copper beetle skeletonizing upper grape and raspberry leaves into lace, webbed hollowed grape berries
symptom_progression: SWD populations build modestly in early summer (so June-bearing strawberries and early June blueberries often escape!), then explode exponentially from July through October on summer/fall raspberries, blackberries, and late blueberries, completing a generation every 8–14 days.
distinguishing_features: Perform the 'Salt-Water Float Test' on suspect berries: dissolve 1 tablespoon of salt in 1 cup of warm water, gently mash 10–15 ripe berries in a zip-top bag with the salt water, and wait 15 minutes—any white SWD maggots inside will float to the top of the liquid! Male SWD flies have a single distinct dark spot near the tip of each wing.
similar_conditions: Sap Beetles / Common Vinegar Flies (only enter already split, bird-pecked, or overripe rotting fruit), Raspberry Fruitworm (light-brown beetle larva in early summer)

topic: Cherry Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits (Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae)
problem_name: Bacterial Canker and Coryneum Blight (Shot Hole) of Stone Fruits
causal_agent: Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae (Bacterial Canker) and Wilsonomyces carpophilus (Coryneum Blight / Shot Hole)

growth_stage: Autumn leaf drop through winter dormancy and spring budbreak
season: Cool, wet autumn, winter, and early spring weather
humidity_conditions: Rainy autumn/winter/spring weather and freeze-thaw cycles
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Bacterial Canker: sunken, dark, water-soaked elliptical cankers on branches and trunks that ooze copious amounts of thick, amber-to-orange gummy sap ('gummosis') in spring and emit a distinct sour, fermented beer-like odor when the dead brown inner bark is sliced open; whole spurs, buds, or scaffold limbs fail to leaf out or suddenly wilt and die in spring; on leaves, small circular purple-brown spots dry up and fall out leaving 'shot-holes'; Coryneum Blight (Fungal Shot Hole): small reddish-purple spots with tan centers on buds, twigs (forming concentric gummy twig cankers), leaves (falling out as shot-holes), and raised rough purple-scabby spots on peach/apricot fruit.
symptom_keywords: amber gummy sap oozing from bark cankers, sour fermented bark odor, circular leaf spots dropping out as shot-holes, dead dormant buds, purple scabby fruit spots
symptom_progression: Pseudomonas bacteria colonize leaf scars in autumn rain and ice-nucleate inside dormant buds/bark during winter freezes; in spring, cankers girdle branches and ooze gum.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished from Cytospora/Leucostoma Perennial Canker and Peach Tree Borer by: (1) Bacterial Canker produces a sour odor under the bark and lacks insect sawdust/frass inside the gum (unlike Peach Tree Borer at the soil line, which mixes dark sawdust frass into the gum), and (2) Coryneum Blight kills dormant winter buds with tiny gummy twig lesions.

favorable_conditions: Cool, wet autumn and early-spring rains (50–65°F) combined with winter freeze events.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 45–70°F (7–21°C) and rainy autumn/winter/spring weather and freeze-thaw cycles.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Peach, Plum, Cherry).

topic: Cherry Bacterial Spot (Xanthomonas spp.)
problem_name: Bacterial Spot
causal_agent: Xanthomonas spp. (X. euvesicatoria, X. vesicatoria, X. perforans, X. gardneri on Solanaceae; X. arboricola pv. pruni on Stone Fruits; X. cucurbitae on Cucurbits)

growth_stage: Seedling transplant stage through fruit maturation
season: Warm, rainy, humid summer weather
humidity_conditions: High humidity, driving rain, wind-blown mist, and overhead irrigation
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Small (1/8 inch / 3 mm), irregular, greasy water-soaked dark brown-to-black spots on leaves that often develop yellow halos, coalesce into ragged necrotic blotches, and cause severe defoliation (especially in pepper, or 'shot-hole' drop-out in peach/plum leaves); on green tomato and pepper fruit, small water-soaked blisters enlarge into raised, scabby, corky brown-to-black warts (1/8–1/4 inch) with sunken centers.

symptom_progression: Bacteria enter through stomata and hydathodes or wind/sand wounds; foliar spots multiply rapidly after summer thunderstorms, causing heavy leaf drop and sunscald of exposed scabby fruit.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished on fruit by raised, rough, scabby brown spots without white halos (whereas Bacterial Canker produces 'bird's-eye' spots with flat white halos and Septoria rarely spots fruit); on leaves, lesions look greasy on the underside and lack fungal pycnidia or concentric target rings.
similar_conditions: Bacterial Speck (prefers cooler <75°F weather and tiny <1 mm superficial black fruit specks), Bacterial Canker, Septoria Leaf Spot, Early Blight
risk_factors: Contaminated seed or commercial transplants, working in wet gardens, overhead watering, and warm driving rainstorms.
favorable_conditions: Warm temperatures (75–86°F) with frequent rain, high humidity, and wind-driven water splash.

management_actions: Never handle, prune, or harvest plants when leaves are wet; use drip irrigation; apply fixed copper + mancozeb or biological bactericides preventatively when warm rainy weather is forecast; remove heavily infected early transplants.
prevention_actions: Purchase certified pathogen-free seed (or hot-water treat seed at 122°F/50°C for 25 minutes) and disease-resistant pepper cultivars (carrying Bs1, Bs2, Bs3, Bs4 resistance genes); rotate away from host crops for 2–3 years; mulch beds to reduce splash.
recommended_observations: Scout Cherry (leaves, stems, petioles, pedicels, blossoms, and developing green fruit) weekly during warm, rainy, humid summer weather (75–86°F (24–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Bacterial Spot from Bacterial Speck (prefers cooler <75°F weather and tiny <1 mm superficial black fruit specks), Bacterial Canker, Septoria Leaf Spot, Early Blight.

geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 75–86°F (24–30°C) and high humidity, driving rain, wind-blown mist, and overhead irrigation.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Tomato, Pepper, Peach, Plum, Cherry).

topic: Cherry Black Knot of Plum and Cherry (Apiosporina morbosa)
problem_name: Black Knot of Plum and Cherry
causal_agent: Apiosporina morbosa
affected_plant_parts: Twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs
growth_stage: Spring shoot elongation through perennial woody growth (2-year lifecycle)
season: Wet spring weather for infection; visible year-round (especially in dormant winter)
humidity_conditions: Spring rain wetting emerging green shoots
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Elongated, rough, coal-black, hard, warty, charcoal-like cylindrical swellings ('knots', 1 to 12+ inches long) encasing twigs and branches; first-year knots start in late summer as subtle olive-green velvety corky swellings that rupture the bark, then turn hard, rough, and jet-black in their second summer/winter, gradually girdling and killing the branch beyond the knot.
symptom_keywords: coal-black warty branch swellings, charcoal-like twig galls, rough black cylindrical knots on plum branches, girdled dead limbs
symptom_progression: Ascospores ejected from 2-year-old knots during spring rains infect succulent new green twigs; soft olive-green swellings appear the first autumn and harden into rough jet-black spore-releasing knots the second year.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the hard, rough, coal-black tar-like woody knots wrapped around plum and cherry twigs.
similar_conditions: Crown Gall (occurs at roots/crown base), Bacterial Canker (sunken gummy bark lesions rather than raised black knots)
risk_factors: Nearby wild cherry or wild plum trees (especially chokecherry Prunus virginiana and black cherry P. serotina) harboring black knots in woodlots/hedgerows, and susceptible plum cultivars ('Stanley', 'Damson', 'Shiro').
favorable_conditions: Rainy spring weather between budbreak and shuck split at 55–77°F.
transmission_or_spread: Wind- and rain-borne ascospores discharged from 2-year-old black knots in spring.
management_actions: PRUNE OUT KNOTS IN WINTER: during late-winter dormancy (before March bud swell when spores are released), prune out all knotted branches by cutting at least 4–6 inches BELOW the visible swelling (as internal fungal mycelium extends several inches beyond the knot), sterilize loppers with 70% alcohol between cuts, and burn or bag/trash the pruned knots immediately (disconnected knots left on the ground still shoot spores!).
prevention_actions: Remove wild plum and chokecherry trees within 500 ft of the garden; plant resistant plum cultivars ('President'); inspect trees every winter.
recommended_observations: Scout Cherry (twigs, fruiting spurs, branches, and main scaffold limbs) weekly during wet spring weather for infection; visible year-round (especially in dormant winter) (55–77°F (13–25°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Black Knot of Plum and Cherry from Crown Gall (occurs at roots/crown base), Bacterial Canker (sunken gummy bark lesions rather than raised black knots).
severity_or_impact: High on plums and cherries (unchecked knots girdle scaffold limbs and ruin the entire tree within a few years)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–77°F (13–25°C) and spring rain wetting emerging green shoots.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Plum, Cherry, Peach).

topic: Cherry Brown Rot of Stone Fruits (Monilinia fructicola)
problem_name: Brown Rot of Stone Fruits
causal_agent: Monilinia fructicola (and Monilinia laxa)
affected_plant_parts: Blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits
growth_stage: Spring bloom and final 3 weeks of fruit ripening through post-harvest
season: Warm, wet, humid spring bloom and summer harvest periods
humidity_conditions: High humidity and rain or prolonged wetness during bloom and fruit ripening
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Blossom & Twig Blight: open spring flowers suddenly turn brown, wither, and cling to the twig inside a drop of amber gum, girdling the fruiting twig; Fruit Rot: small circular light-brown soft spots on ripening peaches, plums, or cherries that expand across the entire fruit within 24–48 hours and erupt in concentric tufts of dusty tan-to-ash-gray conidia spores; rotted fruits shrivel into wrinkled, hard black/gray 'mummies' that hang on the tree through winter.
symptom_keywords: soft brown fruit rot, dusty tan-gray spore tufts on fruit, shriveled hanging fruit mummies, blighted gummy blossoms, twig dieback
symptom_progression: Spring spores from overwintered mummies infect blossoms and twigs; as fruits ripen and sugar rises in summer, secondary conidia invade through microscopic cuticle cracks or insect wounds (plum curculio, oriental fruit moth, Japanese beetle, stink bugs), rotting whole crops in days.
distinguishing_features: Distinguished by the rapid, firm-yet-soft brown decay covered in powdery tan/buff-gray spore tufts (unlike black Rhizopus rot whiskers) and the shriveled mummified fruits hanging on branches.
similar_conditions: Rhizopus Rot (black coarse mold whiskers in storage), Bacterial Spot, Anthracnose, Botrytis Gray Mold
risk_factors: Leaving mummified fruits hanging in trees or lying on the ground over winter, unharvested overripe fruit, insect feeding punctures, fruit cracking from rain, and dense unpruned canopies.
favorable_conditions: Warm (70–80°F), rainy, or humid weather during spring bloom and the final 3 weeks before harvest.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in hanging and fallen fruit mummies and twig cankers; conidia and ascospores spread by wind, rain splash, and fruit-feeding insects.
management_actions: SANITATION IS PARAMOUNT: pick up and destroy all fallen fruit during summer and remove every single shriveled mummy from the tree and ground during winter pruning; thin fruits so they do not touch each other in clusters; control plum curculio and oriental fruit moth whose feeding holes let brown rot in.
prevention_actions: Prune peach, plum, and cherry trees to an open center for sunlight and rapid drying; harvest fruit promptly as it matures.
recommended_observations: Scout Cherry (blossoms, fruiting spurs, young twigs, and ripening fruits) weekly during warm, wet, humid spring bloom and summer harvest periods (68–80°F (20–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Brown Rot of Stone Fruits from Rhizopus Rot (black coarse mold whiskers in storage), Bacterial Spot, Anthracnose, Botrytis Gray Mold.
severity_or_impact: Critical (the most destructive disease of peaches, plums, and cherries; can rot 50–100% of ripening fruit in wet summers)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–80°F (20–27°C) and high humidity and rain or prolonged wetness during bloom and fruit ripening.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Peach, Plum, Cherry).

problem_name: Crown Gall
causal_agent: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (syn. Rhizobium radiobacter) and Allorhizobium vitis (Grape Crown Gall)
affected_plant_parts: Root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes
growth_stage: Nursery transplant establishment through mature perennial growth
season: Spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking)
humidity_conditions: Moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks
visible_symptoms: On Cherry (Prunus avium): Rough, rounded, warty, tumor-like woody outgrowths ('galls', ranging from pea-sized nodules to 2–6+ inch gnarled masses) developing on major roots, at the root collar/graft union near the soil line, or along the lower trunk and bramble/grape canes; young galls in spring are light tan, spongy, or fleshy with no bark covering, then turn dark brown-to-black, hard, corky, and deeply fissured as they age; severely galled plants show stunted shoot growth, small chlorotic leaves, and reduced winter hardiness.
symptom_keywords: rough woody tumor-like galls at soil line, warty gnarled root collar swelling, corky fissured cane galls on grape or raspberry, stunted woody growth
symptom_progression: During root pruning, planting, cultivation, or winter freeze cracking, Agrobacterium attaches to wounded plant cells and transfers a segment of its Ti (tumor-inducing) plasmid DNA directly into the plant's own chromosomes, reprogramming the plant cells to overproduce auxin and cytokinin hormones and divide uncontrollably into a gall.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified by the rounded, rough, corky tumor-like galls on the root crown, graft union, or lower canes (note: once the Ti plasmid DNA is inserted into the plant cells, the gall continues growing even if the bacteria are killed, so chemical sprays cannot cure existing galls!).
similar_conditions: Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors)
risk_factors: Planting visibly galled nursery stock, winter trunk splitting from cold snaps (especially in Vitis vinifera grapes and brambles), cultivation/string-trimmer wounds at the trunk base, and planting into infested soil.
favorable_conditions: Warm growing temperatures following winter freeze cracks or mechanical root/crown wounding.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne bacteria surviving for years in soil and systemic inside asymptomatic nursery propagation wood (especially grape and bramble cuttings); spread by contaminated nursery stock, soil movement, and pruning tools.
management_actions: CAREFULLY INSPECT EVERY BARE-ROOT TREE, VINE, AND BRAMBLE BEFORE PLANTING: reject and discard any nursery plant with abnormal swellings or galls on the roots or crown; protect lower trunks from string-trimmer injury and hill soil or mulch around cold-tender grape graft unions in winter to prevent freeze cracking.
prevention_actions: Dip bare-root nursery fruit trees and caneberries prior to planting in a biological control suspension of non-pathogenic Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 or K1026 (which produces agrocin 84 antibiotic to block crown gall bacteria from infecting planting wounds); rotate out of infested sites into grass/corn cover crops for 3–4 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Cherry (root crown (at the soil line), structural roots, graft unions, and lower woody trunks/canes) weekly during spring and summer active growth (especially following winter freeze cracking) (68–86°F (20–30°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Crown Gall from Black Knot of Plum/Cherry (elongated coal-black fungal swellings on upper twigs rather than root crown), Graft Union Burl/Callus (smooth uniform swelling around graft line), Root-Knot Nematode (small bead-like galls inside fine feeder roots rather than woody surface tumors).
severity_or_impact: High on grapes, brambles, stone fruits, and walnuts (girdles vascular flow at the crown and weakens or kills vines/trees)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–86°F (20–30°C) and moist soils and winter freeze-thaw injury to lower trunks.
host_range: Documented on Cherry (Prunus avium, Rosaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Grape, Raspberry, Blackberry, Apple, Pear, Peach, Plum, Cherry).
