topic: Avocado Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs Management
problem_name: Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs
causal_agent: Diaphorina citri (Asian Citrus Psyllid), Phyllocnistis citrella (Citrus Leafminer), Aonidiella / Coccus / Ceroplastes spp. (Armored and Soft Scales), and Planococcus / Pseudococcus spp. (Mealybugs)
affected_plant_parts: New tender leaf flushes (Citrus Psyllid & Citrus Leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (Scales & Mealybugs)
growth_stage: New vegetative shoot flushes and year-round perennial growth
season: Spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates)
humidity_conditions: Warm, humid growing conditions
visible_symptoms: On Avocado (Persea americana): Asian Citrus Psyllid: tiny (3–4 mm) mottled brown insects that rest on new citrus shoots with their bodies tilted up at a distinctive 45-degree angle; yellow-orange nymphs feed exclusively on unfolded feather-stage new flush leaves, excreting curly white waxy tubules and twisting/notching the shoot tips while transmitting fatal Citrus Greening (HLB); Citrus Leafminer: tiny silvery moth larvae tunnel serpentine, glistening silvery mines packed with a central dark line of frass on the underside of young citrus leaves, curling and twisting new leaves (without harming mature leaves!); Scales & Mealybugs: immobile, dome-shaped brown/tan shells (Soft Scales) or flattened circular armored shields (Armored Scales) encrusted on twigs and leaves, or oval soft pink/white insects coated in fluffy white cottony wax (Mealybugs) tucked in stem axils and fruit clusters, causing yellowing, twig dieback, sticky honeydew, and black sooty mold.
symptom_keywords: mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot, yellow nymphs with curly white waxy tubules on feather flush, glistening silvery serpentine mines curling new citrus leaves, immobile brown bumps on twigs, fluffy white cottony mealybug masses in fruit clusters and stem nodes
symptom_progression: Citrus Psyllid and Citrus Leafminer attack ONLY tender, newly expanding leaf flushes; Scales release microscopic mobile 'crawlers' in spring/summer before cementing down under waxy shields.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish Citrus Leafminer curling from Aphid curling on lemon/lime trees: Citrus Leafminer leaves a shiny, silvery serpentine mine with a dark central frass line inside the curled young leaf; distinguish Scales from normal woody lenticels by flicking a bump with a fingernail—a Scale insect pops off easily!
similar_conditions: Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks)
risk_factors: Frequent light nitrogen applications or frequent summer pruning of citrus trees (which forces continuous flushes of tender young leaves that breed Psyllids and Leafminers all summer!), ant tending of scales and mealybugs, and winter indoor stress on container citrus.
favorable_conditions: Warm weather during new shoot flushes.
transmission_or_spread: Wind-borne flight (Psyllids and Leafminer moths), crawling ants, and infested nursery stock.
management_actions: For Citrus Leafminer: DO NOT prune off the curled mined leaves (even though they look twisted, the green parts still photosynthesize for the tree!) and apply horticultural/neem oil or spinosad onto new leaf flushes as soon as tiny feather leaves reach 1/2 inch; for Scales and Mealybugs: apply a 1–2% horticultural oil spray during dormancy and when spring crawlers emerge, dab indoor mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol, and band tree trunks with sticky barriers over tape to block ants from protecting scales/mealybugs from ladybugs (Cryptolaemus montrouzieri).
prevention_actions: Fertilize and prune citrus trees ONLY once in late winter/early spring so the tree produces a single strong spring flush when Citrus Leafminer numbers are lowest, rather than continuous summer flushes.
recommended_observations: Scout Avocado (new tender leaf flushes (citrus psyllid & citrus leafminer), woody twigs/bark, leaf midribs, and fruit surfaces (scales & mealybugs)) twice weekly during spring through autumn (and year-round in warm climates) (68–92°F (20–33°C)); inspect for mottled brown insect resting at 45-degree angle on citrus shoot to distinguish Citrus Psyllid, Citrus Leafminer, Scales, and Mealybugs from Aphids, Whiteflies, Citrus Canker (raised corky lesions with yellow halos that often colonize Citrus Leafminer tracks).
severity_or_impact: High to Critical (Asian Citrus Psyllid vectors fatal HLB; Scales and Mealybugs weaken branches and coat fruit in sooty mold)

problem_name: Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm
causal_agent: Helicoverpa zea
affected_plant_parts: Sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads
growth_stage: Silking, flowering, and fruit/pod set
season: Mid-summer through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm weather and southerly summer wind currents
visible_symptoms: On Artichoke (Cynara cardunculus): In Sweet Corn: caterpillars hatch on fresh silks, clip silks, and tunnel down the silk channel into the tip of the cob, chewing kernels in the top 1–2 inches of the ear and packing the tip with moist brown frass (usually only ONE large caterpillar per ear tip because larvae are cannibalistic!); In Tomato, Pepper, & Okra ('Tomato Fruitworm'): caterpillars bore a deep, circular hole right next to the stem/calyx attachment of green or ripening fruit, hollowing out an internal cavity filled with wet brown frass and cast skins that causes premature ripening and watery rot; caterpillars (1.5 inches long) vary wildly in color from pale yellow-green or pink to dark brown with alternating light and dark stripes and tiny microscopic spines ('microspines') on the skin.
symptom_keywords: caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear, moist brown frass in corn silk channel, deep circular bore hole at stem end of green tomato, hollowed frass-filled fruit cavity
symptom_progression: Nocturnal tan moths lay single, dome-shaped, ribbed creamy-white eggs directly on fresh green corn silks or on tomato leaves adjacent to flower clusters; hatching larvae immediately crawl into the silk channel or under the fruit calyx within hours.
distinguishing_features: In Sweet Corn, Corn Earworm feeds strictly down from the silk tip (and is cannibalistic so only 1 large worm occupies the tip), whereas European Corn Borer bores through the side husk or ear shank as well; on Tomato, Fruitworm bores deep into the fruit interior at the calyx end (unlike Hornworms which chew open surface craters).
similar_conditions: European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm
risk_factors: Late-planted sweet corn and late-summer tomatoes maturing in August–September when migratory moth flights peak.
favorable_conditions: Warm summer nights (>70°F) during corn silking and tomato fruit set.
transmission_or_spread: Adult moths overwinter in southern states (south of ~40°N latitude) and migrate hundreds of miles northward each summer on warm nocturnal wind currents.
management_actions: In Sweet Corn: apply 5–10 drops (1/4 teaspoon) of food-grade mineral oil or vegetable oil mixed with Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad directly into the silk channel at the tip of each ear 3–5 days after silks first appear (once silks begin to brown at the tips, so pollination is not blocked!); in Tomatoes/Beans/Okra: apply Bt or spinosad when eggs/small larvae appear on leaves before they bore under the fruit calyx.
prevention_actions: Plant early-maturing sweet corn cultivars as early in spring as soil temperature allows to harvest before peak late-summer moth flights; select sweet corn hybrids with tight, long husk extensions beyond the ear tip; encourage Trichogramma egg-parasitoid wasps and Orius minute pirate bugs (which eat earworm eggs on silks).
recommended_observations: Scout Artichoke (sweet corn silks and ear tips, tomato/pepper fruits (stem/calyx end), bean/cowpea/okra pods, and lettuce heads) twice weekly during mid-summer through autumn (75–92°F (24–33°C)); inspect for caterpillar feeding in top tip of sweet corn ear to distinguish Corn Earworm / Tomato Fruitworm / Cotton Bollworm from European Corn Borer (bores through stalk, tassel, and side of ear husk), Fall Armyworm (chews ragged holes in whorl leaves and side of ear), Pinworm.

affected_plant_parts: Leaves and petioles (stalks)
growth_stage: Mid-vegetative growth through harvest

management_actions: Use drip irrigation only and never walk through or harvest parsley, celery, or lettuce while foliage is wet; strip and destroy spotted outer leaves.

topic: Artichoke (Cynara cardunculus) Frost Epidermal Blistering ('Winter Kissed' Bronzing) & Crown Freeze of Artichoke: Environmental Injury Symptoms & Recovery Management

affected_plant_parts: Outer involucral bracts of globes and vegetative rosette leaves
growth_stage: Light frost (28–31°F) vs. hard freeze (<24°F)
season: Perennial in USDA Zones 7–10 (plant crowns/transplants in fall or early spring); grown as an annual in Zones 4–6 by exposing 6-week-old transplants to 10–14 days of 40–50°F chilling in spring
temperature_range: Optimal growth 55–75°F (13–24°C) with cool moist air; requires ~250 chill hours below 50°F to induce flower bud formation; hot dry weather (>85°F) causes buds to open prematurely and bracts to turn tough and leathery; crowns rot below 15–20°F without heavy winter protection

distinguishing_features: Whitish flaky cuticle blisters turning bronze on outer bracts after a light frost with healthy internal flesh.
similar_conditions: Botrytis gray mold (which can invade hard-frozen bracts); Calcium bract tipburn.

topic: Artichoke (Cynara cardunculus) Calcium (Ca) Deficiency (Bract Tipburn of Globe Artichoke Buds): Visual Diagnosis, Mobility & Soil Correction
problem_name: Calcium (Ca) Deficiency (Bract Tipburn of Globe Artichoke Buds)
affected_plant_parts: Inner and outer fleshy bracts of developing floral buds (globes) and young leaves
growth_stage: Bud (globe) enlargement in warm or dry weather
season: Perennial in USDA Zones 7–10 (plant crowns/transplants in fall or early spring); grown as an annual in Zones 4–6 by exposing 6-week-old transplants to 10–14 days of 40–50°F chilling in spring
temperature_range: Optimal growth 55–75°F (13–24°C) with cool moist air; requires ~250 chill hours below 50°F to induce flower bud formation; hot dry weather (>85°F) causes buds to open prematurely and bracts to turn tough and leathery; crowns rot below 15–20°F without heavy winter protection
humidity_conditions: See favorable_conditions for moisture and relative humidity interactions.
visible_symptoms: Margins and tips of the fleshy involucral bracts on developing artichoke globes turn water-soaked and then dark brown to black and leathery ('bract tipburn'), accompanied by hooked necrotic tips on young inner leaves.
symptom_keywords: artichoke, calcium (ca) deficiency, strictly immobile in phloem (transported exclusively upward via xylem transpiration stream), inner and outer fleshy bracts of developing floral buds (globes) and young leaves, chlorosis, stunting
symptom_progression: Site of onset: Youngest expanding upper leaves, enclosed heart leaves, apical meristems, root tips, and low-transpiring developing fruits or storage tissues. Develops during warm, windy, or moisture-stressed periods when rapid transpiration by the massive silvery leaves diverts xylem calcium away from the low-transpiring floral buds.
distinguishing_features: Phloem mobility: Strictly immobile in phloem (transported exclusively upward via xylem transpiration stream). Dry, dark-brown necrotic bract tips without grayish-brown fuzzy sporulation in cool wet weather distinguish Calcium bract tipburn from Botrytis cinerea gray mold.
similar_conditions: Other nutrient deficiencies with contrasting phloem mobility, root rot or vascular wilt restricting nutrient uptake, or viral chlorosis on Artichoke.
risk_factors: Fluctuating soil moisture (drought alternating with heavy watering), high relative humidity or enclosed leaf morphology suppressing xylem transpiration into inner leaves/fruits, acidic unlimed soils (pH < 5.5), high soil salinity, or excess ammonium (NH4+), potassium (K+), or magnesium (Mg2+) competing for root uptake.
favorable_conditions: Fluctuating soil moisture (drought alternating with heavy watering), high relative humidity or enclosed leaf morphology suppressing xylem transpiration into inner leaves/fruits, acidic unlimed soils (pH < 5.5), high soil salinity, or excess ammonium (NH4+), potassium (K+), or magnesium (Mg2+) competing for root uptake.
management_actions: Regulate soil moisture immediately with consistent irrigation and organic mulch; apply foliar calcium sprays (calcium chloride or calcium nitrate at 3–5 lb/100 gal or labeled home-garden rate) directly onto young expanding leaves and developing fruit clusters, and side-dress with calcium nitrate or gypsum.
prevention_actions: Lime acidic soils to pH 6.2–6.8 using calcitic limestone or apply gypsum (calcium sulfate) where pH is already optimal, use nitrate-N rather than ammonium-N fertilizers, avoid pruning feeder roots during cultivation, and maintain steady soil moisture.
recommended_observations: Inspect whether symptoms initiate on older lower foliage vs. youngest upper leaves/meristems on Artichoke, verify soil pH (optimal for Artichoke: 6.0–7.0) and soil moisture, and confirm with a soil or plant tissue test.

topic: Parsnip Black Swallowtail Caterpillar Management
problem_name: Black Swallowtail Caterpillar (Parsleyworm) and Carrot Weevil
causal_agent: Papilio polyxenes (Black Swallowtail / Parsleyworm) and Listronotus oregonensis (Carrot Weevil)
affected_plant_parts: Feathery foliage and flower umbels (Parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (Carrot Weevil)
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through umbel flowering and root bulking
season: Late spring through autumn
humidity_conditions: Warm sunny spring and summer weather
visible_symptoms: On Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa): Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail Caterpillar): young caterpillars are tiny black, saddle-backed larvae with a white band across the middle (mimicking bird droppings!), which molt into large (2-inch), smooth, bright-green caterpillars banded across each segment with black stripes dotted with bright yellow-orange spots; when poked, the caterpillar everts a bright orange, Y-shaped fleshy horn (osmeterium) from behind its head that emits a pungent citrus-terpene scent to deter birds; Carrot Weevil: small (1/4 inch) coppery-brown snout beetles chew small oval cavities in celery/carrot petioles to lay eggs, and legless creamy-white C-shaped grubs with amber-brown heads tunnel zig-zag cavities across the UPPER one-third and crown shoulder of carrot, parsnip, and celery roots.
symptom_keywords: green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley, orange Y-shaped horn behind head when poked, young black caterpillar with white saddle mimicking bird dropping, zig-zag tunnels in upper crown shoulder of carrot root
symptom_progression: Black Swallowtail butterflies lay single round yellow eggs on feathery umbellifer tips; Carrot Weevils walk from overwintering grassy borders in spring to lay eggs in young petioles at the 3–4 true-leaf stage.
distinguishing_features: Parsleyworm is a prized native butterfly larva unmistakable for its green-black-and-yellow bands and reversible orange Y-shaped osmeterium horn; Carrot Weevil larvae have a distinct amber-brown head capsule and tunnel in the UPPER third/crown of the carrot root (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots are headless and tunnel in the LOWER two-thirds of the root!).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms
risk_factors: Uncovered carrot/celery beds adjacent to last year's carrot patch (for Carrot Weevil).
favorable_conditions: Warm sunny days from May through September.
transmission_or_spread: Swallowtail butterflies fly on the wing; Carrot Weevils rarely fly and walk primarily along the ground from overwintering borders.
management_actions: For Parsleyworm (Black Swallowtail): because Papilio polyxenes transforms into the magnificent native Eastern Black Swallowtail butterfly and rarely kills established plants, most gardeners simply plant 2–3 extra dill, fennel, or parsley plants as a dedicated 'butterfly nursery' and gently move caterpillars onto those extra plants rather than spraying! For Carrot Weevil: place wooden wooden-slat Boivin traps baited with carrot slices along bed borders at the 2-leaf stage or cover carrot/celery beds with insect netting.
prevention_actions: Rotate carrots, celery, and parsnips away from last year's umbellifer bed so walking Carrot Weevils cannot easily reach young seedlings; remove all cull carrots at harvest.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsnip (feathery foliage and flower umbels (parsleyworm); leaf petioles and upper taproot crown (carrot weevil)) twice weekly during late spring through autumn (65–88°F (18–31°C)); inspect for green caterpillar with black bands and yellow dots on dill and parsley to distinguish Black Swallowtail Caterpillar from Carrot Rust Fly Maggot (headless white maggot tunneling in lower two-thirds of root with rust-red frass), Armyworms.
severity_or_impact: Low to Moderate for Parsleyworm (beneficial pollinator butterfly); Moderate to High for Carrot Weevil
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 65–88°F (18–31°C) and warm sunny spring and summer weather.
host_range: Documented on Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Parsley, Dill, Fennel, Coriander, Celery, Carrot, Parsnip).

topic: Parsnip Root Maggots Management
problem_name: Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly)
causal_agent: Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly)
affected_plant_parts: Taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds
growth_stage: Seed germination and seedling/root establishment through harvest
season: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather
humidity_conditions: Cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds
visible_symptoms: On Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots.
symptom_keywords: white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots, winding brown root grooves, rusty-red frass tunnels on carrot taproot, wilted bluish-green young cabbage transplant, hollowed germinating bean and corn seeds in cold wet soil
symptom_progression: Small dark-gray housefly-like adult flies (or shiny black flies with yellow heads for Carrot Rust Fly) emerge from overwintering brown football-shaped puparia in spring soil and lay tiny white oblong eggs in soil cracks right against plant stems or over freshly turned manure/organic matter.
distinguishing_features: Root Maggots are completely legless and headless (tapering to tiny black internal mouthhooks at the front end), immediately distinguishing them from Wireworms (hard yellow with 6 legs), White Grubs (C-shaped with brown head and 6 legs), and Fungus Gnat larvae (tiny translucent worms with a shiny black head capsule).
similar_conditions: Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off
risk_factors: Incorporating fresh animal manure, uncomposted green cover crops, or fish/blood meal right before spring planting (whose decaying odor strongly attracts egg-laying Seedcorn and Onion Maggot flies!), cool wet spring weather delaying germination, and leaving carrots in the ground over winter.
favorable_conditions: Cool, moist spring and autumn weather (55–70°F); adult flies seek shade and egg survival drops sharply when soil surface temperatures exceed 90°F in mid-summer.
transmission_or_spread: Overwinters in garden soil as hard reddish-brown puparia; adult flies fly low from neighboring beds and wild hosts (wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, wild mustard).
management_actions: COVER BEDS WITH FLOATING ROW COVERS OR INSECT NETTING AT PLANTING: seal edges with soil over radish, turnip, rutabaga, carrot, onion, and brassica beds (in rotating beds that did NOT host those crops last year) to physically block adult flies from laying eggs at the plant base; for individual brassica transplants, fit a 5-inch square collar of stiff felt, tarpaper, or window screen with a center slit flat on the soil around each stem so flies cannot reach the soil crack.
prevention_actions: Delay planting beans, peas, sweet corn, and cucurbits until soil warms above 60°F (and plant shallowly for fast emergence); use only fully cured compost rather than fresh manure or raw organic meals at planting; harvest all carrots before winter and destroy cull onion/carrot piles.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsnip (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds) twice weekly during cool, moist spring and autumn weather (50–72°F (10–22°C)); inspect for white legless cone-shaped maggots tunneling in radish and turnip roots to distinguish Root Maggots from Wireworms, Clubroot (swollen clubbed roots without maggot tunnels), White Rot / Damping-Off.
severity_or_impact: High in cool northern and coastal gardens (ruins marketable radishes, turnips, carrots, and spring onions)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 50–72°F (10–22°C) and cool, damp spring soils and high-organic/manured beds.
host_range: Documented on Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa, Apiaceae) and related susceptible garden hosts (Cabbage, Broccoli, Cauliflower, Kale, Collards, Brussels sprouts, Kohlrabi, Bok choy).
knowledge_text: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) Root Maggots (Cabbage Maggot, Onion Maggot, Seedcorn Maggot, and Carrot Rust Fly) is a subterranean dipteran maggot pest caused by Delia radicum (Cabbage Maggot), Delia antiqua (Onion Maggot), Delia platura (Seedcorn Maggot), and Psila rosae (Carrot Rust Fly). Visible signs and feeding damage on parsnip (taproots, hypocotyls, underground bulbs, and large germinating seeds): Small (1/4 inch / 6 mm), legless, headless, cone-shaped creamy-white fly maggots (tapered to a point at the mouthhooks and blunt at the rear) that tunnel into underground roots, bulbs, and germinating seeds: (1) Cabbage Maggot: chews winding brown grooves and tunnels across the white flesh of radishes and turnips and severs the feeder roots of young cabbage/broccoli transplants, causing plants to turn bluish-gray, stunt, and wilt on sunny days; (2) Onion Maggot: bores into the basal plate of young onion seedlings and bulbs, causing central leaves to wilt pale green and rot with foul bacterial soft rot; (3) Seedcorn Maggot: hollows out large germinating bean, pea, corn, and cucurbit seeds in cold wet spring soil before they can emerge ('baldhead' seedlings with missing growing points); (4) Carrot Rust Fly: slender yellowish maggots chew superficial winding tunnels packed with rusty-red frass across the lower two-thirds of carrot and parsnip roots. affected_plant_parts: Underground storage roots, tubers, taproots, bulbs, crowns, and germinating seeds
growth_stage: Planting through root/tuber bulking, harvest, and storage
season: Spring planting through autumn harvest
humidity_conditions: Moist soils (especially beds newly converted from turfgrass, pasture, or weedy sod)

symptom_progression: Click beetles and scarab beetles lay eggs in grassy sod and weedy beds; Wireworms and White Grubs live in the soil for 1–5 years before pupating, attacking root crops planted into former sod; Sweetpotato Weevils breed continuously in roots both in the field and in warm storage.
distinguishing_features: Distinguish the 3 underground root chewers by the injury and larva: Wireworms are hard, shiny, jointed yellow-brown 'wires' that drill narrow clean pinholes straight into tubers; White Grubs are soft, C-shaped 6-legged white grubs that chew broad shallow craters; Sweetpotato Weevils leave winding frass-packed tunnels that make sweet potatoes smell and taste like bitter turpentine.
similar_conditions: Common Scab (corky surface crust, no tunnels), Millipedes (2 pairs of legs per body segment scavenging inside already-cracked or wireworm-damaged holes), Slug holes
risk_factors: Converting lawn, pasture, or grassy sod directly into a potato, sweet potato, carrot, strawberry, or sweet corn bed in the first 1–2 years without summer fallowing; leaving volunteer sweet potatoes or morning glory weeds in weevil zones.
favorable_conditions: Warm soils and grassy sod history.
transmission_or_spread: Sweetpotato Weevil spreads primarily via infested sweet potato slips and seed roots; Wireworms and White Grubs persist multi-year in grassy soils.
management_actions: BAIT STATION MONITORING FOR WIREWORMS BEFORE PLANTING: 2 weeks before planting potatoes, sweet potatoes, or carrots in a new bed, bury half a raw potato or a mesh bag of soaked corn/wheat seed 4 inches deep at several spots and dig them up after 7 days—if >1–2 wireworms per bait are found, plant leaf/fruiting crops instead of root crops in that bed! recommended_observations: Conduct a soil test prior to planting Parsnip to verify soil pH (6.0–7.0 (acidic soil below 5.8 stunts roots and increases parsnip canker)) and drainage rate after rainfall or irrigation.

topic: Parsnip Aster Yellows (Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris)
problem_name: Aster Yellows
causal_agent: Candidatus Phytoplasma asteris
affected_plant_parts: Phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures
growth_stage: Vegetative growth through root/head maturation
season: Mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration
humidity_conditions: Warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement
visible_symptoms: On Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa): In Carrot: inner crown leaves turn bright yellow, bronze-red, and proliferate into a dense, upright 'witches'-broom' tuft of stunted twisted shoots, while the underground taproot becomes woody, bitter, pale, and covered in dense mats of woolly hairy secondary lateral roots; In Lettuce & Celery: inner heart leaves twist, turn yellow/blanched with pink-to-tan latex deposits on veins ('rio grande disease'), and fail to head; In Flowers/Umbels: 'phyllody' and 'virescence' where flower petals turn into weird green leafy shoots.
symptom_keywords: witches'-broom yellow crown tuft, woolly hairy carrot taproot, twisted yellow inner heart leaves, green leafy flowers phyllody, bitter woody root
symptom_progression: Aster leafhoppers inject the cell-wall-less phytoplasma into phloem sieve tubes during feeding; after a 10–21 day incubation period, systemic hormone disruption causes yellow witches'-brooming of the crown and hairy bitter roots.
distinguishing_features: Unmistakably identified in carrots by the broom-like cluster of yellow-bronze stunted center leaves coupled with a dense beard of fibrous woolly rootlets along a bitter, woody taproot.
similar_conditions: Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus
risk_factors: High populations of migrating six-spotted aster leafhoppers (Macrosteles quadrilineatus) and nearby perennial broadleaf weeds (dandelion, plantain, wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace, thistle, horseweed).
favorable_conditions: Warm summer winds carrying infective aster leafhoppers from southern grain/forage fields and grassy margins.
transmission_or_spread: Vectored persistently by the aster leafhopper (Macrosteles quadrilineatus); leafhoppers must feed on an infected plant for several hours and undergo a 2-week latent period before transmitting the phytoplasma (not seed- or touch-transmitted).
management_actions: Immediately pull and destroy any plant showing yellow witches'-broom crowns or twisted inner leaves so leafhoppers cannot acquire the pathogen from it; there is no cure once infected.
prevention_actions: Cover high-value carrot, lettuce, and celery beds with fine floating row covers or insect netting to exclude aster leafhoppers; mow and control broadleaf weeds around the garden perimeter.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsnip (phloem vascular system, central crown/heart leaves, taproots, and floral structures) weekly during mid-to-late summer following aster leafhopper migration (70–85°F (21–29°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Aster Yellows from Root-Knot Nematode (causes beaded root galls and forking rather than a crown witches'-broom), Herbicide Drift, Carrot Motley Dwarf Virus.
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High on carrots, lettuce, and celery (infected roots and heads are bitter and inedible)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 70–85°F (21–29°C) and warm weather favoring aster leafhopper vector movement.
host_range: Documented on Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Celery, Lettuce, Spinach, Parsley, Coriander, Dill, Parsnip).

topic: Parsnip Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking) (Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum)
problem_name: Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking)
causal_agent: Pythium violae and Pythium sulcatum
affected_plant_parts: Taproot tip (young seedlings) and mature taproot periderm/cortex
growth_stage: Seedling taproot elongation (Forking) and mid-to-late root sizing (Cavity Spot)
season: Cool, wet, poorly drained soil conditions
humidity_conditions: High soil moisture, compacted beds, or delayed harvest in wet autumn soils
visible_symptoms: On Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa): Two distinct syndromes caused by the same soil-borne Pythium species: (1) Cavity Spot on mature carrots/parsnips: small, sunken, elliptical, horizontal (crosswise) greyish-brown to dark craters/cavities (1/8 to 1/2 inch wide) scattered along the side of an otherwise normal-sized taproot where the outer skin collapses over a shallow subsurface pocket; (2) Pythium Root Dieback: when Pythium kills the delicate apical meristem tip of a 1-to-3-week-old seedling taproot, the root loses apical dominance and splits into multiple 'forked', 'stubbed', or 'fanged' roots.
symptom_keywords: sunken horizontal elliptical pits on carrot root, crosswise root cavities, forked fanged taproots, stubbed stunted carrots, completely healthy green tops
symptom_progression: In spring, Pythium zoospores nip the young primary root tip causing forking; later in summer/autumn, infections along the secondary root emergence sites of the maturing taproot form sunken horizontal cavities under the periderm.
distinguishing_features: Cavity Spot is distinguished by horizontal (crosswise) elliptical sunken lesions with tattered skin margins and no insect tunnels inside (whereas Carrot Rust Fly maggots leave winding rust-colored tunnels filled with frass).
similar_conditions: Carrot Rust Fly Maggot tunnels, Root-Knot Nematode (round bead-like galls on lateral roots), Streptomyces Common Scab (raised corky warts in dry alkaline soil)
risk_factors: Poorly drained or compacted soils, over-irrigation, high soil nitrogen, growing carrots repeatedly in the same bed, and leaving mature carrots in wet soil too long in autumn.
favorable_conditions: Cool-to-moderate (59–68°F), wet soils.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne oomycetes surviving as thick-walled oospores in soil and spreading via swimming zoospores in saturated soil pores.
management_actions: Harvest carrots and parsnips promptly once they reach marketable maturity rather than holding them in wet fall beds; avoid overwatering once roots size up.
prevention_actions: Grow carrots and parsnips on deep (10–12 inch) raised beds for rapid drainage; maintain soil pH around 6.5–6.8; plant Cavity-Spot-tolerant carrot hybrids (such as 'Bolero' or 'Napoli'); rotate out of umbellifers for 3 years.
recommended_observations: Scout Parsnip (taproot tip (young seedlings) and mature taproot periderm/cortex) weekly during cool, wet, poorly drained soil conditions (55–70°F (13–21°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Cavity Spot and Pythium Root Dieback (Forking) from Carrot Rust Fly Maggot tunnels, Root-Knot Nematode (round bead-like galls on lateral roots), Streptomyces Common Scab (raised corky warts in dry alkaline soil).
severity_or_impact: Moderate to High (mars root appearance and causes severe taproot forking)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 55–70°F (13–21°C) and high soil moisture, compacted beds, or delayed harvest in wet autumn soils.
host_range: Documented on Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa, Apiaceae) and related susceptible hosts (Carrot, Parsnip, Beet, Radish, Turnip).

topic: Parsnip Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato (Streptomyces scabies)
problem_name: Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato
causal_agent: Streptomyces scabies (Common Scab - filamentous bacterium) and Rhizoctonia solani (Black Scurf)
affected_plant_parts: Underground tubers, stolons, stems, and swollen storage roots
growth_stage: Tuber initiation and early bulking (first 3–5 weeks after stolon tips swell)
season: Warm, dry soil conditions during early summer tuber set
humidity_conditions: Dry soil during the 4-week window of tuber initiation (for Common Scab); cool wet spring soil (for Black Scurf)
visible_symptoms: On Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa): Common Scab: circular-to-irregular, rough, raised corky brown wart-like crusts ('russet/superficial scab') or sunken crater-like corky pits ('pitted scab') up to 1/4 inch deep on the skin of potato tubers, beets, radishes, and turnips (with normal healthy above-ground foliage!); Black Scurf: hard, irregular, coal-black crusty specks on the potato tuber skin resembling dried bits of soil that will NOT wash off ('the dirt that won't wash off'), plus reddish-brown sunken cankers on underground sprouts in spring.
symptom_keywords: rough corky scabs on potato skin, sunken corky tuber pits, black scurf specks that won't wash off, reddish-brown underground stem cankers
symptom_progression: Streptomyces invades young tubers exclusively through immature unsuberized lenticels during the first 3–5 weeks of tuberization when soil is dry and pH is above 5.5; tubers remain completely edible once peeled.
distinguishing_features: Common Scab forms tan-brown corky raised or pitted skin lesions; Black Scurf forms jet-black superficial sclerotia crusts that look like tar or dried dirt stuck to the skin.
similar_conditions: Powdery Scab (Spongospora subterranea - forms small volcano-like pustules in cool wet soil), Colorado Potato Beetle/Wireworm holes, Physiological Enlarged Lenticels (white puffy dots in wet soil)
risk_factors: Soil pH above 5.5–6.0 (liming or applying wood ashes before potatoes/beets), applying fresh animal manure, dry soil during early tuber set, and planting scabby seed tubers.
favorable_conditions: Soil pH 5.8–7.8 combined with dry soil during the 4 weeks following stolon tip swelling.
transmission_or_spread: Soil-borne actinomycete/fungus and tuber-borne on infected seed potatoes.
management_actions: Keep soil consistently moist (near field capacity) during the critical 4–6 week window of tuber initiation (starting when stolon tips begin to swell, just before bloom)—moisture encourages beneficial antagonistic bacteria on lenticels that block Streptomyces!
prevention_actions: Maintain potato soil pH between 5.0 and 5.5 (never apply lime, wood ash, or fresh manure before planting potatoes); plant only certified scab-free seed tubers and scab-resistant cultivars (such as 'Superior', 'Norland', 'Chieftain', 'Russet Burbank', 'Goldrush').
recommended_observations: Scout Parsnip (underground tubers, stolons, stems, and swollen storage roots) weekly during warm, dry soil conditions during early summer tuber set (68–80°F (20–27°C)); inspect lesion margins, undersides of leaves, and vascular or fruit tissues to distinguish Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato from Powdery Scab (Spongospora subterranea - forms small volcano-like pustules in cool wet soil), Colorado Potato Beetle/Wireworm holes, Physiological Enlarged Lenticels (white puffy dots in wet soil).
severity_or_impact: Moderate (strictly cosmetic skin blemish on peeled tubers, though deep pits increase peeling waste and reduce storage life)
geographic_or_climate_notes: Favored by 68–80°F (20–27°C) and dry soil during the 4-week window of tuber initiation (for common scab); cool wet spring soil (for black scurf).

knowledge_text: Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) Common Scab and Black Scurf of Potato is a bacterial disease caused by Streptomyces scabies (Common Scab - filamentous bacterium) and Rhizoctonia solani (Black Scurf). Symptoms on parsnip (underground tubers, stolons, stems, and swollen storage roots): Common Scab: circular-to-irregular, rough, raised corky brown wart-like crusts ('russet/superficial scab') or sunken crater-like corky pits ('pitted scab') up to 1/4 inch deep on the skin of potato tubers, beets, radishes, and turnips (with normal healthy above-ground foliage!); Black Scurf: hard, irregular, coal-black crusty specks on the potato tuber skin resembling dried bits of soil that will NOT wash off ('the dirt that won't wash off'), plus reddish-brown sunken cankers on underground sprouts in spring. Distinguishing features: Common Scab forms tan-brown corky raised or pitted skin lesions; Black Scurf forms jet-black superficial sclerotia crusts that look like tar or dried dirt stuck to the skin. Favored by soil ph 5.8–7.8 combined with dry soil during the 4 weeks following stolon tip swelling. (68–80°F (20–27°C)). Management and prevention: Keep soil consistently moist (near field capacity) during the critical 4–6 week window of tuber initiation (starting when stolon tips begin to swell, just before bloom)—moisture encourages beneficial antagonistic bacteria on lenticels that block Streptomyces! Maintain potato soil pH between 5.0 and 5.5 (never apply lime, wood ash, or fresh manure before planting potatoes); plant only certified scab-free seed tubers and scab-resistant cultivars (such as 'Superior', 'Norland', 'Chieftain', 'Russet Burbank', 'Goldrush').

distinguishing_features: Healthy Parsnip foliage exhibits uniform species-typical coloration, turgor, and leaf margin geometry without chlorotic halos, necrotic lesions, water-soaked spots, powdery mycelia, insect stippling, or vascular wilting.
recommended_observations: Compare observed leaf color, leaf arrangement, surface pubescence/waxiness, and stem turgor against this healthy Parsnip baseline before diagnosing nutrient deficiency, pest feeding, or foliar disease.
knowledge_text: Healthy baseline vegetative appearance for Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa): Healthy parsnip plants form a bold, upright rosette of coarse, once-pinnately compound medium-green leaves (12–24 inches long) with 5–11 broad, ovate, sessile, coarsely saw-toothed and lobed leaflets and grooved petioles. Extension morphological profile: The large alternate compound leaves are in a basal rosette the first year and are single pinnate. They can be up to 18 inches long and 6 inches wide with long stems. They consist of 9 leaflets that are 3 inches long and 2 inches across. Leaflets can have margins with cleft lobes and coarse teeth. The upper compound leaves that appear in the second year are smaller with shorter stems. Leaflets are ovate or elliptic and 3 inches long by 2 inches wide. Stem profile: Tall green hollow stems are glabrous, angular, and furrowed Plants should display vigorous apical and lateral shoot growth appropriate to their stage without interveinal chlorosis, necrotic spotting, curling, or stunting.
